title: DHS Geometry
text:
Welcome to Geometry
Welcome to Geometry at Frederick Douglass High School!
A builder makes a perfect square corner with three numbers: 3, 4, and 5. A wheelchair ramp must rise 1 inch for every 12 inches it goes forward. You can find the height of a tree from the length of its shadow.
All of these are geometry. Geometry is the math of shape, size, and position. In this class you will measure things you cannot reach, check if a shape is what it looks like, and use algebra to answer questions about pictures.

title: Introduction
text:
What You’ll Learn
Welcome to Unit 1! Geometry starts with a few simple objects: points, lines, and angles.
Look at a door frame, a road map, or the hands of a clock. You see lines that cross and angles that open and close. In this unit you learn to name these objects and measure them. Then you write equations about them, the same kind of equations you solved in Algebra.
By the end of this unit, you will be able to:

title: Introduction
text:
Name and draw points, lines, segments, rays, and angles with the correct symbols
Measure and classify angles
Write and solve equations with segment lengths and angle measures
Use complementary, supplementary, and vertical angles to find missing angles
Find the angles made when a line crosses two parallel lines
Find missing angles in triangles and other polygons

title: Introduction
text:
Topics in This Unit
Points, Lines, Segments, and Angles
Name the basic objects of geometry and write them with the right symbols.
Segment and Angle Addition
Add the parts to get the whole. Write and solve equations for missing lengths and angles.
Complementary, Supplementary, and Vertical Angles
Use angle pairs that add to \(90^\circ\) or \(180^\circ\), or that are always equal.
Parallel Lines and Transversals
Find every angle when a line crosses two parallel lines.
Angles in Triangles and Polygons
The angles in a triangle add to \(180^\circ\). Use that to find the angles in any polygon.

title: 1.1 - Points, Lines, Segments, and Angles
text:
🔥 Warm Up
Look at this map. Three straight streets cross each other.
Each corner is one exact spot on the map. Each street is straight. Where two streets cross, they make a corner that opens a certain amount.
Geometry has a word for each of these things. A corner is a point. A straight street is part of a line. Two streets that leave the same corner make an angle. In this lesson you learn these words and the symbols we use to write them.

title: 1.1 - Points, Lines, Segments, and Angles
text:
Plot the points \(A(3, 2)\), \(B(-3, 2)\), and \(C(-3, -4)\) on a coordinate plane.
Draw a path from \(A\) to \(B\). Then draw a path from \(B\) to \(C\). What kind of corner does the path make at \(B\)?
Solve \(x + 35 = 90\).

title: 1.1 - Points, Lines, Segments, and Angles
text:
👥 Learn Together

1.1.1 - Points, Lines, and Planes
The tip of a sharp pencil makes a tiny dot. In geometry, a point is an exact location. It has no size at all. We name a point with a capital letter.
A line is straight and goes on forever in both directions. We draw an arrow on each end to show that it never stops.
A plane is a flat surface that goes on forever in every direction. A floor or a wall is part of a plane.









Object
Picture
Name
Symbol




point

point \(A\)
\(A\)


line

line \(AB\), or one small letter like line \(\ell\)
\(\overleftrightarrow{AB}\)


plane

plane \(P\), or three points in it that are not on one line





Through any two points there is exactly one line.

Points that lie on the same line are collinear. Points that lie in the same plane are coplanar.

Example 1: Points, lines, and planes






Name line \(\ell\) another way.
Use any two points on the line: \(\overleftrightarrow{AB}\). (\(\overleftrightarrow{AC}\) and \(\overleftrightarrow{BC}\) also work.)
Name three collinear points.
\(A\), \(B\), and \(C\). They are all on line \(\ell\).
Are \(A\), \(B\), and \(D\) collinear?
No. Point \(D\) is not on line \(\ell\).
Name a point that is not in plane \(M\).
Point \(E\).



Name line \(\ell\) using points \(B\) and \(C\).
Name three points in plane \(M\) that are not collinear.




\(\overleftrightarrow{BC}\) (or \(\overleftrightarrow{CB}\))
\(A\), \(B\), and \(D\). (Any two of \(A\), \(B\), \(C\) with point \(D\) also work.)





1.1.2 - Segments and Rays
A real street does not go on forever. It starts at one corner and stops at another. In geometry, part of a line with two ends is a segment. The two ends are its endpoints.
A flashlight beam starts at the flashlight and keeps going. In geometry, part of a line that starts at one endpoint and goes on forever in one direction is a ray.









Object
Picture
Name
Symbol




segment

segment \(AB\)
\(\overline{AB}\)


ray

ray \(AB\)
\(\overrightarrow{AB}\)




\(\overline{AB}\) and \(\overline{BA}\) are the same segment.
\(\overrightarrow{AB}\) and \(\overrightarrow{BA}\) are different rays. \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) starts at \(A\). \(\overrightarrow{BA}\) starts at \(B\). The first letter of a ray is always its endpoint.


\(\overline{AB}\), with a bar, is the segment. It is something you can draw.
\(AB\), with no bar, is the length of the segment. It is a number, like \(AB = 5\).


Example 2: Opposite rays






Name the two rays that start at \(Q\).
\(\overrightarrow{QP}\) and \(\overrightarrow{QR}\).
These two rays have the same endpoint and go in opposite directions. Together they make a line. They are opposite rays.
Name every segment in the figure.
\(\overline{PQ}\), \(\overline{QR}\), and \(\overline{PR}\).



Is \(\overrightarrow{PQ}\) the same ray as \(\overrightarrow{PR}\)?
Is \(\overrightarrow{QP}\) the same ray as \(\overrightarrow{PQ}\)?




Yes. Both start at \(P\) and go to the right forever. They pass through the same points.
No. \(\overrightarrow{QP}\) starts at \(Q\) and goes left. \(\overrightarrow{PQ}\) starts at \(P\) and goes right.





1.1.3 - Angles
Look at corner \(A\) on the street map. Main St and Oak St both leave corner \(A\), in two different directions. That makes an angle.
An angle is two rays with the same endpoint. The rays are the sides of the angle. The shared endpoint is the vertex.





You can name this angle three ways:

\(\angle ABC\) or \(\angle CBA\): three letters, with the vertex in the middle
\(\angle B\): the vertex only
\(\angle 1\): the number written inside the angle

We measure angles in degrees (\(^\circ\)). One full turn is \(360^\circ\). This angle measures \(130^\circ\). We write \(m\angle ABC = 130^\circ\). Read it as “the measure of angle \(ABC\) is 130 degrees.”

Example 3: Angles that share a vertex





Name the three angles that have their vertex at \(B\).
\(\angle ABC\), \(\angle CBD\), and \(\angle ABD\).

In Example 3, the name \(\angle B\) could mean any of the three angles. When two or more angles share a vertex, always use three letters.



Name \(\angle CBD\) another way with three letters.
Which of the three angles is the largest?




\(\angle DBC\)
\(\angle ABD\). It is made of the other two angles together.





1.1.4 - Classifying Angles
We sort angles into four types by their measure.








Type
Measure




acute
more than \(0^\circ\) and less than \(90^\circ\)


right
exactly \(90^\circ\)


obtuse
more than \(90^\circ\) and less than \(180^\circ\)


straight
exactly \(180^\circ\)



A small square at the vertex means the angle is a right angle.

Example 4: Angles on a clock





The hands of a clock make an angle. What angle do they make at 2:00?
A full turn is \(360^\circ\), and a clock has 12 hour marks. So the angle from one hour mark to the next is
\[
360^\circ \div 12 = 30^\circ.
\]
At 2:00 the hands are 2 hour marks apart:
\[
2 \times 30^\circ = 60^\circ.
\]
\(60^\circ\) is less than \(90^\circ\), so the angle is acute.

The hands are 5 hour marks apart: \(5 \times 30^\circ = 150^\circ\).
\(150^\circ\) is between \(90^\circ\) and \(180^\circ\), so the angle is obtuse.




1.1.5 - What a Figure Shows
A drawing can fool your eyes. In geometry, we only trust two things: what we are told, and what the figure marks.

A small square at a vertex means a right angle.
Matching tick marks mean segments have the same length.

Example 5: Marks and looks






Which angle is a right angle for sure?
\(\angle 1\). It has the square mark.
Is \(\angle 2\) a right angle?
We cannot tell. It looks close to \(90^\circ\), but it has no mark. (It really measures \(86^\circ\).)
Which segments have the same length for sure?
\(\overline{AB}\) and \(\overline{CD}\). They have matching tick marks, so \(AB = CD\).
Do \(\overline{EF}\) and \(\overline{GH}\) have the same length?
We cannot tell. They have no marks. (\(\overline{GH}\) is a little longer.)

Remember that lines go on forever. A drawing shows only part of a line.






Yes. On the page they do not touch. But lines go on forever. These two lines get closer as they go to the right, so they meet past the edge of the page.

title: 1.2 - Segment and Angle Addition
text:
🔥 Warm Up
A truck driver leaves Town A and drives 13 miles to Town B. Then she drives 4 more miles to Town C. How far is it from A to C?
You add: \(13 + 4 = 17\) miles. The whole is the sum of its parts. This is true for segments, and it is also true for angles. In this lesson you use that idea to write equations and find missing lengths and angles.

title: 1.2 - Segment and Angle Addition
text:
Write the symbol for segment \(AB\). Then write the symbol for the length of segment \(AB\).
Solve \(3x + 4 = 25\).
Solve \(5x - 6 = 2x + 9\).

title: 1.2 - Segment and Angle Addition
text:
👥 Learn Together

1.2.1 - Length on a Number Line
A ruler is a number line. To find the length of a segment, subtract the two numbers at its ends.
Example 1: Length on a number line





Point \(A\) is at \(-3\). Point \(B\) is at \(4\). Find \(AB\).
\[
AB = |4 - (-3)| = |7| = 7
\]
You can also count the steps from \(-3\) to \(4\). There are 7.

A length is a distance. We use absolute value so the answer is never negative. For points at \(a\) and \(b\), the length is \[
AB = |a - b|.
\] The order does not matter. \(|4 - (-3)| = 7\) and \(|-3 - 4| = 7\).



Point \(P\) is at \(-6\) and point \(Q\) is at \(2\). Find \(PQ\).
Point \(R\) is at \(5\) and point \(S\) is at \(-1.5\). Find \(RS\).




\(|2 - (-6)| = 8\)
\(|-1.5 - 5| = 6.5\)





1.2.2 - Segment Addition
Look at the truck driver again. Town \(B\) is between Town \(A\) and Town \(C\), and all three towns are on one straight road. Then the two short pieces add up to the whole.

If \(B\) is between \(A\) and \(C\) on a line, then \[
AB + BC = AC.
\]

Example 2: Segment addition with \(x\)





Point \(B\) is between \(A\) and \(C\). \(AB = 2x + 3\), \(BC = x - 1\), and \(AC = 17\). Find \(x\), \(AB\), and \(BC\).
Step 1. Write the equation.
\[
(2x + 3) + (x - 1) = 17
\]
Step 2. Combine like terms.
\[
3x + 2 = 17
\]
Step 3. Solve.
\[
3x = 15 \quad\text{so}\quad x = 5
\]
Step 4. Put \(x = 5\) back in to find each length.
\[
AB = 2(5) + 3 = 13 \qquad BC = 5 - 1 = 4
\]
Step 5. Check. \(13 + 4 = 17\). It works.

Point \(E\) is between \(D\) and \(F\). \(DE = x + 6\), \(EF = 3x - 2\), and \(DF = 32\). Find \(x\), \(DE\), and \(EF\).


\((x + 6) + (3x - 2) = 32\), so \(4x + 4 = 32\) and \(x = 7\).
\(DE = 13\) and \(EF = 19\). Check: \(13 + 19 = 32\).


Segment addition only works when \(B\) is on the line between \(A\) and \(C\). If \(AB = 7\) and \(BC = 5\), then \(AC\) is \(12\) only when \(B\) is between them. If \(B\) is on the other side of \(A\), then \(AC = 2\).




1.2.3 - Congruent Segments and Midpoints
Two segments can have the same length. Then we say they are congruent. We use the symbol \(\cong\).
\[
\overline{AB} \cong \overline{CD} \quad\text{means}\quad AB = CD
\]
Use \(\cong\) for figures, like segments. Use \(=\) for numbers, like lengths. Tick marks on a figure show which segments are congruent.
The midpoint of a segment is the point exactly halfway between the endpoints. It cuts the segment into two congruent segments. A segment bisector is any point, line, ray, or segment that goes through the midpoint.
Example 3: A midpoint





\(M\) is the midpoint of \(\overline{AB}\). \(AM = 3x + 4\) and \(MB = 5x - 6\). Find \(x\) and \(AB\).
Step 1. The two halves are equal.
\[
3x + 4 = 5x - 6
\]
Step 2. Solve.
\[
10 = 2x \quad\text{so}\quad x = 5
\]
Step 3. Find each half. \(AM = 3(5) + 4 = 19\). \(MB = 5(5) - 6 = 19\).
Step 4. Add the halves. \(AB = 19 + 19 = 38\).

\(M\) is the midpoint of \(\overline{PQ}\). \(PM = 4x - 3\) and \(MQ = 2x + 9\). Find \(x\) and \(PQ\).


\(4x - 3 = 2x + 9\), so \(2x = 12\) and \(x = 6\).
\(PM = 21\), so \(PQ = 42\).


Example 4: Looks or marks?





Which point is the midpoint for sure?
\(M\) in Figure 1. The tick marks show \(\overline{AM} \cong \overline{MB}\).
We cannot tell for \(N\) in Figure 2. It looks close to the middle, but there are no marks. (It is really a little left of the middle.)



1.2.4 - Angle Addition and Angle Bisectors
Angles add the same way segments do. A point \(D\) is in the interior of \(\angle ABC\) when it is between the two sides of the angle.

If \(D\) is in the interior of \(\angle ABC\), then \[
m\angle ABD + m\angle DBC = m\angle ABC.
\]

Example 5: Angle addition with \(x\)





\(m\angle ABD = (2x + 5)^\circ\), \(m\angle DBC = (3x - 1)^\circ\), and \(m\angle ABC = 79^\circ\). Find \(x\) and each angle.
\[
(2x + 5) + (3x - 1) = 79 \quad\text{so}\quad 5x + 4 = 79 \quad\text{so}\quad x = 15
\]
\(m\angle ABD = 2(15) + 5 = 35^\circ\) and \(m\angle DBC = 3(15) - 1 = 44^\circ\). Check: \(35 + 44 = 79\).

\(m\angle XYW = (x + 20)^\circ\), \(m\angle WYZ = (2x + 4)^\circ\), and \(m\angle XYZ = 90^\circ\). Find \(x\) and each angle.


\(3x + 24 = 90\), so \(x = 22\).
\(m\angle XYW = 42^\circ\) and \(m\angle WYZ = 48^\circ\). Check: \(42 + 48 = 90\).

An angle bisector is a ray that cuts an angle into two congruent angles.
Example 6: An angle bisector





Ray \(\overrightarrow{BD}\) bisects \(\angle ABC\). \(m\angle ABD = (4x + 2)^\circ\) and \(m\angle DBC = (6x - 14)^\circ\). Find \(x\) and \(m\angle ABC\).
The two parts are equal: \(4x + 2 = 6x - 14\), so \(16 = 2x\) and \(x = 8\).
Each part is \(4(8) + 2 = 34^\circ\). The whole angle is \(34 + 34 = 68^\circ\).

Ray \(\overrightarrow{QS}\) bisects \(\angle PQR\). \(m\angle PQS = (5x - 7)^\circ\) and \(m\angle SQR = (3x + 13)^\circ\). Find \(x\) and \(m\angle PQR\).


\(5x - 7 = 3x + 13\), so \(2x = 20\) and \(x = 10\).
Each part is \(43^\circ\), so \(m\angle PQR = 86^\circ\).


Reading a protractor. A protractor measures an angle in degrees. It has two scales, an outer scale and an inner scale. One scale starts at \(0\) on the right. The other starts at \(0\) on the left. Put one side of the angle on a \(0\). Then read the scale that starts at that \(0\).
Example 7: A protractor





Find \(m\angle AOB\).
Side \(\overrightarrow{OA}\) points left, along the \(0\) of the inner scale. Read the inner scale where \(\overrightarrow{OB}\) crosses it: \(50^\circ\).
The outer scale says \(130^\circ\) at the same place. That is the wrong scale. The angle looks small, so \(50^\circ\) makes sense. It is acute.


Find \(m\angle AOC\).
Find \(m\angle BOC\). (Hint: use angle addition.)




\(\overrightarrow{OC}\) is at \(75^\circ\) on the outer scale, so it is \(105^\circ\) on the inner scale. \(m\angle AOC = 105^\circ\).
\(m\angle AOB + m\angle BOC = m\angle AOC\), so \(m\angle BOC = 105 - 50 = 55^\circ\).

title: 1.3 - Complementary, Supplementary, and Vertical Angles
text:
🔥 Warm Up
Hold a pair of scissors. Open them a little. The two blades make an angle. Now open them wider. The angle between the blades grows, and the angle between the handles grows by exactly the same amount.
Some pairs of angles always have a special link. Two crossing lines make four angles. The angles across from each other are always equal. In this lesson you learn the names of these pairs and use them to find missing angles.

title: 1.3 - Complementary, Supplementary, and Vertical Angles
text:
A ray \(\overrightarrow{BD}\) is inside \(\angle ABC\). \(m\angle ABD = 30^\circ\) and \(m\angle DBC = 45^\circ\). Find \(m\angle ABC\).
Solve \(4x - 10 = 2x + 30\).
Solve \((5x + 10) + (3x - 6) = 180\).

title: 1.3 - Complementary, Supplementary, and Vertical Angles
text:
👥 Learn Together

1.3.1 - Complementary and Supplementary Angles
Two angles are complementary if their measures add to \(90^\circ\). Two angles are supplementary if their measures add to \(180^\circ\).





The angles do not have to touch. \(25^\circ\) and \(65^\circ\) are complementary even when they are in different places.
To find the complement of an angle, subtract it from \(90^\circ\). To find the supplement, subtract it from \(180^\circ\).
Example 1: Complement and supplement

Find the complement of \(38^\circ\).
\(90 - 38 = 52\). The complement is \(52^\circ\).
Find the supplement of \(38^\circ\).
\(180 - 38 = 142\). The supplement is \(142^\circ\).
Find the complement and the supplement of \(x^\circ\).
The complement is \((90 - x)^\circ\). The supplement is \((180 - x)^\circ\).



The complement of \(63^\circ\).
The supplement of \(63^\circ\).
The supplement of \(105^\circ\).




\(90 - 63 = 27\), so \(27^\circ\).
\(180 - 63 = 117\), so \(117^\circ\).
\(180 - 105 = 75\), so \(75^\circ\).



An angle that is more than \(90^\circ\) has no complement. The complement would be negative. A way to remember: C comes before S in the alphabet, and \(90\) comes before \(180\).




1.3.2 - Adjacent Angles and Linear Pairs
Two angles are adjacent if they share a vertex and one side, and they do not overlap.





Example 2: Adjacent angles
Look at the two figures. In Figure 1, \(\angle 1\) and \(\angle 2\) share the vertex \(B\) and the side \(\overrightarrow{BD}\). They do not overlap. They are adjacent.
In Figure 2, \(\angle ABD\) and \(\angle ABC\) share the vertex and the side \(\overrightarrow{BA}\). But \(\angle ABD\) is inside \(\angle ABC\), so they overlap. They are not adjacent.
A linear pair is two adjacent angles whose outside sides are opposite rays. Together they make a straight line.

The angles in a linear pair add to \(180^\circ\), because together they make a straight angle.

Example 3: A linear pair





\(A\), \(B\), and \(C\) are on a line. \(m\angle 1 = 62^\circ\). Find \(m\angle 2\).
\(\angle 1\) and \(\angle 2\) are a linear pair, so \(m\angle 1 + m\angle 2 = 180^\circ\).
\[
m\angle 2 = 180 - 62 = 118
\]

Suppose \(m\angle 1 = 47^\circ\). Find \(m\angle 2\).


\(180 - 47 = 133\), so \(m\angle 2 = 133^\circ\).




1.3.3 - Vertical Angles
Two lines that cross make four angles. Vertical angles are the two angles that are across from each other. They share only the vertex.





\(\angle 1\) and \(\angle 3\) are vertical angles. \(\angle 2\) and \(\angle 4\) are also vertical angles.
Example 4: Vertical angles
\(m\angle 1 = 60^\circ\). Find \(m\angle 2\), \(m\angle 3\), and \(m\angle 4\).

\(\angle 1\) and \(\angle 2\) are a linear pair, so \(m\angle 2 = 180 - 60 = 120^\circ\).
\(\angle 3\) is vertical to \(\angle 1\), so \(m\angle 3 = 60^\circ\).
\(\angle 4\) is vertical to \(\angle 2\), so \(m\angle 4 = 120^\circ\).


Suppose \(m\angle 2 = 135^\circ\). Find \(m\angle 1\), \(m\angle 3\), and \(m\angle 4\).


\(m\angle 1 = 180 - 135 = 45^\circ\). \(m\angle 3 = 45^\circ\). \(m\angle 4 = 135^\circ\).


Do not just trust the picture. Look at the figure below. Call the first angle \(x\).





The top angle makes a linear pair with the first angle. So the top angle is \(180 - x\).
The left angle makes a linear pair with the top angle. So the left angle is \(180 - (180 - x) = x\).
The left angle and the first angle are vertical angles. Both are \(x\).
This works for any \(x\). Vertical angles are always equal.




1.3.4 - Solving for \(x\)
Now we use the pairs to write equations. First decide which pair you have. Then pick the rule.








Pair
Rule
Equation




complementary
add to \(90^\circ\)
\(\text{angle} + \text{angle} = 90\)


supplementary or linear pair
add to \(180^\circ\)
\(\text{angle} + \text{angle} = 180\)


vertical
equal
\(\text{angle} = \text{angle}\)



Example 5: Complementary angles





\(\angle ABC\) is a right angle. \(m\angle ABD = (3x + 5)^\circ\) and \(m\angle DBC = (2x)^\circ\). Find \(x\) and each angle.
The two angles are complementary.
\[
(3x + 5) + 2x = 90 \quad\text{so}\quad 5x + 5 = 90 \quad\text{so}\quad x = 17
\]
\(m\angle ABD = 3(17) + 5 = 56^\circ\) and \(m\angle DBC = 2(17) = 34^\circ\). Check: \(56 + 34 = 90\).

Two complementary angles measure \((5x + 6)^\circ\) and \((3x + 12)^\circ\). Find \(x\) and each angle.


\(8x + 18 = 90\), so \(x = 9\). The angles are \(51^\circ\) and \(39^\circ\).


Example 6: Vertical angles





The two marked angles are vertical angles. Find \(x\) and the marked angles.
Vertical angles are equal.
\[
4x - 10 = 2x + 30 \quad\text{so}\quad 2x = 40 \quad\text{so}\quad x = 20
\]
Each angle is \(4(20) - 10 = 70^\circ\). Check: \(2(20) + 30 = 70\). The other two angles are \(180 - 70 = 110^\circ\).

Two vertical angles measure \((6x + 1)^\circ\) and \((4x + 31)^\circ\). Find \(x\) and the angles.


\(6x + 1 = 4x + 31\), so \(x = 15\). Each angle is \(91^\circ\).


Example 7: Find the mistake
Lucía has two vertical angles, \((3x + 10)^\circ\) and \((5x - 30)^\circ\). She writes \((3x + 10) + (5x - 30) = 180\) and gets \(x = 25\). What did she do wrong?
Lucía used the rule for a linear pair. Vertical angles are not a linear pair. They are equal.
Check her answer. With \(x = 25\) the angles are \(85^\circ\) and \(95^\circ\). They are not equal, so \(x = 25\) cannot be right.
The correct equation is \(3x + 10 = 5x - 30\). Then \(40 = 2x\) and \(x = 20\). Each angle is \(70^\circ\).

Example 8: Three expressions





Lines \(\overleftrightarrow{AB}\) and \(\overleftrightarrow{CD}\) cross at \(E\). Find \(x\), \(y\), and the three angles.
Step 1. \(\angle AEC\) and \(\angle CEB\) are a linear pair.
\[
(3x + 5) + (2x + 15) = 180 \quad\text{so}\quad 5x + 20 = 180 \quad\text{so}\quad x = 32
\]
\(m\angle AEC = 3(32) + 5 = 101^\circ\) and \(m\angle CEB = 2(32) + 15 = 79^\circ\).
Step 2. \(\angle BED\) is vertical to \(\angle AEC\), so they are equal.
\[
5y + 1 = 101 \quad\text{so}\quad 5y = 100 \quad\text{so}\quad y = 20
\]

Use the same figure. Now \(m\angle AEC = (2x + 9)^\circ\), \(m\angle CEB = (3x + 1)^\circ\), and \(m\angle BED = (4y - 3)^\circ\). Find \(x\), \(y\), and the three angles.


\(5x + 10 = 180\), so \(x = 34\). \(m\angle AEC = 77^\circ\) and \(m\angle CEB = 103^\circ\).
\(4y - 3 = 77\), so \(y = 20\). \(m\angle BED = 77^\circ\).

title: 1.3 - Complementary, Supplementary, and Vertical Angles
text:

Complements and supplements.

Can an obtuse angle have a complement? Explain.


Pairs of angles. Lines \(\overleftrightarrow{WY}\) and \(\overleftrightarrow{XZ}\) cross at \(P\). Use the figure for problems 11 to 15.






Name a pair of vertical angles.
Name a linear pair.
Find \(m\angle XPY\).
Find \(m\angle YPZ\).
Find \(m\angle ZPW\).


Solve for \(x\).

Vertical angles measure \((7x - 12)^\circ\) and \((4x + 21)^\circ\). Find \(x\) and the angles.
Complementary angles measure \((4x + 3)^\circ\) and \((2x + 9)^\circ\). Find \(x\) and the angles.

A linear pair measures \((4x - 5)^\circ\) and \((2x + 17)^\circ\). Find \(x\) and the angles.
Two lines cross. \(m\angle 1 = (3x + 7)^\circ\) and \(m\angle 2 = (2x + 8)^\circ\) are a linear pair. \(m\angle 3 = (6y - 8)^\circ\) is vertical to \(\angle 1\). Find \(x\), \(y\), and the three angles.
An angle is \(20^\circ\) more than its complement. Find the angle.


Real problems.

Mohammed builds a sawhorse. The legs cross in an X. One angle between the legs is \(68^\circ\). Find the other three angles.
A pair of scissors has handles that make an angle of \(38^\circ\). The blades make an angle vertical to it. Find the angle between the blades. Then find the angle next to it.


Find the mistake.

Samir has a linear pair, \((2x + 10)^\circ\) and \((3x - 20)^\circ\). He writes \(2x + 10 = 3x - 20\) and gets \(x = 30\). What did he do wrong? Find the correct \(x\).


What does the figure show?

In a drawing, \(A\), \(B\), and \(C\) look like they are on one line, and \(D\) is a point off the line. The problem does not say \(A\), \(B\), and \(C\) are collinear. Can you say \(\angle ABD\) and \(\angle DBC\) are supplementary? Explain.


Test practice

Two angles are supplementary. One angle is 3 times as large as the other. What is the measure of the smaller angle?
A. \(30^\circ\)
B. \(45^\circ\)
C. \(60^\circ\)
D. \(135^\circ\)
Two lines cross. One angle measures \((4x + 6)^\circ\). The angle vertical to it measures \((7x - 21)^\circ\). What is the measure of an angle next to them?
A. \(42^\circ\)
B. \(48^\circ\)
C. \(132^\circ\)
D. \(138^\circ\)


Challenge

Three lines cross at one point. How many pairs of vertical angles are there? Draw a picture.
The complement of an angle is \(10^\circ\) less than half of its supplement. Find the angle.

title: 1.4 - Parallel Lines and Transversals
text:
🔥 Warm Up
Look at the stripes in a parking lot. They run side by side and never meet. Now look at the line along the edge of the lot. It crosses every stripe.
When one line crosses two others, it makes eight angles. If the two lines are parallel, these angles follow a pattern. In this lesson you learn the pattern and use it to find missing angles.

title: 1.4 - Parallel Lines and Transversals
text:
Two angles are a linear pair. One measures \(65^\circ\). Find the other.
Solve \(4x + 6 = 6x - 24\).
Solve \((3x - 5) + (2x + 20) = 180\).

title: 1.4 - Parallel Lines and Transversals
text:
👥 Learn Together

1.4.1 - Parallel, Perpendicular, and Skew Lines
Parallel lines are in the same plane and never meet. We write \(\ell \parallel m\). Matching arrows on a figure show that lines are parallel.
Perpendicular lines cross to make right angles. We write \(p \perp q\). A small square shows the right angle.





Skew lines are in space, not in one plane. They do not meet, and they are not parallel. A box shows them well.
Example 1: Lines on a box





Each edge of the box is part of a line.

Name an edge parallel to \(\overline{AB}\).
\(\overline{DC}\). (Also \(\overline{EF}\) and \(\overline{HG}\).) They go in the same direction and never meet.
Name an edge perpendicular to \(\overline{AB}\).
\(\overline{AD}\). (Also \(\overline{BC}\).) They meet at a right angle.
Name an edge skew to \(\overline{AB}\).
\(\overline{CG}\). It does not meet \(\overline{AB}\), and it does not go in the same direction.



Name an edge parallel to \(\overline{AD}\).
Name an edge skew to \(\overline{BC}\).




\(\overline{BC}\). (Also \(\overline{EH}\) and \(\overline{FG}\).)
\(\overline{AE}\). (Also \(\overline{DH}\), \(\overline{EF}\), and \(\overline{HG}\).)



On the coordinate plane. On a grid, two lines are parallel when they go up and over by the same amount. They have the same slope.
Example 2: Parallel on a grid





Are \(\overleftrightarrow{AB}\) and \(\overleftrightarrow{CD}\) parallel? \(A(1, 1)\), \(B(5, 3)\), \(C(1, 4)\), \(D(5, 6)\).
Slope of \(\overleftrightarrow{AB}\): \(\dfrac{3 - 1}{5 - 1} = \dfrac{2}{4} = \dfrac{1}{2}\).
Slope of \(\overleftrightarrow{CD}\): \(\dfrac{6 - 4}{5 - 1} = \dfrac{2}{4} = \dfrac{1}{2}\).
The slopes are equal, so the lines are parallel.

\(J(0, 2)\), \(K(4, 4)\), \(L(1, 0)\), \(M(4, 3)\). Are \(\overleftrightarrow{JK}\) and \(\overleftrightarrow{LM}\) parallel?


Slope of \(\overleftrightarrow{JK}\) is \(\frac{2}{4} = \frac{1}{2}\). Slope of \(\overleftrightarrow{LM}\) is \(\frac{3}{3} = 1\). The slopes are different, so the lines are not parallel.




1.4.2 - Angles Made by a Transversal
A transversal is a line that crosses two or more other lines. In the figure, line \(t\) is a transversal of lines \(\ell\) and \(m\). It makes eight angles.





Angles between \(\ell\) and \(m\) are interior. Angles outside are exterior. These are the four kinds of pairs.













Pair
Where they are
Example




corresponding
same position at each crossing
\(\angle 1\) and \(\angle 5\)


alternate interior
between the lines, opposite sides of \(t\)
\(\angle 3\) and \(\angle 6\)


alternate exterior
outside the lines, opposite sides of \(t\)
\(\angle 1\) and \(\angle 8\)


same-side interior
between the lines, same side of \(t\)
\(\angle 3\) and \(\angle 5\)



Example 3: Name the pair
Use the figure above.

\(\angle 2\) and \(\angle 6\): both are in the upper right position. They are corresponding.
\(\angle 4\) and \(\angle 6\): both are between the lines, on the right side of \(t\). They are same-side interior.



\(\angle 2\) and \(\angle 7\)
\(\angle 3\) and \(\angle 7\)
\(\angle 4\) and \(\angle 5\)




alternate exterior
corresponding
alternate interior





1.4.3 - Parallel Lines and the Eight Angles

If \(\ell \parallel m\), then:

corresponding angles are equal
alternate interior angles are equal
alternate exterior angles are equal
same-side interior angles are supplementary (they add to \(180^\circ\))


Example 4: Find all eight angles
\(\ell \parallel m\) in the figure above, and \(m\angle 1 = 115^\circ\). Find the other seven angles.



Angle
Measure
Reason




\(\angle 2\)
\(65^\circ\)
linear pair with \(\angle 1\)


\(\angle 3\)
\(65^\circ\)
vertical to \(\angle 2\)


\(\angle 4\)
\(115^\circ\)
vertical to \(\angle 1\)


\(\angle 5\)
\(115^\circ\)
corresponding to \(\angle 1\)


\(\angle 6\)
\(65^\circ\)
corresponding to \(\angle 2\)


\(\angle 7\)
\(65^\circ\)
vertical to \(\angle 6\)


\(\angle 8\)
\(115^\circ\)
vertical to \(\angle 5\)



Every angle is either \(115^\circ\) or \(65^\circ\). The two numbers add to \(180^\circ\).

Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One angle is \(48^\circ\). How many of the eight angles measure \(48^\circ\)? What do the others measure?


Four angles measure \(48^\circ\). The other four measure \(180 - 48 = 132^\circ\).


Example 5: Corresponding angles





\(\ell \parallel m\). Find \(x\) and the angles.
The marked angles are corresponding, so they are equal.
\[
4x + 6 = 6x - 24 \quad\text{so}\quad 30 = 2x \quad\text{so}\quad x = 15
\]
Each angle is \(4(15) + 6 = 66^\circ\). Check: \(6(15) - 24 = 66\).
Example 6: Same-side interior angles





\(\ell \parallel m\). Find \(x\) and the angles.
The marked angles are same-side interior, so they add to \(180^\circ\).
\[
(3x - 5) + (2x + 20) = 180 \quad\text{so}\quad 5x + 15 = 180 \quad\text{so}\quad x = 33
\]
The angles are \(3(33) - 5 = 94^\circ\) and \(2(33) + 20 = 86^\circ\). Check: \(94 + 86 = 180\).

\(\ell \parallel m\).

Alternate interior angles measure \((2x + 25)^\circ\) and \((3x - 5)^\circ\). Find \(x\) and the angles.
Same-side interior angles measure \((4x + 2)^\circ\) and \((2x + 16)^\circ\). Find \(x\) and the angles.




They are equal. \(2x + 25 = 3x - 5\), so \(x = 30\). Each angle is \(85^\circ\).
They add to \(180\). \(6x + 18 = 180\), so \(x = 27\). The angles are \(110^\circ\) and \(70^\circ\).





1.4.4 - Are the Lines Parallel?
The rules also work backward. If a transversal makes equal corresponding angles, the lines are parallel. The same is true for equal alternate interior angles, equal alternate exterior angles, and same-side interior angles that add to \(180^\circ\).
Example 7: Use angles to decide





The lines look parallel. The marked angles are corresponding. Are \(\ell\) and \(m\) parallel?
\(88^\circ \ne 92^\circ\). The corresponding angles are not equal, so the lines are not parallel.
(The picture is drawn to scale. The bottom line leans just \(4^\circ\).)
Example 8: Looks or marks?





Are \(\ell\) and \(m\) parallel?
We cannot tell. There are no arrow marks and no angle measures. A drawing that only looks parallel is not enough.


A transversal makes same-side interior angles of \(104^\circ\) and \(76^\circ\).
A transversal makes alternate interior angles of \(65^\circ\) and \(115^\circ\).




\(104 + 76 = 180\), so the lines are parallel.
\(65 \ne 115\), so the lines are not parallel.

Find the angles. \(\ell \parallel m\) in the figure above.

\(m\angle 1 = 128^\circ\). Find \(m\angle 5\), \(m\angle 6\), and \(m\angle 3\).

Real problems.

A diagonal avenue crosses two parallel streets, Oak St and Elm St. The avenue makes a \(38^\circ\) angle with Oak St, as shown. Find the angles \(a\) and \(b\).





Two rails of a train track are parallel. A cable crosses both rails. One of the eight angles measures \(72^\circ\). Every angle is one of two numbers. What are they?


Find the mistake.

\(\ell \parallel m\). Ana has same-side interior angles \((2x + 10)^\circ\) and \((3x - 5)^\circ\). She says same-side interior angles are equal, so \(2x + 10 = 3x - 5\) and \(x = 15\). What did she do wrong? Find the correct \(x\).


Are the lines parallel?

A transversal makes corresponding angles of \(74^\circ\) and \(74^\circ\).
A transversal makes alternate interior angles of \(65^\circ\) and \(115^\circ\).
Same-side interior angles measure \((3x + 10)^\circ\) and \((2x + 20)^\circ\). Find \(x\) so that the lines are parallel.
Two lines in a drawing look parallel. No arrows and no angles are given. Can you say they are parallel? Explain.


Test practice

\(\ell \parallel m\). Alternate interior angles measure \((5x - 20)^\circ\) and \((3x + 16)^\circ\). What is the measure of each angle?
A. \(18^\circ\)
B. \(54^\circ\)
C. \(70^\circ\)
D. \(110^\circ\)

A. Corresponding angles are supplementary.
B. Alternate interior angles are equal.
C. Same-side interior angles are equal.
D. Vertical angles are supplementary.


Challenge

Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One of the eight angles is \(90^\circ\). What are the other seven? What does this tell you about the transversal?
The line through \((0, 0)\) and \((4, 3)\) is given. Line \(n\) goes through \((1, -1)\). Find a second point on \(n\) so that \(n\) is parallel to the given line. Then find a second point so that \(n\) is perpendicular to it.

title: 1.5 - Angles in Triangles and Polygons
text:
🔥 Warm Up
A stop sign is a regular octagon. A honeycomb cell is a regular hexagon. A gazebo floor, a floor tile, and a soccer ball panel are all polygons. Each corner of these shapes is an angle.
Every triangle has angles that add to the same number. Because of that, we can find the angles in any polygon. In this lesson you learn the rules and use them to solve for missing angles.

title: 1.5 - Angles in Triangles and Polygons
text:
Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. Two alternate interior angles are \((2x + 5)^\circ\) and \((3x - 20)^\circ\). Find \(x\).
Find the supplement of \(115^\circ\).
Solve \(6x + 6 = 180\).

title: 1.5 - Angles in Triangles and Polygons
text:
👥 Learn Together

1.5.1 - The Triangle Angle Sum
Cut the three corners off a paper triangle. Put the corners together at one point. They make a straight line.






The three angles of a triangle add to \(180^\circ\).

Paper can fool us, so here is the reason. Draw a line through \(B\) parallel to \(\overline{AC}\).





The angle marked \(1\) at \(B\) is equal to the angle marked \(1\) at \(A\). They are alternate interior angles. The angle marked \(3\) at \(B\) is equal to the angle marked \(3\) at \(C\). The three angles at \(B\) make a straight line, so \(1 + 2 + 3 = 180^\circ\).
Example 1: Find the third angle
A triangle has angles of \(48^\circ\) and \(67^\circ\). Find the third angle.
\[
48 + 67 + x = 180 \quad\text{so}\quad 115 + x = 180 \quad\text{so}\quad x = 65
\]

A triangle has a right angle and a \(37^\circ\) angle. Find the third angle.


\(90 + 37 + x = 180\), so \(x = 53^\circ\).

Example 2: Solve for \(x\)
The angles of a triangle are \((2x)^\circ\), \((3x + 10)^\circ\), and \((x - 4)^\circ\). Find \(x\) and each angle.
\[
2x + (3x + 10) + (x - 4) = 180 \quad\text{so}\quad 6x + 6 = 180 \quad\text{so}\quad x = 29
\]
The angles are \(2(29) = 58^\circ\), \(3(29) + 10 = 97^\circ\), and \(29 - 4 = 25^\circ\). Check: \(58 + 97 + 25 = 180\).

The angles of a triangle are \((x + 15)^\circ\), \((2x - 5)^\circ\), and \((3x + 2)^\circ\). Find \(x\) and each angle.


\(6x + 12 = 180\), so \(x = 28\). The angles are \(43^\circ\), \(51^\circ\), and \(86^\circ\).




1.5.2 - Classifying Triangles
We name a triangle two ways: by its sides and by its angles.








By sides
Meaning




scalene
no sides the same length


isosceles
at least two sides the same length


equilateral
all three sides the same length






By angles
Meaning




acute
all three angles less than \(90^\circ\)


right
one \(90^\circ\) angle


obtuse
one angle more than \(90^\circ\)


equiangular
all three angles the same (\(60^\circ\) each)




In an isosceles triangle, the two angles across from the equal sides are equal. They are the base angles.

Example 3: Name it two ways

A triangle has sides \(4\), \(4\), and \(4\) and angles \(60^\circ\), \(60^\circ\), \(60^\circ\).
It is equilateral and equiangular.
A triangle has angles \(90^\circ\), \(45^\circ\), and \(45^\circ\).
It has a \(90^\circ\) angle, so it is right. It has two equal angles, so it is isosceles.

Example 4: Base angles





The tick marks show \(AB = BC\). The angle at \(B\) is \(40^\circ\). Find the base angles.
The base angles are equal. The three angles add to \(180\), so the two base angles add to \(180 - 40 = 140\). Each one is \(140 \div 2 = 70^\circ\).

An isosceles triangle has a base angle of \(55^\circ\). Find the angle at the top.


The base angles are \(55^\circ\) and \(55^\circ\). \(180 - 55 - 55 = 70^\circ\).

Example 5: An isosceles triangle with \(x\)





The tick marks show \(AB = BC\). Find \(x\) and the perimeter.
\[
3x + 1 = 2x + 9 \quad\text{so}\quad x = 8
\]
Each equal side is \(3(8) + 1 = 25\). The perimeter is \(25 + 25 + 12 = 62\).

The equal sides of an isosceles triangle are \((5x - 4)\) and \((3x + 10)\). The third side is \(20\). Find \(x\) and the perimeter.


\(5x - 4 = 3x + 10\), so \(x = 7\). Each equal side is \(31\). The perimeter is \(31 + 31 + 20 = 82\).




1.5.3 - Exterior Angles
Extend one side of a triangle. The angle outside the triangle, next to an inside angle, is an exterior angle. The two inside angles far from it are the remote interior angles.






An exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of its two remote interior angles.

Why? The exterior angle and its inside neighbor are a linear pair, so they add to \(180^\circ\). The three inside angles also add to \(180^\circ\). So the exterior angle equals the other two inside angles together.
Example 6: Find an exterior angle
In the figure, the remote angles are \(50^\circ\) and \(65^\circ\). The exterior angle is \(50 + 65 = 115^\circ\).

An exterior angle is \(130^\circ\). One remote angle is \(80^\circ\). Find the other remote angle.


\(130 - 80 = 50^\circ\).

Example 7: Solve for \(x\)





Find \(x\) and the exterior angle.
\[
4x - 6 = (x + 30) + (x + 36) \quad\text{so}\quad 4x - 6 = 2x + 66 \quad\text{so}\quad x = 36
\]
The exterior angle is \(4(36) - 6 = 138^\circ\). The remote angles are \(66^\circ\) and \(72^\circ\).

An exterior angle is \((7x - 3)^\circ\). The remote angles are \((2x + 22)^\circ\) and \((3x + 5)^\circ\). Find \(x\) and the exterior angle.


\(7x - 3 = 5x + 27\), so \(x = 15\). The exterior angle is \(102^\circ\).




1.5.4 - Polygons
A polygon is a closed figure made of segments. We name a polygon by its number of sides.

A polygon with \(n\) sides is an \(n\)-gon. A polygon is convex if no corner points inward (see the figure at the top of the lesson). A regular polygon has all sides equal and all angles equal.
The angle sum. Pick one corner. Draw all the diagonals from it. They cut the polygon into triangles.





A hexagon makes \(4\) triangles, and each triangle has \(180^\circ\). So the angles of a hexagon add to \(4 \cdot 180 = 720^\circ\).

A polygon with \(n\) sides makes \(n - 2\) triangles. The interior angles add to \[
(n - 2) \cdot 180^\circ.
\]

Example 8: Angle sum
Find the angle sum of a pentagon and of an octagon.
Pentagon: \((5 - 2) \cdot 180 = 540^\circ\).
Octagon: \((8 - 2) \cdot 180 = 1080^\circ\).

Find the angle sum of a hexagon. Check it with the figure above.


\((6 - 2) \cdot 180 = 720^\circ\). It matches the \(4\) triangles.

Example 9: One angle of a regular polygon
In a regular polygon, all angles are equal. Divide the sum by \(n\).

Regular pentagon: \(540 \div 5 = 108^\circ\).
Regular decagon: \((10 - 2) \cdot 180 = 1440\), and \(1440 \div 10 = 144^\circ\).


Find one angle of a regular hexagon.


\(720 \div 6 = 120^\circ\).

Exterior angles. Walk around a polygon. At each corner you turn by the exterior angle. After one trip around you have turned one full circle, \(360^\circ\).






The exterior angles of any convex polygon add to \(360^\circ\).

For a regular polygon with \(n\) sides, each exterior angle is \(360 \div n\). Each interior angle is \(180\) minus the exterior angle.
Example 10: Find the number of sides

The angles of a polygon add to \(1260^\circ\). Find \(n\).
\((n - 2) \cdot 180 = 1260\), so \(n - 2 = 7\) and \(n = 9\).
Each angle of a regular polygon is \(150^\circ\). Find \(n\).
The exterior angle is \(180 - 150 = 30^\circ\). So \(n = 360 \div 30 = 12\).


The angles of a polygon add to \(1620^\circ\). Find \(n\).


\(n - 2 = 9\), so \(n = 11\).

Example 11: Solve for \(x\)
A quadrilateral has angles \(x^\circ\), \((2x)^\circ\), \((x + 50)^\circ\), and \(90^\circ\). Find \(x\) and each angle.
The sum for a quadrilateral is \((4 - 2) \cdot 180 = 360\).
\[
x + 2x + (x + 50) + 90 = 360 \quad\text{so}\quad 4x + 140 = 360 \quad\text{so}\quad x = 55
\]
The angles are \(55^\circ\), \(110^\circ\), \(105^\circ\), and \(90^\circ\).

A quadrilateral has angles \(x^\circ\), \((x + 20)^\circ\), \((2x)^\circ\), and \((x + 40)^\circ\). Find \(x\) and each angle.


\(5x + 60 = 360\), so \(x = 60\). The angles are \(60^\circ\), \(80^\circ\), \(120^\circ\), and \(100^\circ\).

title: Unit 1 Summary
text:
1.1 - Points, Lines, Segments, and Angles
Example: Clock hands at 4:00: \(4 \cdot 30^\circ = 120^\circ\), obtuse.

title: Unit 1 Summary
text:
A point is an exact location. A line goes on forever both ways. A plane is a flat surface that goes on forever.
Segment \(\overline{AB}\): two endpoints. Ray \(\overrightarrow{AB}\): starts at \(A\), goes on forever. Line \(\overleftrightarrow{AB}\). Length \(AB\) is a number.
\(\overrightarrow{AB}\) and \(\overrightarrow{BA}\) are different rays. The first letter is the endpoint.
An angle has two sides and a vertex. Name it \(\angle ABC\) with the vertex in the middle. Write the measure as \(m\angle ABC\).
Acute: less than \(90^\circ\). Right: \(90^\circ\). Obtuse: between \(90^\circ\) and \(180^\circ\). Straight: \(180^\circ\).
Trust what is told and what is marked: square marks, tick marks, arrows. Do not trust how a figure looks.

title: Unit 1 Summary
text:
1.2 - Segment and Angle Addition

Length on a number line: \(AB = |a - b|\). Length is never negative.
Segment addition: if \(B\) is between \(A\) and \(C\), then \(AB + BC = AC\).
Congruent (\(\cong\)) is for figures. \(=\) is for numbers. \(\overline{AB} \cong \overline{CD}\) means \(AB = CD\).
A midpoint makes two congruent segments. A segment bisector goes through the midpoint.
Angle addition: if \(D\) is inside \(\angle ABC\), then \(m\angle ABD + m\angle DBC = m\angle ABC\). An angle bisector makes two congruent angles.
Protractor: put one side on a \(0\). Read the scale that starts at that \(0\).






Example: \(AB = 2x + 3\), \(BC = x - 1\), \(AC = 17\). \(3x + 2 = 17\), so \(x = 5\), \(AB = 13\), \(BC = 4\).

title: Unit 1 Summary
text:
1.3 - Complementary, Supplementary, and Vertical Angles

Complementary angles add to \(90^\circ\). Supplementary angles add to \(180^\circ\). They do not have to touch.
Complement of \(x^\circ\): \((90 - x)^\circ\). Supplement of \(x^\circ\): \((180 - x)^\circ\).
Adjacent angles share a vertex and a side and do not overlap. A linear pair is adjacent with outside sides that are opposite rays. A linear pair is supplementary.
Vertical angles are across from each other. They are equal.
To solve for \(x\): name the pair, then write angle \(+\) angle \(= 90\) (complementary), \(= 180\) (supplementary or linear pair), or angle \(=\) angle (vertical).






Example: Vertical angles \((4x - 10)^\circ\) and \((2x + 30)^\circ\). \(4x - 10 = 2x + 30\), so \(x = 20\) and each angle is \(70^\circ\).

title: Unit 1 Summary
text:
1.4 - Parallel Lines and Transversals

Parallel (\(\parallel\)): same plane, never meet. Perpendicular (\(\perp\)): right angles. Skew: not in one plane, never meet.
A transversal crosses two lines and makes 8 angles. Pairs: corresponding, alternate interior, alternate exterior, same-side interior.
If the lines are parallel: corresponding, alternate interior, and alternate exterior angles are equal. Same-side interior angles are supplementary.
The rules work backward. Equal corresponding or alternate angles, or same-side interior angles that add to \(180^\circ\), show the lines are parallel.
On a grid, parallel lines have the same slope.






Example: \(\ell \parallel m\). Corresponding angles \((4x + 6)^\circ\) and \((6x - 24)^\circ\). \(x = 15\), each angle \(66^\circ\).

title: Unit 1 Summary
text:
1.5 - Angles in Triangles and Polygons

The angles of a triangle add to \(180^\circ\).
By sides: scalene, isosceles (two equal), equilateral (three equal). By angles: acute, right, obtuse, equiangular. Base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal.
An exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles.
A polygon with \(n\) sides: angle sum \((n - 2) \cdot 180^\circ\). Exterior angles of a convex polygon add to \(360^\circ\).
Regular polygon: each exterior angle is \(\dfrac{360}{n}\) and each interior angle is \(180\) minus that.






Example: Regular pentagon: \((5 - 2) \cdot 180 = 540\), and \(540 \div 5 = 108^\circ\).

Example 1: Write the symbol for the ray that starts at \(K\) and goes through \(L\). Write the symbol for the line through \(K\) and \(L\). Classify an angle of \(137^\circ\).
Ray: \(\overrightarrow{KL}\). Line: \(\overleftrightarrow{KL}\). \(137^\circ\) is between \(90^\circ\) and \(180^\circ\), so it is obtuse.

\((5x - 2) + (3x + 6) = 44\), so \(8x + 4 = 44\) and \(x = 5\). \(AB = 23\) and \(BC = 21\). Check: \(23 + 21 = 44\).


1.3 - Complementary, Supplementary, and Vertical Angles
Example 3: Two supplementary angles measure \((7x + 3)^\circ\) and \((5x + 9)^\circ\). Find \(x\) and the angles.
\((7x + 3) + (5x + 9) = 180\), so \(12x + 12 = 180\) and \(x = 14\). The angles are \(101^\circ\) and \(79^\circ\).


1.4 - Parallel Lines and Transversals
Example 4: \(\ell \parallel m\). Alternate interior angles measure \((5x + 12)^\circ\) and \((8x - 18)^\circ\). Find \(x\) and the angles.
Alternate interior angles are equal. \(5x + 12 = 8x - 18\), so \(30 = 3x\) and \(x = 10\). Each angle is \(62^\circ\).

Example 5: Each angle of a regular polygon is \(144^\circ\). Find the number of sides and the angle sum.
Exterior angle: \(180 - 144 = 36^\circ\). \(n = 360 \div 36 = 10\). Angle sum: \((10 - 2) \cdot 180 = 1440^\circ\).

title: 2.1 - Square Roots and Simplifying Radicals
text:
👥 Learn Together

2.1.1 - Perfect Squares and Square Roots
A square tile is 3 inches on each side. Its area is \(3 \times 3 = 9\) square inches. The number 9 is a perfect square. A perfect square is the square of a whole number.
Now go backward. A square has area 9 square inches. How long is its side? It is 3 inches. We say 3 is the square root of 9, and we write \(\sqrt{9} = 3\). The symbol \(\sqrt{\ \ }\) is the radical sign. The number under it is the radicand.





Here are the perfect squares you should know. Learn them. You will see them all unit long.

\(\sqrt{49} = 7\). We do not write \(-7\). Both \(7 \cdot 7\) and \((-7) \cdot (-7)\) equal 49, but the radical sign asks for the positive root only.


Example 1: Find each square root.

\(\sqrt{64}\). Think: what number times itself is 64? \(8 \cdot 8 = 64\), so \(\sqrt{64} = 8\).
\(\sqrt{144} = 12\), because \(12 \cdot 12 = 144\).
A square tile has area 81 square inches. Its side length is \(\sqrt{81} = 9\) inches.



\(\sqrt{121}\)
\(\sqrt{225}\)




\(\sqrt{121} = 11\)
\(\sqrt{225} = 15\)


Most numbers are not perfect squares. Look at this tilted square on a grid. Its corners sit on the grid points. Cut off the four small triangles and the area is 2 square units. So the side length is \(\sqrt{2}\). No whole number times itself gives 2.







2.1.2 - Estimating Square Roots
The area of the garden is 50 square feet, and 50 is not a perfect square. But \(49 < 50 < 64\), so \(7 < \sqrt{50} < 8\). The side is a little more than 7 feet.
To decide if the root is closer to 7 or to 8, test the middle, \(7.5\). Since \(7.5^2 = 56.25\), a radicand less than \(56.25\) has a root closer to 7.






Example 3: Estimate \(\sqrt{50}\). Then use a calculator and round to the nearest tenth.
\(7^2 = 49\) and \(8^2 = 64\). So \(\sqrt{50}\) is between 7 and 8.
Test the middle: \(7.5^2 = 56.25\). Since \(50 < 56.25\), \(\sqrt{50}\) is closer to 7.
Calculator: \(\sqrt{50} \approx 7.071\). To the nearest tenth, \(\sqrt{50} \approx 7.1\).

\(6^2 = 36\) and \(7^2 = 49\), so \(\sqrt{45}\) is between 6 and 7. Since \(6.5^2 = 42.25\) and \(45 > 42.25\), it is closer to 7. Calculator: \(\sqrt{45} \approx 6.7\).


\(\sqrt{40}\) is not \(40 \div 2\). Square roots are much smaller than the number. \(6^2 = 36\) and \(7^2 = 49\), so \(\sqrt{40}\) is a little more than 6.



2.1.3 - Simplifying Square Roots
The garden side \(\sqrt{50}\) can be written a shorter way. \(50 = 25 \cdot 2\), and 25 is a perfect square. So \(\sqrt{50} = \sqrt{25} \cdot \sqrt{2} = 5\sqrt{2}\).
The rule: \(\sqrt{a \cdot b} = \sqrt{a} \cdot \sqrt{b}\) for \(a\) and \(b\) that are 0 or more. A radical is simplified when the radicand has no perfect square factor except 1. We usually give answers in this form. We call it the exact answer.

Example 5: Simplify \(\sqrt{72}\) two ways.
Method 1: perfect square factor. \(72 = 36 \cdot 2\).
\[
\sqrt{72} = \sqrt{36} \cdot \sqrt{2} = 6\sqrt{2}
\]
Method 2: prime factors. \(72 = 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 3\). Circle the pairs: \((2 \cdot 2)\) and \((3 \cdot 3)\). One 2 is left over.
\[
\sqrt{72} = 2 \cdot 3 \cdot \sqrt{2} = 6\sqrt{2}
\]

Example 6: Simplify each square root.

\(\sqrt{48}\). The largest perfect square factor is 16. \(\sqrt{48} = \sqrt{16} \cdot \sqrt{3} = 4\sqrt{3}\).
\(\sqrt{180}\). Prime factors: \(180 = 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 3 \cdot 5\). The pairs give \(2 \cdot 3 = 6\), and 5 is left over. So \(\sqrt{180} = 6\sqrt{5}\).
\(\sqrt{30}\). The factors of 30 are 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 10, 15, 30. None of them is a perfect square except 1. So \(\sqrt{30}\) is already simplified.



\(\sqrt{98}\)
\(\sqrt{150}\)




\(\sqrt{98} = \sqrt{49} \cdot \sqrt{2} = 7\sqrt{2}\)
\(\sqrt{150} = \sqrt{25} \cdot \sqrt{6} = 5\sqrt{6}\)



The side of the garden is \(\sqrt{50} = 5\sqrt{2}\) feet. That is about \(5 \cdot 1.414 = 7.07\) feet, which agrees with the estimate between 7 and 8.


A number in front of a radical means multiply. \(5\sqrt{2}\) is \(5 \cdot \sqrt{2}\). To simplify \(3\sqrt{8}\), first simplify \(\sqrt{8} = 2\sqrt{2}\). Then multiply: \(3 \cdot 2\sqrt{2} = 6\sqrt{2}\).



2.1.4 - Multiplying, Adding, and Rationalizing
Multiply radicals by multiplying the numbers in front and multiplying the radicands: \(\sqrt{3} \cdot \sqrt{12} = \sqrt{36} = 6\). Then simplify.
Add radicals only when the radicands are the same. These are like radicals, like \(3x + 5x = 8x\). So \(3\sqrt{2} + 5\sqrt{2} = 8\sqrt{2}\). If the radicands differ, simplify first. You may find they match.
Rationalize: a simplified answer has no radical in the denominator. Multiply the top and bottom by that radical. In Unit 6 we need this step often.

Example 8: Multiply and simplify: \(2\sqrt{3} \cdot 5\sqrt{6}\).
Numbers in front: \(2 \cdot 5 = 10\). Radicands: \(\sqrt{3} \cdot \sqrt{6} = \sqrt{18}\).
\(\sqrt{18} = \sqrt{9} \cdot \sqrt{2} = 3\sqrt{2}\).
\[
2\sqrt{3} \cdot 5\sqrt{6} = 10 \cdot 3\sqrt{2} = 30\sqrt{2}
\]

Example 9: Add: \(\sqrt{8} + \sqrt{18}\).
The radicands differ, so simplify first. \(\sqrt{8} = 2\sqrt{2}\) and \(\sqrt{18} = 3\sqrt{2}\).
Now they are like radicals: \(2\sqrt{2} + 3\sqrt{2} = 5\sqrt{2}\).

Example 10: Rationalize the denominator: \(\dfrac{6}{\sqrt{2}}\).
\[
\dfrac{6}{\sqrt{2}} \cdot \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{6\sqrt{2}}{2} = 3\sqrt{2}
\]
We multiplied by \(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}}\), which equals 1, so the value did not change.


\(\sqrt{2} \cdot \sqrt{14}\)
\(4\sqrt{5} + 2\sqrt{5}\)
\(\dfrac{9}{\sqrt{3}}\)




\(\sqrt{28} = 2\sqrt{7}\)
\(6\sqrt{5}\)
\(\dfrac{9\sqrt{3}}{3} = 3\sqrt{3}\)



Jamal writes \(\sqrt{9 + 16} = \sqrt{9} + \sqrt{16} = 3 + 4 = 7\).
Find his mistake. First add: \(9 + 16 = 25\), and \(\sqrt{25} = 5\). The rule \(\sqrt{a \cdot b} = \sqrt{a} \cdot \sqrt{b}\) works for multiplying. It does not work for adding. \(\sqrt{9+16}\) is not \(\sqrt{9} + \sqrt{16}\).

title: 2.2 - The Pythagorean Theorem and Its Converse
text:
👥 Learn Together

2.2.1 - Parts of a Right Triangle
A right triangle has one right angle. The two sides that make the right angle are the legs. The side across from the right angle is the hypotenuse. The hypotenuse is always the longest side.
The legs can be turned any way. The hypotenuse is still the side that does not touch the right angle.






Example 1: Name the legs and the hypotenuse of \(\triangle PQR\). The right angle is at \(Q\).





The legs touch the right angle. They are \(\overline{PQ}\) and \(\overline{QR}\), so the legs are \(\overline{PQ}\) and \(\overline{QR}\).
The hypotenuse is across from \(Q\). It is \(\overline{PR}\).

\(\overline{PR}\) is the longest because it is the hypotenuse.



2.2.2 - The Pythagorean Theorem
Look at a right triangle with legs 3 and 4. Build a square on each side. The areas are \(3^2 = 9\), \(4^2 = 16\), and the big square has area 25. Notice that \(9 + 16 = 25\).
This is true for every right triangle. If the legs are \(a\) and \(b\) and the hypotenuse is \(c\), then \(a^2 + b^2 = c^2\).











Take two big squares with the same side length \(a + b\). In each one, place four copies of the same right triangle.
In the first square, the space left over is one tilted square with area \(c^2\). In the second square, the space left over is two squares with areas \(a^2\) and \(b^2\).
Both big squares have the same area. Both have four triangles. So what is left over must match: \(c^2 = a^2 + b^2\).



2.2.3 - Finding a Missing Side
Write the theorem. Put in the two sides you know. Solve for the third. The hypotenuse \(c\) is always alone on one side of the equation.
Leave an exact answer as a simplified radical (Lesson 2.1). Then give a decimal when the problem asks.

Example 3: Find the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs 5 and 7. Give the exact answer and round to the nearest tenth.
\[
5^2 + 7^2 = c^2
\]
\[
25 + 49 = c^2 \quad\text{so}\quad c^2 = 74
\]
\(c = \sqrt{74}\). Since \(74 = 2 \cdot 37\), it does not simplify. \(c \approx 8.6\).

Example 4: A right triangle has hypotenuse 12 and one leg 8. Find the other leg. Give the exact answer and round to the nearest tenth.
\[
8^2 + b^2 = 12^2
\]
\[
64 + b^2 = 144 \quad\text{so}\quad b^2 = 80
\]
\(b = \sqrt{80} = \sqrt{16} \cdot \sqrt{5} = 4\sqrt{5} \approx 8.9\).






Example 5: The legs of a right triangle are \(x\) and \(x + 7\). The hypotenuse is 13. Find \(x\).
\[
x^2 + (x + 7)^2 = 13^2
\]
\[
x^2 + x^2 + 14x + 49 = 169 \quad\text{so}\quad 2x^2 + 14x - 120 = 0
\]
Divide by 2: \(x^2 + 7x - 60 = 0\). Factor: \((x + 12)(x - 5) = 0\). So \(x = 5\) or \(x = -12\).
A length cannot be negative. The legs are 5 and 12. Check: \(25 + 144 = 169\).


Find the hypotenuse when the legs are 4 and 9.
Find the other leg when the hypotenuse is 11 and one leg is 6.




\(c = \sqrt{16 + 81} = \sqrt{97} \approx 9.8\)
\(b = \sqrt{121 - 36} = \sqrt{85} \approx 9.2\)




2.2.4 - Pythagorean Triples
Some right triangles have whole number sides. Three whole numbers \(a\), \(b\), \(c\) with \(a^2 + b^2 = c^2\) form a Pythagorean triple. The triangle with sides 3, 4, 5 is the best known one.
Multiply every number of a triple by the same number and you get another triple. 3-4-5 times 2 is 6-8-10. Times 3 is 9-12-15.

Example 7: Two legs of a right triangle are 15 and 36. Find the hypotenuse.
Is it a multiple of a triple? \(15 = 3 \cdot 5\) and \(36 = 3 \cdot 12\). So it is \(3 \cdot (5, 12, 13)\).
The hypotenuse is \(3 \cdot 13 = 39\). Check: \(225 + 1296 = 1521 = 39^2\).

\(25 = 5 \cdot 5\) and \(15 = 5 \cdot 3\). It is \(5 \cdot (3, 4, 5)\). The other leg is \(5 \cdot 4 = 20\).



2.2.5 - The Converse: Is It a Right Triangle?
The converse of a rule turns it around. The theorem says: right triangle, then \(a^2 + b^2 = c^2\). The converse says: if \(a^2 + b^2 = c^2\), then the triangle is a right triangle. The converse is also true.
Let \(c\) be the longest side. Compare \(c^2\) with \(a^2 + b^2\). Equal means right. If \(a^2 + b^2\) is bigger, the triangle is acute. If \(a^2 + b^2\) is smaller, it is obtuse.
First check that the three lengths can make a triangle. The triangle inequality says the two shorter sides must add to more than the longest side.

Example 9: Is a triangle with sides 7, 24, and 25 a right triangle?
The longest side is 25. Test: \(7^2 + 24^2 = 49 + 576 = 625\).
\(25^2 = 625\). They are equal, so the triangle is a right triangle.

Example 10: Sides 5, 6, and 8. Is the triangle right, acute, or obtuse?
First: \(5 + 6 = 11 > 8\), so it is a triangle.
\(5^2 + 6^2 = 25 + 36 = 61\) and \(8^2 = 64\).
\(61 < 64\), so the triangle is obtuse.






This triangle looks like a right triangle. The picture only suggests it. The numbers show the truth: the largest angle is about \(93^\circ\), so it is obtuse. Always check with numbers, as in Example 7.


Example 11: Can lengths 3, 4, and 9 make a triangle?
\(3 + 4 = 7\), and \(7 < 9\). The short sides are not longer than the long side.
So no, these lengths cannot make a triangle.


9, 40, 41
6, 7, 10




\(81 + 1600 = 1681 = 41^2\). Right.
\(36 + 49 = 85 < 100\). Obtuse.

title: 2.3 - The Pythagorean Theorem in the Real World
text:
👥 Learn Together

2.3.1 - Squaring a Corner
Builders need square corners for decks, floors, and walls. They use the 3-4-5 triangle. Measure 3 feet along one edge and 4 feet along the other. If the marks are exactly 5 feet apart, the corner is a right angle. For a big slab they use 6-8-10 or 9-12-15, because longer measures are more exact.
A rectangle has four right angles. A diagonal is a segment that joins two corners that are not next to each other. If the diagonal is the right length, the corner is square.

Example 1: A deck is 10 ft by 24 ft. Kofi measures the diagonal and gets 26 ft 2 in. Is the deck square?





Draw the rectangle. The diagonal and two sides make a right triangle.
The diagonal should be \(c = \sqrt{10^2 + 24^2} = \sqrt{676} = 26\) ft.
Kofi measured 26 ft 2 in, which is 2 inches too long. The deck is not square. The corner needs to be pushed in.

\(c = \sqrt{15^2 + 20^2} = \sqrt{625} = 25\) ft. (It is \(5 \cdot (3, 4, 5)\).)



2.3.2 - Ladders
A ladder against a wall makes a right triangle. The wall is one leg, the ground is the other leg, and the ladder is the hypotenuse. The base of the ladder should not be too close to the wall. The 4-to-1 rule: the base should be 1 foot from the wall for every 4 feet of height.

Example 3: A 20 ft ladder has its base 5 ft from a wall. How high does it reach? Does it follow the 4-to-1 rule? Round to the nearest tenth.





\[
5^2 + h^2 = 20^2 \quad\text{so}\quad h^2 = 375
\]
\(h = \sqrt{375} = 5\sqrt{15} \approx 19.4\) ft.
Rule: \(19.4 \div 4 \approx 4.9\). The base needs to be at least 4.9 ft out. It is 5 ft out, so the ladder follows the rule.

\(h = \sqrt{24^2 - 6^2} = \sqrt{540} = 6\sqrt{15} \approx 23.2\) ft.



2.3.3 - Screens
TVs, phones, and monitors are measured on the diagonal, from one corner to the opposite corner. A “55 inch TV” has a screen diagonal of 55 inches. The width and the height are the legs.

Example 5: A TV screen is 40 in wide and 22.5 in tall. What is its screen size? Round to the nearest tenth.





\[
d^2 = 40^2 + 22.5^2 = 1600 + 506.25 = 2106.25
\]
\(d = \sqrt{2106.25} \approx 45.9\). It is a 45.9 inch screen (sold as a 46 inch TV).

\(w = \sqrt{24^2 - 12^2} = \sqrt{432} = 12\sqrt{3} \approx 20.8\) in.



2.3.4 - Shortcuts and Distances
A straight path is the shortest path. When a path goes across a rectangle, it is the diagonal. Compare it with walking along the sides.

Example 7: A park is 300 ft by 400 ft. Moses walks from one corner to the opposite corner. How much shorter is the diagonal path than walking along two sides?





Along two sides: \(300 + 400 = 700\) ft.
Diagonal: \(\sqrt{300^2 + 400^2} = \sqrt{250000} = 500\) ft. (It is \(100 \cdot (3, 4, 5)\).)
\(700 - 500 = 200\). The diagonal path is 200 ft shorter.

Example 8: A baseball diamond is a square with 90 ft between bases. How far is it from home plate to second base? Round to the nearest tenth.
Home to first and first to second are the legs. Home to second is the diagonal.
\(d = \sqrt{90^2 + 90^2} = \sqrt{16200} = 90\sqrt{2} \approx 127.3\) ft.

\(\sqrt{36^2 + 3^2} = \sqrt{1305} \approx 36.1\) ft.



2.3.5 - Two Steps: Boxes
How long is the longest pole that fits in a box? It runs from one bottom corner to the opposite top corner. You need two right triangles. First find the diagonal of the floor. Then use that diagonal as a leg of a second right triangle.

Example 10: A box is 12 in long, 9 in wide, and 8 in tall. Find the longest pole that fits.





Step 1, the floor: \(f = \sqrt{12^2 + 9^2} = \sqrt{225} = 15\) in.
Step 2, the pole: \(p = \sqrt{15^2 + 8^2} = \sqrt{289} = 17\) in.
The longest pole is 17 in.

Floor: \(\sqrt{16 + 16} = \sqrt{32}\). Rod: \(\sqrt{32 + 49} = \sqrt{81} = 9\) ft.

title: 2.4 - Distance on the Coordinate Plane
text:
👥 Learn Together

2.4.1 - Horizontal and Vertical Distance
Points on the same horizontal line have the same \(y\)-coordinate. Count the units between them, or subtract the \(x\)-coordinates. The distance is never negative, so use the absolute value: \(|x_2 - x_1|\).
Points on the same vertical line have the same \(x\)-coordinate. The distance is \(|y_2 - y_1|\).






Example 1: Use the figure. Find \(AB\) and \(CD\).
\(A(-3, 2)\) and \(B(4, 2)\) have the same \(y\). \(AB = |4 - (-3)| = 7\).
\(C(5, -4)\) and \(D(5, 2)\) have the same \(x\). \(CD = |2 - (-4)| = 6\).


\(P(-5, -1)\) and \(Q(3, -1)\)
\(R(-2, 6)\) and \(S(-2, -3)\)




\(|3 - (-5)| = 8\)
\(|6 - (-3)| = 9\)




2.4.2 - Slanted Distance: Draw a Right Triangle
Most pairs of points are not on a horizontal or vertical line. Draw a horizontal segment and a vertical segment to make a right triangle. The slanted segment is the hypotenuse. The legs are the horizontal change and the vertical change.

Example 3: Find the distance from \(A(1, 2)\) to \(B(5, 5)\).





Draw the right triangle with the right angle at \((5, 2)\).
Horizontal leg: \(5 - 1 = 4\). Vertical leg: \(5 - 2 = 3\).
\(AB^2 = 4^2 + 3^2 = 25\), so \(AB = 5\).

Example 4: Find the distance from \(A(-2, -1)\) to \(B(3, 4)\). Give the exact answer and round to the nearest tenth.





Horizontal leg: \(3 - (-2) = 5\). Vertical leg: \(4 - (-1) = 5\).
\(AB^2 = 5^2 + 5^2 = 50\). \(AB = \sqrt{50} = 5\sqrt{2} \approx 7.1\).

Legs: \(2 - (-3) = 5\) and \(|-8 - 4| = 12\). \(PQ = \sqrt{25 + 144} = 13\).



2.4.3 - The Distance Formula
The steps in 2.4.2 are always the same. Subtract the \(x\)’s. Subtract the \(y\)’s. Square both. Add. Take the square root. The distance formula writes those steps with symbols.

Subtracting a negative number adds. For \(x_1 = -4\) and \(x_2 = 2\): \(x_2 - x_1 = 2 - (-4) = 6\), not \(-2\). Put the second point in parentheses.


Example 6: Find the distance from \(A(-4, 3)\) to \(B(2, -5)\).
\[
d = \sqrt{(2 - (-4))^2 + (-5 - 3)^2} = \sqrt{6^2 + (-8)^2}
\]
\[
d = \sqrt{36 + 64} = \sqrt{100} = 10
\]

Example 7: Find the distance from \((1, -2)\) to \((-3, 4)\). Give the exact answer and round to the nearest tenth.
\[
d = \sqrt{(-3 - 1)^2 + (4 - (-2))^2} = \sqrt{16 + 36} = \sqrt{52}
\]
\(\sqrt{52} = 2\sqrt{13} \approx 7.2\).

\(d = \sqrt{(-4 - 2)^2 + (1 - (-6))^2} = \sqrt{36 + 49} = \sqrt{85} \approx 9.2\)



2.4.4 - Using Distance
Distance helps you decide things. You can find which point is closer, check if a triangle has two equal sides, or find a missing coordinate. When a coordinate is missing, write the distance formula, square both sides, and solve. There can be two answers.

Example 9: Which point is closer to \(M(1, 1)\): \(P(4, 5)\) or \(Q(-5, 4)\)?
\(MP = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5\).
\(MQ = \sqrt{(-6)^2 + 3^2} = \sqrt{45} \approx 6.7\).
\(5 < 6.7\), so \(P\) is closer.

Example 10: Is the triangle with \(A(1, 1)\), \(B(7, 1)\), and \(C(4, 5)\) isosceles?
\(AB = |7 - 1| = 6\).
\(AC = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5\) and \(BC = \sqrt{(-3)^2 + 4^2} = 5\).
Because \(AC = BC\), triangle \(ABC\) is isosceles.

Example 11: The point \((1, k)\) is 5 units from \((4, 2)\). Find \(k\).
\[
\sqrt{(1 - 4)^2 + (k - 2)^2} = 5 \quad\text{so}\quad 9 + (k - 2)^2 = 25
\]
\((k - 2)^2 = 16\), so \(k - 2 = 4\) or \(k - 2 = -4\). Then \(k = 6\) or \(k = -2\).
There are two points: \((1, 6)\) and \((1, -2)\).

Example 12: A town map has 1 mile for each grid unit. The school is at \(S(2, 1)\) and the library is at \(L(8, 9)\). A car follows the streets. A drone flies straight. How much shorter is the drone’s trip?





Streets: \(6\) miles east and \(8\) miles north is \(6 + 8 = 14\) miles.
Drone: \(\sqrt{6^2 + 8^2} = 10\) miles.
The drone’s trip is \(14 - 10 = 4\) miles shorter.

\((k + 2)^2 + 36 = 100\), so \((k + 2)^2 = 64\) and \(k + 2 = \pm 8\). Then \(k = 6\) or \(k = -10\).

title: 2.5 - Midpoint
text:
🔥 Warm Up
Fatima lives at one point on the town map. Jamal lives at another. They want to meet at the point exactly halfway between their homes. Where is it?
The halfway point of a segment is its midpoint. You can find it by averaging the coordinates. This is one of the tools you will use again and again.

title: 2.5 - Midpoint

title: 2.5 - Midpoint
text:
👥 Learn Together

2.5.1 - Midpoint on a Number Line
The number halfway between two numbers is their average. Add them and divide by 2.
What number is halfway between \(-3\) and \(9\)? \((-3 + 9) \div 2 = 6 \div 2 = 3\). Check by distance: from \(-3\) to \(3\) is 6, and from \(3\) to \(9\) is 6.






Example 1: Find the number halfway between \(-8\) and \(-2\).
\(\dfrac{-8 + (-2)}{2} = \dfrac{-10}{2} = -5\).
Check: the distance from \(-8\) to \(-5\) is 3, and from \(-5\) to \(-2\) is 3.

\(\dfrac{-7 + 4}{2} = \dfrac{-3}{2} = -1.5\)



2.5.2 - The Midpoint Formula
On the plane, the midpoint is halfway across and halfway up. So average the \(x\)-coordinates, and average the \(y\)-coordinates.






From \(A(1, 2)\) to \(B(9, 8)\) you go 8 right and 6 up. Half of that is 4 right and 3 up. \(A\) plus that step is \((1 + 4, 2 + 3) = (5, 5)\). The formula gives the same point: \(\left(\dfrac{1 + 9}{2}, \dfrac{2 + 8}{2}\right) = (5, 5)\).


Example 3: Find the midpoint of \(A(-2, 4)\) and \(B(6, -2)\).
\[
M = \left( \dfrac{-2 + 6}{2},\ \dfrac{4 + (-2)}{2} \right) = \left( \dfrac{4}{2},\ \dfrac{2}{2} \right) = (2,\ 1)
\]

Example 4: Find the midpoint of \((1, -5)\) and \((-6, 2)\).
\[
M = \left( \dfrac{1 + (-6)}{2},\ \dfrac{-5 + 2}{2} \right) = \left( \dfrac{-5}{2},\ \dfrac{-3}{2} \right) = (-2.5,\ -1.5)
\]

\(\left(\dfrac{-7 + 3}{2}, \dfrac{2 + (-6)}{2}\right) = (-2, -2)\)


Amira finds the midpoint of \((2, 6)\) and \((8, 2)\). She writes \(\left(\dfrac{8 - 2}{2}, \dfrac{6 - 2}{2}\right) = (3, 2)\).
She subtracted. The midpoint is an average, so add: \(\left(\dfrac{2 + 8}{2}, \dfrac{6 + 2}{2}\right) = (5, 4)\). Check: \((3, 2)\) is not even between the two points.



2.5.3 - Finding a Missing Endpoint
Sometimes you know the midpoint and one endpoint. Find the other endpoint. There are two ways.

Example 6: \(M(3, 1)\) is the midpoint of \(\overline{AB}\). \(A\) is \((-1, 4)\). Find \(B\).
Way 1. From \(A\) to \(M\): \(x\) goes \(3 - (-1) = 4\) and \(y\) goes \(1 - 4 = -3\). Take the same step from \(M\): \(B = (3 + 4,\ 1 + (-3)) = (7,\ -2)\).
Way 2. \(\dfrac{-1 + x}{2} = 3\) gives \(x = 7\). \(\dfrac{4 + y}{2} = 1\) gives \(y = -2\).
Both ways give \(B(7, -2)\).

\(\dfrac{4 + x}{2} = -2\) gives \(x = -8\). \(\dfrac{-1 + y}{2} = 5\) gives \(y = 11\). \(Q(-8, 11)\).



2.5.4 - Using the Midpoint
The midpoint helps you find meeting places, the center of a circle, and it lets you check a claim. To prove that \(M\) is the midpoint of \(\overline{AB}\) by computation, show two things: \(M\) is the same distance from \(A\) and \(B\), and \(M\) is on the line through \(A\) and \(B\).

Example 8: Fatima lives at \((2, 3)\) and Jamal lives at \((10, 7)\). Each unit is 1 mile. Where do they meet halfway? How far does each walk? Round to the nearest tenth.
\(M = \left(\dfrac{2 + 10}{2}, \dfrac{3 + 7}{2}\right) = (6, 5)\).
The distance between their homes is \(\sqrt{8^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{80}\). Each walks half: \(\dfrac{\sqrt{80}}{2} = \sqrt{20} = 2\sqrt{5} \approx 4.5\) miles.

Example 9: The ends of a diameter of a circle are \((-3, 4)\) and \((5, -2)\). Find the center and the radius.





Center: \(\left(\dfrac{-3 + 5}{2}, \dfrac{4 + (-2)}{2}\right) = (1, 1)\).
Diameter: \(\sqrt{8^2 + 6^2} = 10\). Radius: \(10 \div 2 = 5\).

Example 10: Is \(M(2, 2)\) the midpoint of \(A(-1, -2)\) and \(B(5, 6)\)? Is \(N(3, 4)\) the midpoint of \(A(0, 0)\) and \(B(6, 0)\)?
Part 1. \(AM = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5\) and \(MB = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5\). The slope of \(\overline{AM}\) is \(\dfrac{4}{3}\) and the slope of \(\overline{MB}\) is \(\dfrac{4}{3}\), so the three points are on one line.
Because \(AM = MB\) and the points are collinear, \(M\) is the midpoint.
Part 2. \(AN = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5\) and \(NB = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5\). The distances are equal, but \(N\) is not on the line through \(A\) and \(B\). So \(N\) is not the midpoint. Equal distances alone are not enough.

\(\left(\dfrac{-5 + 7}{2}, \dfrac{2 + (-6)}{2}\right) = (1, -2)\)

title: 2.6 - Slope, Parallel Lines, and Perpendicular Lines
text:
🔥 Warm Up
Look at a city map. Main Street runs at a slant. A new road must run side by side with it and never cross it. Another new road must cross it in a perfect square corner.
How can you tell, using only coordinates? The answer is in the slope. In this lesson you use slope to decide if lines are parallel or perpendicular, and to write equations for new lines.

2.6 - Slope, Parallel Lines, and Perpendicular Lines

title: 2.6 - Slope, Parallel Lines, and Perpendicular Lines
text:
👥 Learn Together

2.6.1 - Slope Review
The slope of a line tells how steep it is. It is the rise over the run: the change in \(y\) divided by the change in \(x\). You learned slope in Algebra 1. We need it often in geometry, so here it is again.

Example 1: Find each slope. a. The line through \((-2, 5)\) and \((4, -1)\). b. The line \(y = -\dfrac{3}{4}x + 2\). c. The line \(y = 3\). d. The line \(x = 4\).

\(m = \dfrac{-1 - 5}{4 - (-2)} = \dfrac{-6}{6} = -1\).
The slope is the number in front of \(x\): \(-\dfrac{3}{4}\).
\(y = 3\) is horizontal. The slope is 0.
\(x = 4\) is vertical. The slope is undefined. (The run is 0, and you cannot divide by 0.)


\(m = \dfrac{0 - (-4)}{3 - (-3)} = \dfrac{4}{6} = \dfrac{2}{3}\)



2.6.2 - Parallel Lines
Parallel lines stay the same distance apart. They never meet. In the picture both lines go up 2 for every 3 to the right. The steps match all along the lines. That is why they never meet.






Example 3: Is the line through \(A(1, 2)\) and \(B(4, 6)\) parallel to the line through \(C(-2, -1)\) and \(D(1, 3)\)?
Slope of \(\overline{AB}\): \(\dfrac{6 - 2}{4 - 1} = \dfrac{4}{3}\).
Slope of \(\overline{CD}\): \(\dfrac{3 - (-1)}{1 - (-2)} = \dfrac{4}{3}\).
The slopes are equal. Is it the same line? The line through \(A\) and \(B\) at \(x = -2\) has \(y = -2\), not \(-1\). So \(C\) is not on it.
Because the slopes are equal and the lines are different, the lines are parallel.

Yes. Both have slope 3 and the \(y\)-intercepts \(-2\) and \(5\) are different, so the lines are different.



2.6.3 - Perpendicular Lines
Perpendicular lines meet at a right angle. Take a slope step with run 3 and rise 2. Turn the step \(90^\circ\) counterclockwise. Now the run is \(-2\) and the rise is 3. The new slope is \(\dfrac{3}{-2} = -\dfrac{3}{2}\). The slope \(\dfrac{2}{3}\) became \(-\dfrac{3}{2}\): flip it and change the sign.






Example 5: Find the slope of a line perpendicular to a line with slope \(\dfrac{3}{4}\). Then for slope \(-5\).
Slope \(\dfrac{3}{4}\): flip to \(\dfrac{4}{3}\) and change the sign: \(-\dfrac{4}{3}\). Check: \(\dfrac{3}{4} \cdot \left(-\dfrac{4}{3}\right) = -1\).
Slope \(-5 = \dfrac{-5}{1}\): flip to \(\dfrac{1}{-5}\) and change the sign: \(\dfrac{1}{5}\). Check: \(-5 \cdot \dfrac{1}{5} = -1\).

\(-\dfrac{2}{7}\)



2.6.4 - Parallel, Perpendicular, or Neither?
Find the slope of each line. Put an equation in the form \(y = mx + b\) first. Then compare.

Example 7: Decide: parallel, perpendicular, or neither?

\(y = 2x + 1\) and \(4x - 2y = 6\). Rewrite the second: \(-2y = -4x + 6\), so \(y = 2x - 3\). Slopes: \(2\) and \(2\). The \(y\)-intercepts differ, so the lines are parallel.
\(2x + 3y = 6\) and \(3x - 2y = 4\). First: \(y = -\dfrac{2}{3}x + 2\), slope \(-\dfrac{2}{3}\). Second: \(y = \dfrac{3}{2}x - 2\), slope \(\dfrac{3}{2}\). Product: \(-\dfrac{2}{3} \cdot \dfrac{3}{2} = -1\). The lines are perpendicular.
The line through \((0, 0)\) and \((4, 2)\), and the line through \((1, 5)\) and \((3, 1)\). Slopes: \(\dfrac{2}{4} = \dfrac{1}{2}\) and \(\dfrac{1 - 5}{3 - 1} = -2\). Product: \(-1\). The lines are perpendicular.



\(y = 3x\) and \(y = -3x\)
\(y = -\dfrac{1}{2}x + 1\) and \(y = 2x + 4\)




Slopes \(3\) and \(-3\). Neither. (The product is \(-9\).)
Slopes \(-\dfrac{1}{2}\) and \(2\). Perpendicular.




2.6.5 - Writing Equations
To write the equation of a line through a point, you need the slope and a point. Find the slope from the given line (the same for parallel, the opposite reciprocal for perpendicular). Then put the point in \(y = mx + b\) and solve for \(b\).

Example 9: Write the equation of the line through \((3, -1)\) that is parallel to \(y = 2x + 5\).
The slope is \(2\) (same slope). Put in the point: \(-1 = 2(3) + b\), so \(b = -7\).
The equation is \(y = 2x - 7\).

Example 10: Main Street is the line \(y = \dfrac{1}{2}x + 2\) on a city grid. A new road goes through \(P(4, -3)\). Write the equation of the road that is parallel to Main Street. Then write the equation of the road that is perpendicular to it.





Parallel: \(m = \dfrac{1}{2}\). \(-3 = \dfrac{1}{2}(4) + b\), so \(b = -5\). The road is \(y = \dfrac{1}{2}x - 5\).
Perpendicular: \(m = -2\). \(-3 = -2(4) + b\), so \(b = 5\). The road is \(y = -2x + 5\).

\(m = -\dfrac{1}{2}\). \(1 = -\dfrac{1}{2}(4) + b\), so \(b = 3\). \(y = -\dfrac{1}{2}x + 3\).

text:
🔥 Warm Up
A hiking trail runs in a straight line from the trailhead to a lookout. The park wants a rest stop part of the way along the trail, say two fifths of the way. Where on the map does the rest stop go?
The midpoint is one special case: it is halfway. In this lesson you find a point at any fraction of the way along a segment. You use the same idea of steps you used for the midpoint.

2.7 - Dividing a Segment in a Ratio

title: 2.7 - Dividing a Segment in a Ratio
text:
👥 Learn Together

2.7.1 - On a Number Line
Find the point \(\dfrac{1}{3}\) of the way from 2 to 14. The distance from 2 to 14 is 12. One third of 12 is 4. So the point is \(2 + 4 = 6\).
A ratio \(a:b\) splits a segment into two parts in the ratio \(a\) to \(b\). The part next to the start is \(a\) parts, and the whole segment is \(a + b\) parts. So the point is \(\dfrac{a}{a + b}\) of the way from the start.






Example 1: Find the point that divides the segment from 4 to 20 in the ratio \(3:1\).
\(k = \dfrac{3}{3 + 1} = \dfrac{3}{4}\).
The distance is \(20 - 4 = 16\). \(\dfrac{3}{4} \cdot 16 = 12\).
The point is \(4 + 12 = 16\). Check: from 4 to 16 is 12, and from 16 to 20 is 4. The ratio is \(12:4 = 3:1\).

The distance is 25. \(\dfrac{2}{5} \cdot 25 = 10\). The point is \(-5 + 10 = 5\).



2.7.2 - On the Coordinate Plane
On the plane, go from \(A\) to \(B\) in two directions: a run and a rise. Take the same fraction of each. Add them to \(A\). Think of the segment as one big staircase. Cut it into equal small steps. The point is a certain number of small steps from \(A\).






Example 3: Find the point \(P\) that divides \(\overline{AB}\) in the ratio \(1:3\) for \(A(1, 2)\) and \(B(13, 10)\).
\(k = \dfrac{1}{1 + 3} = \dfrac{1}{4}\). Run: \(13 - 1 = 12\). Rise: \(10 - 2 = 8\).
\(P = \left(1 + \dfrac{1}{4}(12),\ 2 + \dfrac{1}{4}(8)\right) = (1 + 3,\ 2 + 2) = (4,\ 4)\).

Example 4: Find the point \(\dfrac{2}{5}\) of the way from \(A(-3, 5)\) to \(B(7, -5)\).
Run: \(7 - (-3) = 10\). Rise: \(-5 - 5 = -10\).
\(P = \left(-3 + \dfrac{2}{5}(10),\ 5 + \dfrac{2}{5}(-10)\right) = (-3 + 4,\ 5 + -4) = (1,\ 1)\).

Example 5: Find the point that divides \(\overline{AB}\) in the ratio \(2:3\) for \(A(-4, -2)\) and \(B(6, 8)\).
\(k = \dfrac{2}{5}\). Run \(= 10\) and rise \(= 10\).
\(P = (-4 + 4,\ -2 + 4) = (0,\ 2)\).

\(k = \dfrac{1}{3}\). Run 9, rise 12. \(P = (0 + 3,\ -6 + 4) = (3, -2)\).



2.7.3 - Order Matters
“From \(A\) to \(B\)” and “from \(B\) to \(A\)” are different. The ratio \(3:1\) from \(A\) to \(B\) puts the point close to \(B\). The ratio \(3:1\) from \(B\) to \(A\) puts it close to \(A\). Always find out which endpoint you start from.

Example 7: \(A(1, 1)\) and \(B(9, 5)\). Find the point that divides the segment in the ratio \(3:1\) from \(A\) to \(B\). Then find the point in the ratio \(3:1\) from \(B\) to \(A\).
From \(A\) to \(B\): \(k = \dfrac{3}{4}\). Run 8, rise 4. \(P = (1 + 6,\ 1 + 3) = (7,\ 4)\).
From \(B\) to \(A\): start at \(B\). Run \(1 - 9 = -8\), rise \(1 - 5 = -4\). \(Q = (9 + \dfrac{3}{4}(-8),\ 5 + \dfrac{3}{4}(-4)) = (3,\ 2)\).
\(P\) is near \(B\). \(Q\) is near \(A\). They are different points on the same segment.

\((1 + 2,\ 1 + 1) = (3, 2)\). It is \(Q\). Going \(\dfrac{3}{4}\) of the way from \(B\) is the same as going \(\dfrac{1}{4}\) of the way from \(A\).



2.7.4 - Using Ratios and Checking
You can check an answer with the distance formula. The two parts should add up to the whole, and they should match the ratio.

Example 9: A trail goes from the trailhead \(T(2, 1)\) to the lookout \(L(14, 6)\). Each unit is 1 mile. A rest stop is \(\dfrac{2}{5}\) of the way from \(T\) to \(L\). Find the rest stop \(R\). Then check with distances.





Run 12, rise 5. \(R = \left(2 + \dfrac{2}{5}(12),\ 1 + \dfrac{2}{5}(5)\right) = (2 + 4.8,\ 1 + 2) = (6.8,\ 3)\).
\(TL = \sqrt{12^2 + 5^2} = 13\) miles.
\(TR = \sqrt{4.8^2 + 2^2} = \sqrt{27.04} = 5.2\) miles. And \(\dfrac{2}{5} \cdot 13 = 5.2\). It matches.
\(RL = \sqrt{7.2^2 + 3^2} = \sqrt{60.84} = 7.8\) miles. \(5.2 + 7.8 = 13\) and \(5.2 : 7.8 = 2 : 3\). It checks.

\(k = \dfrac{3}{4}\). Run 20, rise \(-8\). \((0 + 15,\ 12 - 6) = (15, 6)\).

Order matters.

Real problems.
