2.8 - Perimeter and Area on the Coordinate Plane

title: 2.8 - Perimeter and Area on the Coordinate Plane
text:
👥 Learn Together

2.8.1 - Perimeter from Vertices
The perimeter of a polygon is the distance around it. Find the length of each side with the distance formula. Then add the lengths. Sides that are horizontal or vertical are quick: subtract the coordinates.

Example 1: Find the perimeter of triangle \(ABC\) with \(A(-2, 1)\), \(B(4, 1)\), and \(C(4, 5)\). Give the exact answer and round to the nearest tenth.
\(AB = |4 - (-2)| = 6\). \(BC = |5 - 1| = 4\).
\(AC = \sqrt{6^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{52} = 2\sqrt{13}\).
Perimeter \(= 6 + 4 + 2\sqrt{13} = 10 + 2\sqrt{13} \approx 17.2\).

Example 2: Find the perimeter of quadrilateral \(ABCD\) with \(A(1, 1)\), \(B(5, 1)\), \(C(7, 4)\), and \(D(3, 4)\). Round to the nearest tenth.





\(AB = 4\) and \(CD = 4\).
\(BC = \sqrt{2^2 + 3^2} = \sqrt{13}\) and \(DA = \sqrt{(-2)^2 + (-3)^2} = \sqrt{13}\).
Perimeter \(= 8 + 2\sqrt{13} \approx 15.2\).

\(PQ = 5\), \(QR = 3\), \(PR = \sqrt{25 + 9} = \sqrt{34}\). Perimeter \(= 8 + \sqrt{34} \approx 13.8\).



2.8.2 - Area with Horizontal and Vertical Sides
Area is the number of square units inside a figure. When the sides are horizontal or vertical, the base and height come straight from the coordinates.

Example 4: Find the area of the trapezoid with vertices \(A(1, 1)\), \(B(9, 1)\), \(C(7, 5)\), and \(D(3, 5)\).





\(\overline{AB}\) and \(\overline{DC}\) are horizontal, so they are parallel. \(b_1 = 9 - 1 = 8\) and \(b_2 = 7 - 3 = 4\). The height is \(5 - 1 = 4\).
\(A = \dfrac{1}{2}(8 + 4)(4) = 24\) square units.

Example 5: Find the area of the right triangle with vertices \((1, 1)\), \((6, 1)\), and \((6, 4)\).
Base: \(6 - 1 = 5\). Height: \(4 - 1 = 3\).
\(A = \dfrac{1}{2}(5)(3) = 7.5\) square units.

Base \(= 6\), height \(= 4\). \(A = \dfrac{1}{2}(6)(4) = 12\) square units.



2.8.3 - Slanted Figures: The Box Method
What if no side is horizontal or vertical? Draw the smallest rectangle around the figure. Its sides are on the grid lines. This is the bounding box. The figure’s area is the box’s area minus the area of the corner triangles (and rectangles) outside the figure.

Example 7: Find the area of the triangle with vertices \(A(1, 1)\), \(B(7, 3)\), and \(C(3, 6)\).





Bounding box: \(x\) from 1 to 7 and \(y\) from 1 to 6. Area \(= 6 \cdot 5 = 30\).
Corner triangles: bottom right, legs 6 and 2: \(\dfrac{1}{2}(6)(2) = 6\). Top right, legs 4 and 3: \(\dfrac{1}{2}(4)(3) = 6\). Top left, legs 2 and 5: \(\dfrac{1}{2}(2)(5) = 5\).
Total outside: \(6 + 6 + 5 = 17\). Area of \(\triangle ABC = 30 - 17 = 13\) square units.

Box: \(7 \cdot 6 = 42\). Corners: \(\dfrac{1}{2}(7)(1) = 3.5\), \(\dfrac{1}{2}(4)(5) = 10\), \(\dfrac{1}{2}(3)(6) = 9\). Total \(22.5\). Area \(= 42 - 22.5 = 19.5\) square units.



2.8.4 - Slanted Squares and Rectangles
A tilted square or rectangle has a simple area: side times side, or length times width. Find the side lengths with the distance formula. Then check your answer with the box method. Two methods that agree give you confidence.

Example 9: Find the area of the rectangle with vertices \(A(1, 3)\), \(B(3, 1)\), \(C(7, 5)\), and \(D(5, 7)\). Use two methods.





Method 1, side lengths. \(AB = \sqrt{2^2 + 2^2} = \sqrt{8} = 2\sqrt{2}\). \(BC = \sqrt{4^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{32} = 4\sqrt{2}\).
\(A = 2\sqrt{2} \cdot 4\sqrt{2} = 8 \cdot 2 = 16\) square units.
Method 2, box. The box has \(x\) from 1 to 7 and \(y\) from 1 to 7. It is \(6 \cdot 6 = 36\). The four corner triangles have areas \(2\), \(8\), \(2\), \(8\). Their total is \(20\). \(36 - 20 = 16\).
Both methods give 16.

Example 10: A garden on a property map has corners \(A(0, 0)\), \(B(10, 0)\), \(C(10, 6)\), and \(D(0, 3)\). Each unit is 1 foot. How much fence goes around it? How many square feet of mulch cover it? Round to the nearest tenth.
Sides: \(AB = 10\), \(BC = 6\), \(DA = 3\), and \(CD = \sqrt{10^2 + 3^2} = \sqrt{109} \approx 10.4\).
Fence: \(10 + 6 + 3 + 10.4 = 29.4\) feet.
The garden is a trapezoid with parallel sides \(\overline{DA}\) and \(\overline{BC}\) (both vertical) and height 10. Area \(= \dfrac{1}{2}(3 + 6)(10) = 45\) square feet of mulch.

Side \(= \sqrt{3^2 + 2^2} = \sqrt{13}\), so area \(= 13\). Box: \(5 \cdot 5 = 25\). Four triangles with legs 3 and 2 have area 3 each, total 12. \(25 - 12 = 13\).

title: 2.9 - Checking Shapes with Coordinates
text:
🔥 Warm Up
A builder tells you, “This frame is a rectangle.” You look at it, and it looks like a rectangle. Is it? A picture can fool your eyes. A frame can be off by a small amount and still look right.
In geometry, “it looks true” is not enough. We want to know it is true for sure. When a shape sits on a coordinate plane, we can check it with numbers: slopes and distances. If the numbers say yes, no one can argue. This is called computation as proof. In this lesson you use it on triangles and four-sided shapes.
crumbs: Unit 2: The Pythagorean Theorem and the Coordinate Plane

title: 2.9 - Checking Shapes with Coordinates
text:
Find the slope of the line through \((-1, 2)\) and \((3, 5)\).
Find the distance from \((-2, 1)\) to \((1, 5)\).
Solve \(2x - 3 = x + 5\).

title: 2.9 - Checking Shapes with Coordinates
text:
👥 Learn Together

2.9.1 - Is It a Right Triangle?
A right triangle has a \(90^\circ\) angle. There are two ways to check for it with coordinates.
Way 1: slopes. Two sides are perpendicular if their slopes are opposite reciprocals (the product is \(-1\)). Find the slope of each side at a corner.
Way 2: distances. Find all three side lengths. Use the converse of the Pythagorean theorem (Lesson 2.2): the sum of the squares of the two short sides must equal the square of the longest side.
Every time, finish with a sentence that starts with “Because.” This sentence is the proof.

Example 1: Show that triangle \(ABC\) with \(A(2, 1)\), \(B(8, 3)\), and \(C(1, 4)\) is a right triangle. Use both ways.





Way 1. Slope of \(\overline{AB}\): \(\dfrac{3 - 1}{8 - 2} = \dfrac{1}{3}\). Slope of \(\overline{AC}\): \(\dfrac{4 - 1}{1 - 2} = -3\).
The product is \(\dfrac{1}{3} \cdot (-3) = -1\).
Way 2. \(AB^2 = 6^2 + 2^2 = 40\). \(AC^2 = (-1)^2 + 3^2 = 10\). \(BC^2 = (-7)^2 + 1^2 = 50\).
\(AB^2 + AC^2 = 40 + 10 = 50 = BC^2\).
Because the slopes of \(\overline{AB}\) and \(\overline{AC}\) have a product of \(-1\) (and \(AB^2 + AC^2 = BC^2\)), \(\overline{AB} \perp \overline{AC}\). Triangle \(ABC\) is a right triangle with the right angle at \(A\).

Example 2: Is triangle \(PQR\) with \(P(0, 0)\), \(Q(6, 2)\), and \(R(4, 6)\) a right triangle?
Slopes: \(\overline{PQ}\): \(\dfrac{2}{6} = \dfrac{1}{3}\). \(\overline{PR}\): \(\dfrac{6}{4} = \dfrac{3}{2}\). \(\overline{QR}\): \(\dfrac{6 - 2}{4 - 6} = -2\).
Products: \(\dfrac{1}{3} \cdot \dfrac{3}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\), \(\dfrac{1}{3} \cdot (-2) = -\dfrac{2}{3}\), \(\dfrac{3}{2} \cdot (-2) = -3\). None is \(-1\).
Check by distance: \(PQ^2 = 40\), \(PR^2 = 52\), \(QR^2 = 20\). \(40 + 20 = 60\), which is not 52.
Because no pair of sides is perpendicular, triangle \(PQR\) is not a right triangle.

Slope of \(\overline{DE}\) is \(\dfrac{1}{2}\). Slope of \(\overline{DF}\) is \(\dfrac{2}{-1} = -2\). The product is \(-1\). Because \(\overline{DE} \perp \overline{DF}\), the triangle is a right triangle with the right angle at \(D\).



2.9.2 - Isosceles or Equilateral?
An isosceles triangle has two sides of equal length. An equilateral triangle has three. Find the three side lengths with the distance formula and compare them.

Example 4: Is triangle \(ABC\) with \(A(1, 1)\), \(B(7, 1)\), and \(C(4, 5)\) isosceles? Is it equilateral?
\(AB = |7 - 1| = 6\).
\(AC = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5\). \(BC = \sqrt{(-3)^2 + 4^2} = 5\).
Because \(AC = BC = 5\), triangle \(ABC\) is isosceles. It is not equilateral, because \(AB = 6\) is different.

Example 5: Show that the triangle with \(A(1, 1)\), \(B(5, 1)\), and \(C(3, 1 + 2\sqrt{3})\) is equilateral.
\(AB = 4\).
\(AC = \sqrt{2^2 + (2\sqrt{3})^2} = \sqrt{4 + 12} = 4\). \(BC = \sqrt{(-2)^2 + (2\sqrt{3})^2} = \sqrt{16} = 4\).
Because \(AB = AC = BC = 4\), triangle \(ABC\) is equilateral.

\(PQ = 4\). \(PR = \sqrt{4 + 16} = \sqrt{20}\). \(QR = \sqrt{4 + 16} = \sqrt{20}\). Because \(PR = QR\), triangle \(PQR\) is isosceles.



2.9.3 - Four-Sided Shapes
Here are the definitions we use to check shapes. (In Unit 4 you learn many more facts about them.)







Shape
What to check with coordinates




Parallelogram
Opposite sides have equal slopes (both pairs)


Rectangle
A parallelogram, and two sides at a corner have slopes with product \(-1\)


Rhombus
All four sides have the same length (distance formula)


Square
A rectangle and a rhombus together




Example 7: Is \(ABCD\) with \(A(1, 1)\), \(B(5, 2)\), \(C(6, 5)\), \(D(2, 4)\) a parallelogram? A rectangle? A rhombus?





Slopes: \(\overline{AB}\): \(\dfrac{2 - 1}{5 - 1} = \dfrac{1}{4}\). \(\overline{DC}\): \(\dfrac{5 - 4}{6 - 2} = \dfrac{1}{4}\). \(\overline{AD}\): \(\dfrac{4 - 1}{2 - 1} = 3\). \(\overline{BC}\): \(\dfrac{5 - 2}{6 - 5} = 3\).
Because both pairs of opposite sides have equal slopes, \(ABCD\) is a parallelogram.
Rectangle? \(\dfrac{1}{4} \cdot 3 = \dfrac{3}{4}\), not \(-1\). The corner at \(A\) is not a right angle. It is not a rectangle.
Rhombus? \(AB = \sqrt{17}\) and \(AD = \sqrt{10}\). They are not equal. It is not a rhombus.
So \(ABCD\) is a parallelogram and nothing more specific.

Example 8: Is \(ABCD\) with \(A(2, 1)\), \(B(6, 3)\), \(C(5, 5)\), \(D(1, 3)\) a rectangle? A square?





Slopes: \(\overline{AB}\) and \(\overline{DC}\) are both \(\dfrac{1}{2}\). \(\overline{AD}\) and \(\overline{BC}\) are both \(-2\). It is a parallelogram.
At \(A\): \(\dfrac{1}{2} \cdot (-2) = -1\). There is a right angle.
Because \(ABCD\) is a parallelogram with a right angle, it is a rectangle.
Square? \(AB = \sqrt{20}\) and \(AD = \sqrt{5}\). Not equal. So it is a rectangle but not a square.

Example 9: Is \(ABCD\) with \(A(1, 1)\), \(B(6, 1)\), \(C(9, 5)\), \(D(4, 5)\) a rhombus? A square?
\(AB = 5\). \(BC = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5\). \(CD = 5\). \(DA = \sqrt{(-3)^2 + (-4)^2} = 5\).
Because all four sides have length 5, \(ABCD\) is a rhombus.
Square? \(\overline{AB}\) is horizontal (slope 0). \(\overline{AD}\) has slope \(\dfrac{4}{3}\). They are not perpendicular. So it is a rhombus but not a square.

\(AB = 4\) and \(BC = 4\), and all sides are 4. \(\overline{AB}\) is horizontal and \(\overline{BC}\) is vertical, so they are perpendicular. Because \(ABCD\) has four equal sides and a right angle, it is a square.



2.9.4 - Looks Like, or Is?
Drawings can look right and be wrong. Only the numbers tell. Look at these two shapes.

Example 11: The shape \(ABCD\) with \(A(1, 1)\), \(B(8, 2)\), \(C(9, 9)\), \(D(2, 8)\) looks like a tilted square. Is it a square?





\(AB = \sqrt{7^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt{50}\). \(BC = \sqrt{1^2 + 7^2} = \sqrt{50}\). \(CD = \sqrt{50}\). \(DA = \sqrt{50}\). All four sides are equal, so it is a rhombus.
Slope of \(\overline{AB}\): \(\dfrac{1}{7}\). Slope of \(\overline{AD}\): \(\dfrac{7}{1} = 7\). The product is \(\dfrac{1}{7} \cdot 7 = 1\), not \(-1\).
Because \(\overline{AB}\) and \(\overline{AD}\) are not perpendicular, \(ABCD\) is not a square. It is a rhombus.

Example 12: The shape \(ABCD\) with \(A(2, 1)\), \(B(12, 2)\), \(C(11, 11)\), \(D(1, 10)\) looks like a rectangle. Is it?





Slopes: \(\overline{AB}\) and \(\overline{DC}\) are both \(\dfrac{1}{10}\). \(\overline{AD}\) and \(\overline{BC}\) are both \(\dfrac{9}{-1} = -9\). It is a parallelogram.
At \(A\): \(\dfrac{1}{10} \cdot (-9) = -\dfrac{9}{10}\). This is close to \(-1\), but it is not \(-1\).
Because the product is \(-\dfrac{9}{10}\), there is no right angle. \(ABCD\) is not a rectangle. It is a parallelogram.

Does “four equal sides” make a square? No. The rhombus in the example has four equal sides and is not a square. One example that breaks a rule is a counterexample. It is enough to show the rule is false.


Hnin says: “\(ABCD\) with \(A(1, 1)\), \(B(5, 2)\), \(C(6, 5)\), \(D(2, 4)\) is a rectangle because its opposite sides are equal.”
The opposite sides are equal, but that is also true for a parallelogram that is not a rectangle. The missing check is a right angle. Here \(\dfrac{1}{4} \cdot 3 = \dfrac{3}{4}\), so there is no right angle. It is not a rectangle.


Use the rhombus \(A(1, 1)\), \(B(6, 1)\), \(C(9, 5)\), \(D(4, 5)\). All sides are 5, but the corner at \(A\) is not a right angle (slopes 0 and \(\dfrac{4}{3}\)).



2.9.5 - Finding the Fourth Vertex
In a parallelogram, going from \(B\) to \(C\) is the same step as going from \(A\) to \(D\). If you know \(A\), \(B\), and \(C\), take the step from \(B\) to \(C\) and add it to \(A\) to get \(D\).

Example 14: Three vertices of parallelogram \(ABCD\) are \(A(1, 1)\), \(B(6, 2)\), and \(C(8, 6)\). Find \(D\). Check your answer.





Step from \(B\) to \(C\): \((8 - 6,\ 6 - 2) = (2,\ 4)\).
\(D = (1 + 2,\ 1 + 4) = (3,\ 5)\).
Check with slopes: \(\overline{AB}\): \(\dfrac{1}{5}\) and \(\overline{DC}\): \(\dfrac{6 - 5}{8 - 3} = \dfrac{1}{5}\). \(\overline{AD}\): \(\dfrac{4}{2} = 2\) and \(\overline{BC}\): \(\dfrac{4}{2} = 2\).
Because both pairs of opposite sides have equal slopes, \(ABCD\) with \(D(3, 5)\) is a parallelogram.

Step from \(Q\) to \(R\): \((2, 4)\). \(S = P + (2, 4) = (2, 4)\).

title: 2.9 - Checking Shapes with Coordinates
text:
✍️ Practice On Your Own

Name each quadrilateral as specifically as you can: parallelogram, rectangle, rhombus, square, or none of these. Show your checks.

title: Unit 2 Summary
text:
2.1 - Square Roots and Simplifying Radicals
Example: Simplify \(\sqrt{48} + \sqrt{12}\). \(4\sqrt{3} + 2\sqrt{3} = 6\sqrt{3}\)

title: Unit 2 Summary
text:
A perfect square is the square of a whole number: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100, 121, 144, 169, 196, 225.
\(\sqrt{49} = 7\). In geometry we use the positive root.
To estimate \(\sqrt{50}\): \(7^2 = 49\) and \(8^2 = 64\), so it is between 7 and 8. Test the middle, \(7.5^2 = 56.25\). Since \(50 < 56.25\), it is closer to 7.
To simplify, take out the largest perfect square factor: \(\sqrt{72} = \sqrt{36} \cdot \sqrt{2} = 6\sqrt{2}\).
Multiply: \(2\sqrt{3} \cdot 5\sqrt{6} = 10\sqrt{18} = 30\sqrt{2}\). Add like radicals: \(3\sqrt{2} + 5\sqrt{2} = 8\sqrt{2}\).
Rationalize: \(\dfrac{6}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{6\sqrt{2}}{2} = 3\sqrt{2}\).
\(\sqrt{9 + 16}\) is not \(\sqrt{9} + \sqrt{16}\).
crumbs: Unit 2: The Pythagorean Theorem and the Coordinate Plane

title: Unit 2 Summary
section: 2.2 - The Pythagorean Theorem and Its Converse
text:
2.2 - The Pythagorean Theorem and Its Converse

In a right triangle, the legs make the right angle. The hypotenuse is across from it and is the longest side.
Pythagorean theorem: \(a^2 + b^2 = c^2\), where \(c\) is the hypotenuse.
Pythagorean triples: 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 7-24-25, and their multiples.
Converse: let \(c\) be the longest side. If \(a^2 + b^2 = c^2\), the triangle is right. If \(a^2 + b^2 > c^2\), it is acute. If \(a^2 + b^2 < c^2\), it is obtuse.
Triangle inequality: the two shorter sides must add to more than the longest side.






Example: Legs 6 and 8. Find \(c\). \(36 + 64 = 100\), so \(c = 10\)
crumbs: Unit 2: The Pythagorean Theorem and the Coordinate Plane

title: Unit 2 Summary
section: 2.3 - The Pythagorean Theorem in the Real World
text:
2.3 - The Pythagorean Theorem in the Real World

Always: draw and label the right triangle, solve, and answer in a sentence with units.
Squaring a corner: mark 3 and 4. The marks must be 5 apart. Check a rectangle by its diagonal.
Ladders: the ladder is the hypotenuse. 4-to-1 rule: the base is at least height \(\div\) 4 from the wall.
Screens: the size is the diagonal. Width and height are the legs.
Boxes: floor diagonal first, then the box diagonal.

Example: A 13 ft ladder has its base 5 ft from a wall. How high does it reach? \(\sqrt{169 - 25} = 12\) ft
crumbs: Unit 2: The Pythagorean Theorem and the Coordinate Plane

title: Unit 2 Summary
text:
2.4 - Distance on the Coordinate Plane

Same \(y\): distance is \(|x_2 - x_1|\). Same \(x\): distance is \(|y_2 - y_1|\).
Slanted: draw a right triangle. The legs are the horizontal and vertical changes.
Distance formula: \(d = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2}\).
Use it to compare distances, to check for equal sides, and to find a missing coordinate (there can be two answers).






Example: Distance from \((1, 2)\) to \((5, 5)\). \(\sqrt{4^2 + 3^2} = 5\)
crumbs: Unit 2: The Pythagorean Theorem and the Coordinate Plane

title: Unit 2 Summary
text:
2.5 - Midpoint

Midpoint formula: \(M = \left(\dfrac{x_1 + x_2}{2},\ \dfrac{y_1 + y_2}{2}\right)\). Average the \(x\)’s and average the \(y\)’s.
Missing endpoint: take the same step again from the midpoint, or solve \(\dfrac{x_1 + x}{2} = x_M\).
The center of a circle is the midpoint of a diameter.
To check that \(M\) is a midpoint, show \(AM = MB\) and that \(A\), \(M\), \(B\) are collinear.

Example: Midpoint of \((-2, 4)\) and \((6, -2)\). \((2, 1)\)
crumbs: Unit 2: The Pythagorean Theorem and the Coordinate Plane

title: Unit 2 Summary
section: 2.6 - Slope, Parallel Lines, and Perpendicular Lines
text:
2.6 - Slope, Parallel Lines, and Perpendicular Lines

Slope: \(m = \dfrac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}\). Horizontal lines have slope 0. Vertical lines have undefined slope.
Parallel lines have equal slopes (and are different lines).
Perpendicular lines have slopes that are opposite reciprocals. The product is \(-1\).
To write a line through a point: find the slope, put the point in \(y = mx + b\), solve for \(b\).

Example: A line has slope \(\dfrac{3}{4}\). Give the slope of a perpendicular line. \(-\dfrac{4}{3}\)
crumbs: Unit 2: The Pythagorean Theorem and the Coordinate Plane

title: Unit 2 Summary
section: 2.7 - Dividing a Segment in a Ratio
text:
2.7 - Dividing a Segment in a Ratio

Ratio \(a:b\) from \(A\) to \(B\): the point is \(k = \dfrac{a}{a + b}\) of the way.
\(P = \left(x_1 + k(x_2 - x_1),\ y_1 + k(y_2 - y_1)\right)\).
Order matters. The same ratio from \(B\) to \(A\) gives a different point.
Check with distance: \(AP = k \cdot AB\).






Example: Ratio \(1:3\) from \(A(1, 2)\) to \(B(13, 10)\). \(k = \dfrac{1}{4}\). \(P = (4, 4)\)
crumbs: Unit 2: The Pythagorean Theorem and the Coordinate Plane

title: Unit 2 Summary
section: 2.8 - Perimeter and Area on the Coordinate Plane
text:
2.8 - Perimeter and Area on the Coordinate Plane

Perimeter: add the side lengths. Use the distance formula for slanted sides.
Area: rectangle \(bh\), triangle \(\dfrac{1}{2}bh\), trapezoid \(\dfrac{1}{2}(b_1 + b_2)h\).
Box method: area of the bounding box minus the corner triangles.
Slanted rectangle or square: length times width from the distance formula. Check with the box method.

Example: Area of the triangle with vertices \((0, 0)\), \((6, 0)\), \((6, 8)\). \(\dfrac{1}{2}(6)(8) = 24\)
crumbs: Unit 2: The Pythagorean Theorem and the Coordinate Plane

title: Unit 2 Summary
text:
2.9 - Checking Shapes with Coordinates

Computation as proof: use slopes and distances to show a fact for sure. End with “Because …, the shape is a …”.
Right triangle: two sides have slopes with product \(-1\), or the side squares satisfy \(a^2 + b^2 = c^2\).
Isosceles: two equal sides. Equilateral: three equal sides.
Looks vs is: a shape that looks like a square can be a rhombus. Check slopes and lengths. A counterexample shows a rule is false.
Fourth vertex of a parallelogram \(ABCD\): \(D = A + C - B\).

Example: What do you check to show a parallelogram is a rectangle? Show two sides at a corner have slopes with a product of \(-1\).







Shape
What to check




Parallelogram
Opposite sides have equal slopes


Rectangle
A parallelogram with a right angle (slopes with product \(-1\))


Rhombus
Four equal sides


Square
A rectangle and a rhombus

title: Unit 2 Review
text:
2.1 - Square Roots and Simplifying Radicals
Example 1: Simplify \(\sqrt{96}\) and \(\sqrt{20} + \sqrt{45}\).
\(\sqrt{96} = \sqrt{16} \cdot \sqrt{6} = 4\sqrt{6}\).
\(\sqrt{20} = 2\sqrt{5}\) and \(\sqrt{45} = 3\sqrt{5}\). Add: \(5\sqrt{5}\).


2.2 - The Pythagorean Theorem and Its Converse
Example 2: The legs of a right triangle are 6 and 10. Find the hypotenuse (exact and to the nearest tenth). Is a triangle with sides 7, 10, and 12 right, acute, or obtuse?
\(c^2 = 36 + 100 = 136\). \(c = \sqrt{136} = 2\sqrt{34} \approx 11.7\).
\(7^2 + 10^2 = 149\) and \(12^2 = 144\). \(149 > 144\), so the triangle is acute.


2.3 - The Pythagorean Theorem in the Real World
Example 3: A 15 ft wire runs from the top of a pole to the ground 9 ft from the base of the pole. How tall is the pole?
\(9^2 + h^2 = 15^2\), so \(h^2 = 225 - 81 = 144\).
\(h = 12\). The pole is 12 ft tall.


2.4 - Distance on the Coordinate Plane
Example 4: Find the distance from \((-3, -2)\) to \((5, 4)\).
\(d = \sqrt{(5 - (-3))^2 + (4 - (-2))^2} = \sqrt{64 + 36} = 10\).


2.5 - Midpoint
Example 5: Find the midpoint of \((-6, 1)\) and \((8, 9)\). Then find \(B\) if \(M(0, 4)\) is the midpoint of \(\overline{AB}\) and \(A\) is \((-3, 6)\).
\(M = \left(\dfrac{-6 + 8}{2}, \dfrac{1 + 9}{2}\right) = (1, 5)\).
Step from \(A\) to \(M\): \((3, -2)\). \(B = (0 + 3, 4 - 2) = (3, 2)\).


2.6 - Slope, Parallel Lines, and Perpendicular Lines
Example 6: Write the equation of the line through \((1, 4)\) that is parallel to \(y = -2x + 3\).
The slope is \(-2\). \(4 = -2(1) + b\), so \(b = 6\). The equation is \(y = -2x + 6\).


2.7 - Dividing a Segment in a Ratio
Example 7: Find the point that divides the segment from \(A(-2, 3)\) to \(B(10, -6)\) in the ratio \(1:2\).
\(k = \dfrac{1}{3}\). Run \(= 12\), rise \(= -9\).
\(P = (-2 + 4,\ 3 + (-3)) = (2, 0)\).


2.8 - Perimeter and Area on the Coordinate Plane
Example 8: Find the perimeter and the area of the triangle with vertices \((0, 0)\), \((6, 0)\), and \((6, 8)\).
Sides: \(6\), \(8\), and \(\sqrt{36 + 64} = 10\). Perimeter \(= 24\).
Area \(= \dfrac{1}{2}(6)(8) = 24\) square units.


2.9 - Checking Shapes with Coordinates
Example 9: Show that the triangle with \(A(-1, 0)\), \(B(3, 2)\), and \(C(1, 6)\) is a right triangle.
Slope of \(\overline{BA}\): \(\dfrac{0 - 2}{-1 - 3} = \dfrac{1}{2}\). Slope of \(\overline{BC}\): \(\dfrac{6 - 2}{1 - 3} = -2\).
Because the slopes have a product of \(-1\), \(\overline{BA} \perp \overline{BC}\), and triangle \(ABC\) is a right triangle with the right angle at \(B\).

title: Introduction
text:
What You’ll Learn
Welcome to Unit 3! When you move a picture on a phone screen, turn it, flip it, or zoom in, the phone moves every point of the picture by a rule.
These moves are called transformations. In this unit you learn the rules for slides, flips, turns, and size changes on the coordinate plane. You use distance and slope from Unit 2 to check what stays the same and what changes.
By the end of this unit, you will be able to:

title: Introduction
text:
Translate, reflect, rotate, and dilate figures on the coordinate plane
Write and use a rule like \((x, y) \rightarrow (x + 3, y - 2)\)
Find the transformation that moves one figure onto another
Tell which transformations keep lengths and angles the same
Do two or more transformations in a row
Find lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry

title: Introduction
text:
Topics in This Unit
Translations
Slide a figure with a rule. Check that lengths stay the same.
Reflections
Flip a figure over a line. Find the line of reflection.
Rotations
Turn a figure around a point by \(90^\circ\), \(180^\circ\), or \(270^\circ\).
Dilations
Make a figure larger or smaller with a scale factor.
Sequences of Transformations and Symmetry
Do transformations one after another. Find symmetry in shapes and designs.

title: 3.1 - Translations
text:
🔥 Warm Up
Open a floor plan on a screen. Drag a desk to a new spot. The whole desk slides. It does not turn. It does not change size.
Every corner of the desk moves the same way. Here each corner moves 5 units right and 3 units up. In this lesson you write that move as a rule. Then you use the rule on the coordinate plane.

title: 3.1 - Translations
text:
Plot \(A(1, 2)\) and \(B(5, 5)\) on a coordinate plane. Find the distance \(AB\).
Find the slope of the line through \(A(1, 2)\) and \(B(5, 5)\).
Solve \(-2 + a = 4\).

title: 3.1 - Translations
text:
👥 Learn Together

3.1.1 - Moving a Figure
A transformation moves a figure, or changes its size, by a rule. A translation is the simplest one. It slides the whole figure.

The starting figure is the preimage. The new figure is the image.
The image of point \(A\) is \(A'\). Read it as “A prime”.
A translation slides every point the same distance in the same direction.


Example 1: Preimage and image





The desk \(ABCD\) slides to \(A'B'C'D'\) (see the figure).

Name the image of \(C\). \(C'\)
\(A\) is at \((1, 1)\) and \(A'\) is at \((6, 4)\). How far did \(A\) move? 5 right and 3 up
\(D\) is at \((1, 3)\). Where is \(D'\)? \((6, 6)\). Every point moves the same way.



Name the preimage of \(B'\).
\(C\) is at \((4, 3)\). Where is \(C'\)?




\(B\)
\((9, 6)\)




3.1.2 - Translation Rules
Moving 5 right and 3 up adds 5 to every \(x\) and 3 to every \(y\). We write that as a rule:
\[(x, y) \rightarrow (x + 5, y + 3)\]

The rule \((x, y) \rightarrow (x + a, y + b)\) slides a figure.
If \(a\) is positive, move right. If \(a\) is negative, move left.
If \(b\) is positive, move up. If \(b\) is negative, move down.




Move
Rule




3 right
\((x + 3, y)\)


5 down
\((x, y - 5)\)


2 left and 6 up
\((x - 2, y + 6)\)


7 right and 1 down
\((x + 7, y - 1)\)




Example 2: Use a rule
Apply \((x, y) \rightarrow (x - 3, y + 5)\) to \(P(2, -4)\).
\(x\): \(2 - 3 = -1\)
\(y\): \(-4 + 5 = 1\)
\(P' = (-1, 1)\)

Example 3: Find the rule
\(A(-2, 3)\) moves to \(A'(4, -1)\). Write the rule.
Change in \(x\): \(4 - (-2) = 6\)
Change in \(y\): \(-1 - 3 = -4\)
Rule: \((x, y) \rightarrow (x + 6, y - 4)\)
In words: 6 right and 4 down.

To find the change, always do image minus preimage. If you subtract the other way, you get the wrong direction.



Apply \((x, y) \rightarrow (x + 7, y - 2)\) to \(Q(-5, -3)\).
\(B(1, -6)\) moves to \(B'(-3, 0)\). Write the rule and say it in words.




\(Q' = (2, -5)\)
\(-3 - 1 = -4\) and \(0 - (-6) = 6\). Rule: \((x - 4, y + 6)\). 4 left and 6 up.




3.1.3 - Graphing the Image
To graph the image of a figure, move each vertex with the rule. Then connect the new points in the same order.

Step 1: Apply the rule to every vertex.
Step 2: Plot the new points and label them \(A'\), \(B'\), \(C'\).
Step 3: Connect them in the same order as the preimage.


Example 4: Translate a triangle





Graph the image of \(\triangle ABC\) with \(A(-4, 1)\), \(B(-1, 1)\), \(C(-3, 4)\) under \((x, y) \rightarrow (x + 5, y - 3)\).
\(A' = (-4 + 5, 1 - 3) = (1, -2)\)
\(B' = (-1 + 5, 1 - 3) = (4, -2)\)
\(C' = (-3 + 5, 4 - 3) = (2, 1)\)

Example 5: Translate a quadrilateral





Graph the image of \(PQRS\) with \(P(1, -1)\), \(Q(4, -2)\), \(R(5, 1)\), \(S(2, 2)\) under \((x, y) \rightarrow (x - 6, y + 2)\).
\(P' = (-5, 1)\), \(Q' = (-2, 0)\)
\(R' = (-1, 3)\), \(S' = (-4, 4)\)

\(J'(1, 2)\), \(K'(4, 1)\), \(L'(3, 5)\)


A game screen is a coordinate plane. A character that steps 1 right and 2 up uses the rule \((x, y) \rightarrow (x + 1, y + 2)\). A chess knight that jumps 2 squares right and 1 up uses \((x + 2, y + 1)\).



3.1.4 - What Stays the Same
A translation slides a figure. It does not stretch it or turn it. We can check this with the tools from Unit 2.

A translation keeps every side length and every angle the same.
Each side is parallel to its image. (They have the same slope.)
A transformation that keeps lengths and angles is a rigid motion. A translation is a rigid motion.


Example 6: Check with coordinates
In the first triangle example, \(A(-4, 1)\) and \(C(-3, 4)\) move to \(A'(1, -2)\) and \(C'(2, 1)\). Compare \(\overline{AC}\) and \(\overline{A'C'}\).
Length of \(\overline{AC}\): \(\sqrt{1^2 + 3^2} = \sqrt{10}\)
Length of \(\overline{A'C'}\): \(\sqrt{1^2 + 3^2} = \sqrt{10}\)
Slope of \(\overline{AC}\): \(\dfrac{4 - 1}{-3 - (-4)} = 3\)
Slope of \(\overline{A'C'}\): \(\dfrac{1 - (-2)}{2 - 1} = 3\)
The lengths are equal and the slopes are equal. So \(\overline{AC} \cong \overline{A'C'}\) and \(\overline{AC} \parallel \overline{A'C'}\).

\(XY = \sqrt{36 + 64} = 10\) and \(X'Y' = \sqrt{36 + 64} = 10\). Both slopes are \(\dfrac{8}{6} = \dfrac{4}{3}\).

\((x, y) \rightarrow (x + 9, y - 4)\) to \((-6, 0)\).
\((x, y) \rightarrow (x - 3, y + 8)\) to \((4, -8)\).


Write the rule that moves \(A\) to \(A'\). Then say it in words.

\(A(2, 5) \rightarrow A'(7, 3)\)
\(A(-4, -1) \rightarrow A'(-1, -6)\)
\(A(0, 6) \rightarrow A'(-8, 2)\)
\(A(3, -3) \rightarrow A'(3, 4)\)


Graph the image. Give its coordinates.






Use \((x, y) \rightarrow (x + 4, y - 5)\) on \(\triangle TUV\).


Graph the image. Give its coordinates.






Use \((x, y) \rightarrow (x - 5, y + 3)\) on \(WXYZ\).


Graph the image on your own grid.

Triangle \(MNO\) has \(M(1, -4)\), \(N(5, -3)\), \(O(2, -1)\). Use \((x, y) \rightarrow (x - 3, y + 6)\). Give the image coordinates.


Check with distance and slope.

\(A(1, 2)\) and \(B(4, 6)\) move to \(A'(6, 0)\) and \(B'(9, 4)\). Show \(AB = A'B'\) and that the slopes are equal.
A translation maps \(\triangle XYZ\) to \(\triangle X'Y'Z'\). \(XY = 13\) and \(m\angle Y = 72^\circ\). Find \(X'Y'\) and \(m\angle Y'\).
Amira says the triangle with \((0, 0)\), \((4, 0)\), \((0, 3)\) was translated to the triangle with \((5, 1)\), \((9, 1)\), \((5, 5)\) because it looks the same. Is she right? Use lengths to decide.


Solve for the unknown.

The point \((2k, k + 1)\) is moved by \((x, y) \rightarrow (x + 3, y - 2)\) to \((11, 3)\). Find \(k\).
The image of \(P(x, 3)\) under \((x, y) \rightarrow (x - 5, y + 2)\) is \(P'(4, 5)\). Find \(x\).


Real problems.

On a floor plan, each unit is 1 foot. A table has corners \((2, 1)\), \((6, 1)\), \((6, 4)\), \((2, 4)\). It moves 7 feet right and 3 feet up. Give the new corners and the area before and after.
A game character is at \((3, 3)\). Each move uses \((x, y) \rightarrow (x + 2, y + 1)\). Where is the character after 4 moves?
Hnin moves a game piece with \((x, y) \rightarrow (x + 2, y - 1)\) three times in a row. Write one rule for all three moves.


Find the mistake.

Diego applies \((x, y) \rightarrow (x - 4, y + 1)\) to \((3, -2)\) and gets \((7, -1)\). What did he do wrong? What is the correct image?


Test practice

The point \(P(-3, 5)\) is translated by the rule \((x, y) \rightarrow (x + 6, y - 8)\). What are the coordinates of \(P'\)?
A. \((3, -3)\)
B. \((-9, 13)\)
C. \((3, 13)\)
D. \((-9, -3)\)
Quadrilateral \(WXYZ\) is translated to form quadrilateral \(W'X'Y'Z'\). \(WX = 8\) cm and \(m\angle X = 105^\circ\). Which statement must be true?
A. \(W'X' = 8\) cm and \(m\angle X' = 105^\circ\)
B. \(W'X' > 8\) cm and \(m\angle X' = 105^\circ\)
C. \(W'X' = 8\) cm and \(m\angle X' = 75^\circ\)
D. \(W'X' = 8\) cm and \(m\angle X'\) cannot be found


Challenge

A translation maps \(A(2, 5)\) to \(A'(-1, 9)\). The same translation maps \(B(-3, k)\) to \(B'(m, 1)\). Find \(m\) and \(k\).

title: 3.2 - Reflections
text:
🔥 Warm Up
Look at the front of an ambulance. The word is printed backward.
A driver sees the front of the ambulance in a rear-view mirror. The mirror flips the word, so the driver reads it the right way. A flip like this is a reflection. In this lesson you reflect figures over a line on the coordinate plane.

title: 3.2 - Reflections
text:
Find the midpoint of \(A(1, 2)\) and \(B(5, 6)\).
Find the slope of the line through \(A(1, 2)\) and \(B(5, 6)\). Then give the slope of a line perpendicular to it.
Solve \(2a - 4 = 10\).

title: 3.2 - Reflections
text:
👥 Learn Together

3.2.1 - Reflecting Over the Axes
A reflection flips a figure over a line. The line is the line of reflection. A point and its image are the same distance from the line, on opposite sides.

Over the \(x\)-axis, the \(y\)-coordinate changes sign: \((x, y) \rightarrow (x, -y)\).
Over the \(y\)-axis, the \(x\)-coordinate changes sign: \((x, y) \rightarrow (-x, y)\).
Points on the line of reflection do not move.


Example 1: Reflect a point
Reflect \(P(3, -4)\) over the \(x\)-axis. Then reflect \(P\) over the \(y\)-axis.
Over the \(x\)-axis: \((x, y) \rightarrow (x, -y)\), so \(P' = (3, 4)\).
Over the \(y\)-axis: \((x, y) \rightarrow (-x, y)\), so \(P' = (-3, -4)\).

Example 2: Reflect a triangle





Graph the image of \(\triangle ABC\) over the \(x\)-axis. \(A(1, 2)\), \(B(5, 1)\), \(C(3, 5)\).
\(A' = (1, -2)\)
\(B' = (5, -1)\)
\(C' = (3, -5)\)


Reflect \(Q(-5, 2)\) over the \(x\)-axis and over the \(y\)-axis.
\(R(4, -3)\) has image \(R'(-4, -3)\). Over which axis was it reflected? Write the rule.




\(x\)-axis: \((-5, -2)\). \(y\)-axis: \((5, 2)\).
The \(y\)-axis. \((x, y) \rightarrow (-x, y)\).




3.2.2 - Other Lines of Reflection
Two diagonal lines are also useful: \(y = x\) and \(y = -x\). For a vertical line \(x = a\) or a horizontal line \(y = b\), count the distance to the line.



Line of reflection
Rule




\(x\)-axis
\((x, y) \rightarrow (x, -y)\)


\(y\)-axis
\((x, y) \rightarrow (-x, y)\)


\(y = x\)
\((x, y) \rightarrow (y, x)\)


\(y = -x\)
\((x, y) \rightarrow (-y, -x)\)




For \(x = a\) or \(y = b\): count how far the point is from the line. Go the same distance to the other side.


Example 3: Reflect over a diagonal line
Reflect \(A(2, 5)\) over \(y = x\). Reflect \(B(-3, 1)\) over \(y = -x\).
\(A' = (5, 2)\)
\(B' = (-y, -x) = (-1, 3)\)

Example 4: Reflect over a vertical line





Reflect \(\triangle ABC\) over the line \(x = 2\). \(A(-1, 1)\), \(B(1, 3)\), \(C(0, -2)\).
\(A\) is 3 units left of the line, so \(A'\) is 3 units right: \((5, 1)\).
\(B\) is 1 unit left, so \(B' = (3, 3)\).
\(C\) is 2 units left, so \(C' = (4, -2)\).


Reflect \(S(-2, -4)\) over the line \(y = -1\).
Reflect \(T(6, 3)\) over \(y = -x\).




\(S\) is 3 units below the line, so \(S'\) is 3 units above: \((-2, 2)\).
\((-3, -6)\)



Still water reflects a tree. The top of a tree 12 feet above the water has a reflection 12 feet below the water. The water line is the line of reflection.



3.2.3 - Finding the Line of Reflection
Look at a point \(A\) and its image \(A'\). The line of reflection is exactly halfway between them. It also meets \(\overline{AA'}\) at a right angle.

The line of reflection is the perpendicular bisector of \(\overline{AA'}\).
It goes through the midpoint of \(\overline{AA'}\).
It is perpendicular to \(\overline{AA'}\). The slopes multiply to \(-1\).


Example 5: Find the line





\(A(1, 2)\) is reflected to \(A'(5, 6)\). Find the line of reflection.
Midpoint: \(\left(\dfrac{1 + 5}{2}, \dfrac{2 + 6}{2}\right) = (3, 4)\)
Slope of \(\overline{AA'}\): \(\dfrac{6 - 2}{5 - 1} = 1\)
Perpendicular slope: \(-1\)
The line has slope \(-1\) and goes through \((3, 4)\): \(y - 4 = -(x - 3)\), so \(y = -x + 7\).

Midpoint: \((1, 4)\). The slope of \(\overline{PP'}\) is undefined (vertical), so the line is horizontal: \(y = 4\).



3.2.4 - What a Reflection Keeps and Changes
A reflection keeps lengths and angles. It is a rigid motion. But a reflection flips the figure.

A reflection keeps every length and every angle the same.
It reverses the orientation. Labels that go counterclockwise now go clockwise.
A reflection is not a translation. You cannot make it by sliding.


Example 6: Check with distance





\(\triangle ABC\) has \(A(1, 1)\), \(B(5, 1)\), \(C(1, 4)\). Reflect it over the \(y\)-axis to get \(A'(-1, 1)\), \(B'(-5, 1)\), \(C'(-1, 4)\).
\(AB = 4\) and \(A'B' = 4\)
\(AC = 3\) and \(A'C' = 3\)
\(BC = 5\) and \(B'C' = 5\)
Going \(A \rightarrow B \rightarrow C\) is counterclockwise. Going \(A' \rightarrow B' \rightarrow C'\) is clockwise.

Both \(\overline{AB}\) and \(\overline{A'B'}\) are horizontal, so the slopes are equal (0). \(\overline{AC}\) and \(\overline{A'C'}\) are both vertical, so they are parallel. This works here because the line of reflection is vertical. In general, a side is not parallel to its image.

Test practice

Triangle \(ABC\) is reflected over a line to form triangle \(A'B'C'\). Which statement must be true?
A. \(\triangle A'B'C'\) is the same size and shape as \(\triangle ABC\), but its labels go the opposite way around.
B. \(\triangle A'B'C'\) is larger than \(\triangle ABC\).
C. \(\triangle A'B'C'\) has the same orientation as \(\triangle ABC\).
D. Each side of \(\triangle A'B'C'\) is parallel to its pre-image side.


Challenge

A river runs along the \(x\)-axis. Hnin is at \(A(1, 3)\) and her house is at \(B(7, 5)\). She walks to the river and then to the house. Reflect \(A\) over the \(x\)-axis. Use \(A'\) and \(B\) to find where she should touch the river to walk the shortest path. How long is the path?

title: 3.3 - Rotations
text:
🔥 Warm Up
A Ferris wheel turns around its center. Every seat moves along a circle. Every seat turns by the same angle.
Here a seat at \(A(3, 0)\) turns a quarter of the way around and lands at \(A'(0, 3)\). A turn like this is a rotation. In this lesson you rotate figures about the origin and find the rotation that moves one figure onto another.

title: 3.3 - Rotations
text:
Find the distance from the origin to \(A(4, 1)\).
Find the slope of the line through \((0, 0)\) and \((4, 1)\). Then give the slope of a perpendicular line.
Find \(-y\) when \(y = -3\).

title: 3.3 - Rotations
text:
👥 Learn Together

3.3.1 - Center, Angle, and Direction
A rotation needs three facts: the center it turns about, the angle it turns, and the direction it turns.

A rotation turns every point of a figure about a fixed point, the center of rotation.
Counterclockwise is the positive direction. Clockwise is negative.
A turn of \(90^\circ\) clockwise is the same as a turn of \(270^\circ\) counterclockwise.


Example 1: Read a rotation





In the Ferris wheel figure, the seat moves from \(A(3, 0)\) to \(A'(0, 3)\) about \(O(0, 0)\).
Center: \(O(0, 0)\)
Angle: \(90^\circ\)
Direction: counterclockwise (the arrow turns left, up from the \(x\)-axis)

Example 2: Same turn, two names
Write each rotation as a counterclockwise angle.

\(90^\circ\) clockwise: \(360^\circ - 90^\circ = 270^\circ\) counterclockwise
\(270^\circ\) clockwise: \(360^\circ - 270^\circ = 90^\circ\) counterclockwise
\(180^\circ\) clockwise: \(180^\circ\) counterclockwise



Write \(90^\circ\) counterclockwise as a clockwise angle.
The minute hand of a clock moves from 12 to 6. What is the angle and direction?




\(360^\circ - 90^\circ = 270^\circ\) clockwise
\(180^\circ\) clockwise (or \(180^\circ\) counterclockwise)




3.3.2 - Rotating About the Origin
These rules turn a point \((x, y)\) about the origin \(O(0, 0)\).



Rotation (counterclockwise)
Rule




\(90^\circ\)
\((x, y) \rightarrow (-y, x)\)


\(180^\circ\)
\((x, y) \rightarrow (-x, -y)\)


\(270^\circ\) (or \(90^\circ\) clockwise)
\((x, y) \rightarrow (y, -x)\)




A point and its image are the same distance from the center.
For \(90^\circ\), the segments from the center to \(A\) and to \(A'\) are perpendicular.


Example 3: Check a rotation with coordinates





Rotate \(A(4, 1)\) by \(90^\circ\) counterclockwise about the origin. Then check.
\(A' = (-y, x) = (-1, 4)\)
Distance \(OA\): \(\sqrt{4^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt{17}\). Distance \(OA'\): \(\sqrt{(-1)^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{17}\).
Slope of \(\overline{OA}\): \(\dfrac{1}{4}\). Slope of \(\overline{OA'}\): \(-4\).
The slopes multiply to \(\dfrac{1}{4} \cdot (-4) = -1\), so \(\overline{OA} \perp \overline{OA'}\).

Example 4: Use the rules

Rotate \(B(-3, 2)\) by \(180^\circ\): \((-x, -y) = (3, -2)\).
Rotate \(C(2, 5)\) by \(270^\circ\) counterclockwise: \((y, -x) = (5, -2)\).



Rotate \(P(-2, 6)\) by \(90^\circ\) counterclockwise about the origin.
Rotate \(Q(5, -3)\) by \(90^\circ\) clockwise about the origin.




\((-y, x) = (-6, -2)\)
\(90^\circ\) clockwise is \(270^\circ\) counterclockwise: \((y, -x) = (-3, -5)\)




3.3.3 - Graphing the Image
Rotate each vertex with the rule. Then connect the new points in the same order.

Example 5: Rotate a triangle





Rotate \(\triangle ABC\) by \(90^\circ\) counterclockwise about the origin. \(A(1, 1)\), \(B(5, 1)\), \(C(1, 3)\).
Use \((x, y) \rightarrow (-y, x)\).
\(A' = (-1, 1)\), \(B' = (-1, 5)\), \(C' = (-3, 1)\)

Example 6: Rotate a quadrilateral





Rotate \(PQRS\) by \(180^\circ\) about the origin. \(P(2, -1)\), \(Q(5, -2)\), \(R(6, 2)\), \(S(3, 3)\).
Use \((x, y) \rightarrow (-x, -y)\).
\(P' = (-2, 1)\), \(Q' = (-5, 2)\)
\(R' = (-6, -2)\), \(S' = (-3, -3)\)

A fan has 4 blades. Turning the fan \(90^\circ\) puts each blade where the next blade was. The fan looks the same. You will see this again in 3.5 as rotational symmetry.


\((y, -x)\): \(J'(-1, 4)\), \(K'(-3, 1)\), \(L'(2, 2)\)



3.3.4 - Finding the Rotation
To find a rotation, test one point. Try \(90^\circ\), \(180^\circ\), and \(270^\circ\) until a rule gives the image. Then check a second point.

A rotation keeps every length and every angle. It is a rigid motion.
A rotation does not reverse orientation. Labels go the same way around.


Example 7: Find the rotation





\(\triangle ABC\) is mapped to \(\triangle A'B'C'\). Find the rotation about the origin.
Test \(A(2, 1) \rightarrow A'(-1, 2)\).
\(90^\circ\) rule: \((-y, x) = (-1, 2)\). It matches.
Check \(B(5, 1)\): \((-y, x) = (-1, 5)\). It matches \(B'\).
The rotation is \(90^\circ\) counterclockwise about the origin.


\(P(3, -2) \rightarrow P'(-3, 2)\). Find the rotation.
\(Q(4, 1) \rightarrow Q'(1, -4)\). Find the rotation.




\((-x, -y) = (-3, 2)\). It is a \(180^\circ\) rotation.
\((y, -x) = (1, -4)\). It is \(270^\circ\) counterclockwise, or \(90^\circ\) clockwise.

Test practice

A. \((5, 3)\)
B. \((-5, -3)\)
C. \((3, -5)\)
D. \((-3, -5)\)
Segment \(AB\) has endpoints \(A(2, 1)\) and \(B(6, 1)\). It is rotated \(90^\circ\) counterclockwise about the origin to form \(\overline{A'B'}\). Which statement is true?
A. \(A'B' = 4\) and \(\overline{A'B'}\) is vertical.
B. \(A'B' = 4\) and \(\overline{A'B'}\) is horizontal.
C. \(A'B' = 5\) and \(\overline{A'B'}\) is vertical.
D. \(A'B' = 8\) and \(\overline{A'B'}\) is horizontal.


Challenge

title: 3.4 - Dilations
text:
🔥 Warm Up
A projector shines a small slide onto a big wall. The picture on the wall has the same shape as the slide. It is much bigger.
The figure shows the idea. Each point moves along a ray from the center \(O\). Each new point is twice as far from \(O\) as the old point. This kind of size change is a dilation. In this lesson you enlarge and reduce figures on the coordinate plane.

title: 3.4 - Dilations
text:
Find the distance from \((0, 0)\) to \((3, 4)\).
Find the slope of the line through \((2, 1)\) and \((4, 3)\).
Solve \(\dfrac{x}{4} = 6\).

title: 3.4 - Dilations
text:
👥 Learn Together

3.4.1 - Scale Factor
A dilation makes a figure bigger or smaller. It keeps the shape. The number that tells how much the size changes is the scale factor, \(k\).

A dilation changes the size of a figure from a fixed point, the center. The shape stays the same.
If \(k > 1\), the image is larger: an enlargement. If \(0 < k < 1\), the image is smaller: a reduction.
With the center at the origin: \((x, y) \rightarrow (kx, ky)\).


Example 1: Dilate points
The center is the origin. Dilate \(P(4, -6)\) with \(k = \dfrac{1}{2}\). Dilate \(Q(-2, 5)\) with \(k = 3\).
\(P' = \left(\dfrac{1}{2} \cdot 4, \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot (-6)\right) = (2, -3)\)
\(Q' = (3 \cdot (-2), 3 \cdot 5) = (-6, 15)\)
\(P'\) is closer to the origin, so this is a reduction. \(Q'\) is farther, so this is an enlargement.

Example 2: Enlarge a triangle





Dilate \(\triangle ABC\) with \(k = 2\) about the origin. \(A(2, 1)\), \(B(4, 1)\), \(C(2, 3)\).
\(A' = (4, 2)\)
\(B' = (8, 2)\)
\(C' = (4, 6)\)

Example 3: Reduce a triangle





Dilate \(\triangle PQR\) with \(k = \dfrac{1}{3}\) about the origin. \(P(-6, 6)\), \(Q(6, 6)\), \(R(0, -3)\).
\(P' = (-2, 2)\), \(Q' = (2, 2)\), \(R' = (0, -1)\)

\(J'(1, -2)\), \(K'(3, 0)\), \(L'(2, 2)\)



3.4.2 - What Changes and What Stays
A dilation changes lengths. It does not change angles. We can check both with coordinates.

Every length is multiplied by \(k\).
Every angle measure stays the same.
Each side is parallel to its image. (They have the same slope.)
A dilation is not a rigid motion, because lengths change (unless \(k = 1\)).


Example 4: Check a dilation





In the triangle with \(A(2, 1)\), \(B(4, 1)\), \(C(2, 3)\) and \(k = 2\), compare the sides.
\(AB = 2\) and \(A'B' = 4\). \(A'B' = 2 \cdot AB\).
\(BC = \sqrt{4 + 4} = 2\sqrt{2}\) and \(B'C' = \sqrt{16 + 16} = 4\sqrt{2}\). \(B'C' = 2 \cdot BC\).
Slope of \(\overline{BC}\): \(\dfrac{3 - 1}{2 - 4} = -1\). Slope of \(\overline{B'C'}\): \(\dfrac{6 - 2}{4 - 8} = -1\).
The slopes are equal, so \(\overline{BC} \parallel \overline{B'C'}\). The angle at \(A\) is \(90^\circ\) and the angle at \(A'\) is \(90^\circ\).

A dilation makes a similar figure. It does not make a congruent one. Do not say that a dilation keeps lengths. It multiplies them by \(k\).


\(P'(3, 6)\), \(Q'(12, 18)\). \(PQ = 5\) and \(P'Q' = 15\). Both slopes are \(\dfrac{4}{3}\).



3.4.3 - Finding the Scale Factor
Compare a length in the image to the same length in the original.

\(k = \dfrac{\text{image length}}{\text{original length}}\)
If \(k\) is more than 1, it is an enlargement. If \(k\) is less than 1, it is a reduction.


Example 5: Find \(k\) from a figure





Rectangle \(WXYZ\) is dilated about the origin to \(W'X'Y'Z'\). Find the scale factor.
Original width \(WZ = 4\). Image width \(W'Z' = 6\).
\(k = \dfrac{6}{4} = \dfrac{3}{2}\)
Check with a point: \(W(2, 2) \rightarrow W'(3, 3)\), and \(3 \div 2 = \dfrac{3}{2}\).
\(k > 1\), so it is an enlargement.


A side of 12 cm becomes 30 cm. Find \(k\).
\(A(-4, 6)\) maps to \(A'(-2, 3)\) about the origin. Find \(k\).




\(k = \dfrac{30}{12} = \dfrac{5}{2} = 2.5\)
\(k = \dfrac{-2}{-4} = \dfrac{1}{2}\). It is a reduction.



A model car has a scale of \(1:24\). That is \(k = \dfrac{1}{24}\). A real car 180 inches long becomes a model \(180 \cdot \dfrac{1}{24} = 7.5\) inches long.



3.4.4 - A Center That Is Not the Origin
When the center is \(C(h, j)\), move the center to the origin first. Then dilate. Then move back.

Step 1: Subtract the center: \((x - h, y - j)\).
Step 2: Multiply by \(k\).
Step 3: Add the center back.


Example 6: Dilate about a point





Dilate \(\triangle ABC\) with \(k = 2\) about the center \(P(1, 1)\). \(A(3, 1)\), \(B(3, 3)\), \(C(2, 3)\).
\(A\): \((3 - 1, 1 - 1) = (2, 0)\). Times 2: \((4, 0)\). Add back: \(A' = (5, 1)\).
\(B\): \((2, 2) \rightarrow (4, 4) \rightarrow B' = (5, 5)\).
\(C\): \((1, 2) \rightarrow (2, 4) \rightarrow C' = (3, 5)\).

\((4 - 2, 2 - 1) = (2, 1)\). Times 3: \((6, 3)\). Add back: \((8, 4)\).

title: 3.5 - Sequences of Transformations and Symmetry
text:
🔥 Warm Up
Look at this hubcap. It has 5 spokes that look the same.
Turn the hubcap one fifth of the way around. It looks exactly the same. That turn is a transformation that maps the hubcap onto itself. In this lesson you do two or more transformations in a row. Then you use transformations to find symmetry.

title: 3.5 - Sequences of Transformations and Symmetry
text:
Reflect \((3, -4)\) over the \(y\)-axis.
Rotate \((2, 5)\) by \(90^\circ\) counterclockwise about the origin.
Solve \(\dfrac{360}{n} = 72\).

title: 3.5 - Sequences of Transformations and Symmetry
text:
👥 Learn Together

3.5.1 - One After Another
Do one transformation. Then do another to the image. The first image is \(A'\). The second image is \(A''\) (read “A double prime”).

A sequence of transformations does one transformation after another.
\(A \rightarrow A'\rightarrow A''\). Always do the moves in the order given.
A combined rule shows the whole sequence in one rule.


Example 1: Do a sequence
Translate \(P(2, 5)\) by \((x + 3, y - 2)\). Then reflect the image over the \(y\)-axis.
Step 1: \(P' = (2 + 3, 5 - 2) = (5, 3)\)
Step 2: \(P'' = (-5, 3)\), so \(P'' = (-5, 3)\)
Combined rule: \((x, y) \rightarrow (-x - 3, y - 2)\). Check: \((-2 - 3, 5 - 2) = (-5, 3)\).


Reflect \(Q(-4, 1)\) over the \(x\)-axis. Then translate by \((x + 6, y + 2)\). Find \(Q''\).
Translate by \((x + 2, y + 5)\). Then translate by \((x - 7, y - 1)\). Write one rule.




\(Q' = (-4, -1)\). \(Q'' = (2, 1)\).
\((x + 2 - 7, y + 5 - 1) = (x - 5, y + 4)\)




3.5.2 - Does Order Matter?
Sometimes the order does not change the result. Often it does.

Two translations in either order give the same image.
A reflection and a translation, in a different order, often give a different image.
One example that gives different images is a counterexample to the claim “order never matters.”


Example 2: A counterexample
Use \(P(2, 1)\). Do these two moves in both orders: reflect over the \(x\)-axis, and translate by \((x + 4, y - 3)\).
Reflect first: \((2, -1)\). Then translate: \((6, -4)\).
Translate first: \((6, -2)\). Then reflect: \((6, 2)\).
The images are different. So order matters here.

Example 3: See it on a triangle





\(A(1, 2)\), \(B(3, 2)\), \(C(1, 4)\). Reflect over the \(x\)-axis, then translate by \((x + 4, y - 3)\). This gives \(A_1\), \(B_1\), \(C_1\). Do the moves in the other order to get \(A_2\), \(B_2\), \(C_2\).
\(A_1 = (5, -5)\), \(B_1 = (7, -5)\), \(C_1 = (5, -7)\)
\(A_2 = (5, 1)\), \(B_2 = (7, 1)\), \(C_2 = (5, -1)\)

First way: \((5, 4) \rightarrow (-5, 4)\). Second way: \((-3, 4) \rightarrow (-1, 4)\). They are not the same.



3.5.3 - Describing a Sequence
To describe a sequence, find the moves that take the preimage to the final image. There is often more than one correct answer.

Look at the orientation. If it reversed, the sequence needs a reflection.
Compare sizes. If the size changed, the sequence needs a dilation.
Check your sequence with one or two vertices.


Example 4: Describe a sequence





\(\triangle ABC\) with \(A(1, 1)\), \(B(4, 1)\), \(C(1, 3)\) maps to \(\triangle A''B''C''\). Describe a sequence.
The labels go the other way around, so the sequence includes a reflection.
Reflect over the \(y\)-axis: \(A' = (-1, 1)\). Then translate: \(A'' = (-1, -4)\), which is 5 down: \((x, y - 5)\).
Another answer: translate 5 down first, then reflect over the \(y\)-axis. It gives the same \(\triangle A''B''C''\).

Rotate \(90^\circ\) counterclockwise about the origin: \(D'(-3, 2)\). Then translate \((x + 1, y + 2)\): \(D''(-2, 4)\). Check \(E\): \((-3, 5) \rightarrow (-2, 7)\).



3.5.4 - Rigid Motions and Dilations
Which transformations keep lengths and angles?



Transformation
Keeps lengths?
Keeps angles?
Rigid motion?




translation
yes
yes
yes


reflection
yes
yes
yes


rotation
yes
yes
yes


dilation (\(k \ne 1\))
no
yes
no




Any sequence of rigid motions is a rigid motion. It keeps lengths and angles.
A dilation changes lengths. It keeps angles.


Example 5: Choose the transformation
Which transformation fits each description?

Lengths and angles stay the same. The figure is flipped. reflection
All lengths double. Angles stay the same. dilation
Lengths and angles stay the same. The figure is only moved over. translation


No. Rigid motions keep lengths. A dilation with \(k = 2\) is needed.



3.5.5 - Symmetry
A figure has symmetry if a transformation maps it onto itself.

Line symmetry: a reflection over a line maps the figure onto itself. The line is a line of symmetry.
Rotational symmetry: a rotation of less than \(360^\circ\) maps the figure onto itself.
The order \(n\) is the number of times it fits in one full turn. The smallest angle is \(\dfrac{360^\circ}{n}\).


Example 6: Symmetry of letters





Find the lines of symmetry and the order of rotational symmetry.
H: 2 lines (vertical and horizontal). Turn \(180^\circ\) and it fits. Order 2.
S: 0 lines. Turn \(180^\circ\) and it fits. Order 2.
A: 1 line (vertical). No turn less than \(360^\circ\) fits. Order 1.

Example 7: Regular polygons





A regular polygon with \(n\) sides has \(n\) lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry of order \(n\) (see 1.5).
Equilateral triangle: 3 lines, order 3, smallest angle \(\dfrac{360}{3} = 120^\circ\).
Square: 4 lines, order 4, smallest angle \(\dfrac{360}{4} = 90^\circ\).
Regular pentagon: 5 lines, order 5, smallest angle \(\dfrac{360}{5} = 72^\circ\).

Order 6, smallest angle \(\dfrac{360}{6} = 60^\circ\), and 6 lines of symmetry.


A rectangle that is not a square has 2 lines of symmetry, not 4. Folding it along a diagonal does not make the halves match.

Test practice

The point \((3, -2)\) is translated by \((x - 4, y + 1)\). Then the image is reflected over the \(x\)-axis. What are the coordinates of the final image?

D. \((-7, 3)\)

A. regular octagon
B. regular hexagon
C. regular nonagon
D. regular decagon


Challenge

Reflect \(P(3, 2)\) over the line \(x = 1\). Then reflect the image over the line \(x = 4\). Find \(P''\). Compare \(P\) and \(P''\). What single translation does this equal? How does its size relate to the distance between the two lines?

title: Unit 3 Summary
text:
3.1 - Translations
Example: \((x - 3, y + 5)\) applied to \(P(2, -4)\) gives \(P' = (-1, 1)\).

title: Unit 3 Summary
text:
A transformation moves a figure by a rule. The starting figure is the preimage. The new figure is the image. Point \(A\) becomes \(A'\).
A translation slides every point the same distance in the same direction: \((x, y) \rightarrow (x + a, y + b)\).
Positive \(a\) moves right and negative \(a\) moves left. Positive \(b\) moves up and negative \(b\) moves down.
To find the rule, use image minus preimage for \(x\) and for \(y\).
To graph an image, move every vertex and connect the new points in the same order.
A translation keeps lengths and angles. Each side is parallel to its image. It is a rigid motion.

title: Unit 3 Summary
text:
3.2 - Reflections

A reflection flips a figure over a line of reflection. A point and its image are the same distance from the line.
Over the \(x\)-axis: \((x, -y)\). Over the \(y\)-axis: \((-x, y)\). Over \(y = x\): \((y, x)\). Over \(y = -x\): \((-y, -x)\).
Over \(x = a\) or \(y = b\): count the distance to the line and go the same distance to the other side.
The line of reflection is the perpendicular bisector of \(\overline{AA'}\). It goes through the midpoint and is perpendicular.
A reflection is a rigid motion. It reverses orientation.






Example: reflect \((3, -4)\) over \(y = -x\). \((-y, -x) = (4, -3)\).

title: Unit 3 Summary
text:
3.3 - Rotations

A rotation turns a figure about a center by an angle in a direction. Counterclockwise is positive.
\(90^\circ\) clockwise is the same as \(270^\circ\) counterclockwise.
About the origin: \(90^\circ\) is \((-y, x)\). \(180^\circ\) is \((-x, -y)\). \(270^\circ\) is \((y, -x)\).
A point and its image are the same distance from the center. For \(90^\circ\), the two radii are perpendicular (slopes multiply to \(-1\)).
A rotation is a rigid motion. It does not reverse orientation.






Example: rotate \((2, 5)\) by \(270^\circ\) counterclockwise. \((y, -x) = (5, -2)\).

title: Unit 3 Summary
text:
3.4 - Dilations

A dilation has a center and a scale factor \(k\). About the origin: \((x, y) \rightarrow (kx, ky)\).
\(k > 1\) is an enlargement. \(0 < k < 1\) is a reduction.
Every length is multiplied by \(k\). Angles stay the same. Each side is parallel to its image.
A dilation is not a rigid motion. \(k = \dfrac{\text{image length}}{\text{original length}}\).
Center \((h, j)\): subtract the center, multiply by \(k\), add the center back.






Example: dilate \(B(4, 2)\) with \(k = 3\) about \((2, 1)\). \((2, 1) \rightarrow (6, 3) \rightarrow (8, 4)\).

title: Unit 3 Summary
text:
3.5 - Sequences of Transformations and Symmetry

A sequence does one transformation after another: \(A \rightarrow A' \rightarrow A''\).
Order can matter. Two translations commute, but a reflection and a translation usually do not.
To describe a sequence, check orientation (reflection?) and size (dilation?). Test a vertex. More than one answer can be right.
Any sequence of translations, reflections, and rotations is a rigid motion. A dilation is not.
A regular polygon with \(n\) sides has \(n\) lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry of order \(n\). The smallest angle of rotation is \(\dfrac{360^\circ}{n}\).






Example: translate \((x + 3, y)\), then reflect over the \(y\)-axis. One rule: \((-x - 3, y)\).

title: Unit 3 Review
text:
3.1 - Translations
Example 1: Translate \(P(-3, 4)\) by \((x + 5, y - 6)\). Then find the rule that moves \(A(2, -1)\) to \(A'(-4, 3)\).
\(P' = (2, -2)\). Change in \(x\): \(-4 - 2 = -6\). Change in \(y\): \(3 - (-1) = 4\). Rule: \((x - 6, y + 4)\).


3.2 - Reflections
Example 2: Reflect \((-4, 3)\) over the \(y\)-axis and over \(y = x\). Find the line of reflection that maps \(A(0, 2)\) to \(A'(6, 2)\).
\(y\)-axis: \((4, 3)\). \(y = x\): \((3, -4)\). The midpoint of \(\overline{AA'}\) is \((3, 2)\) and \(\overline{AA'}\) is horizontal, so the line is \(x = 3\).


3.3 - Rotations
Example 3: Rotate \((3, -2)\) by \(90^\circ\) and by \(180^\circ\) counterclockwise about the origin. Find the rotation that maps \((-1, -5)\) to \((-5, 1)\).
\(90^\circ\): \((-y, x) = (2, 3)\). \(180^\circ\): \((-3, 2)\). For \((-1, -5) \rightarrow (-5, 1)\) the rule \((y, -x)\) works, so it is \(270^\circ\) counterclockwise (\(90^\circ\) clockwise).


3.4 - Dilations
Example 4: Dilate \((6, -9)\) with \(k = \dfrac{1}{3}\) about the origin. A side of 8 becomes 20. Find \(k\). Dilate \(B(5, 3)\) with \(k = 2\) about \((1, 1)\).
\((2, -3)\). \(k = \dfrac{20}{8} = \dfrac{5}{2}\). \(B\): \((4, 2) \rightarrow (8, 4) \rightarrow (9, 5)\).


3.5 - Sequences of Transformations and Symmetry
Example 5: Do “translate by \((x + 2, y)\), then reflect over the \(y\)-axis” on \(P(1, 3)\). Do the moves in the other order. Then give the order of rotational symmetry and the smallest angle for a regular octagon.
First order: \((3, 3) \rightarrow (-3, 3)\). Other order: \((-1, 3) \rightarrow (1, 3)\). Different. A regular octagon has order 8 and smallest angle \(\dfrac{360^\circ}{8} = 45^\circ\).

title: Introduction
text:
What You’ll Learn
Welcome to Unit 4! Two parts made in a factory must be exactly the same size and shape, or they will not fit. Same size and same shape is called congruent.
In this unit you learn how to tell when two figures are congruent. For triangles, you only need to check three parts. You also learn the properties of special quadrilaterals and how to make exact drawings with a compass and a straightedge.
By the end of this unit, you will be able to:

title: Introduction
text:
Use rigid motions to decide if two figures are congruent
Write a congruence statement and name the matching parts
Decide which triangles are congruent by SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, or HL
Explain why SSA and AAA are not enough
Use the angles and sides of isosceles and equilateral triangles

A shelf maker cuts a board along its diagonal. The cut makes two triangles.
Lay piece 1 over piece 2 and they match exactly. They have the same size and the same shape. Figures like this are congruent. In this lesson you learn how to tell when figures are congruent. You also use matching parts to find missing lengths and angles.

title: 4.1 - Congruent Figures and Rigid Motions
text:
👥 Learn Together

4.1.1 - Congruent Figures

Two figures are congruent if one can be moved onto the other with rigid motions.
Rigid motions are translations, reflections, and rotations. They keep every length and every angle the same.
Congruent figures have the same size and the same shape.
A dilation changes the size. It can not show that figures are congruent.


Example 1: Find the rigid motions





Is \(\triangle DEF\) congruent to \(\triangle ABC\)? \(A(2, 2)\), \(B(6, 2)\), \(C(2, 5)\), \(D(-3, -7)\), \(E(-3, -3)\), \(F(-6, -7)\).
Step 1: Rotate \(90^\circ\) counterclockwise about the origin. \((x, y) \rightarrow (-y, x)\).
$A’ = $ \((-2, 2)\), $B’ = $ \((-2, 6)\), $C’ = $ \((-5, 2)\)
Step 2: Translate by \((x - 1, y - 9)\).
$A’’ = $ \((-3, -7)\), $B’’ = $ \((-3, -3)\), $C’’ = $ \((-6, -7)\)
The points land on \(D\), \(E\), and \(F\). Both motions are rigid, so the triangles are congruent.

Example 2: Same shape is not enough
Amira says \(\triangle ABC\) and \(\triangle GHI\) are congruent because they have the same shape. \(\triangle ABC\) has sides \(3\), \(4\), \(5\). \(\triangle GHI\) has sides \(6\), \(8\), \(10\). Is she right?
No. Every side of \(\triangle GHI\) is 2 times as long as the matching side of \(\triangle ABC\).
A dilation with scale factor 2 moves one onto the other. A dilation is not a rigid motion, so the triangles are not congruent.


A figure is reflected over the \(x\)-axis and then translated 4 units left. Is the image congruent to the original? Why?
A figure is dilated with scale factor \(\frac{3}{2}\). Is the image congruent to the original? Why?




Yes. A reflection and a translation are both rigid motions. They keep size and shape.
No. A dilation changes the size. It is not a rigid motion.




4.1.2 - Corresponding Parts and Congruence Statements

Corresponding parts are the sides and angles that match when one figure is moved onto the other.
In a congruence statement, the order of the letters matters. In \(\triangle ABC \cong \triangle FDE\), \(A\) matches \(F\), \(B\) matches \(D\), and \(C\) matches \(E\).
So \(\overline{AB}\) matches \(\overline{FD}\), and \(\angle A\) matches \(\angle F\).
Tick marks on sides and arcs on angles show which parts are congruent.


Example 3: Match the parts





\(\triangle ABC \cong \triangle FDE\). Name every pair of corresponding parts.
Sides: \(\overline{AB}\) and \(\overline{FD}\), \(\overline{BC}\) and \(\overline{DE}\), \(\overline{AC}\) and \(\overline{FE}\).
Angles: \(\angle A\) and \(\angle F\), \(\angle B\) and \(\angle D\), \(\angle C\) and \(\angle E\).
Check with the marks. One tick is on \(\overline{AB}\) and \(\overline{FD}\). Two ticks are on \(\overline{BC}\) and \(\overline{DE}\). Three ticks are on \(\overline{AC}\) and \(\overline{FE}\).


\(\triangle JKL \cong \triangle MNP\). Which side matches \(\overline{KL}\)?
Which angle matches \(\angle P\)?




\(\overline{NP}\)
\(\angle L\)



Example 4: Find the mistake
Kofi looks at the marks in the figure above. He writes \(\triangle ABC \cong \triangle DEF\). Find his mistake. Write a correct statement.
The marks show that \(\angle A\) matches \(\angle F\), not \(\angle D\).
Kofi wrote the letters in the order he saw them. The statement must follow the marks.
Correct statement: \(\triangle ABC \cong \triangle FDE\)

\(\triangle ABC \cong \triangle DEF\) and \(\triangle ABC \cong \triangle FDE\) say different things. Always match the letters in the same positions.



4.1.3 - Using Corresponding Parts

Corresponding parts of congruent figures are congruent. Matching sides have the same length. Matching angles have the same measure.
To find a missing part, find its corresponding part. Then write an equation.


Example 5: Find \(x\) and \(y\)





\(ABCD \cong EFGH\). \(AB = 3x - 2\) and \(EF = x + 10\). \(m\angle C = (4y + 6)^\circ\) and \(m\angle G = 78^\circ\). Find \(x\), \(y\), and \(AB\).
\(\overline{AB}\) matches \(\overline{EF}\), so \(3x - 2 = x + 10\).
\(2x = 12\), so $x = $ 6
$AB = 3(6) - 2 = $ 16
\(\angle C\) matches \(\angle G\), so \(4y + 6 = 78\).
\(4y = 72\), so $y = $ 18

\(2a + 5 = 17\), so \(a = 6\). \(3b - 4 = 59\), so \(b = 21\).


A factory stamps out thousands of the same bracket. Each bracket must be congruent to the plan, or the bolt holes will not line up.



4.1.4 - Congruence on a Grid

On a grid, find the rigid motions that move one figure onto the other.
Or use the distance formula on every side. If one pair of matching sides has different lengths, the figures are not congruent.
If all three sides of one triangle match all three sides of another, the triangles are congruent. You will see why in 4.2.


Example 6: Show with distances





Show that \(\triangle ABC \cong \triangle DEF\). \(A(-4, 2)\), \(B(-2, 5)\), \(C(-6, 6)\), \(D(2, -4)\), \(E(5, -6)\), \(F(6, -2)\).
$AB = = $ \(\sqrt{13}\) and $DE = = $ \(\sqrt{13}\)
$BC = = $ \(\sqrt{17}\) and $EF = = $ \(\sqrt{17}\)
$AC = = $ \(\sqrt{20}\) and $DF = = $ \(\sqrt{20}\)
All three pairs match, so \(\triangle ABC \cong \triangle DEF\).

Example 7: Show they are not congruent





Are \(\triangle GHI\) and \(\triangle JKL\) congruent? \(G(2, 2)\), \(H(6, 2)\), \(I(2, 5)\), \(J(-7, -3)\), \(K(-3, -3)\), \(L(-7, -7)\).
$GH = $ 4 and $JK = $ 4. They match.
$GI = $ 3 but $JL = $ 4. They do not match.
One pair of sides is different, so the triangles are not congruent. Both are right triangles, but the sides decide.

\(PQ = 4\), \(PR = 3\), \(QR = 5\). \(XY = 4\), \(XZ = 3\), \(YZ = 5\). All three pairs match, so \(\triangle PQR \cong \triangle XYZ\).

Test practice

title: 4.2 - Triangle Congruence: SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, and HL
text:
🔥 Warm Up
Build a square from four sticks and four bolts. Push on one corner. The square tilts. Now build a triangle from three sticks. Push on it. It does not move.
Three sides lock a triangle into one shape. This is why bridges, roofs, and bike frames are built from triangles. In this lesson you find out which three parts are enough to know that two triangles are congruent.

title: 4.2 - Triangle Congruence: SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, and HL
text:
👥 Learn Together

4.2.1 - Why Triangles? SSS

A triangle with three fixed side lengths can have only one shape. A four-sided frame can tilt.
SSS (side, side, side): If three sides of one triangle are congruent to three sides of another triangle, the triangles are congruent.
SSS is the rule behind the distance check on a grid in 4.1.


Example 1: Use SSS





Are the triangles congruent? Write a congruence statement.
The marks show \(AB \cong YZ\) (one tick), \(BC \cong ZX\) (two ticks), and \(AC \cong YX\) (three ticks).
All three pairs of sides are congruent. By SSS, \(\triangle ABC \cong\) \(\triangle YZX\).
The letters follow the marks: \(A\) matches \(Y\), \(B\) matches \(Z\), and \(C\) matches \(X\).

Yes, by SSS. \(\triangle PQR \cong \triangle STU\).


A bridge truss, a roof truss, and a bike frame are made of triangles. A triangle cannot be pushed out of shape. A rectangle can.



4.2.2 - SAS, ASA, AAS, and HL

SAS (side, angle, side): two sides and the angle between them. The angle between two sides is the included angle.
ASA (angle, side, angle): two angles and the side between them. The side between two angles is the included side.
AAS (angle, angle, side): two angles and a side that is not between them.
HL (hypotenuse, leg): works for right triangles only. The hypotenuse and one leg are congruent.







Example 2: Use SAS





The marks show \(AB \cong DE\), \(AC \cong DF\), and \(\angle A \cong \angle D\).
Angle \(A\) is between \(\overline{AB}\) and \(\overline{AC}\). Angle \(D\) is between \(\overline{DE}\) and \(\overline{DF}\).
Two sides and the included angle match. By SAS, \(\triangle ABC \cong\) \(\triangle DEF\).

Example 3: Use AAS





The marks show \(\angle G \cong \angle J\), \(\angle H \cong \angle K\), and \(HI \cong KL\).
Side \(\overline{HI}\) is not between \(\angle G\) and \(\angle H\). It touches \(\angle H\) and \(\angle I\).
Two angles and a side that is not between them match. By AAS, \(\triangle GHI \cong\) \(\triangle JKL\).

Example 4: Use HL





The figure shows right angles at \(A\) and \(D\). The hypotenuses \(\overline{BC}\) and \(\overline{EF}\) are congruent. The legs \(\overline{AC}\) and \(\overline{DF}\) are congruent.
Both triangles are right triangles, and the hypotenuse and a leg match. By HL, \(\triangle ABC \cong\) \(\triangle DEF\).


In \(\triangle ABC\) and \(\triangle DEF\), \(\angle A \cong \angle D\), \(AB \cong DE\), and \(\angle B \cong \angle E\). Which rule shows the triangles are congruent?
In \(\triangle ABC\) and \(\triangle DEF\), \(AB \cong DE\), \(BC \cong EF\), and \(\angle B \cong \angle E\). Which rule?




ASA. Side \(\overline{AB}\) is between \(\angle A\) and \(\angle B\).
SAS. Angle \(B\) is between \(\overline{AB}\) and \(\overline{BC}\).




4.2.3 - What Is Not Enough: SSA and AAA

SSA (two sides and an angle that is not between them) is not enough. Two different triangles can have these parts.
AAA (three angles) is not enough. The triangles have the same shape but can have different sizes.
A counterexample is one example that shows a rule does not always work.


Example 5: A counterexample for SSA





In the figure, \(AB = 5\), \(BC = BD = 3.2\), and \(\angle A = 30^\circ\) in both triangles. Two sides and a non-included angle match.
But \(AC\) is about 2.3 and \(AD\) is about 6.3. The triangles are not congruent.
So SSA does not show that triangles are congruent.

Example 6: A counterexample for AAA





Both triangles have angles \(40^\circ\), \(60^\circ\), and \(80^\circ\). The larger triangle has sides that are 2 times as long.
The angles match, but the sizes are different. The triangles are not congruent. AAA does not work.

No. The angles match (AAA), but AAA is not enough. The sizes are different.


If the marks give only SSA or AAA, the triangles might be congruent. You just cannot tell from those facts. Write “not enough information”.



4.2.4 - Which Shortcut? Use the Marks and the Given Facts

Use only the marks and the facts you are given. A picture can look congruent and not be.
A side that both triangles share is congruent to itself. It counts as one pair of sides.
Vertical angles are equal (1.3). Parallel lines make equal alternate interior angles (1.4).
Write the congruence statement with the letters in matching order. If no rule fits, write “not enough information”.


Example 7: A shared side





\(AB \cong AD\) and \(BC \cong DC\). Are \(\triangle ABC\) and \(\triangle ADC\) congruent?
Both triangles share \(\overline{AC}\), so \(AC \cong AC\).
Three pairs of sides are congruent. By SSS, \(\triangle ABC \cong\) \(\triangle ADC\).

Example 8: Vertical angles





\(\overline{AD}\) and \(\overline{BC}\) cross at \(E\). \(AE \cong DE\) and \(BE \cong CE\). Which rule shows \(\triangle AEB \cong \triangle DEC\)?
\(\angle AEB\) and \(\angle DEC\) are vertical angles, so they are equal.
Two sides and the included angle match. By SAS, \(\triangle AEB \cong\) \(\triangle DEC\).

Example 9: Parallel lines





\(\overline{AB} \parallel \overline{DC}\) and \(AB \cong DC\). Which rule shows \(\triangle ABD \cong \triangle CDB\)?
\(\overline{BD}\) is a shared side. Because \(\overline{AB} \parallel \overline{DC}\), the alternate interior angles \(\angle ABD\) and \(\angle CDB\) are equal.
Two sides and the included angle match. By SAS, \(\triangle ABD \cong\) \(\triangle CDB\).

Example 10: Not enough information





The triangles look the same. The marks show \(AB \cong DE\), \(BC \cong EF\), and \(\angle A \cong \angle D\).
Angle \(A\) is not between \(\overline{AB}\) and \(\overline{BC}\). This is SSA.
SSA is not enough. The answer is: not enough information.

The angles at \(T\) are vertical angles, so they are equal. Two sides and the included angle match: SAS.



4.2.5 - Solve for \(x\) in Congruent Triangles

First use the marks to decide that the triangles are congruent.
Then matching parts are congruent. Set them equal and solve.


Example 11: Find \(x\), \(y\), and \(z\)





\(AC \cong DF\), \(BC \cong EF\), and \(\angle C \cong \angle F\). Find \(x\), \(y\), \(z\), and \(AB\).
Two sides and the included angle match. By SAS, \(\triangle ABC \cong \triangle DEF\).
\(BC = EF\), so \(2y + 3 = 15\) and $y = $ 6.
\(\angle C \cong \angle F\), so \(5z + 1 = 61\) and $z = $ 12.
\(\overline{AB}\) matches \(\overline{DE}\), so \(3x + 1 = 5x - 9\). Then \(10 = 2x\) and $x = $ 5.
$AB = 3(5) + 1 = $ 16

\(4x - 7 = 2x + 9\), so \(x = 8\). \(y + 5 = 3y - 7\), so \(y = 6\). \(BC = 11\).

Real problems.

Test practice

text:

An A-frame cabin has a roof shaped like a triangle. The two sloping sides are the same length. If you cut the cabin down the middle, the two halves match.
A triangle with two equal sides is isosceles. Equal sides always come with equal angles. In this lesson you use this fact to find missing angles and sides.

title: 4.3 - Isosceles and Equilateral Triangles

title: 4.3 - Isosceles and Equilateral Triangles
text:
👥 Learn Together

4.3.1 - Parts of an Isosceles Triangle

An isosceles triangle has at least two congruent sides. They are the legs. The third side is the base.
The angle between the legs is the vertex angle.
The two angles that touch the base are the base angles.


Example 1: Name the parts





\(AB \cong AC\) in the figure. Name the legs, the base, the vertex angle, and the base angles.
Legs: \(\overline{AB}\) and \(\overline{AC}\)
Base: \(\overline{BC}\)
Vertex angle: \(\angle A\)
Base angles: \(\angle B\) and \(\angle C\)

Legs: \(\overline{PQ}\) and \(\overline{QR}\). Base: \(\overline{PR}\). Vertex angle: \(\angle Q\). Base angles: \(\angle P\) and \(\angle R\).



4.3.2 - The Base Angles Theorem

Base angles theorem: In an isosceles triangle, the base angles are congruent.
Converse: If two angles of a triangle are congruent, the sides across from them are congruent.
Why it works: fold the triangle along the line from the vertex to the midpoint of the base. This is a reflection (Unit 3). The two halves match, so \(\angle B\) lands on \(\angle C\).
The vertex angle and the two base angles add to \(180^\circ\).







Example 2: Find the base angles
The vertex angle of an isosceles triangle is \(40^\circ\). Find each base angle.
The base angles are equal. Together they measure $180 - 40 = $ \(140^\circ\).
Each base angle is $140 = $ \(70^\circ\).

Example 3: Find the vertex angle
A base angle of an isosceles triangle is \(52^\circ\). Find the vertex angle.
Both base angles are \(52^\circ\). Their sum is $2(52) = $ \(104^\circ\).
The vertex angle is $180 - 104 = $ \(76^\circ\).

Example 4: Use the converse





In \(\triangle ABC\), \(m\angle B = m\angle C = 65^\circ\) and \(AB = 9\). Find \(AC\).
\(\overline{AC}\) is across from \(\angle B\) and \(\overline{AB}\) is across from \(\angle C\). The angles are equal, so the sides across from them are equal.
$AC = $ 9


The vertex angle of an isosceles triangle is \(80^\circ\). Find each base angle.
A base angle of an isosceles triangle is \(35^\circ\). Find the vertex angle.




\((180 - 80) \div 2 = 50^\circ\)
\(180 - 2(35) = 110^\circ\)




4.3.3 - Equilateral Triangles

An equilateral triangle has three congruent sides. It is also equiangular: all three angles are congruent.
Each angle measures $180 = $ \(60^\circ\).
If all three angles of a triangle are \(60^\circ\), the triangle is equilateral.


Example 5: Equilateral with algebra





\(\triangle ABC\) is equilateral. \(AB = 2x + 1\) and \(BC = 3x - 4\). Find \(x\) and the perimeter.
All sides are equal, so \(2x + 1 = 3x - 4\).
\(5 = x\), so $x = $ 5.
Each side is $2(5) + 1 = $ 11. The perimeter is $3 = $ 33.

\(5x - 5 = 60\), so \(5x = 65\) and \(x = 13\).


A yield sign is an equilateral triangle. If one side is 36 inches, all three sides are 36 inches, and every angle is \(60^\circ\).



4.3.4 - Solve for \(x\) in Isosceles Triangles

Equal sides: set the two sides equal. Equal angles: set the two angles equal.
Use the angle sum, \(180^\circ\), when the vertex angle is also needed.
With two triangles that share a side, find the angles in one triangle at a time.


Example 6: Angles with \(x\)





\(AB \cong AC\). The vertex angle is \(50^\circ\). The base angle \(\angle B\) is \((3x + 5)^\circ\). Find \(x\).
Base angles together: \(180 - 50 = 130\). Each base angle is $130 = $ 65.
\(3x + 5 = 65\), so \(3x = 60\) and $x = $ 20.

Example 7: Sides with \(x\)





\(AB \cong AC\). \(AB = 2x + 1\), \(AC = x + 8\), and \(BC = 12\). Find \(x\) and the perimeter.
The legs are equal, so \(2x + 1 = x + 8\) and $x = $ 7.
Each leg is $7 + 8 = $ 15. The perimeter is $15 + 15 + 12 = $ 42.

Example 8: Two triangles that share a side





\(AB \cong BC\) and \(AD \cong DC\). \(m\angle B = 40^\circ\) and \(m\angle D = 100^\circ\). Find \(m\angle BAD\).
In \(\triangle ABC\), each base angle is $(180 - 40) = $ \(70^\circ\). So \(m\angle BAC = 70^\circ\).
In \(\triangle ADC\), each base angle is $(180 - 100) = $ \(40^\circ\). So \(m\angle CAD = 40^\circ\).
$mBAD = 70 + 40 = $ \(110^\circ\) (angle addition).

\(4x - 10 = 2x + 20\), so \(x = 15\). Each base angle is \(50^\circ\). The vertex angle is \(180 - 100 = 80^\circ\).



4.3.5 - Check on a Grid

In an isosceles triangle, the line from the vertex angle to the midpoint of the base is perpendicular to the base.
To check: find the midpoint of the base. Then find the slopes. Slopes of perpendicular lines multiply to \(-1\).


Example 9: Show it with slopes





\(A(7, 2)\), \(B(3, 5)\), \(C(7, 7)\). Show that \(\triangle ABC\) is isosceles with base \(\overline{BC}\). Show that the line from \(A\) to the midpoint \(M\) of \(\overline{BC}\) is perpendicular to \(\overline{BC}\).
$AB = = $ 5 and $AC = = $ 5. The legs are equal.
Midpoint of \(\overline{BC}\): $M = $ \((5, 6)\)
Slope of \(\overline{BC}\): $ = $ \(\dfrac{1}{2}\)
Slope of \(\overline{AM}\): $ = $ \(-2\)
\(\dfrac{1}{2} \cdot (-2) = -1\), so \(\overline{AM} \perp \overline{BC}\).

\(AB = \sqrt{16 + 4} = \sqrt{20}\) and \(AC = \sqrt{4 + 16} = \sqrt{20}\). \(M = (3, 1)\). Slope of \(\overline{AM}\) is \(\frac{1 - (-2)}{3 - 4} = -3\). Slope of \(\overline{BC}\) is \(\frac{1}{3}\). The product is \(-1\).

title: 4.4 - Quadrilaterals and Their Properties
