title: 4.4 - Quadrilaterals and Their Properties
text:
👥 Learn Together

4.4.1 - The Quadrilateral Family

A quadrilateral has 4 sides. Its 4 angles add to \(360^\circ\).
Trapezoid: exactly one pair of parallel sides. Kite: two pairs of congruent sides that are next to each other.
Parallelogram: both pairs of opposite sides are parallel.
Rectangle: a parallelogram with 4 right angles. Rhombus: a parallelogram with 4 congruent sides.
Square: a rectangle and a rhombus. It has 4 right angles and 4 congruent sides.







Example 1: Name the shape
Give the most specific name for each quadrilateral.

Four congruent sides and four right angles: square
Both pairs of opposite sides parallel, four right angles, sides not all equal: rectangle
Exactly one pair of parallel sides: trapezoid
Four congruent sides, angles not right angles: rhombus



A quadrilateral has two pairs of congruent sides that are next to each other. The opposite sides are not congruent. What is it?
Is every square a rectangle? Use the family tree.




A kite.
Yes. A square is below rectangle on the tree. It has 4 right angles.




4.4.2 - Parallelograms

Opposite sides of a parallelogram are congruent.
Opposite angles are congruent.
Consecutive angles (angles next to each other) are supplementary. They add to \(180^\circ\).
The diagonals bisect each other. They meet at the midpoint of each diagonal.
The converse works too: if the diagonals of a quadrilateral bisect each other, it is a parallelogram.


Example 2: Find \(x\) and \(y\)





In parallelogram \(ABCD\), \(AB = 2x + 3\), \(CD = 4x - 9\), \(m\angle A = (5y - 10)^\circ\), and \(m\angle C = 70^\circ\). Find \(x\), \(y\), and \(m\angle B\).
Opposite sides are equal: \(2x + 3 = 4x - 9\). So \(12 = 2x\) and $x = $ 6.
Opposite angles are equal: \(5y - 10 = 70\). So \(5y = 80\) and $y = $ 16.
\(\angle B\) and \(\angle A\) are consecutive: $mB = 180 - 70 = $ \(110^\circ\).

Example 3: Check the diagonals with coordinates





\(A(2, 2)\), \(B(7, 3)\), \(C(9, 7)\), \(D(4, 6)\). Show that \(ABCD\) is a parallelogram.
Midpoint of \(\overline{AC}\): $(, ) = $ \((5.5, 4.5)\)
Midpoint of \(\overline{BD}\): $(, ) = $ \((5.5, 4.5)\)
The diagonals have the same midpoint, so they bisect each other. \(ABCD\) is a parallelogram.

Midpoint of \(\overline{EG}\): \((3.5, 2.5)\). Midpoint of \(\overline{FH}\): \((3.5, 2.5)\). They match, so yes.


A car jack and the arms of a desk lamp are parallelograms. As the arms move, opposite sides stay parallel and the same length. The top stays level.



4.4.3 - Rectangles, Rhombuses, and Squares

A rectangle has all the properties of a parallelogram. Its diagonals are congruent.
A rhombus has all the properties of a parallelogram. Its diagonals are perpendicular, and each diagonal bisects a pair of opposite angles.
A square has all of these properties. Its diagonals are congruent and perpendicular.


Example 4: Rectangle diagonals





\(ABCD\) is a rectangle. \(AC = 3x + 2\) and \(BD = 5x - 12\). Find \(x\) and \(AC\).
The diagonals of a rectangle are congruent: \(3x + 2 = 5x - 12\).
\(14 = 2x\), so $x = $ 7.
$AC = 3(7) + 2 = $ 23

Example 5: Rhombus angles





\(ABCD\) is a rhombus. \(m\angle CAB = 28^\circ\). Find \(m\angle DAB\), \(m\angle ABC\), and \(m\angle AEB\).
Diagonal \(\overline{AC}\) bisects \(\angle DAB\): $mDAB = 2(28) = $ \(56^\circ\).
Consecutive angles add to \(180^\circ\): $mABC = 180 - 56 = $ \(124^\circ\).
The diagonals are perpendicular: $mAEB = $ \(90^\circ\).


Rectangle \(PQRS\) has diagonal \(PR = 18\). Find \(QS\).
The diagonals of a rhombus cross at \(E\). Find \(m\angle AEB\).




\(QS = 18\). The diagonals of a rectangle are congruent.
\(90^\circ\). The diagonals of a rhombus are perpendicular.



A builder measures both diagonals of a frame. If the opposite sides match and the diagonals match, the frame is a rectangle. The corners are square.



4.4.4 - Trapezoids and Kites

A trapezoid has one pair of parallel sides, the bases. The other two sides are the legs.
The midsegment of a trapezoid connects the midpoints of the legs. It is parallel to the bases. Its length is the average of the bases: \(\dfrac{b_1 + b_2}{2}\).
Isosceles trapezoid: the legs are congruent. Each pair of base angles is congruent. The diagonals are congruent.
Kite: the diagonals are perpendicular. One pair of opposite angles is congruent (the angles between the unequal sides).


Example 6: Midsegment





The bases of a trapezoid are 12 and 28. The midsegment is \((3x + 5)\). Find \(x\).
Midsegment $= = $ 20.
\(3x + 5 = 20\), so \(3x = 15\) and $x = $ 5.

Example 7: Isosceles trapezoid





\(ABCD\) is an isosceles trapezoid with \(\overline{AB} \parallel \overline{DC}\). \(m\angle D = 70^\circ\). Find \(m\angle C\), \(m\angle A\), and \(m\angle B\).
Base angles are congruent: $mC = $ \(70^\circ\).
\(\angle A\) and \(\angle D\) are consecutive angles between parallel lines: $mA = 180 - 70 = $ \(110^\circ\).
$mB = $ \(110^\circ\)

Example 8: Kite





\(ABCD\) is a kite. \(AB = AD\) and \(CB = CD\). \(m\angle A = 80^\circ\) and \(m\angle B = 110^\circ\). Find \(m\angle D\) and \(m\angle C\).
The angles between the unequal sides are congruent: $mD = $ \(110^\circ\).
The four angles add to \(360^\circ\): $mC = 360 - 80 - 110 - 110 = $ \(60^\circ\).

\(m\angle S = 100^\circ\). \(m\angle R = 360 - 70 - 100 - 100 = 90^\circ\).



4.4.5 - Always, Sometimes, or Never?

A shape is always a member of every group above it on the family tree.
To show a statement is not always true, find a counterexample: one example where it fails.
Use one of the four ways to justify: a drawing to scale, a coordinate check, a counterexample, or a mark on a figure.


Example 9: Decide and explain

A square is a rectangle. Always. A square has 4 right angles and opposite sides parallel.
A rectangle is a rhombus. Sometimes. A rectangle 2 by 5 is a counterexample: the sides are not all equal. A square is a rectangle that is also a rhombus.
A trapezoid is a parallelogram. Never. A trapezoid has exactly one pair of parallel sides. A parallelogram has two.



A rhombus is a square. Always, sometimes, or never? Explain.




Sometimes. A rhombus with angles \(60^\circ\) and \(120^\circ\) is a counterexample. It has no right angles.

title: 4.5 - Constructions
text:
🔥 Warm Up
Before computers, builders and mapmakers drew exact figures with two tools. A straightedge draws straight lines. A compass draws arcs and circles. There is no ruler and no protractor.
The figure above is an equilateral triangle made with only these two tools. In this lesson you learn eight constructions. For each one you also learn why it works. The reason is always congruent triangles or equal compass widths.

title: 4.5 - Constructions

title: 4.5 - Constructions
text:
👥 Learn Together

4.5.1 - Copy a Segment and Copy an Angle

A construction uses only a compass (draws arcs and circles) and a straightedge (draws straight lines). Keep your arcs. They show your work.
Copy a segment \(\overline{AB}\) onto a ray from \(C\). Step 1: Set the compass width to the length of \(\overline{AB}\).
Step 2: Put the compass point on \(C\). Draw an arc across the ray. Label the point \(D\). Now \(CD = AB\).
Why it works: \(CD\) and \(AB\) are both the same compass width.
Copy an angle \(\angle A\) onto a ray from \(D\). Step 1: Put the compass point on \(A\). Draw an arc across both sides. Label the points \(P\) and \(Q\).
Step 2: Keep the same width. Put the point on \(D\). Draw an arc across the ray. Label the point \(R\).
Step 3: Set the compass to the length \(PQ\). Put the point on \(R\). Draw an arc that crosses the other arc at \(S\).
Step 4: Draw ray \(DS\). Now \(\angle SDR \cong \angle A\).
Why it works: \(AP = DR\), \(AQ = DS\), and \(PQ = RS\) (equal compass widths). So \(\triangle APQ \cong \triangle DRS\) by SSS.


Example 1: Copy a segment





Copy \(\overline{AB}\) onto the ray from \(C\). Label the new segment \(\overline{CD}\).
Why does \(CD = AB\)?
Same compass width

Example 2: Copy an angle





Copy \(\angle A\) onto the ray from \(D\).
Which rule shows \(\triangle APQ \cong \triangle DRS\)?
SSS


4.5.2 - Perpendicular Bisector and Midpoint

Step 1: Set the compass wider than half of \(AB\). Put the point on \(A\). Draw an arc above and below \(\overline{AB}\).
Step 2: Keep the same width. Put the point on \(B\). Draw arcs that cross the first arcs at \(P\) and \(Q\).
Step 3: Draw line \(PQ\). It crosses \(\overline{AB}\) at the midpoint \(M\). Line \(PQ\) is the perpendicular bisector of \(\overline{AB}\).
Why it works: \(AP = BP\) and \(AQ = BQ\) (equal compass widths). Also \(PQ = PQ\). So \(\triangle APQ \cong \triangle BPQ\) by SSS.
Then \(\angle APM \cong \angle BPM\). With \(AP = BP\) and \(PM = PM\), \(\triangle APM \cong \triangle BPM\) by SAS. So \(AM = BM\) and the two angles at \(M\) are equal. Equal angles on a straight line are each \(90^\circ\).


Example 3: Construct the perpendicular bisector





Construct the perpendicular bisector of \(\overline{AB}\). Label the midpoint \(M\).
Name two equal segments you constructed.
\(AM\) and \(MB\)


4.5.3 - Bisect an Angle

Step 1: Put the compass point on the vertex \(A\). Draw an arc across both sides. Label the points \(P\) and \(Q\).
Step 2: Put the point on \(P\). Draw an arc inside the angle. Keep the same width. Put the point on \(Q\) and draw an arc that crosses the first arc at \(R\).
Step 3: Draw ray \(AR\). It is the angle bisector. \(\angle PAR \cong \angle QAR\).
Why it works: \(AP = AQ\) and \(PR = QR\) (equal compass widths). Also \(AR = AR\). So \(\triangle APR \cong \triangle AQR\) by SSS. The matching angles \(\angle PAR\) and \(\angle QAR\) are equal.


Example 4: Bisect an angle





Bisect \(\angle A\).
If \(m\angle A = 66^\circ\), how large is each new angle?
\(33^\circ\)


4.5.4 - Perpendicular and Parallel Lines Through a Point

Perpendicular from \(P\) to line \(\ell\). Step 1: Put the point on \(P\). Draw an arc that crosses \(\ell\) twice, at \(A\) and \(B\).
Step 2: Put the point on \(A\), then on \(B\), with the same width. Draw arcs that cross below \(\ell\) at \(Q\).
Step 3: Draw line \(PQ\). It is perpendicular to \(\ell\).
Why it works: \(PA = PB\) and \(QA = QB\). So \(PQ\) is the perpendicular bisector of \(\overline{AB}\).
Parallel to \(\ell\) through \(P\). Step 1: Draw a line through \(P\) that crosses \(\ell\) at \(A\). Step 2: Copy the angle at \(A\) to \(P\), using the same four steps as before.
Why it works: the two angles are corresponding angles and they are congruent. So the lines are parallel (1.4).


Example 5: Construct a perpendicular line





Construct the line through \(P\) that is perpendicular to \(\ell\). Label the foot \(F\).
What is \(m\angle PFA\)?
\(90^\circ\)

Example 6: Construct a parallel line





Construct the line through \(P\) that is parallel to \(\ell\).
Which angles did you copy?
corresponding angles


4.5.5 - Equilateral Triangle and Regular Hexagon

Equilateral triangle on \(\overline{AB}\). Step 1: Set the compass width to \(AB\). Draw an arc from \(A\) and an arc from \(B\). They cross at \(C\).
Step 2: Draw \(\overline{AC}\) and \(\overline{BC}\). Why it works: \(AC = AB\) and \(BC = AB\) (the same compass width). All three sides are equal, and each angle is \(60^\circ\).
Regular hexagon. Step 1: Draw a circle with center \(O\). Do not change the compass width. Put the point on a point 1 on the circle. Mark point 2.
Step 2: Move the point to 2 and mark 3. Keep going until you have 6 points. Draw the six sides.
Why it works: each side equals the radius, so each triangle with \(O\) is equilateral. Each center angle is \(60^\circ\), and $6 ^= $ \(360^\circ\).


Example 7: Construct an equilateral triangle





Construct an equilateral triangle on \(\overline{AB}\).
How long is each side if \(AB = 4.6\)?
4.6

Example 8: Construct a regular hexagon





Construct a regular hexagon in the circle. Start at point 1.
If the radius is 2.2, how long is each side?
2.2

title: Unit 4 Summary
text:
4.1 - Congruent Figures and Rigid Motions
Example: \(\triangle ABC \cong \triangle DEF\), \(AB = 2x + 1\), and \(DE = 15\). Then \(2x + 1 = 15\), so \(x = 7\).

title: Unit 4 Summary
text:
Congruent figures have the same size and the same shape. Write \(\triangle ABC \cong \triangle DEF\).
The order of the letters shows the matching parts. \(\overline{AB}\) matches \(\overline{DE}\) and \(\angle A\) matches \(\angle D\).
Matching parts of congruent figures are congruent. Use them to find missing sides and angles.
A rigid motion keeps all lengths and angles. Translations, reflections, and rotations are rigid motions.
Two figures are congruent if a sequence of rigid motions maps one onto the other.
On a grid, use the distance formula to check that matching sides are equal.

title: Unit 4 Summary
text:
4.2 - Triangle Congruence

SSS: three pairs of congruent sides.
SAS: two pairs of congruent sides and the included angle (the angle between them).
ASA: two pairs of congruent angles and the included side.
AAS: two pairs of congruent angles and a side that is not between them.
HL: right triangles with congruent hypotenuses and one pair of congruent legs.
SSA and AAA are not enough. A counterexample shows it: AAA gives the same shape in different sizes.






Example: Two triangles have sides 6 and 9 and the included angle \(50^\circ\) in each. They are congruent by SAS.

title: Unit 4 Summary
text:
4.3 - Isosceles and Equilateral Triangles

An isosceles triangle has two congruent sides, the legs. The third side is the base.
Base angles theorem: the angles opposite the congruent sides are congruent.
Converse: if two angles are congruent, the sides opposite them are congruent.
The angles of a triangle add to \(180^\circ\). Vertex angle \(= 180^\circ -\) two base angles.
An equilateral triangle has three congruent sides and three \(60^\circ\) angles.
On a grid, find the distances to show two sides are equal.






Example: The vertex angle is \(48^\circ\). Each base angle is \(\dfrac{180 - 48}{2} = 66^\circ\).

title: Unit 4 Summary
text:
4.4 - Quadrilaterals and Their Properties

The four angles of a quadrilateral add to \(360^\circ\).
Parallelogram: opposite sides and opposite angles are congruent. Consecutive angles add to \(180^\circ\). The diagonals bisect each other.
Rectangle: a parallelogram with four right angles. The diagonals are congruent.
Rhombus: a parallelogram with four congruent sides. The diagonals are perpendicular and bisect the angles.
Square: a rectangle and a rhombus.
Trapezoid: exactly one pair of parallel sides. The midsegment is parallel to the bases. Its length is the average of the bases.
Kite: two pairs of congruent sides that are next to each other. The diagonals are perpendicular.
A counterexample shows a statement is not always true.






Example: The bases of a trapezoid are 10 and 18. The midsegment is \(\dfrac{10 + 18}{2} = 14\).

title: Unit 4 Summary
text:
4.5 - Constructions

A construction uses only a compass and a straightedge.
Copy a segment or an angle: use the same compass width for each arc.
Perpendicular bisector of \(\overline{AB}\): open the compass wider than half of \(AB\). Draw arcs from \(A\) and from \(B\). Draw the line through the two crossing points.
Angle bisector: draw an arc across both sides. Draw equal arcs from those two points. Draw the ray through the vertex and the crossing point.
Perpendicular and parallel lines through a point \(P\) use the same arcs and copy an angle.
An equilateral triangle on \(\overline{AB}\): arcs of width \(AB\) from \(A\) and from \(B\). A regular hexagon: step the radius around a circle.
A construction works because equal compass widths make congruent triangles (SSS).






Example: An angle of \(84^\circ\) is bisected. Each new angle is \(84 \div 2 = 42^\circ\).

title: Unit 4 Review
text: 👥 Learn Together

title: Unit 4 Review
text:
4.1 - Congruent Figures and Rigid Motions
Example 1: \(\triangle ABC \cong \triangle DEF\). \(AB = 3x - 4\) and \(DE = 17\). \(m\angle C = 2y + 10\) and \(m\angle F = 70^\circ\). Find \(x\) and \(y\). Which side matches \(\overline{BC}\)?
\(3x - 4 = 17\), so \(x = 7\). \(2y + 10 = 70\), so \(y = 30\). \(\overline{BC}\) matches \(\overline{EF}\).


4.2 - Triangle Congruence
Example 2: \(AB = 7\), \(BC = 9\), \(m\angle B = 40^\circ\). \(DE = 7\), \(EF = 9\), \(m\angle E = 40^\circ\). Are the triangles congruent? Then try \(PQ = 5\), \(QR = 8\), \(m\angle P = 30^\circ\) and \(ST = 5\), \(TU = 8\), \(m\angle S = 30^\circ\).
The first pair is congruent by SAS. The angle is between the two sides. In the second pair the angle is not between the sides. That is SSA, which is not enough. We cannot tell.


4.3 - Isosceles and Equilateral Triangles
Example 3: \(AB = AC\) in \(\triangle ABC\). \(m\angle B = (3x + 5)^\circ\) and \(m\angle C = (5x - 15)^\circ\). Find \(x\) and \(m\angle A\).
Base angles are equal: \(3x + 5 = 5x - 15\), so \(x = 10\). Each base angle is \(35^\circ\). \(m\angle A = 180 - 35 - 35 = 110^\circ\).


4.4 - Quadrilaterals and Their Properties
Example 4: In parallelogram \(ABCD\), \(m\angle A = (2x + 20)^\circ\) and \(m\angle B = (3x - 10)^\circ\). Find \(x\) and the four angles.
Consecutive angles add to \(180^\circ\): \(5x + 10 = 180\), so \(x = 34\). \(m\angle A = 88^\circ\) and \(m\angle B = 92^\circ\). Opposite angles are equal, so \(m\angle C = 88^\circ\) and \(m\angle D = 92^\circ\).


4.5 - Constructions
Example 5: List the steps to bisect \(\angle A\). Say why the construction works. If \(m\angle A = 84^\circ\), how large is each new angle?
Draw an arc across both sides, at \(P\) and \(Q\). Draw equal arcs from \(P\) and from \(Q\) that cross at \(R\). Draw \(\overrightarrow{AR}\). It works because \(\triangle APR \cong \triangle AQR\) by SSS. Each new angle is \(42^\circ\).

title: Introduction
text:
What You’ll Learn
Welcome to Unit 5! A map, a model car, and a photo on your phone all show something at a different size. The shape stays the same. Only the size changes.
Figures with the same shape are similar. In this unit you use ratios and proportions to find missing lengths in similar figures. Then you use similar triangles to measure things you cannot reach, like the height of a tree or the width of a river.
By the end of this unit, you will be able to:

title: Introduction
text:
Write and solve proportions
Use a scale factor to find missing lengths
Decide if two figures are similar
Decide if two triangles are similar by AA, SSS, or SAS
Use parallel lines to find lengths in triangles
Measure heights and distances with shadows and mirrors

title: Introduction
text:
Topics in This Unit
Ratios and Proportions
Write ratios, solve proportions, and use scale drawings and maps.
Similar Figures and Scale Factor
Same shape, different size. Find missing sides with a scale factor.
Similar Triangles
Decide if two triangles are similar. Find missing sides.
Triangle Proportionality
A line parallel to one side of a triangle cuts the other sides in the same ratio.
Indirect Measurement
Find the height of a tree or a building with similar triangles.
Unit 5 Summary
Every tool from the unit in one place, to keep beside you.
Unit 5 Review
Practice every skill from the unit before the quiz.

title: 5.1 - Ratios and Proportions
text:
🔥 Warm Up
Amira is making lemonade for a school party. Her recipe uses 2 cups of lemon juice and 3 cups of water. She needs more, so she doubles the recipe. Now she uses 4 cups of juice and 6 cups of water.
The amounts changed. The taste did not, because the ratio of juice to water is still the same. Maps, floor plans, and recipes all work this way. In this lesson you learn to write ratios and to solve for a missing number. Later in this unit, these skills help you find missing lengths in figures with the same shape.

title: 5.1 - Ratios and Proportions
text:
Simplify \(\dfrac{18}{24}\).
Solve \(4x = 30\).
Solve \(2x + 3 = 3x - 5\).

title: 5.1 - Ratios and Proportions
text:
👥 Learn Together

5.1.1 - Ratios
A ratio compares two numbers by division. Amira’s recipe has 2 cups of juice for every 3 cups of water. The ratio of juice to water is 2 to 3.
You can write the same ratio three ways:

2 to 3
\(2 : 3\)
\(\dfrac{2}{3}\)

A ratio can be simplified like a fraction. Divide both numbers by the same number. The ratio \(4 : 6\) simplifies to \(2 : 3\) because \(4 \div 2 = 2\) and \(6 \div 2 = 3\).

The ratio of juice to water is \(2 : 3\). The ratio of water to juice is \(3 : 2\). These are different. The first number goes with the first thing named.


Example 1: Write and simplify a ratio
A box has 15 red tiles and 25 blue tiles.

Write the ratio of red tiles to blue tiles.
Write the ratio of blue tiles to all the tiles.
\(15 : 25\). Divide both by 5. The ratio is \(3 : 5\).
There are \(15 + 25 = 40\) tiles. The ratio is \(25 : 40\). Divide both by 5. The ratio is \(5 : 8\).



Write the ratio of tablets to laptops in lowest terms.
Write the ratio of laptops to all the devices in lowest terms.




\(30 : 18 = 5 : 3\)
\(18 : 48 = 3 : 8\)


Use the same units. To compare 2 feet and 8 inches, change them to the same unit first.

Example 3: Ratios with units
Ahmad has a board that is 2 feet long. He cuts a piece that is 8 inches long. Write the ratio of the board to the piece in lowest terms.
Change feet to inches: \(2 \text{ ft} = 24 \text{ in}\).
The ratio is \(24 : 8\). Divide both by 8. The ratio is \(3 : 1\).
The board is 3 times as long as the piece.

What is the ratio of 3 yards to 6 feet?


\(3 \text{ yd} = 9 \text{ ft}\). The ratio is \(9 : 6 = 3 : 2\).



5.1.2 - Proportions
A proportion is an equation that says two ratios are equal. Start with Amira’s lemonade. The recipe uses 2 cups of juice for 3 cups of water. How much juice goes with 12 cups of water?
Let \(x\) be the cups of juice. Juice is on top and water is on the bottom in both ratios:
\[
\dfrac{2}{3} = \dfrac{x}{12}
\]
Multiply both sides by \(3\) and by \(12\). The left side becomes \(2 \cdot 12\). The right side becomes \(3 \cdot x\). So \(24 = 3x\). Then \(x = 8\).
That shortcut always works. It is called cross products. Multiply along the two diagonals.
\[
\dfrac{a}{b} = \dfrac{c}{d} \quad \text{means} \quad ad = bc
\]

Example 5: Solve a proportion
Solve \(\dfrac{x}{12} = \dfrac{5}{8}\).
Cross products: \(8 \cdot x = 12 \cdot 5\).
\(8x = 60\)
\(x = 7.5\)
Check: \(\dfrac{7.5}{12} = 0.625\) and \(\dfrac{5}{8} = 0.625\).

\(\dfrac{x}{10} = \dfrac{7}{4}\)


\(4x = 70\), so \(x = 17.5\).


Example 7: A proportion from a word problem
Moses walks 6 miles in 2 hours. He keeps the same speed. How long does it take him to walk 15 miles?
Put miles on top and hours on the bottom in both ratios. Let \(t\) be the hours.
\(\dfrac{6}{2} = \dfrac{15}{t}\)
\(6t = 2 \cdot 15 = 30\)
\(t = 5\)
It takes 5 hours.

A printer prints 45 pages in 6 minutes. How many pages does it print in 20 minutes?


\(\dfrac{45}{6} = \dfrac{p}{20}\), so \(6p = 900\) and \(p = 150\) pages.

Sometimes the unknown is part of an expression. Use cross products, then solve the equation.

Example 9: Expressions in a proportion
Solve \(\dfrac{5}{x + 2} = \dfrac{4}{x}\).
Cross products: \(5 \cdot x = 4(x + 2)\).
\(5x = 4x + 8\)
\(x = 8\)
Check: \(\dfrac{5}{10} = 0.5\) and \(\dfrac{4}{8} = 0.5\).

\(\dfrac{7}{x} = \dfrac{3}{x - 4}\)


\(7(x - 4) = 3x\), so \(7x - 28 = 3x\) and \(4x = 28\). \(x = 7\).


Example 11: A proportion with two answers
Solve \(\dfrac{x - 2}{5} = \dfrac{20}{x - 2}\).
Cross products: \((x - 2)(x - 2) = 5 \cdot 20\).
\((x - 2)^2 = 100\)
\(x - 2 = 10\) or \(x - 2 = -10\)
\(x = 12\) or \(x = -8\)
Both work in the equation. In a figure, a length cannot be negative, so you would keep only \(x = 12\).

\(\dfrac{x + 1}{4} = \dfrac{9}{x + 1}\)


\((x + 1)^2 = 36\), so \(x + 1 = 6\) or \(x + 1 = -6\). \(x = 5\) or \(x = -7\).



5.1.3 - Scale Drawings and Maps
A scale drawing is a smaller or larger copy of something real. A map and a floor plan are scale drawings. The scale tells how a length on the drawing matches the real length.
A scale of \(1 \text{ in} : 20 \text{ ft}\) means that 1 inch on the drawing stands for 20 feet in real life. Put the drawing length in one ratio and the real length in the other. Keep the same units in the same place.

Example 13: Use a scale





The plan of a lot has the scale \(1 \text{ in} : 20 \text{ ft}\). On the plan, the lot is 3.5 in long and 2 in wide.

Find the real length of the lot.
A shed is 12 ft wide. How wide is the shed on the plan?
Let \(L\) be the real length in feet.

\(\dfrac{1}{20} = \dfrac{3.5}{L}\), so \(L = 20 \cdot 3.5 = 70\) ft.
The lot is 70 ft long (and \(2 \cdot 20 = 40\) ft wide).

Let \(d\) be the width on the plan in inches.

\(\dfrac{1}{20} = \dfrac{d}{12}\), so \(20d = 12\) and \(d = 0.6\).
The shed is 0.6 in wide on the plan.


Two towns are 3.5 in apart on the map. Find the real distance.
Two lakes are 50 mi apart. How far apart are they on the map?




\(3.5 \cdot 8 = 28\) mi.
\(\dfrac{1}{8} = \dfrac{d}{50}\), so \(8d = 50\) and \(d = 6.25\) in.


A scale can also have no units, like \(1 : 50\). Then both numbers use the same unit. On a \(1 : 50\) plan, 1 cm on the plan stands for 50 cm in real life.


5.1.4 - Ratios in a Figure
A ratio can split a total into parts. Write each part as a number times \(x\). Add the parts to equal the total. Solve for \(x\).

Example 15: Angles in a ratio





The angles of a triangle are in the ratio \(2 : 3 : 4\). Find each angle.
The angles add to \(180^\circ\).
\(2x + 3x + 4x = 180\)
\(9x = 180\), so \(x = 20\).
The angles are \(2(20) = 40^\circ\), \(3(20) = 60^\circ\), and \(4(20) = 80^\circ\).
Check: \(40 + 60 + 80 = 180\).

Find each angle. Then say whether the triangle is acute, right, or obtuse.


\(x + 2x + 6x = 180\), so \(9x = 180\) and \(x = 20\).
The angles are \(20^\circ\), \(40^\circ\), and \(120^\circ\). The triangle is obtuse.


Example 17: A segment in a ratio





Point \(P\) is on \(\overline{AB}\). \(AB = 40\) in. The ratio \(AP : PB\) is \(3 : 5\). Find \(AP\) and \(PB\).
\(AP + PB = AB\)
\(3x + 5x = 40\)
\(8x = 40\), so \(x = 5\).
\(AP = 3(5) = 15\) in and \(PB = 5(5) = 25\) in.

A mix is cement : sand : gravel \(= 1 : 2 : 3\) by volume. The total is 27 cubic feet. How much of each is there?


\(x + 2x + 3x = 27\), so \(6x = 27\) and \(x = 4.5\).
Cement: 4.5 cubic ft. Sand: 9 cubic ft. Gravel: 13.5 cubic ft.

title: 5.1 - Ratios and Proportions
text:
✍️ Practice On Your Own

14 to 21
36 : 48
45 to 15


Change to the same unit. Then write the ratio in lowest terms.

90 cm to 2 m
45 min to 2 h
2 yd to 3 ft


Solve each proportion.

\(\dfrac{x}{15} = \dfrac{2}{5}\)
\(\dfrac{7}{x} = \dfrac{21}{12}\)
\(\dfrac{5}{8} = \dfrac{x}{20}\)
\(\dfrac{9}{14} = \dfrac{27}{x}\)

\(\dfrac{6}{x - 1} = \dfrac{9}{12}\)
\(\dfrac{x}{x + 3} = \dfrac{2}{5}\)
\(\dfrac{x + 2}{9} = \dfrac{4}{x + 2}\) (two answers)


Find the mistake.

Thu solves \(\dfrac{3}{x} = \dfrac{5}{20}\). She writes \(3 \cdot 5 = 20x\) and gets \(x = 0.75\). Find her mistake. Then solve the proportion correctly.


Write a proportion and solve.

A rice recipe for 4 people uses 3 cups of rice. How many cups does the same recipe need for 14 people?
Kofi’s car uses 5 gallons of gas to drive 140 miles. At the same rate, how far can it go on 12 gallons?
A photo is 4 in by 6 in. It is enlarged so the short side is 10 in. The shape stays the same. How long is the long side?


Use the scale.

A drawing has the scale \(1 \text{ in} : 25 \text{ ft}\). A deck is 130 ft long in real life. How long is it on the drawing?
A map has the scale \(1 \text{ cm} : 4 \text{ km}\). Two cities are 7.5 cm apart on the map. How far apart are they in real life?
A floor plan has the scale \(1 : 50\). A room is 5 m long. How long is the room on the plan? Give your answer in centimeters.


Find the parts.

The angles of a triangle are in the ratio \(1 : 2 : 3\). Find each angle.
Point \(F\) is on \(\overline{DE}\). \(DE = 63\) cm and \(DF : FE = 2 : 7\). Find \(DF\) and \(FE\).
A concrete mix is cement : sand : gravel \(= 1 : 2 : 4\). The total is 28 cubic feet. How much gravel is there?
The angles of a quadrilateral are in the ratio \(2 : 3 : 3 : 4\). Find each angle.


Test practice

The length of a garden to its width is in the ratio 7 to 4. The garden is 28 feet long. Which equation can be used to find the width \(w\)?
A. \(\dfrac{7}{4} = \dfrac{w}{28}\)
B. \(\dfrac{7}{4} = \dfrac{28}{w}\)
C. \(\dfrac{4}{7} = \dfrac{28}{w}\)
D. \(\dfrac{28}{7} = \dfrac{4}{w}\)
On a map, 2.5 centimeters stand for 10 kilometers. Two towns are 14 centimeters apart on the map. What is the real distance between the towns?
A. 35 km
B. 56 km
C. 5.6 km
D. 140 km


Challenge

A map has the scale \(1 \text{ in} : 20 \text{ mi}\). A park is a rectangle 2 in by 3 in on the map. Find the real area of the park in square miles. Hint: do not multiply the map area by 20.

title: 5.2 - Similar Figures and Scale Factor
text:
🔥 Warm Up
You print a photo that is 4 inches by 6 inches. Then you enlarge it to 8 inches by 12 inches. It looks the same, only bigger. Now you enlarge it to 8 inches by 10 inches. This time the picture looks stretched.
Photos A and B have the same shape. Photo C does not. Figures with the same shape are similar. In this lesson you learn how to tell, and how to use the scale factor to find missing lengths.

title: 5.2 - Similar Figures and Scale Factor
text:
Solve \(\dfrac{x}{6} = \dfrac{10}{4}\).
A segment is 8 cm long. A dilation with scale factor 2.5 is applied. How long is the image?
Find the area and perimeter of a rectangle that is 5 in by 3 in.

title: 5.2 - Similar Figures and Scale Factor
text:
👥 Learn Together

5.2.1 - What Similar Means
Two figures are similar (\(\sim\)) if one can be made from the other by a dilation and rigid motions. You studied both in Unit 3 and Unit 4. A dilation changes the size. Rigid motions move the figure. Neither one changes the shape.
Because of this, similar figures always have two things in common:

Corresponding angles are equal.
Corresponding sides are proportional. The ratio of each pair of matching sides is the same number.

The sides of triangle \(ABC\) below are 4, 6, and 8. The sides of triangle \(DEF\) are 6, 9, and 12. The matching angles have the same marks.






Example 1: Check the sides
Use the figure above. Show that the sides of \(\triangle ABC\) and \(\triangle DEF\) are proportional.
Match the shortest sides, the middle sides, and the longest sides.
\(\dfrac{DE}{AB} = \dfrac{6}{4} = 1.5\)
\(\dfrac{EF}{BC} = \dfrac{9}{6} = 1.5\)
\(\dfrac{FD}{CA} = \dfrac{12}{8} = 1.5\)
All three ratios are 1.5. The sides are proportional, and the angles match. The triangles are similar.

Triangle 1 has sides 5, 7, and 9. Triangle 2 has sides 10, 14, and 18. Are the sides proportional?


\(\dfrac{10}{5} = 2\), \(\dfrac{14}{7} = 2\), \(\dfrac{18}{9} = 2\). Yes, the ratios are all 2.



5.2.2 - Similarity Statements and Scale Factor
A similarity statement names the figures in matching order. \(\triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF\) says that \(A\) matches \(D\), \(B\) matches \(E\), and \(C\) matches \(F\). So \(\overline{AB}\) matches \(\overline{DE}\), and \(\angle B\) matches \(\angle E\).
The scale factor \(k\) is the ratio of the new length to the old length. Always say which figure goes first.
\[
k = \dfrac{\text{length in the new figure}}{\text{length in the old figure}}
\]

Example 3: Write the statement and find \(k\)
Use the triangles in the figure above.

Write the similarity statement and name the side that matches \(\overline{BC}\).
Find the scale factor from \(\triangle ABC\) to \(\triangle DEF\).
Find the scale factor from \(\triangle DEF\) to \(\triangle ABC\).
\(\triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF\). Side \(\overline{BC}\) matches \(\overline{EF}\).
\(k = \dfrac{DE}{AB} = \dfrac{6}{4} = 1.5\). The new triangle is larger.
\(k = \dfrac{AB}{DE} = \dfrac{4}{6} = \dfrac{2}{3}\). The new triangle is smaller.

The two scale factors are reciprocals. \(1.5 \cdot \dfrac{2}{3} = 1\).


Which angle matches \(\angle L\)?
\(JK = 10\) and \(MN = 4\). Find the scale factor from \(\triangle JKL\) to \(\triangle MNP\).




\(\angle P\)
\(k = \dfrac{MN}{JK} = \dfrac{4}{10} = \dfrac{2}{5} = 0.4\)




5.2.3 - Are Two Figures Similar?
To decide if two polygons are similar, check both things. Matching angles are not enough. Proportional sides are not enough either (a square and a rhombus have equal side ratios, but their angles differ). You need both.

Example 5: Are the photos similar?





All the angles are \(90^\circ\).

Are photos A and B similar?
Are photos A and C similar?
Short sides: \(\dfrac{8}{4} = 2\). Long sides: \(\dfrac{12}{6} = 2\). The ratios are equal. Yes, A and B are similar, with \(k = 2\).
Short sides: \(\dfrac{8}{4} = 2\). Long sides: \(\dfrac{10}{6} \approx 1.67\). The ratios are not equal. No.

Photos A and C have equal angles, but they are not similar. This is a counterexample to the claim “rectangles with equal angles are similar.”

A photo is 6 in by 10 in. Another photo is 9 in by 15 in. Are they similar? If so, find \(k\) from the small photo to the large one.


\(\dfrac{9}{6} = 1.5\) and \(\dfrac{15}{10} = 1.5\). Yes, they are similar and \(k = 1.5\).



5.2.4 - Find a Missing Side
To find a missing side, write a proportion with two pairs of matching sides. Then use cross products.

Example 7: Find \(x\)





\(\triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF\). Find \(EF\).
\(\overline{AB}\) matches \(\overline{DE}\). \(\overline{BC}\) matches \(\overline{EF}\).
\(\dfrac{AB}{DE} = \dfrac{BC}{EF}\), so \(\dfrac{6}{10} = \dfrac{9}{x}\).
\(6x = 90\), so \(x = 15\).
Check with \(k\): \(k = \dfrac{10}{6} = \dfrac{5}{3}\) and \(9 \cdot \dfrac{5}{3} = 15\).

\(AB = 8\), \(DE = 12\), and \(BC = 14\). Find \(EF\).


\(\dfrac{8}{12} = \dfrac{14}{x}\), so \(8x = 168\) and \(x = 21\).


Example 9: Sides as expressions
\(\triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF\). \(AB = 6\), \(DE = 15\), \(BC = x + 4\), and \(EF = 5x\). Find \(x\) and \(EF\).
\(\dfrac{AB}{DE} = \dfrac{BC}{EF}\), so \(\dfrac{6}{15} = \dfrac{x + 4}{5x}\).
\(6 \cdot 5x = 15(x + 4)\)
\(30x = 15x + 60\)
\(15x = 60\), so \(x = 4\).
\(EF = 5(4) = 20\).
Check: \(BC = 8\), and \(\dfrac{8}{20} = 0.4 = \dfrac{6}{15}\).

\(AB = 8\), \(DE = 20\), \(BC = x + 1\), and \(EF = 3x + 1\). Find \(x\).


\(\dfrac{8}{20} = \dfrac{x + 1}{3x + 1}\), so \(8(3x + 1) = 20(x + 1)\).
\(24x + 8 = 20x + 20\), so \(4x = 12\) and \(x = 3\).



5.2.5 - Perimeter and Area
Look at the two rectangles. The small one is 2 by 3. The large one is 4 by 6. The scale factor is \(k = 2\).





Count the grid squares. The small rectangle has 6. The large one has 24. The area is \(4 = 2^2\) times as large. The perimeter goes from 10 to 20, which is 2 times as large.

Perimeters are in the ratio \(k\).
Areas are in the ratio \(k^2\).


Example 11: Perimeter and area
Two similar triangles have scale factor \(k = 3\) from the small one to the large one. The small triangle has sides 3, 4, and 5 and area 6 square inches. Find the perimeter and the area of the large triangle.
Small perimeter: \(3 + 4 + 5 = 12\) in.
Large perimeter: \(3 \cdot 12 = 36\) in.
Large area: \(3^2 \cdot 6 = 9 \cdot 6 = 54\) square in.
Check: the large sides are 9, 12, 15. \(9 + 12 + 15 = 36\).

A small rectangle is 2 cm by 4 cm. A similar rectangle has \(k = 5\). Find the perimeter and area of the large rectangle.


Small perimeter: \(12\) cm, so large: \(60\) cm.
Small area: \(8\) square cm, so large: \(25 \cdot 8 = 200\) square cm.


If \(k = 3\), the area is not 3 times as large. It is \(3^2 = 9\) times as large.

title: 5.3 - Similar Triangles
text:
🔥 Warm Up
A wheelchair ramp rises 1 foot over a length of 12 feet. A builder puts a support post under the ramp. Another post goes in at a different spot. The ramp, the ground, and each post make a triangle. All of these triangles have the same shape.
How can the builder be sure of this without measuring every angle? Triangles are special. You do not need to check every angle and every side. In this lesson you learn three short tests for similar triangles.

title: 5.3 - Similar Triangles
text:
A triangle has angles of \(48^\circ\) and \(75^\circ\). Find the third angle.
Solve \(\dfrac{x}{x + 4} = \dfrac{3}{5}\).
Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. What can you say about corresponding angles?

title: 5.3 - Similar Triangles
text:
👥 Learn Together

5.3.1 - AA Similarity
In Unit 4 you learned that three equal angles (AAA) do not make triangles congruent. They can be different sizes. Now you know why. Triangles with three equal angles have the same shape. They are similar.
You only need two pairs of equal angles. The angles of a triangle add to \(180^\circ\), so the third pair is equal for free.

If two angles of one triangle are equal to two angles of another triangle, the triangles are similar.


Example 1: Use AA





In the figure, \(m\angle A = m\angle D = 50^\circ\) and \(m\angle B = m\angle E = 60^\circ\).

Find \(m\angle C\) and \(m\angle F\).
Are the triangles similar? Write the statement.
\(m\angle C = 180 - 50 - 60 = 70^\circ\). \(m\angle F = 180 - 50 - 60 = 70^\circ\).
Two pairs of angles are equal (and the third pair is too). The triangles are similar by AA.

\(\triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF\)

\(\triangle PQR\) has \(m\angle P = 48^\circ\) and \(m\angle Q = 82^\circ\). \(\triangle XYZ\) has \(m\angle X = 48^\circ\) and \(m\angle Z = 50^\circ\). Are they similar?


\(m\angle R = 180 - 48 - 82 = 50^\circ\) and \(m\angle Y = 180 - 48 - 50 = 82^\circ\).
\(\angle P = \angle X\) and \(\angle R = \angle Z\) (and \(\angle Q = \angle Y\)). Yes, similar by AA. \(\triangle PQR \sim \triangle XYZ\).



5.3.2 - SSS and SAS Similarity
There are two more tests. They look like SSS and SAS for congruent triangles. The difference is that the sides do not have to be equal. They have to be proportional.

SSS similarity: the ratios of all three pairs of matching sides are equal.
SAS similarity: the ratios of two pairs of matching sides are equal, and the angles between those sides are equal.


Example 3: SSS
Triangle 1 has sides 4, 6, and 8. Triangle 2 has sides 10, 15, and 20. Are the triangles similar? Then try 6, 8, 10 and 9, 12, 16.
Match the shortest with the shortest, and so on.
\(\dfrac{10}{4} = 2.5\), \(\dfrac{15}{6} = 2.5\), \(\dfrac{20}{8} = 2.5\)
All three ratios are equal. The triangles are similar by SSS.
For 6, 8, 10 and 9, 12, 16: \(\dfrac{9}{6} = 1.5\), \(\dfrac{12}{8} = 1.5\), but \(\dfrac{16}{10} = 1.6\). The ratios are not all equal. Not similar.

Triangle 1 has sides 7, 9, and 12. Triangle 2 has sides 14, 18, and 24.


\(\dfrac{14}{7} = 2\), \(\dfrac{18}{9} = 2\), \(\dfrac{24}{12} = 2\). Similar by SSS, with \(k = 2\).


Example 5: SAS
In \(\triangle ABC\), \(AB = 6\), \(AC = 9\), and \(m\angle A = 40^\circ\). In \(\triangle DEF\), \(DE = 10\), \(DF = 15\), and \(m\angle D = 40^\circ\). Are the triangles similar?
The angle \(A\) is between \(\overline{AB}\) and \(\overline{AC}\). The angle \(D\) is between \(\overline{DE}\) and \(\overline{DF}\).
\(\dfrac{DE}{AB} = \dfrac{10}{6} = \dfrac{5}{3}\) and \(\dfrac{DF}{AC} = \dfrac{15}{9} = \dfrac{5}{3}\).
The ratios are equal and the included angles are equal. Similar by SAS. \(\triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF\).

In \(\triangle KLM\), \(KL = 4\), \(KM = 10\), and \(m\angle K = 65^\circ\). In \(\triangle RST\), \(RS = 6\), \(RT = 15\), and \(m\angle R = 65^\circ\).


\(\dfrac{6}{4} = 1.5\) and \(\dfrac{15}{10} = 1.5\). The angles \(K\) and \(R\) are between the sides. Similar by SAS. \(\triangle KLM \sim \triangle RST\).



5.3.3 - Which Test Works?
Here is how the tests for congruence (4.2) and similarity compare.








Test
Congruent triangles
Similar triangles




SSS
all three sides equal
all three sides proportional


SAS
two sides equal, included angle equal
two sides proportional, included angle equal


AA
not enough alone (use ASA or AAS)
two angles equal is enough



When you write the similarity statement, put matching vertices in the same position. \(\triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF\) means \(A \to D\), \(B \to E\), \(C \to F\).

Example 7: Pick the test
For each pair, write AA, SSS, SAS, or not similar. If they are similar, write the statement.

\(\triangle ABC\): \(m\angle A = 55^\circ\), \(m\angle B = 45^\circ\). \(\triangle XYZ\): \(m\angle X = 55^\circ\), \(m\angle Y = 45^\circ\).
\(\triangle ABC\): \(AB = 6\), \(BC = 8\), \(AC = 12\). \(\triangle DEF\): \(DE = 9\), \(EF = 12\), \(DF = 18\).
\(\triangle JKL\): \(JK = 5\), \(KL = 8\), \(m\angle K = 70^\circ\). \(\triangle MNP\): \(MN = 10\), \(NP = 12\), \(m\angle N = 70^\circ\).
AA. \(\triangle ABC \sim \triangle XYZ\).
\(\dfrac{9}{6} = \dfrac{12}{8} = \dfrac{18}{12} = 1.5\). SSS. \(\triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF\).
The angles \(K\) and \(N\) are between the sides. \(\dfrac{10}{5} = 2\) but \(\dfrac{12}{8} = 1.5\). The ratios are not equal. Not similar.


\(\triangle ABC\): \(AB = 9\), \(BC = 12\), \(m\angle B = 30^\circ\). \(\triangle DEF\): \(DE = 6\), \(EF = 8\), \(m\angle E = 30^\circ\). Which test works? Write the statement.


\(\dfrac{6}{9} = \dfrac{2}{3}\) and \(\dfrac{8}{12} = \dfrac{2}{3}\). The angles are between the sides. SAS. \(\triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF\).



5.3.4 - Overlapping Triangles
Sometimes one triangle sits inside another. They share an angle. If \(\overline{DE} \parallel \overline{BC}\), then \(\angle ADE\) and \(\angle ABC\) are corresponding angles, so they are equal. With the shared \(\angle A\), that is AA.
Tip: draw the two triangles apart. Then match the sides. Remember that the big triangle uses the whole side: \(AB\), not \(DB\).

Example 9: Nested triangles





\(\overline{DE} \parallel \overline{BC}\). \(AD = 6\), \(DB = 3\), and \(DE = 8\). Find \(BC\).
\(\angle A\) is shared. \(\angle ADE = \angle ABC\) (corresponding angles). So \(\triangle ADE \sim \triangle ABC\) by AA.
The big triangle uses the whole side: \(AB = 6 + 3 = 9\).
\(\dfrac{AD}{AB} = \dfrac{DE}{BC}\), so \(\dfrac{6}{9} = \dfrac{8}{x}\).
\(6x = 72\), so \(x = 12\).

\(AD = 9\), \(DB = 3\), and \(DE = 15\). Find \(BC\).


\(AB = 12\). \(\dfrac{9}{12} = \dfrac{15}{x}\), so \(9x = 180\) and \(x = 20\).


Example 11: Nested triangles with expressions





\(\overline{DE} \parallel \overline{BC}\). \(AD = x\), \(DB = 4\), \(AE = 6\), and \(EC = 3\). Find \(x\).
\(\triangle ADE \sim \triangle ABC\) by AA.
\(AB = x + 4\) and \(AC = 6 + 3 = 9\).
\(\dfrac{AD}{AB} = \dfrac{AE}{AC}\), so \(\dfrac{x}{x + 4} = \dfrac{6}{9}\).
\(9x = 6(x + 4)\), so \(9x = 6x + 24\) and \(3x = 24\).
\(x = 8\). Check: \(\dfrac{8}{12} = \dfrac{6}{9}\).

\(AD = 5\), \(DB = x\), \(AE = 4\), and \(EC = 6\). Find \(x\).


\(\dfrac{5}{5 + x} = \dfrac{4}{10}\), so \(50 = 4(5 + x)\).
\(50 = 20 + 4x\), so \(x = 7.5\).



5.3.5 - Similar Triangles on a Grid
On a coordinate grid, you can prove two triangles are similar with computation. Use the distance formula to check side ratios (SSS). Use slopes to check that sides are parallel (equal angles).

Example 13: Check with distances





Show that \(\triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF\). Find \(k\).
\(A(1, 1)\), \(B(3, 1)\), \(C(1, 4)\). \(D(5, 1)\), \(E(9, 1)\), \(F(5, 7)\).
\(AB = 2\), \(AC = 3\), \(BC = \sqrt{2^2 + 3^2} = \sqrt{13}\).
\(DE = 4\), \(DF = 6\), \(EF = \sqrt{4^2 + 6^2} = \sqrt{52} = 2\sqrt{13}\).
\(\dfrac{DE}{AB} = 2\), \(\dfrac{DF}{AC} = 2\), \(\dfrac{EF}{BC} = \dfrac{2\sqrt{13}}{\sqrt{13}} = 2\).
All ratios are 2. Similar by SSS, with \(k = 2\).

\(P(1, 1)\), \(Q(4, 1)\), \(R(1, 5)\) and \(S(5, 1)\), \(T(11, 1)\), \(U(5, 9)\). Use the distance formula.


\(PQ = 3\), \(PR = 4\), \(QR = 5\). \(ST = 6\), \(SU = 8\), \(TU = \sqrt{36 + 64} = 10\).
\(\dfrac{6}{3} = \dfrac{8}{4} = \dfrac{10}{5} = 2\). Similar by SSS.


Example 15: Check with slopes
\(P(0, 0)\), \(Q(4, 2)\), \(R(2, 6)\) and \(S(6, 1)\), \(T(12, 4)\), \(U(9, 10)\). Show that matching sides are parallel.
Slope of \(\overline{PQ}\): \(\dfrac{2 - 0}{4 - 0} = \dfrac{1}{2}\). Slope of \(\overline{ST}\): \(\dfrac{4 - 1}{12 - 6} = \dfrac{1}{2}\).
Slope of \(\overline{QR}\): \(\dfrac{6 - 2}{2 - 4} = -2\). Slope of \(\overline{TU}\): \(\dfrac{10 - 4}{9 - 12} = -2\).
Slope of \(\overline{PR}\): \(\dfrac{6}{2} = 3\). Slope of \(\overline{SU}\): \(\dfrac{9}{3} = 3\).
Every pair is parallel, so the angles are equal. The triangles are similar by AA.

Light from the top of a tree goes through a tiny hole and lands on the back wall of a dark box. The tree and its image make similar triangles. The image is upside down and much smaller.

title: 5.3 - Similar Triangles
text:
✍️ Practice On Your Own

Are the triangles similar? If yes, write the statement and the test.

\(\triangle ABC\): \(m\angle A = 62^\circ\), \(m\angle B = 48^\circ\). \(\triangle DEF\): \(m\angle D = 62^\circ\), \(m\angle E = 48^\circ\).

Are the triangles similar by SSS? Give the ratios.

Sides 3, 5, 7 and 9, 15, 21
Sides 4, 6, 9 and 6, 9, 14
Sides 5, 12, 13 and 15, 36, 39
Sides 8, 10, 12 and 12, 15, 19


Are the triangles similar by SAS? If you cannot tell, explain.

\(AB = 6\), \(AC = 10\), \(m\angle A = 50^\circ\). \(DE = 9\), \(DF = 15\), \(m\angle D = 50^\circ\).
\(AB = 8\), \(AC = 12\), \(m\angle A = 70^\circ\). \(DE = 12\), \(DF = 20\), \(m\angle D = 70^\circ\).
\(JK = 5\), \(KL = 7\), \(m\angle J = 40^\circ\). \(MN = 10\), \(NP = 14\), \(m\angle M = 40^\circ\).
\(AB = 3\), \(BC = 5\), \(m\angle B = 100^\circ\). \(DE = 9\), \(EF = 15\), \(m\angle E = 100^\circ\).


Write the statement.

\(m\angle P = m\angle T\) and \(m\angle Q = m\angle U\) in \(\triangle PQR\) and \(\triangle STU\). Write the similarity statement.


Use the figure. \(\overline{DE} \parallel \overline{BC}\).






Explain why \(\triangle ADE \sim \triangle ABC\). Name the test.
\(AD = 4\), \(DB = 2\), and \(DE = 6\). Find \(BC\).
\(AD = 5\), \(AB = 15\), and \(AE = 4\). Find \(AC\).
\(AD = x\), \(DB = 3\), \(AE = 6\), and \(EC = 4\). Find \(x\).
Mohammed has \(AD = 4\), \(AB = 10\), and \(DE = 3\). He writes \(\dfrac{4}{10} = \dfrac{BC}{3}\) and gets \(BC = 1.2\). Find his mistake and fix it.


Use the coordinate plane.

\(A(0, 0)\), \(B(6, 0)\), \(C(0, 8)\) and \(D(2, 2)\), \(E(5, 2)\), \(F(2, 6)\). Use the distance formula to show \(\triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF\). Find \(k\) from \(\triangle ABC\) to \(\triangle DEF\).
\(G(0, 0)\), \(H(4, 0)\), \(J(4, 3)\) and \(K(1, -2)\), \(L(9, -2)\), \(M(9, 4)\). Use slopes to show the triangles are similar. Find \(k\) from \(\triangle GHJ\) to \(\triangle KLM\).
\(A(1, 1)\), \(B(4, 1)\), \(C(1, 5)\) and \(D(6, 1)\), \(E(10, 1)\), \(F(6, 7)\). Both triangles have a right angle (\(A\) and \(D\)). Are they similar? Use side ratios.


Real problems.

A ramp is 12 ft long and rises 1 ft. A post stands under the ramp 8 ft along its length. The post and the ramp make a triangle that is similar to the whole ramp triangle. How tall is the post in inches?
A pinhole camera is a box 0.2 m deep. A tree is 12 m tall and 30 m from the hole. The tree and its image make similar triangles. How tall is the image in centimeters?
Lucía says, “Any two right triangles that each have a \(30^\circ\) angle are similar.” Is she right? Explain.


Test practice

In \(\triangle ABC\) and \(\triangle DEF\), \(m\angle A = m\angle D = 50^\circ\), \(AB = 6\), \(AC = 8\), and \(DE = 9\). What value of \(DF\) shows that \(\triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF\) by SAS?
A. 10
B. 12
C. 14
D. 16
In \(\triangle ABC\), point \(D\) is on \(\overline{AB}\) and point \(E\) is on \(\overline{AC}\). \(\overline{DE} \parallel \overline{BC}\), \(AD = 6\), \(AB = 10\), and \(DE = 9\). What is \(BC\)?
A. 5.4
B. 12
C. 15
D. 25


Challenge

Jamal says, “Any two isosceles triangles are similar.” Give a counterexample. Then tell one extra fact that would make two isosceles triangles similar.

title: 5.4 - Triangle Proportionality
text:
🔥 Warm Up
A lot owner wants to divide a triangle-shaped yard with a fence. The fence must run parallel to the street side. Where should the fence meet the two other sides?
A line parallel to one side of a triangle cuts the other two sides in the same ratio. This is a very useful fact. You can use it to find lengths, to prove two lines are parallel, and to see why a segment joining two midpoints is half as long as the third side.

title: 5.4 - Triangle Proportionality
text:
Solve \(\dfrac{x}{12} = \dfrac{5}{8}\).
Find the midpoint of \((2, 5)\) and \((8, -1)\).
\(\triangle ADE \sim \triangle ABC\), \(AD = 3\), \(AB = 9\), and \(DE = 5\). Find \(BC\).

title: 5.4 - Triangle Proportionality
text:
👥 Learn Together

5.4.1 - A Line Parallel to a Side
In 5.3 you saw that a line parallel to a side makes a small triangle that is similar to the big one. That gives a new fact about the pieces of the sides.
Triangle Proportionality Theorem. If a line is parallel to one side of a triangle and meets the other two sides, it divides those sides in the same ratio.
\[
\dfrac{AD}{DB} = \dfrac{AE}{EC}
\]
Why? Look at the numbers. If \(AD = 6\), \(DB = 4\), \(AE = 9\), and \(EC = 6\), then \(\dfrac{6}{4} = 1.5\) and \(\dfrac{9}{6} = 1.5\). The two parts on each side have the same ratio. Also \(\dfrac{AD}{AB} = \dfrac{6}{10}\) and \(\dfrac{AE}{AC} = \dfrac{9}{15}\). Both are \(0.6\), which is what similar triangles give.

Example 1: Find a missing part





\(\overline{DE} \parallel \overline{BC}\). \(AD = 6\), \(DB = 4\), and \(AE = 9\). Find \(EC\).
\(\dfrac{AD}{DB} = \dfrac{AE}{EC}\), so \(\dfrac{6}{4} = \dfrac{9}{x}\).
\(6x = 36\), so \(x = 6\).
\(EC = 6\).

\(AD = 10\), \(DB = 4\), and \(EC = 6\). Find \(AE\).


\(\dfrac{10}{4} = \dfrac{x}{6}\), so \(4x = 60\) and \(AE = 15\).


Example 3: Expressions





\(\overline{DE} \parallel \overline{BC}\). \(AD = x\), \(DB = 6\), \(AE = x + 2\), and \(EC = 9\). Find \(x\).
\(\dfrac{x}{6} = \dfrac{x + 2}{9}\)
\(9x = 6(x + 2)\)
\(9x = 6x + 12\), so \(3x = 12\) and \(x = 4\).
Check: \(\dfrac{4}{6} = \dfrac{6}{9}\).


5.4.2 - The Converse
The converse also works. If a segment cuts two sides of a triangle in the same ratio, it is parallel to the third side. Look at the two triangles. Both look like they have a parallel segment. Only one does.






Example 4: Is it parallel?
Use the figure above.

In triangle (a), is \(\overline{DE} \parallel \overline{BC}\)?
In triangle (b), is \(\overline{DE} \parallel \overline{BC}\)?
\(\dfrac{AD}{DB} = \dfrac{6}{9} = \dfrac{2}{3}\) and \(\dfrac{AE}{EC} = \dfrac{8}{12} = \dfrac{2}{3}\). The ratios are equal. Yes, \(\overline{DE} \parallel \overline{BC}\).
\(\dfrac{AD}{DB} = \dfrac{4}{8} = \dfrac{1}{2}\) and \(\dfrac{AE}{EC} = \dfrac{5}{15} = \dfrac{1}{3}\). The ratios are not equal. No.


A segment that looks parallel may not be. Only numbers (equal ratios) or parallel marks tell you for sure.



5.4.3 - The Midsegment of a Triangle
A midsegment of a triangle joins the midpoints of two sides. Each midpoint makes the ratio \(\dfrac{AD}{DB} = 1\). So the converse says \(\overline{DE} \parallel \overline{BC}\). The triangles \(ADE\) and \(ABC\) have scale factor \(\dfrac{1}{2}\).





Midsegment Theorem. A midsegment is parallel to the third side. It is half as long: \(DE = \dfrac{1}{2} BC\).

Example 5: Use the midsegment
\(D\) and \(E\) are the midpoints of \(\overline{AB}\) and \(\overline{AC}\).

\(BC = 18\). Find \(DE\).
\(DE = 3x + 1\) and \(BC = 5x + 12\). Find \(x\) and \(BC\).
\(DE = \dfrac{1}{2}(18) = 9\).
\(BC = 2 \cdot DE\), so \(5x + 12 = 2(3x + 1)\).

\(5x + 12 = 6x + 2\), so \(x = 10\).
\(BC = 5(10) + 12 = 62\). (Check: \(DE = 31\).)


\(DE = 7.5\). Find \(BC\).
\(DE = 2x + 4\) and \(BC = 6x - 4\). Find \(x\).




\(BC = 2(7.5) = 15\).
\(6x - 4 = 2(2x + 4)\), so \(6x - 4 = 4x + 8\), \(2x = 12\), and \(x = 6\).



Example 7: Check with coordinates





\(A(2, 8)\), \(B(0, 0)\), \(C(10, 2)\). \(D\) is the midpoint of \(\overline{AB}\). \(E\) is the midpoint of \(\overline{AC}\). Show that \(\overline{DE} \parallel \overline{BC}\) and \(DE = \dfrac{1}{2} BC\).
Midpoints: \(D = \left(\dfrac{2 + 0}{2}, \dfrac{8 + 0}{2}\right) = (1, 4)\) and \(E = \left(\dfrac{2 + 10}{2}, \dfrac{8 + 2}{2}\right) = (6, 5)\).
Slope of \(\overline{DE}\): \(\dfrac{5 - 4}{6 - 1} = \dfrac{1}{5}\). Slope of \(\overline{BC}\): \(\dfrac{2 - 0}{10 - 0} = \dfrac{1}{5}\). Equal slopes, so parallel.
\(DE = \sqrt{5^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt{26}\) and \(BC = \sqrt{10^2 + 2^2} = \sqrt{104} = 2\sqrt{26}\).
So \(DE = \dfrac{1}{2} BC\).


5.4.4 - Parallel Lines and Transversals
Three parallel cross streets cut two avenues. The lots along the avenues are cut in proportion.





If three or more parallel lines cut two transversals, the transversals are cut proportionally.

Example 8: Lots on a street
Use the street map above. Pine St, Oak St, and Elm St are parallel. Find \(x\).
\(\dfrac{60}{90} = \dfrac{80}{x}\)
\(60x = 7200\), so \(x = 120\).
The second lot on 2nd Ave is 120 ft long.

Three parallel streets cross two avenues. On one avenue, the lots are 45 ft and 75 ft. On the other, the first lot is 60 ft. How long is the second lot?


\(\dfrac{45}{75} = \dfrac{60}{x}\), so \(45x = 4500\) and \(x = 100\) ft.

title: 5.5 - Indirect Measurement
text:
🔥 Warm Up
How tall is the tree in front of your school? You cannot climb it with a tape measure. How wide is a river? You cannot walk across it. In both cases you can still find the answer.
You measure things that are easy to reach. Then you use similar triangles to find the length you cannot reach. This is called indirect measurement. People who build bridges, make maps, and survey land use it every day.

title: 5.5 - Indirect Measurement
text:
Solve \(\dfrac{6}{4} = \dfrac{h}{30}\).
Two right triangles each have a \(35^\circ\) angle. Are they similar? Say why.
Change 5 ft 6 in to feet.

title: 5.5 - Indirect Measurement
text:
👥 Learn Together

5.5.1 - Shadows

1. Draw a sketch and label it.
2. Name the similar triangles.
3. Write a proportion with matching sides in the same positions.
4. Solve, and answer with units.

At the same time of day, the sun hits everything at the same angle. A person and a tree each stand straight up. Each makes a right triangle with its shadow. Both triangles have a right angle and the same sun angle, so they are similar by AA.

Example 1: Height of a tree





A person 5 ft tall has a shadow 8 ft long. At the same time, a tree has a shadow 40 ft long. How tall is the tree?
The triangles are similar. Put height over shadow on both sides.
\(\dfrac{5}{8} = \dfrac{h}{40}\)
\(8h = 200\), so \(h = 25\).
The tree is 25 ft tall.

A stick 3 ft tall casts a shadow 2 ft long. At the same time, a pole casts a shadow 18 ft long. How tall is the pole?


\(\dfrac{3}{2} = \dfrac{h}{18}\), so \(2h = 54\) and \(h = 27\) ft.



5.5.2 - Mirrors
Put a mirror flat on the ground. Stand where you can see the top of the building in the mirror. The light from the top of the building hits the mirror and bounces to your eye. The two angles at the mirror are equal. The person and the building each make a right angle with the ground. So the two triangles are similar by AA.

Example 3: Height of a building





Mei’s eyes are 1.6 m above the ground. She stands 2 m from a mirror on the ground and sees the top of a building in it. The mirror is 30 m from the building. How tall is the building?
The small triangle has legs 1.6 and 2. The large triangle has legs \(h\) and 30.
\(\dfrac{1.6}{2} = \dfrac{h}{30}\)
\(2h = 48\), so \(h = 24\).
The building is 24 m tall.

Daniel’s eyes are 1.5 m above the ground. He stands 3 m from a mirror and sees the top of a tree. The mirror is 36 m from the tree. How tall is the tree?


\(\dfrac{1.5}{3} = \dfrac{h}{36}\), so \(3h = 54\) and \(h = 18\) m.



5.5.3 - Across a River
You want to know the width of a river. A tree \(A\) stands on the far bank. Follow these steps:

Stand at \(B\) on your bank, straight across from the tree. This makes \(\overline{AB}\) the width you want.
Walk along your bank and put a stake at \(C\). Walk a little farther and put a stake at \(D\).
At \(D\), turn and walk straight away from the river to a point \(E\) where you see the tree \(A\) and the stake \(C\) in a line.

Now \(\triangle ABC \sim \triangle EDC\). Both have a right angle, and the angles at \(C\) are vertical angles.

Example 5: Width of a river





\(BC = 20\) m, \(CD = 5\) m, and \(DE = 6\) m. Find the width \(AB\) of the river.
\(\triangle ABC \sim \triangle EDC\). Match \(\overline{AB}\) with \(\overline{ED}\) and \(\overline{BC}\) with \(\overline{DC}\).
\(\dfrac{AB}{DE} = \dfrac{BC}{CD}\), so \(\dfrac{x}{6} = \dfrac{20}{5}\).
\(5x = 120\), so \(x = 24\).
The river is 24 m wide.

\(BC = 15\) m, \(CD = 5\) m, and \(DE = 4\) m. Find \(AB\).


\(\dfrac{x}{4} = \dfrac{15}{5}\), so \(5x = 60\) and \(x = 12\) m.



5.5.4 - Mixed Real Problems
Some problems hide which lengths match. Always draw the sketch. In the next example, the small triangle is Tomás and his shadow. The big triangle is the lamp and the whole ground length from the lamp to the tip of the shadow.

Example 7: Which lengths match?





A lamp stands on a level street. Tomás is 6 ft tall. He stands 10 ft from the base of the lamp. His shadow is 5 ft long. How tall is the lamp?
The small triangle: height 6, base 5 (the shadow).
The big triangle: height \(h\), base \(10 + 5 = 15\) (from the lamp to the tip of the shadow).
\(\dfrac{6}{5} = \dfrac{h}{15}\)
\(5h = 90\), so \(h = 18\).
The lamp is 18 ft tall.

Maria is 5 ft tall. She stands 12 ft from a lamp post. Her shadow is 6 ft long. How tall is the lamp post?


Big base: \(12 + 6 = 18\). \(\dfrac{5}{6} = \dfrac{h}{18}\), so \(6h = 90\) and \(h = 15\) ft.


Example 9: Test wording
A vertical post that is 2.5 feet tall casts a shadow that is 1.5 feet long. At the same time, a nearby tower casts a shadow that is 36 feet long. What is the height of the tower?
A. 21.6 ft B. 40 ft C. 60 ft D. 100 ft
Draw the sketch. Height over shadow:
\(\dfrac{2.5}{1.5} = \dfrac{h}{36}\), so \(1.5h = 90\) and \(h = 60\).
The answer is C, 60 ft.

Find the height of the school flagpole. Work with a partner. Measure your height, your shadow, and the flagpole’s shadow with a tape measure. Write a proportion and solve. Then check with a mirror on the ground.

title: Unit 5 Summary
text:
5.1 - Ratios and Proportions
Example: \(\dfrac{x}{12} = \dfrac{5}{8}\) gives \(8x = 60\), so \(x = 7.5\). Angles in the ratio \(2 : 3 : 4\): \(9x = 180\), so \(x = 20\) and the angles are \(40^\circ\), \(60^\circ\), \(80^\circ\).

title: Unit 5 Summary
text:
A ratio compares two numbers by division: \(2 : 3\), \(\dfrac{2}{3}\), or “2 to 3”. Use the same units.
A proportion says that two ratios are equal. Cross products: \(\dfrac{a}{b} = \dfrac{c}{d}\) means \(ad = bc\).
Put the same kind of number in the same place in both ratios.
A scale like \(1 \text{ in} : 20 \text{ ft}\) turns a drawing length into a real length, and the other way.
To split a total in the ratio \(3 : 5\), write the parts \(3x\) and \(5x\) and add them to the total.

title: Unit 5 Summary
text:
5.2 - Similar Figures and Scale Factor

Similar figures (\(\sim\)) have the same shape. Matching angles are equal and matching sides are proportional.
The order of the letters in \(\triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF\) shows which parts match.
The scale factor \(k\) is the new length divided by the old length. The other direction uses the reciprocal.
To find a missing side, write a proportion with matching sides, then use cross products.
Perimeters change by \(k\). Areas change by \(k^2\).
Equal angles alone are not enough. Two rectangles with equal angles can be different shapes.






Example: If \(k = 1.5\), a side of 4 becomes 6. A perimeter of 18 becomes 27. An area of 10 becomes \(1.5^2 \cdot 10 = 22.5\).

title: Unit 5 Summary
text:
5.3 - Similar Triangles

AA: two pairs of equal angles make triangles similar.
SSS: all three pairs of sides are proportional.
SAS: two pairs of sides are proportional and the included angles are equal.
If \(\overline{DE} \parallel \overline{BC}\), then \(\triangle ADE \sim \triangle ABC\). Draw the triangles apart and use the whole side \(AB\) for the big triangle.
On a grid, use the distance formula for side ratios and slopes for parallel sides.






Example: Sides 4, 6, 8 and 10, 15, 20 have equal ratios of 2.5. The triangles are similar by SSS.

title: Unit 5 Summary
text:
5.4 - Triangle Proportionality

If \(\overline{DE} \parallel \overline{BC}\), then \(\dfrac{AD}{DB} = \dfrac{AE}{EC}\).
Converse: if the two ratios are equal, then \(\overline{DE} \parallel \overline{BC}\).
A midsegment joins the midpoints of two sides. It is parallel to the third side and half as long.
Three parallel lines cut two transversals into proportional parts.
On a grid, use the midpoint formula and slopes to check a midsegment.






Example: \(AD = 6\), \(DB = 4\), and \(AE = 9\). Then \(\dfrac{6}{4} = \dfrac{9}{x}\), so \(x = 6\).

title: Unit 5 Summary
text:
5.5 - Indirect Measurement

Use similar triangles to find a length you cannot measure.
Four steps: draw a sketch, name the similar triangles, write a proportion, solve and use units.
Shadows: a person and a tree at the same time make similar right triangles.
Mirrors: the angle in equals the angle out. Use eye height.
River: with stakes \(B\), \(C\), \(D\) and point \(E\), \(\dfrac{AB}{DE} = \dfrac{BC}{CD}\).






Example: A 5 ft person has an 8 ft shadow. A tree has a 40 ft shadow. \(\dfrac{5}{8} = \dfrac{h}{40}\), so \(h = 25\) ft.

title: Unit 5 Review
text:
5.1 - Ratios and Proportions
Example 1: a. Solve \(\dfrac{x - 3}{4} = \dfrac{9}{x - 3}\).

The angles of a triangle are in the ratio \(3 : 4 : 5\). Find each angle.
\((x - 3)^2 = 36\), so \(x - 3 = 6\) or \(x - 3 = -6\). \(x = 9\) or \(x = -3\).
\(3x + 4x + 5x = 180\), so \(x = 15\). The angles are \(45^\circ\), \(60^\circ\), and \(75^\circ\).



5.2 - Similar Figures and Scale Factor
Example 2: \(\triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF\). \(AB = 8\) and \(DE = 12\). The perimeter of \(\triangle ABC\) is 30 and its area is 40 square units. Find \(k\) from \(\triangle ABC\) to \(\triangle DEF\). Then find the perimeter and area of \(\triangle DEF\).
\(k = \dfrac{12}{8} = 1.5\). Perimeter: \(1.5 \cdot 30 = 45\). Area: \(1.5^2 \cdot 40 = 90\) square units.


5.3 - Similar Triangles
Example 3: \(AB = 9\), \(AC = 12\), and \(m\angle A = 55^\circ\). \(DE = 6\), \(DF = 8\), and \(m\angle D = 55^\circ\). Are the triangles similar? Write the statement.
\(\dfrac{6}{9} = \dfrac{2}{3}\) and \(\dfrac{8}{12} = \dfrac{2}{3}\). The angles are between the sides. Similar by SAS. \(\triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF\).


5.4 - Triangle Proportionality
Example 4: a. \(\overline{DE} \parallel \overline{BC}\). \(AD = 5\), \(DB = x\), \(AE = 6\), and \(EC = 9\). Find \(x\).

A midsegment is \(2x - 1\) long. The side it is parallel to is \(3x + 5\) long. Find \(x\).
\(\dfrac{5}{x} = \dfrac{6}{9}\), so \(6x = 45\) and \(x = 7.5\).
\(3x + 5 = 2(2x - 1)\), so \(3x + 5 = 4x - 2\) and \(x = 7\). The midsegment is 13 and the side is 26.



5.5 - Indirect Measurement
Example 5: A person 6 ft tall casts a shadow 4.5 ft long. At the same time a flagpole casts a shadow 27 ft long. How tall is the flagpole?
\(\dfrac{6}{4.5} = \dfrac{h}{27}\), so \(4.5h = 162\) and \(h = 36\) ft.

title: Introduction
text:
What You’ll Learn
Welcome to Unit 6! How long must a wheelchair ramp be? How tall is a cell tower? How steep is a roof? People who build things answer these questions every day with right triangles.
In this unit you learn trigonometry. Trigonometry connects the angles of a right triangle to the lengths of its sides. With one side and one angle, you can find everything else about the triangle.
By the end of this unit, you will be able to:

title: Introduction
text:
Find the sides of \(45^\circ\)-\(45^\circ\)-\(90^\circ\) and \(30^\circ\)-\(60^\circ\)-\(90^\circ\) triangles
Write the sine, cosine, and tangent of an angle
Use trigonometry to find a missing side
Use inverse trigonometry to find a missing angle
Use the relationship between sine and cosine of complementary angles
Solve problems with angles of elevation and depression
Solve real problems with ramps, roofs, towers, and maps

title: Introduction
text:
Topics in This Unit
Special Right Triangles
Find missing sides of two special triangles without a calculator.
The Trigonometric Ratios
Sine, cosine, and tangent compare the sides of a right triangle.
Solving for a Side
Use one angle and one side to find another side.
Solving for an Angle
Use two sides to find an angle.
Sine and Cosine of Complementary Angles
The sine of one acute angle is the cosine of the other.
Angles of Elevation and Depression
Look up or look down to find heights and distances.
Modeling with Right Triangles
Plan ramps, roofs, and routes with right triangles.
Unit 6 Summary
Every tool from the unit in one place, to keep beside you.
Unit 6 Review
Practice every skill from the unit before the quiz.

title: 6.1 - Special Right Triangles
text:
🔥 Warm Up
A baseball diamond is a square. Each side is \(90\) feet. The catcher at home plate must throw the ball to second base. How far is that throw?
The throw is the diagonal of the square. It cuts the square into two right triangles. These triangles always have the same angles, so their sides always have the same pattern. In this lesson you learn two triangles whose sides you can find with no calculator and no table.

title: 6.1 - Special Right Triangles
text:
A right triangle has legs \(5\) and \(12\). Find the hypotenuse.
Simplify \(\sqrt{48}\).
Solve \(5x - 3 = 2x + 12\).

title: 6.1 - Special Right Triangles
text:
👥 Learn Together

6.1.1 - The 45°-45°-90° Triangle
Cut a square in half along its diagonal. You get two identical right triangles.





Each triangle has a right angle at \(B\). The two legs are sides of the square, so they are equal. That makes the other two angles equal, so each is \(45^\circ\). This is a \(45^\circ\)-\(45^\circ\)-\(90^\circ\) triangle. It is one kind of special right triangle.
Try a square with side \(6\). The Pythagorean theorem gives the diagonal:
\[
d^2 = 6^2 + 6^2 = 72, \qquad d = \sqrt{72} = 6\sqrt{2}.
\]
Now use any side \(s\):
\[
d^2 = s^2 + s^2 = 2s^2, \qquad d = s\sqrt{2}.
\]






The two legs are equal. The hypotenuse is the leg times \(\sqrt{2}\).
\[
\text{hypotenuse} = \text{leg} \cdot \sqrt{2}
\]


Example 1: Find the hypotenuse from a leg
A \(45^\circ\)-\(45^\circ\)-\(90^\circ\) triangle has a leg of \(7\). Find the hypotenuse. Give the exact answer and the answer to the nearest tenth.
\[
\text{hypotenuse} = 7\sqrt{2} \approx 9.9
\]
The hypotenuse is \(7\sqrt{2}\), or about \(9.9\).

\(11\sqrt{2} \approx 15.6\)


Example 2: The baseball diamond
The bases are \(90\) feet apart. How far is it from home plate to second base? Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
The path home, first, second makes a \(45^\circ\)-\(45^\circ\)-\(90^\circ\) triangle. Its legs are \(90\) feet. The throw is the hypotenuse.
\[
d = 90\sqrt{2} \approx 127.3
\]
The throw is about \(127.3\) feet.

Going the other way: from the hypotenuse
If you know the hypotenuse, divide by \(\sqrt{2}\) to find a leg. Then rationalize the denominator (Lesson 2.1).
Example 3: Find a leg from the hypotenuse
The hypotenuse of a \(45^\circ\)-\(45^\circ\)-\(90^\circ\) triangle is \(8\). Find each leg. Give the exact answer and the answer to the nearest tenth.
\[
\text{leg} = \frac{8}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{8}{\sqrt{2}} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{8\sqrt{2}}{2} = 4\sqrt{2} \approx 5.7
\]
Each leg is \(4\sqrt{2}\), or about \(5.7\).

\(\dfrac{12}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{12\sqrt{2}}{2} = 6\sqrt{2} \approx 8.5\)


Dividing by \(\sqrt{2}\) is the same as multiplying by \(\sqrt{2}\) and then dividing by \(2\). Check with Example 3: \(8 \cdot \sqrt{2} \div 2 = 4\sqrt{2}\).


Example 4: Show it with coordinates





Points \(A(0, 0)\), \(B(5, 0)\), and \(C(5, 5)\) make a triangle. Show that it is a \(45^\circ\)-\(45^\circ\)-\(90^\circ\) triangle. Find \(AC\).

\(\overline{AB}\) is horizontal and \(\overline{BC}\) is vertical. So the angle at \(B\) is \(90^\circ\).
\(AB = 5\) and \(BC = 5\). The legs are equal, so the other two angles are equal. Each is \((180^\circ - 90^\circ) \div 2 = 45^\circ\).
Use the distance formula: \(AC = \sqrt{5^2 + 5^2} = \sqrt{50} = 5\sqrt{2} \approx 7.1\).

This matches the rule: hypotenuse = leg \(\cdot \sqrt{2}\).


Show that \(\triangle PQR\) is a \(45^\circ\)-\(45^\circ\)-\(90^\circ\) triangle.
Find \(PR\) exactly.




\(\overline{PQ}\) is horizontal and \(\overline{QR}\) is vertical, so the angle at \(Q\) is \(90^\circ\). \(PQ = 6\) and \(QR = 6\), so the legs are equal.
\(PR = 6\sqrt{2}\)





6.1.2 - The 30°-60°-90° Triangle
Start with an equilateral triangle. All sides are \(2x\) and all angles are \(60^\circ\). Draw the height \(\overline{CM}\). It makes a right angle with the base and cuts the base in half.





Each half is a \(30^\circ\)-\(60^\circ\)-\(90^\circ\) triangle. Its hypotenuse is \(2x\). Its shortest leg is \(x\). Use the Pythagorean theorem to find the height \(h\):
\[
x^2 + h^2 = (2x)^2 \quad\Rightarrow\quad h^2 = 4x^2 - x^2 = 3x^2 \quad\Rightarrow\quad h = x\sqrt{3}.
\]







The short leg is across from the \(30^\circ\) angle. Call it \(x\).
The hypotenuse is \(2x\).
The long leg is across from the \(60^\circ\) angle. It is \(x\sqrt{3}\).


The shortest side is across from the smallest angle. The longest side is across from the largest angle. Always find the short leg first.

Example 5: Find the sides from the short leg
The short leg of a \(30^\circ\)-\(60^\circ\)-\(90^\circ\) triangle is \(5\). Find the other two sides.

Hypotenuse: \(2 \cdot 5 = 10\).
Long leg: \(5\sqrt{3} \approx 8.7\).


Hypotenuse: \(2 \cdot 9 = 18\). Long leg: \(9\sqrt{3} \approx 15.6\).


Example 6: Find the sides from the hypotenuse
The hypotenuse of a \(30^\circ\)-\(60^\circ\)-\(90^\circ\) triangle is \(14\). Find the other two sides.

Short leg: half the hypotenuse, \(14 \div 2 = 7\).
Long leg: \(7\sqrt{3} \approx 12.1\).


Short leg: \(20 \div 2 = 10\). Long leg: \(10\sqrt{3} \approx 17.3\).


Example 7: Find the sides from the long leg
The long leg of a \(30^\circ\)-\(60^\circ\)-\(90^\circ\) triangle is \(6\). Find the other two sides.
The long leg is \(x\sqrt{3}\). So \(x\sqrt{3} = 6\). Divide by \(\sqrt{3}\) and rationalize:
\[
x = \frac{6}{\sqrt{3}} = \frac{6\sqrt{3}}{3} = 2\sqrt{3} \approx 3.5
\]

Short leg: \(2\sqrt{3} \approx 3.5\).
Hypotenuse: \(2x = 4\sqrt{3} \approx 6.9\).


Short leg: \(\dfrac{9}{\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{9\sqrt{3}}{3} = 3\sqrt{3} \approx 5.2\). Hypotenuse: \(2 \cdot 3\sqrt{3} = 6\sqrt{3} \approx 10.4\).


The \(\sqrt{3}\) belongs on the long leg. The hypotenuse is a whole number multiple of the short leg: \(2x\). It never has \(\sqrt{3}\) when you start from the short leg.




6.1.3 - Choosing the Right Rule
Look at the angles first.



The triangle has angles
Legs and hypotenuse




\(45^\circ\), \(45^\circ\), \(90^\circ\)
\(s\), \(s\), \(s\sqrt{2}\)


\(30^\circ\), \(60^\circ\), \(90^\circ\)
\(x\), \(x\sqrt{3}\), \(2x\)



When a side is an expression, write an equation and solve for \(x\).
Example 8: Sides that are expressions






A \(45^\circ\)-\(45^\circ\)-\(90^\circ\) triangle has legs \(3x - 2\) and \(2x + 2\). Find \(x\), the legs, and the hypotenuse.
The legs are equal: \(3x - 2 = 2x + 2\), so \(x = 4\).
Each leg is \(3(4) - 2 = 10\). The hypotenuse is \(10\sqrt{2} \approx 14.1\).
In the figure, the short leg is \(x + 4\) and the hypotenuse is \(3x - 1\). Find \(x\) and all three sides.
The hypotenuse is twice the short leg: \(3x - 1 = 2(x + 4)\). So \(3x - 1 = 2x + 8\) and \(x = 9\).
Short leg: \(9 + 4 = 13\). Hypotenuse: \(3(9) - 1 = 26\). Long leg: \(13\sqrt{3} \approx 22.5\).



A \(45^\circ\)-\(45^\circ\)-\(90^\circ\) triangle has legs \(5x - 3\) and \(2x + 9\). Find \(x\) and the hypotenuse (nearest tenth).
A \(30^\circ\)-\(60^\circ\)-\(90^\circ\) triangle has short leg \(x + 6\) and hypotenuse \(3x - 4\). Find \(x\) and the long leg (nearest tenth).




\(5x - 3 = 2x + 9\), so \(x = 4\). Each leg is \(17\). The hypotenuse is \(17\sqrt{2} \approx 24.0\).
\(3x - 4 = 2(x + 6)\), so \(x = 16\). The short leg is \(22\). The long leg is \(22\sqrt{3} \approx 38.1\).



Example 9: Error analysis
Kofi says: “A \(30^\circ\)-\(60^\circ\)-\(90^\circ\) triangle has a short leg of \(6\). So the hypotenuse is \(6\sqrt{3}\).” Find his mistake and fix it.
Kofi put \(\sqrt{3}\) on the hypotenuse. The hypotenuse is twice the short leg: \(2 \cdot 6 = 12\). The long leg is \(6\sqrt{3}\). Check: \(6^2 + (6\sqrt{3})^2 = 36 + 108 = 144 = 12^2\).



6.1.4 - Special Triangles in the Real World
Example 10: A ramp





A ramp is \(16\) feet long. It makes a \(30^\circ\) angle with the ground. How high does it rise? How far does it reach along the ground? Round to the nearest tenth.
The ramp is the hypotenuse of a \(30^\circ\)-\(60^\circ\)-\(90^\circ\) triangle. The rise \(h\) is across from the \(30^\circ\) angle, so it is the short leg.

\(h = 16 \div 2 = 8\) feet.
\(d = 8\sqrt{3} \approx 13.9\) feet.

The ramp rises \(8\) feet and reaches about \(13.9\) feet along the ground.

Example 11: A square tile
A square floor tile has sides of \(18\) inches. A crack runs along the diagonal. How long is the crack? Round to the nearest tenth of an inch.
The diagonal is the hypotenuse of a \(45^\circ\)-\(45^\circ\)-\(90^\circ\) triangle with legs \(18\).
\[
18\sqrt{2} \approx 25.5 \text{ inches}
\]

The height cuts the triangle into two 30-60-90 triangles. The short leg is \(30 \div 2 = 15\). The height is the long leg: \(15\sqrt{3} \approx 26.0\) feet.


A hexagon is made of six equilateral triangles. The distance across a hexagon nut from one flat side to the opposite flat side is two heights of those triangles. Wrench makers use the \(30^\circ\)-\(60^\circ\)-\(90^\circ\) rule to find it.

Challenge

title: 6.2 - The Trigonometric Ratios
text:
🔥 Warm Up
A ramp rises \(1\) foot for every \(12\) feet of ground it covers. A roof rises \(6\) inches for every \(12\) inches across. A road climbs \(6\) feet for every \(100\) feet of flat ground.
All three are right triangles. In each one, the ratio of two sides tells how steep the slope is. Steeper slopes have bigger ratios. In this lesson you learn three ratios that connect the angles of a right triangle to its sides. They are the foundation of trigonometry.

title: 6.2 - The Trigonometric Ratios
text:
Two right triangles each have a \(35^\circ\) angle. Are they similar? Say why.
Find the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs \(6\) and \(7\). Give the exact answer.
Write \(\dfrac{3}{8}\) as a decimal, rounded to the nearest thousandth.

title: 6.2 - The Trigonometric Ratios
text:
👥 Learn Together

6.2.1 - Naming the Sides
Choose one acute angle in a right triangle. The three sides get names that depend on that angle.

The hypotenuse is across from the right angle. It is always the longest side.
The opposite side is across from the angle you chose. It does not touch the angle.
The adjacent side is next to the angle you chose. It is the leg that touches the angle (the hypotenuse touches it too, but it is not called adjacent).






Now choose the other acute angle. The names of the two legs trade places.






The hypotenuse never changes. The opposite and adjacent sides change when you pick a different angle. Always say which angle you are using.


Example 1: Name the sides






For angle \(A\), name the side with length \(8\), the side with length \(15\), and the side with length \(17\).
\(BC = 8\) is across from \(A\), so it is opposite. \(AC = 15\) touches \(A\), so it is adjacent. \(AB = 17\) is the hypotenuse.
Now use angle \(B\). Which side is opposite? Which is adjacent?
\(AC = 15\) is across from \(B\), so it is opposite. \(BC = 8\) touches \(B\), so it is adjacent.



For angle \(B\), which side is the hypotenuse?
The side of length \(8\) is adjacent to which angle?




\(\overline{AB}\), with length \(17\). The hypotenuse is the same for both acute angles.
Angle \(B\).





6.2.2 - Why the Ratios Work
Look at three right triangles that share the \(35^\circ\) angle at \(A\). The figure is drawn to scale.





All three triangles have a \(35^\circ\) angle and a right angle. By AA similarity (Lesson 5.3), they are similar. Similar triangles have equal ratios for matching sides. Here are the measurements, to the nearest hundredth.
