The three ratios are the same in every row. They depend only on the angle, not on how big the triangle is. A \(35^\circ\) angle always gives an opposite-to-hypotenuse ratio of about \(0.57\). That is why one angle gives one number we can look up.



6.2.3 - Sine, Cosine, and Tangent
The three ratios have names. Use the angle \(A\).









Ratio
Name
Short form
Memory aid




\(\dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}\)
sine
\(\sin A\)
SOH


\(\dfrac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}\)
cosine
\(\cos A\)
CAH


\(\dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}\)
tangent
\(\tan A\)
TOA



Say it as SOH CAH TOA: Sine is Opposite over Hypotenuse, Cosine is Adjacent over Hypotenuse, Tangent is Opposite over Adjacent.

Write each ratio as a fraction first. Then divide to get a decimal. Round only at the end.


Example 2: Ratios from the side lengths
Use the triangle in Example 1. Find \(\sin A\), \(\cos A\), and \(\tan A\). Write each as a fraction and as a decimal rounded to four places.
\[
\sin A = \frac{\text{opp}}{\text{hyp}} = \frac{8}{17} \approx 0.4706 \qquad
\cos A = \frac{\text{adj}}{\text{hyp}} = \frac{15}{17} \approx 0.8824 \qquad
\tan A = \frac{\text{opp}}{\text{adj}} = \frac{8}{15} \approx 0.5333
\]
Example 3: Ratios for the other angle
Find \(\sin B\), \(\cos B\), and \(\tan B\) in the same triangle.
For angle \(B\), the opposite side is \(15\) and the adjacent side is \(8\).
\[
\sin B = \frac{15}{17} \approx 0.8824 \qquad
\cos B = \frac{8}{17} \approx 0.4706 \qquad
\tan B = \frac{15}{8} = 1.8750
\]
Notice that \(\sin B = \cos A\). You will see why in Lesson 6.5.


Write \(\sin A\), \(\cos A\), and \(\tan A\) as fractions.
Write each as a decimal rounded to four places.




\(\sin A = \dfrac{7}{25}\), \(\cos A = \dfrac{24}{25}\), \(\tan A = \dfrac{7}{24}\)
\(\sin A = 0.2800\), \(\cos A = 0.9600\), \(\tan A = 0.2917\)



Example 4: Find the hypotenuse first
A right triangle has legs \(6\) and \(7\). Angle \(A\) is across from the leg of length \(6\). Find \(\sin A\), \(\cos A\), and \(\tan A\) to four decimal places.
Use the Pythagorean theorem for the hypotenuse: \(6^2 + 7^2 = 85\), so the hypotenuse is \(\sqrt{85} \approx 9.2195\).
\[
\sin A = \frac{6}{\sqrt{85}} \approx 0.6508 \qquad
\cos A = \frac{7}{\sqrt{85}} \approx 0.7593 \qquad
\tan A = \frac{6}{7} \approx 0.8571
\]

The hypotenuse is \(\sqrt{81 + 144} = 15\). So \(\sin A = \dfrac{9}{15} = 0.6\), \(\cos A = \dfrac{12}{15} = 0.8\), and \(\tan A = \dfrac{9}{12} = 0.75\).


Example 5: Error analysis
Hnin looks at the triangle in Example 1. She writes \(\sin A = \dfrac{15}{17}\). Find her mistake.
For angle \(A\), the side of length \(15\) is adjacent, not opposite. \(\dfrac{15}{17}\) is adjacent over hypotenuse, which is \(\cos A\). The correct answer is \(\sin A = \dfrac{8}{17}\).



6.2.4 - Using a Calculator
You do not need to measure a triangle to find a ratio. A scientific calculator has a \(\boxed{\sin}\) key, a \(\boxed{\cos}\) key, and a \(\boxed{\tan}\) key.

A calculator can measure angles in degrees or in radians. In this book, always use degree mode. Check your calculator: \(\sin 30^\circ\) must give \(0.5\) and \(\tan 45^\circ\) must give \(1\). If you see \(-0.9880\) for \(\sin 30\), the calculator is in radian mode. Change the mode and try again.

Example 6: Calculator values
Find each value to four decimal places.

\(\sin 35^\circ \approx 0.5736\)
\(\cos 62^\circ \approx 0.4695\)
\(\tan 71^\circ \approx 2.9042\)

Compare \(\sin 35^\circ \approx 0.5736\) with the table in 6.2.2. The table gave \(0.57\) for the same angle. The calculator is just a faster way to get the ratio.


\(\sin 18^\circ\)
\(\cos 18^\circ\)
\(\tan 64^\circ\)




\(0.3090\)
\(0.9511\)
\(2.0503\)


Look for patterns. As an angle gets bigger, its sine and tangent get bigger and its cosine gets smaller. The sine and cosine of an acute angle are always between \(0\) and \(1\) because a leg is shorter than the hypotenuse.



6.2.5 - Tangent Is Slope
Remember that slope is rise over run. In a right triangle, the opposite side is the rise and the adjacent side is the run. So
\[
\tan\theta = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}} = \frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}} = \text{slope}.
\]
(The Greek letter \(\theta\), “theta,” often names an angle.)
Example 7: A line on the coordinate plane





A line passes through the origin and makes a \(40^\circ\) angle with the \(x\)-axis. What is its slope? Find the \(y\)-coordinate of point \(P\) where \(x = 10\).
The slope is \(\tan 40^\circ \approx 0.8391\). Slope is rise over run, so \(y = 10 \cdot \tan 40^\circ \approx 8.4\). Point \(P\) is about \((10, 8.4)\).

Slope \(= \tan 25^\circ \approx 0.4663\). At \(x = 20\), \(y \approx 20 \cdot 0.4663 \approx 9.3\).


Example 8: Road grade





A road climbs \(6\) feet for every \(100\) feet of flat ground. The grade of a road is the slope written as a percent. Find the grade and write \(\tan\theta\).
\[
\tan\theta = \frac{6}{100} = 0.06 \quad\text{so the grade is } 6\%.
\]

\(\tan\theta = \dfrac{9}{120} = 0.075\). The grade is \(7.5\%\).


The law says a wheelchair ramp must rise at most \(1\) foot for each \(12\) feet of run. That is \(\tan\theta = \dfrac{1}{12} \approx 0.0833\), a grade of about \(8.3\%\). To rise \(3\) feet, the ramp needs \(36\) feet of run.

What is \(\tan 45^\circ\)? Why does a \(45^\circ\)-\(45^\circ\)-\(90^\circ\) triangle give this answer?
Which is larger, \(\sin 10^\circ\) or \(\sin 80^\circ\)? Check with a calculator.

Tangent is slope. Use the figure for problem 21.






Look at the grid figure. The line through the origin and \((12, 5)\) makes angle \(\theta\) with the \(x\)-axis. Find \(\tan\theta\) as a fraction and a decimal to four places.

Real problems.

A ladder reaches \(12\) feet up a wall. Its base is \(5\) feet from the wall. The ladder makes angle \(\theta\) with the ground. Find the length of the ladder. Then find \(\sin\theta\) and \(\cos\theta\) to four places.
A roof has a \(9/12\) pitch. That means it rises \(9\) inches for every \(12\) inches of run. Find \(\tan\theta\). How many feet does the roof rise over a run of \(14\) feet?
A ramp rises \(2\) feet over \(20\) feet of run. The legal limit is \(\tan\theta = \frac{1}{12} \approx 0.0833\). Is this ramp steeper than the limit? Show with \(\tan\theta\).
A skateboard ramp makes a \(25^\circ\) angle with the ground. How many feet does it rise for each \(10\) feet of horizontal run? Round to the nearest tenth.


Find the mistake.

Samir says: “\(\cos 40^\circ \approx 0.7660\), so \(\cos 80^\circ\) must be double that, \(1.5320\).” Find his mistake. Check with a calculator.


Test practice

In right triangle \(ABC\), the right angle is at \(C\). \(AC = 21\), \(BC = 20\), and \(AB = 29\). Which fraction equals \(\sin B\)?
A. \(\dfrac{20}{29}\)
B. \(\dfrac{21}{29}\)
C. \(\dfrac{20}{21}\)
D. \(\dfrac{21}{20}\)
A line passes through the origin and makes a \(50^\circ\) angle with the positive \(x\)-axis. Which number is closest to the slope of the line?
A. \(0.6428\)
B. \(0.7660\)
C. \(1.1918\)
D. \(50\)


Challenge

In a right triangle, \(\sin A = \dfrac{20}{29}\). Draw the triangle and label two sides. Find \(\cos A\) and \(\tan A\) as fractions. Hint: use the Pythagorean theorem.

title: 6.3 - Solving for a Side
text:
🔥 Warm Up
How high does a \(24\)-foot ladder reach when it leans against a wall at \(75^\circ\)? You cannot hold a tape measure to the top. You can still find the answer.
The ladder is the hypotenuse. The angle is known. The height is the opposite side. One angle and one side are enough. In this lesson you use sine, cosine, and tangent to find a missing side.

title: 6.3 - Solving for a Side
text:
Solve \(\dfrac{x}{12} = 0.6428\).
Solve \(\dfrac{8}{x} = 0.9063\). Round to the nearest tenth.
Find \(\sin 40^\circ\), \(\cos 40^\circ\), and \(\tan 40^\circ\) to four decimal places.

title: 6.3 - Solving for a Side
text:
👥 Learn Together

6.3.1 - Choose the Ratio
To find a missing side, use these steps.

Draw the triangle. Mark the angle you know.
Label the sides opposite, adjacent, and hypotenuse for that angle.
Find the side you know and the side you want.
Pick the ratio that uses exactly those two sides.
Write the equation, solve, and round.




I know
I want
Use




opposite and hypotenuse (either one)
the other one
sin


adjacent and hypotenuse (either one)
the other one
cos


opposite and adjacent (either one)
the other one
tan




Say the two sides out loud. “Opposite and hypotenuse” is SOH, so use sine. “Adjacent and hypotenuse” is CAH, so use cosine. “Opposite and adjacent” is TOA, so use tangent.




6.3.2 - The Unknown Is on Top
When the side you want is on top of the fraction, multiply both sides by the number on the bottom.
Example 1: Opposite from the hypotenuse





Find \(x\). Round to the nearest tenth.

The known side, \(12\), is the hypotenuse. The wanted side, \(x\), is opposite the \(40^\circ\) angle.
Opposite and hypotenuse: use sine.

\[
\sin 40^\circ = \frac{x}{12} \quad\Rightarrow\quad x = 12\sin 40^\circ \approx 7.7
\]
Example 2: Opposite from the adjacent





Find \(x\) to the nearest tenth. The side of length \(15\) is adjacent to the \(52^\circ\) angle. The side \(x\) is opposite it. Use tangent.
\[
\tan 52^\circ = \frac{x}{15} \quad\Rightarrow\quad x = 15\tan 52^\circ \approx 19.2
\]
Example 3: Adjacent from the hypotenuse





Find \(x\) to the nearest tenth. The side \(x\) is adjacent to the \(28^\circ\) angle. The hypotenuse is \(20\). Use cosine.
\[
\cos 28^\circ = \frac{x}{20} \quad\Rightarrow\quad x = 20\cos 28^\circ \approx 17.7
\]


A right triangle has a \(23^\circ\) angle and a hypotenuse of \(18\). Find the side opposite the angle.
A right triangle has a \(61^\circ\) angle. The adjacent side is \(9\). Find the opposite side.




\(x = 18\sin 23^\circ \approx 7.0\)
\(x = 9\tan 61^\circ \approx 16.2\)





6.3.3 - The Unknown Is on the Bottom
Sometimes the unknown is the denominator. Then you divide.
Example 4: The hypotenuse from the adjacent side





Find \(x\) to the nearest tenth. The side \(8\) is adjacent to the \(25^\circ\) angle. The side \(x\) is the hypotenuse. Use cosine.
\[
\cos 25^\circ = \frac{8}{x}
\]
Multiply both sides by \(x\). Then divide both sides by \(\cos 25^\circ\):
\[
x \cdot \cos 25^\circ = 8 \quad\Rightarrow\quad x = \frac{8}{\cos 25^\circ} \approx 8.8
\]

Do not write \(x = 8\cos 25^\circ\). That gives \(7.3\), and a leg cannot be longer than the hypotenuse. Check: the hypotenuse must be the longest side. If your answer for the hypotenuse is smaller than a leg, you multiplied when you should have divided.

Example 5: The adjacent side from the opposite side





Find \(x\) to the nearest tenth. The side \(9\) is opposite the \(34^\circ\) angle. The side \(x\) is adjacent. Use tangent.
\[
\tan 34^\circ = \frac{9}{x} \quad\Rightarrow\quad x = \frac{9}{\tan 34^\circ} \approx 13.3
\]
Example 6: The hypotenuse from the opposite side





Find \(x\) to the nearest tenth. The side \(14\) is opposite the \(63^\circ\) angle. The side \(x\) is the hypotenuse. Use sine.
\[
\sin 63^\circ = \frac{14}{x} \quad\Rightarrow\quad x = \frac{14}{\sin 63^\circ} \approx 15.7
\]


A right triangle has a \(55^\circ\) angle. The adjacent side is \(10\). Find the hypotenuse.
A right triangle has a \(47^\circ\) angle. The opposite side is \(6\). Find the adjacent side.
A right triangle has a \(41^\circ\) angle. The opposite side is \(11\). Find the hypotenuse.




\(x = \dfrac{10}{\cos 55^\circ} \approx 17.4\)
\(x = \dfrac{6}{\tan 47^\circ} \approx 5.6\)
\(x = \dfrac{11}{\sin 41^\circ} \approx 16.8\)





6.3.4 - Find All the Missing Sides
Example 7: Both legs





The hypotenuse is \(20\) and an acute angle is \(35^\circ\). Find \(x\) and \(y\) to the nearest tenth. Then check with the Pythagorean theorem.

\(x\) is opposite \(35^\circ\): \(x = 20\sin 35^\circ \approx 11.5\).
\(y\) is adjacent to \(35^\circ\): \(y = 20\cos 35^\circ \approx 16.4\).
Check: \(11.5^2 + 16.4^2 \approx 401.2\), and \(20^2 = 400\). The small difference comes from rounding.

If you use the exact calculator values instead of the rounded ones, the check is closer. Always use the numbers you were given when you can, and do not use rounded answers to find other sides.



6.3.5 - Real Problems
Draw the right triangle first. Label the angle and the sides you know. Answer in a sentence with units.
Example 8: The ladder





A \(24\)-foot ladder leans against a wall. It makes a \(75^\circ\) angle with the ground. How high up the wall does it reach? How far is the base from the wall? Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.

Height \(h\) is opposite \(75^\circ\): \(h = 24\sin 75^\circ \approx 23.2\) feet.
Base distance is adjacent: \(24\cos 75^\circ \approx 6.2\) feet.

The ladder reaches about \(23.2\) feet up the wall. Its base is about \(6.2\) feet from the wall.
Example 9: The guy wire





A guy wire holds up a cell tower. It is anchored \(30\) feet from the base of the tower. The wire makes a \(58^\circ\) angle with the ground. How tall is the tower where the wire is attached? How long is the wire? Round to the nearest tenth.

The \(30\) ft side is adjacent. The height \(h\) is opposite. Use tangent: \(h = 30\tan 58^\circ \approx 48.0\) feet.
The wire \(L\) is the hypotenuse. Use cosine: \(\cos 58^\circ = \dfrac{30}{L}\), so \(L = \dfrac{30}{\cos 58^\circ} \approx 56.6\) feet.

Example 10: A kite





A kite string is \(100\) feet long. It makes a \(52^\circ\) angle with the ground. Ignore the sag in the string. How high is the kite? Round to the nearest foot.
\(h = 100\sin 52^\circ \approx 78.8\). The kite is about \(79\) feet high.

Height: \(12\sin 38^\circ \approx 7.4\) feet. Ground distance: \(12\cos 38^\circ \approx 9.5\) feet.


Moses solves \(\cos 25^\circ = \dfrac{8}{x}\) and writes \(x = 8\cos 25^\circ \approx 7.3\). What is wrong?
He multiplied. The unknown is in the denominator, so he must divide: \(x = \dfrac{8}{\cos 25^\circ} \approx 8.8\). His answer is also impossible, because the hypotenuse \(x\) must be longer than the leg \(8\).

title: 6.4 - Solving for an Angle
text:
🔥 Warm Up
A roof must be steep enough to shed rain and snow. A wheelchair ramp must be gentle enough to climb. How steep is each one, in degrees?
So far you found sides from an angle. In this lesson you go the other way. You know two sides, and you find the angle. The tool is the inverse of sine, cosine, and tangent.

title: 6.4 - Solving for an Angle
text:
Find \(\tan 40^\circ\) to four decimal places.
Solve \(\dfrac{7}{x} = 0.8\).
Find the slope of the line through \((0, 0)\) and \((10, 4)\).

title: 6.4 - Solving for an Angle
text:
👥 Learn Together

6.4.1 - Inverse Ratios
You know that \(\sin 30^\circ = 0.5\). The inverse sine goes the other way. It starts with the ratio and gives the angle:
\[
\sin^{-1}(0.5) = 30^\circ
\]
Read \(\sin^{-1}(0.5)\) as “the angle whose sine is \(0.5\).” There are three inverse keys: \(\sin^{-1}\), \(\cos^{-1}\), and \(\tan^{-1}\). On most calculators you press \(\boxed{2\text{nd}}\) or \(\boxed{\text{shift}}\) and then the \(\boxed{\sin}\), \(\boxed{\cos}\), or \(\boxed{\tan}\) key.

\(\sin^{-1}(0.5)\) does not mean \(\dfrac{1}{\sin 0.5}\). The small \(-1\) only says “inverse.” Keep the calculator in degree mode. Check: \(\sin^{-1}(0.5)\) must give \(30\).

Example 1: Inverse values
Find each angle to the nearest tenth of a degree.

\(\sin^{-1}(0.4) \approx 23.6^\circ\)
\(\cos^{-1}(0.25) \approx 75.5^\circ\)
\(\tan^{-1}(1.5) \approx 56.3^\circ\)



\(\sin^{-1}(0.3)\)
\(\cos^{-1}(0.8)\)
\(\tan^{-1}(0.7)\)




\(17.5^\circ\)
\(36.9^\circ\)
\(35.0^\circ\)





6.4.2 - Find an Angle from Two Sides
Use the same steps as before. Label the sides for the angle you want. Pick the ratio that uses the two sides you know. Then use the inverse key.
Example 2: Opposite and hypotenuse





Find \(m\angle A\) to the nearest tenth. The opposite side is \(7\) and the hypotenuse is \(13\). Use sine.
\[
\sin A = \frac{7}{13} \quad\Rightarrow\quad m\angle A = \sin^{-1}\left(\frac{7}{13}\right) \approx 32.6^\circ
\]
Example 3: Opposite and adjacent





Find \(m\angle A\) to the nearest tenth. The opposite side is \(9\) and the adjacent side is \(12\). Use tangent.
\[
\tan A = \frac{9}{12} = 0.75 \quad\Rightarrow\quad m\angle A = \tan^{-1}(0.75) \approx 36.9^\circ
\]
Example 4: Adjacent and hypotenuse





Find \(m\angle A\) to the nearest tenth. The adjacent side is \(8\) and the hypotenuse is \(11\). Use cosine.
\[
\cos A = \frac{8}{11} \quad\Rightarrow\quad m\angle A = \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{8}{11}\right) \approx 43.3^\circ
\]


The opposite side is \(5\) and the adjacent side is \(8\).
The adjacent side is \(15\) and the hypotenuse is \(17\).




\(\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{5}{8}\right) \approx 32.0^\circ\)
\(\cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{15}{17}\right) \approx 28.1^\circ\)



Type the fraction in parentheses: \(\sin^{-1}(7 \div 13)\). If you type \(\sin^{-1}(7) \div 13\), you get an error, because a sine can never be greater than \(1\).




6.4.3 - Solve a Right Triangle
To solve a triangle means to find every missing side and every missing angle. Use the Pythagorean theorem for a side, trigonometry for an angle, and the angle sum (\(90^\circ\) for the two acute angles) for the last angle.
Example 5: Solve a triangle from two legs





The legs are \(10\) and \(7\). Find \(c\), \(m\angle A\), and \(m\angle B\).

Hypotenuse: \(c = \sqrt{10^2 + 7^2} = \sqrt{149} \approx 12.2\).
Angle \(A\) is opposite the leg \(7\): \(m\angle A = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{7}{10}\right) \approx 35.0^\circ\).
Angle \(B\): \(90^\circ - 35.0^\circ = 55.0^\circ\).
Check by a second method: \(m\angle B = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{10}{7}\right) \approx 55.0^\circ\). It matches.


Hypotenuse: \(13\). The angle opposite \(5\): \(\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{5}{12}\right) \approx 22.6^\circ\). The other angle: \(90^\circ - 22.6^\circ = 67.4^\circ\).




6.4.4 - Angles in the Real World
Example 6: Roof pitch





Builders say a roof has a \(6/12\) pitch when it rises \(6\) inches for every \(12\) inches of run. Find the roof angle \(\theta\).
\[
\tan\theta = \frac{6}{12} = 0.5 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \theta = \tan^{-1}(0.5) \approx 26.6^\circ
\]
Example 7: A wheelchair ramp





The most a ramp may rise is \(1\) foot for each \(12\) feet of run. What angle does it make with the ground?
\[
\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{12}\right) \approx 4.8^\circ
\]
A ramp is gentle. It is less than \(5^\circ\).
Example 8: Stairs





Each step rises \(7\) inches and runs \(11\) inches. Find the angle of the stairs.
\[
\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{7}{11}\right) \approx 32.5^\circ
\]
Example 9: The sun’s angle





A person \(6\) feet tall casts a shadow \(9.5\) feet long. Find the angle of the sun above the ground.
\[
\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{6}{9.5}\right) \approx 32.3^\circ
\]
Example 10: Road grade
A road has a grade of \(8\%\). Find the angle it makes with the horizontal. A grade of \(8\%\) is a slope of \(0.08\), so \(\theta = \tan^{-1}(0.08) \approx 4.6^\circ\).
Example 11: The angle of a line





A line passes through \(P(2, 1)\) and \(Q(10, 6)\). What angle does it make with the \(x\)-axis?
The slope is \(\dfrac{6 - 1}{10 - 2} = \dfrac{5}{8}\). So \(\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{5}{8}\right) \approx 32.0^\circ\).

\(\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{9}{12}\right) = \tan^{-1}(0.75) \approx 36.9^\circ\).


A carpenter does not carry a protractor to the roof. A \(6/12\) pitch means rise \(6\), run \(12\). A framing square marks that triangle directly on the wood. The angle \(26.6^\circ\) is what the ratio \(\frac{6}{12}\) means in degrees.


Ana looks at a right triangle with an opposite side of \(5\) and an adjacent side of \(8\). She writes \(\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{8}{5}\right) \approx 58.0^\circ\). What is wrong?
She flipped the fraction. Tangent is opposite over adjacent, so the fraction is \(\dfrac{5}{8}\) and the angle is about \(32.0^\circ\). Her answer is the other acute angle.

title: 6.5 - Sine and Cosine of Complementary Angles
text:
🔥 Warm Up
A \(20\)-foot ladder leans against a wall. The ladder makes a \(70^\circ\) angle with the ground. It also makes a \(20^\circ\) angle with the wall.
Mia finds the height with \(20\sin 70^\circ\). Jamal finds it with \(20\cos 20^\circ\). They get the same answer. Is that luck? In this lesson you learn why the sine of one angle equals the cosine of the other angle.
crumbs: 6.5 - Sine and Cosine of Complementary Angles

title: 6.5 - Sine and Cosine of Complementary Angles
text:
Two angles are complementary. One is \(35^\circ\). Find the other.

crumbs: 6.5 - Sine and Cosine of Complementary Angles

title: 6.5 - Sine and Cosine of Complementary Angles
text:
👥 Learn Together

6.5.1 - The Acute Angles Are Complementary
The three angles of a triangle add to \(180^\circ\). A right triangle has one \(90^\circ\) angle. So the other two angles add to \(90^\circ\):
\[
m\angle A + m\angle B = 90^\circ \qquad\text{so}\qquad m\angle B = 90^\circ - m\angle A.
\]
Angles that add to \(90^\circ\) are complementary (Lesson 1.3). In a right triangle, the two acute angles are always complementary.








6.5.2 - Sine and Cosine Trade Places
Look at the triangle. The side \(a\) is opposite \(A\). It is adjacent to \(B\). The side \(b\) is adjacent to \(A\). It is opposite \(B\).
\[
\sin A = \frac{a}{c} \qquad \cos B = \frac{a}{c}
\]
The two ratios are the same fraction. So \(\sin A = \cos B\). Since \(B = 90^\circ - A\):

\[
\sin A = \cos(90^\circ - A) \qquad\qquad \cos A = \sin(90^\circ - A)
\]
The sine of an angle equals the cosine of its complement.

Check it with a calculator. Round to four decimal places.

Complement

In every row the two values match. That is the reason for the name cosine: it is the sine of the complement.



6.5.3 - Using the Rule
Example 1: Find a complement
Write each value as the sine or cosine of another angle.

\(\cos 15^\circ = \sin(90^\circ - 15^\circ) = \sin 75^\circ\)
\(\sin 41^\circ = \cos(90^\circ - 41^\circ) = \cos 49^\circ\)

Example 2: Use a known value
You know that \(\sin 28^\circ \approx 0.4695\). Find \(\cos 62^\circ\) without a calculator.
The angles \(28^\circ\) and \(62^\circ\) add to \(90^\circ\). So \(\cos 62^\circ = \sin 28^\circ \approx 0.4695\).


Write \(\sin 12^\circ\) as a cosine.
You know \(\cos 73^\circ \approx 0.2924\). Find \(\sin 17^\circ\).




\(\cos 78^\circ\)
\(\sin 17^\circ = \cos 73^\circ \approx 0.2924\)





6.5.4 - Solving Equations
If \(\sin(\text{one angle}) = \cos(\text{another angle})\), the two angles are complementary. They add to \(90^\circ\).
Example 3: Solve for \(x\)
Solve \(\sin(2x + 10)^\circ = \cos(3x)^\circ\).
The angles are complementary:
\[
(2x + 10) + 3x = 90 \quad\Rightarrow\quad 5x + 10 = 90 \quad\Rightarrow\quad 5x = 80 \quad\Rightarrow\quad x = 16.
\]
Check: \(2(16) + 10 = 42\) and \(3(16) = 48\). Then \(\sin 42^\circ \approx 0.6691\) and \(\cos 48^\circ \approx 0.6691\). They match.
Example 4: Solve for \(x\)
Solve \(\sin(x + 20)^\circ = \cos(2x - 5)^\circ\).
\[
(x + 20) + (2x - 5) = 90 \quad\Rightarrow\quad 3x + 15 = 90 \quad\Rightarrow\quad x = 25.
\]
The angles are \(45^\circ\) and \(45^\circ\). Check: \(\sin 45^\circ = \cos 45^\circ \approx 0.7071\).


\(\sin(4x - 6)^\circ = \cos(x + 16)^\circ\)
\(\sin(x + 5)^\circ = \cos(3x + 15)^\circ\)




\((4x - 6) + (x + 16) = 90\), so \(5x + 10 = 90\) and \(x = 16\). The angles are \(58^\circ\) and \(32^\circ\).
\((x + 5) + (3x + 15) = 90\), so \(4x + 20 = 90\) and \(x = 17.5\). The angles are \(22.5^\circ\) and \(67.5^\circ\).



\(\sin A = \cos A\) is true only when \(A = 45^\circ\). For other angles, \(\sin A\) and \(\cos A\) are different. For example, \(\sin 35^\circ \approx 0.5736\) but \(\cos 35^\circ \approx 0.8192\). The rule pairs an angle with its complement.




6.5.5 - Two More Facts
Tangent from sine and cosine. Divide the side ratios:
\[
\frac{\sin A}{\cos A} = \frac{a/c}{b/c} = \frac{a}{b} = \tan A.
\]
Tangent and the complement. The side \(a\) is opposite \(A\) and adjacent to \(B\). So \(\tan A = \dfrac{a}{b}\) and \(\tan B = \dfrac{b}{a}\). These are reciprocals:
\[
\tan A \cdot \tan(90^\circ - A) = 1.
\]
Example 5: Tangent from sine and cosine
Check that \(\tan 35^\circ = \dfrac{\sin 35^\circ}{\cos 35^\circ}\).
\(\dfrac{0.5736}{0.8192} \approx 0.7002\), and a calculator gives \(\tan 35^\circ \approx 0.7002\).
Example 6: Use the product rule
\(\tan 40^\circ \approx 0.8391\). Find \(\tan 50^\circ\) without a calculator.
The angles \(40^\circ\) and \(50^\circ\) are complementary, so \(\tan 50^\circ = \dfrac{1}{\tan 40^\circ} \approx \dfrac{1}{0.8391} \approx 1.1918\).


Find \(\tan A\).
Find \(\tan B\), where \(B\) is the other acute angle.




\(\tan A = \dfrac{0.6}{0.8} = 0.75\)
\(\tan B = \dfrac{1}{0.75} \approx 1.3333\). (Also \(\sin B = \cos A = 0.8\) and \(\cos B = \sin A = 0.6\), so \(\tan B = \frac{0.8}{0.6}\).)



Example 7: Two ways to find the height





A \(20\)-foot ladder makes a \(70^\circ\) angle with the ground and a \(20^\circ\) angle with the wall. Find how high it reaches in two ways. Round to the nearest tenth.

From the ground angle: \(h = 20\sin 70^\circ \approx 18.8\) feet.
From the wall angle: \(h\) is adjacent to \(20^\circ\), so \(h = 20\cos 20^\circ \approx 18.8\) feet.

Both ways give the same height, because \(\sin 70^\circ = \cos 20^\circ\).

Lucía says: “\(\sin 30^\circ = \cos 30^\circ\), because the sine of an angle is the cosine of the angle.” What is wrong?
The rule pairs an angle with its complement, not with itself. \(\sin 30^\circ = \cos 60^\circ = 0.5\). But \(\cos 30^\circ \approx 0.8660\).

text:

\(\sin A\)
\(\cos B\)
What do you notice about your answers to problems 18 and 19?

Real problems. Round to the nearest tenth.

A \(15\)-foot ladder makes a \(65^\circ\) angle with the ground. Find the height it reaches using \(\sin 65^\circ\). Then find it again using the angle the ladder makes with the wall.

Find the mistake.

Kofi says: “\(\sin 35^\circ = \cos 35^\circ\), so both are \(0.7071\).” Find his mistake. What is \(\sin 35^\circ\) equal to?


Test practice

In a right triangle, one acute angle \(A\) measures \(37^\circ\) and \(\sin A \approx 0.6018\). The other acute angle is \(B\). Which statement must be true?
A. \(\cos B \approx 0.6018\)
B. \(\sin B \approx 0.6018\)

title: 6.6 - Angles of Elevation and Depression
text:
🔥 Warm Up
A pilot lands a plane. A lifeguard watches a swimmer from a tall chair. A student looks up at the top of a cell tower. Each person looks along a line of sight. The angle the line of sight makes with the flat ground tells how high or how far away something is.
In this lesson you use that angle, and one side, to find a height or a distance you cannot measure with a tape.

title: 6.6 - Angles of Elevation and Depression
text:
Solve \(\tan 40^\circ = \dfrac{h}{50}\) for \(h\). Round to the nearest tenth.
Solve \(\tan 25^\circ = \dfrac{120}{d}\) for \(d\). Round to the nearest tenth.
Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One alternate interior angle is \(34^\circ\). What is the other?

title: 6.6 - Angles of Elevation and Depression
text:
👥 Learn Together

6.6.1 - Elevation and Depression
Imagine a flat, level line from your eyes. This is the horizontal.

The angle of elevation is the angle from the horizontal up to your line of sight.
The angle of depression is the angle from the horizontal down to your line of sight.

Both angles are measured from the horizontal, never from the vertical.

A common error is to use the angle from the vertical (straight up). In the picture, the angle of elevation is \(62^\circ\). The angle from the vertical is \(28^\circ\). They add to \(90^\circ\). Use the one that starts at the horizontal.









6.6.2 - Looking Up and Looking Down
A person at \(A\) looks up at \(B\). A person at \(B\) looks down at \(A\). The two horizontal lines are parallel.





The line of sight is a transversal. The angle of elevation at \(A\) and the angle of depression at \(B\) are alternate interior angles (Lesson 1.4). Parallel lines make them equal.

The angle of elevation from \(A\) to \(B\) equals the angle of depression from \(B\) to \(A\).




6.6.3 - Finding Heights and Distances
Use these steps.

Draw a picture. Draw the horizontal line and the line of sight.
Mark the angle from the horizontal.
Draw the right triangle. Label the sides opposite and adjacent to the angle.
Pick sine, cosine, or tangent. Solve.
If the observer’s eyes are above the ground, add the eye height to the height you find.

Example 1: A cell tower, with eye height





Hana stands \(80\) feet from a cell tower. Her eyes are \(5.5\) feet above the ground. The angle of elevation to the top is \(62^\circ\). How tall is the tower? Round to the nearest tenth.
The side \(x\) is the part of the tower above her eye level. It is opposite the angle, and \(80\) is adjacent. Use tangent.
\[
x = 80\tan 62^\circ \approx 150.5
\]
Add her eye height: \(150.5 + 5.5 = 156.0\).
The tower is about \(156.0\) feet tall.
Example 2: A lighthouse and a boat





The top of a lighthouse is \(120\) feet above the sea. The angle of depression to a boat is \(25^\circ\). How far is the boat from the base of the lighthouse? Round to the nearest tenth.
The angle of depression at the top equals the angle of elevation at the boat, \(25^\circ\). The height \(120\) is opposite that angle. The distance \(d\) is adjacent.
\[
\tan 25^\circ = \frac{120}{d} \quad\Rightarrow\quad d = \frac{120}{\tan 25^\circ} \approx 257.3
\]
The boat is about \(257.3\) feet from the base.
Example 3: An airplane landing





A plane is \(1500\) feet above the ground. The pilot sees the end of the runway at an angle of depression of \(3^\circ\). How far is the plane from the runway, along the ground? Round to the nearest foot. Then change the answer to miles.
\[
\tan 3^\circ = \frac{1500}{d} \quad\Rightarrow\quad d = \frac{1500}{\tan 3^\circ} \approx 28,622 \text{ feet}
\]
One mile is \(5280\) feet. So \(d \approx 28,622 \div 5280 \approx 5.4\) miles.
Example 4: A drone





An operator stands \(120\) meters from the point on the ground directly under a drone. The angle of elevation to the drone is \(35^\circ\). Ignore the operator’s height. How high is the drone? How far is it from the operator in a straight line? Round to the nearest tenth.

Height: \(h = 120\tan 35^\circ \approx 84.0\) meters.
Straight-line distance \(L\): \(\cos 35^\circ = \dfrac{120}{L}\), so \(L = \dfrac{120}{\cos 35^\circ} \approx 146.5\) meters.



Moses stands \(40\) feet from a tree. His eyes are \(5\) feet above the ground. The angle of elevation to the top of the tree is \(56^\circ\). How tall is the tree?
A hiker stands on a cliff \(60\) feet high. The angle of depression to a boat is \(20^\circ\). How far is the boat from the base of the cliff?




\(40\tan 56^\circ \approx 59.3\), and \(59.3 + 5 = 64.3\) feet.
\(d = \dfrac{60}{\tan 20^\circ} \approx 164.8\) feet.



Example 5: Find the angle





Olena’s eyes are \(5\) feet above the ground. She stands \(50\) feet from a flagpole that is \(35\) feet tall. Find the angle of elevation to the top. Round to the nearest tenth.
The part of the pole above her eye level is \(35 - 5 = 30\) feet.
\[
\tan\theta = \frac{30}{50} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \theta = \tan^{-1}(0.6) \approx 31.0^\circ
\]

Samir says: “The angle of elevation is \(28^\circ\).” He measured from the vertical in the picture of Section 6.6.1. What should it be?
The angle of elevation is measured from the horizontal. It is \(90^\circ - 28^\circ = 62^\circ\).




6.6.4 - Two Angles
Sometimes you see the same object from two places. Then you have two right triangles that share a side. Write an equation for each triangle and solve for the unknown.
Example 6: Moving closer





From point \(A\), the angle of elevation to the top of a tower is \(30^\circ\). After walking \(100\) feet toward the tower to point \(B\), the angle is \(45^\circ\). Find the height \(h\) of the tower. Round to the nearest tenth. (Ignore eye height.)

From \(B\): \(\tan 45^\circ = \dfrac{h}{x}\). Since \(\tan 45^\circ = 1\), \(h = x\).
From \(A\): \(\tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{h}{x + 100}\). So \(h = (x + 100)\tan 30^\circ\).
Replace \(h\) with \(x\): \(x = (x + 100)(0.5774)\). Then \(x - 0.5774x = 57.74\), so \(0.4226x = 57.74\) and \(x \approx 136.6\).

The tower is about \(136.6\) feet tall.

A clinometer measures an angle of elevation. Work with a partner. Tape a drinking straw along the flat edge of a protractor. Tie a string with a washer to the center hole. Look through the straw at the top of a tree or a flagpole. The string hangs straight down. Read the angle between the string and the \(90^\circ\) mark. That is the angle of elevation. Measure how far you stand from the object. Then find the height with tangent, and add your eye height.


Airplanes land along a path of about \(3^\circ\). That is a gentle slope. At \(1500\) feet of height, the plane is more than \(5\) miles from the runway.

title: 6.6 - Angles of Elevation and Depression
text:
✍️ Practice On Your Own
Elevation or depression? Write the name of the angle.

A hiker on the ground looks up at a hawk in a tree.
A pilot looks down at the end of a runway.
A lifeguard sits in a high chair and looks down at a swimmer.
A student on the ground looks up at the top of a flagpole.
The angle of elevation from point \(P\) to point \(Q\) is \(28^\circ\). What is the angle of depression from \(Q\) to \(P\)?


Use the figure.






Which numbered angle is the angle of elevation from \(A\) to \(B\)?
Which numbered angle is the angle of depression from \(B\) to \(A\)?
If \(m\angle 1 = 37^\circ\), find \(m\angle 2\) and \(m\angle 3\).
Why is \(\angle 3\) not an angle of elevation?


Find the height. Draw a picture. Round to the nearest tenth.

You stand \(45\) feet from a building. The angle of elevation to the top is \(52^\circ\). Ignore your eye height.
You stand \(100\) meters from a cliff. Your eyes are \(1.6\) meters above the ground. The angle of elevation to the top is \(38^\circ\).
You stand \(30\) feet from a tree with your eyes \(5\) feet above the ground. The angle of elevation to the top is \(48^\circ\).
A cell tower casts no shadow at noon. You stand \(200\) feet away. The angle of elevation to the top is \(70^\circ\). Ignore your eye height.


Find the distance. Draw a picture. Round to the nearest tenth.

From the top of a lighthouse \(80\) meters above the sea, the angle of depression to a boat is \(15^\circ\). How far is the boat from the base?
A plane is \(3000\) feet above the ground. The angle of depression to the airport is \(8^\circ\). Find the ground distance to the nearest hundred feet.
A swimmer is in the water below a \(45\)-foot cliff. The angle of depression to the swimmer is \(38^\circ\). How far is the swimmer from the base of the cliff?
A drone is \(60\) meters above the ground. The angle of depression from the drone to its landing pad is \(32^\circ\). How far is the drone from the pad in a straight line?


Find the angle. Draw a picture. Round to the nearest tenth of a degree.

Your eyes are \(5\) feet above the ground. You stand \(40\) feet from a wall that is \(25\) feet tall. Find the angle of elevation to the top.
A plane is \(2000\) feet above the ground. Its horizontal distance from the airport is \(9000\) feet. Find the angle of depression to the airport.
Your eyes are \(5\) feet above the ground. You stand \(45\) feet from a tree that is \(60\) feet tall. Find the angle of elevation to the top.


Real problems. Draw a picture first. Round to the nearest tenth.

An operator stands \(85\) meters from the point under a drone. Her eyes are \(1.7\) meters above the ground. The angle of elevation to the drone is \(28^\circ\). How high is the drone above the ground? How far is it from her eyes in a straight line?
A student uses a clinometer. She stands \(60\) feet from her school with her eyes \(5\) feet above the ground. The angle of elevation to the roof is \(41^\circ\). How tall is the school?
A fire truck ladder is \(100\) feet long. It is attached to the truck \(10\) feet above the ground and makes an angle of elevation of \(70^\circ\). How high does the top reach above the ground?
A ski lift cable is \(2000\) feet long. It rises at an angle of elevation of \(15^\circ\). How many feet does it rise?
Hnin sees a kite at an angle of elevation of \(x^\circ\). Her brother, standing on a hill directly above the kite, sees Hnin at an angle of depression of \((2x - 15)^\circ\). Find \(x\).
Ahmad says: “The angle of elevation is \(34^\circ\), so the angle of depression from the top is \(90^\circ - 34^\circ = 56^\circ\).” Find his mistake and fix it.


Test practice

From the top of a \(150\)-foot lighthouse, the angle of depression to a boat is \(20^\circ\). Which expression gives the distance, in feet, from the base of the lighthouse to the boat?
A. \(150\tan 20^\circ\)
B. \(\dfrac{150}{\tan 20^\circ}\)
C. \(150\sin 20^\circ\)
D. \(\dfrac{150}{\sin 20^\circ}\)
A student whose eyes are \(5\) feet above the ground stands \(60\) feet from a building. She measures an angle of elevation of \(40^\circ\) to the top. What is the height of the building to the nearest foot?
A. \(38\) ft
B. \(50\) ft
C. \(55\) ft
D. \(72\) ft


Challenge

Repeat Example 6 with new numbers. From point \(A\), the angle of elevation to the top of a tower is \(25^\circ\). You walk \(100\) feet toward the tower. Now the angle is \(40^\circ\). Find the height of the tower to the nearest tenth. Hint: \(\tan 40^\circ \approx 0.8391\) and \(\tan 25^\circ \approx 0.4663\).
From the top of a \(100\)-foot lighthouse, the angles of depression to two boats in a line are \(20^\circ\) and \(40^\circ\). How far apart are the boats? Round to the nearest tenth.

title: 6.7 - Modeling with Right Triangles
text:
🔥 Warm Up
A carpenter builds a ramp, a stair, and a roof. A pilot plans a route. A drone operator measures a field. None of them has a ready-made triangle. They draw one, name what they know, and choose the right tool.
In this lesson you put everything in Unit 6 together. You solve real problems with several steps.

title: 6.7 - Modeling with Right Triangles
text:
Find \(\sqrt{30^2 + 360^2}\). Round to the nearest tenth.
Find the angle: \(\tan\theta = \dfrac{1}{12}\). Round to the nearest tenth of a degree.
A right triangle has a hypotenuse of \(40\) and a \(60^\circ\) angle. Find the leg opposite the \(60^\circ\) angle.

title: 6.7 - Modeling with Right Triangles
text:
👥 Learn Together

6.7.1 - A Plan and a Choice of Tools
Every worked example in this lesson follows six steps.

Sketch the situation.
Label the right triangle with every number you know.
Choose a tool.
Solve.
Check that the answer makes sense.
Say the answer in a sentence with units.

Use this table to choose a tool.








What you know
What you want
Tool




two sides
the third side
Pythagorean theorem


one side and a \(45^\circ\) or \(30^\circ\)-\(60^\circ\) angle
the other sides
special right triangle


one angle and one side
another side
\(\sin\), \(\cos\), or \(\tan\)


two sides
an angle
\(\sin^{-1}\), \(\cos^{-1}\), or \(\tan^{-1}\)


two angles
the third angle
angle sum, \(90^\circ\) for the acute angles






6.7.2 - Ramps and Stairs
Example 1: A wheelchair ramp





A porch is \(30\) inches above the ground. A ramp must rise at most \(1\) inch for every \(12\) inches of run. How long is the ramp? What angle does it make with the ground? Round to the nearest tenth.

Sketch. Done above. The figure is drawn to scale.
Label. Rise \(30\) in. Run \(12 \cdot 30 = 360\) in. Ramp length \(L\) is the hypotenuse.
Choose. Two legs known: Pythagorean theorem for \(L\). Two sides known: \(\tan^{-1}\) for the angle.
Solve. \(L = \sqrt{30^2 + 360^2} = \sqrt{130{,}500} \approx 361.2\) in. The angle is \(\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{30}{360}\right) = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{12}\right) \approx 4.8^\circ\).
Check. The ramp (\(361.2\) in) is a little longer than its run (\(360\) in). The angle is small. Both fit a gentle ramp.
Say. The ramp is about \(361.2\) inches, or \(30.1\) feet, long. It makes an angle of about \(4.8^\circ\) with the ground.


Run: \(12 \cdot 18 = 216\) in \(= 18\) ft. Length: \(\sqrt{18^2 + 216^2} \approx 18.1\) ft.


Example 2: A staircase





A building code says each riser can be at most \(7.75\) inches. A staircase must rise \(108\) inches. Each tread is \(10\) inches deep. How many risers? What is each riser? What angle do the stairs make? How long is the stringer (the sloping board)? Round to the nearest tenth.

Sketch. Done above.
Label. Total rise \(108\) in. Tread \(10\) in.
Choose. Division for the risers, tangent for the angle, Pythagorean theorem for the stringer.
Solve. \(108 \div 7.75 \approx 13.9\), so the stairs need at least \(14\) risers. With \(14\) risers, each riser is \(108 \div 14 \approx 7.7\) in. There is one fewer tread than risers, so there are \(13\) treads and the run is \(13 \cdot 10 = 130\) in. The angle is \(\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{7.7}{10}\right) \approx 37.6^\circ\). The stringer is \(\sqrt{108^2 + 130^2} \approx 169.0\) in.
Check. \(14 \cdot 7.7 \approx 108\). A stair near \(37.6^\circ\) is steep but common.
Say. The stairs have \(14\) risers of about \(7.7\) inches. They make an angle of about \(37.6^\circ\). The stringer is about \(169.0\) inches, or \(14.1\) feet, long.


\(96 \div 7.75 \approx 12.4\), so \(13\) risers. Riser: \(96 \div 13 \approx 7.4\) in. Angle: \(\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{7.4}{10}\right) \approx 36.4^\circ\).




6.7.3 - Roofs
Example 3: A rafter with an overhang





A house is \(28\) feet wide. The roof has a \(7/12\) pitch and a \(1\)-foot overhang at each edge. Find the roof angle, the height \(h\) of the peak above the walls, and the length \(L\) of a rafter from the peak to the end of the overhang. Round to the nearest tenth.

Sketch. Done above.
Label. The peak is over the middle, so the run is \(28 \div 2 = 14\) ft. The pitch means rise \(7\) per run \(12\).
Choose. Tangent for \(h\) and the angle. Cosine for the rafter.
Solve. \(\tan\theta = \dfrac{7}{12}\), so \(\theta \approx 30.3^\circ\). \(h = 14 \cdot \dfrac{7}{12} \approx 8.2\) ft. The overhang adds \(1\) ft to the horizontal distance, so the rafter covers \(14 + 1 = 15\) ft horizontally: \(\cos\theta = \dfrac{15}{L}\), so \(L = \dfrac{15}{\cos 30.3^\circ} \approx 17.4\) ft.
Check. Without the overhang the rafter is \(\sqrt{14^2 + 8.2^2} \approx 16.2\) ft. The overhang adds a little, so \(17.4\) ft is reasonable.
Say. The roof angle is about \(30.3^\circ\). The peak is about \(8.2\) feet above the walls. Each rafter is about \(17.4\) feet long.


Run \(= 12\) ft. Rise \(= 12 \cdot \dfrac{5}{12} = 5\) ft. Rafter \(= \sqrt{12^2 + 5^2} = 13\) ft. Angle: \(\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{5}{12}\right) \approx 22.6^\circ\).




6.7.4 - Navigation and Maps
A bearing tells a direction. It is the angle measured clockwise from north. A bearing of \(060^\circ\) means \(60^\circ\) clockwise from north, toward the east.
Example 4: A ship’s course





A ship leaves port and sails \(40\) nautical miles on a bearing of \(060^\circ\). How far north and how far east of the port is the ship? Round to the nearest tenth.

Sketch. Done above. The angle between north and the course is \(60^\circ\).
Label. The north distance \(n\) is adjacent to \(60^\circ\). The east distance \(e\) is opposite. The hypotenuse is \(40\).
Choose. Cosine for \(n\), sine for \(e\).
Solve. \(n = 40\cos 60^\circ = 20\). \(e = 40\sin 60^\circ \approx 34.6\).
Check. \(20^2 + 34.6^2 \approx 1600\). It matches \(40^2\). (Also, the triangle is a \(30^\circ\)-\(60^\circ\)-\(90^\circ\) triangle, so \(n\) is half the hypotenuse.)
Say. The ship is \(20\) nautical miles north and about \(34.6\) nautical miles east of the port.


North: \(8\cos 35^\circ \approx 6.6\) km. East: \(8\sin 35^\circ \approx 4.6\) km.


Example 5: A map on the coordinate plane





Airport \(A\) is at \((2, 1)\) and town \(B\) is at \((10, 7)\). One unit is \(1\) mile. How far is the flight from \(A\) to \(B\)? What is the bearing from \(A\) to \(B\)? Round to the nearest tenth.

Sketch. Done above. The legs are \(10 - 2 = 8\) and \(7 - 1 = 6\).
Label. The angle \(\theta\) at \(A\) is measured from east. The bearing is measured from north.
Choose. Distance formula (the Pythagorean theorem). Inverse tangent for \(\theta\).
Solve. \(AB = \sqrt{8^2 + 6^2} = 10\). \(\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{6}{8}\right) \approx 36.9^\circ\). Bearing \(= 90^\circ - 36.9^\circ = 53.1^\circ\).
Check. The town is up and to the right, so the bearing is between \(0^\circ\) and \(90^\circ\). It is closer to east, so a bearing near \(53.1^\circ\) fits.
Say. The flight is \(10\) miles on a bearing of about \(53.1^\circ\).


\(AB = \sqrt{7^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{65} \approx 8.1\) mi. \(\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{4}{7}\right) \approx 29.7^\circ\). Bearing \(= 90^\circ - 29.7^\circ = 60.3^\circ\).




6.7.5 - Drones, Ladders, and Checking
Example 6: A drone surveys a field





A drone hovers \(60\) meters above a field. It sees marker \(M_1\) to the left at an angle of depression of \(50^\circ\). It sees marker \(M_2\) to the right at an angle of depression of \(30^\circ\). How far apart are the markers? Round to the nearest tenth.

Sketch. Done above.
Label. The height \(60\) is opposite each angle at the markers (alternate interior angles).
Choose. Tangent in each right triangle. Then add.
Solve. Left: \(\dfrac{60}{\tan 50^\circ} \approx 50.34\) m. Right: \(\dfrac{60}{\tan 30^\circ} \approx 103.92\) m. Add the unrounded values: \(50.34 + 103.92 = 154.26\), which is about \(154.3\) m.
Check. The \(30^\circ\) marker is farther away than the \(50^\circ\) marker, since a smaller angle means a longer ground distance. Yes.
Say. The markers are about \(154.3\) meters apart.


\(\dfrac{80}{\tan 40^\circ} + \dfrac{80}{\tan 25^\circ} \approx 95.34 + 171.56 = 266.90 \approx 266.9\) m.


Example 7: Is the ladder safe?





A safety rule says a ladder’s base should be \(1\) foot from the wall for every \(4\) feet of height. Ahmad places a \(20\)-foot ladder so that the top reaches \(18\) feet up a wall. Does it follow the rule? Round to the nearest tenth.

Sketch. Done above.
Label. Hypotenuse \(20\). Height \(18\). Base \(b\).
Choose. Pythagorean theorem for \(b\).
Solve. \(b = \sqrt{20^2 - 18^2} = \sqrt{76} \approx 8.7\) ft. The rule needs \(18 \div 4 = 4.5\) ft.
Check. \(8.7\) ft is much more than \(4.5\) ft. The ladder lies too flat. The angle with the ground is \(\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{18}{20}\right) \approx 64.2^\circ\). The rule gives \(\tan^{-1}(4) \approx 76.0^\circ\).
Say. No. The ladder is too flat. The base is about \(8.7\) feet from the wall, not \(4.5\) feet. At \(76.0^\circ\), the same ladder would reach about \(19.4\) feet.


Fatima finds the length of a ramp with a rise of \(2\) feet and a run of \(24\) feet. She writes \(2 + 24 = 26\) feet. What is wrong?
She added the legs. The ramp is the hypotenuse, so she must use the Pythagorean theorem: \(\sqrt{2^2 + 24^2} \approx 24.1\) feet. A ramp cannot be longer than the two legs combined, but it is almost as long as the run.


Builders check answers against the situation. A roof rafter longer than the whole house, a ramp shorter than its run, or a ladder that lies almost flat are all warnings. The number on the calculator is only the first step.

title: Unit 6 Summary
text:
6.1 - Special Right Triangles
Example: a 45-45-90 triangle has a hypotenuse of 10. Each leg is \(5\sqrt{2} \approx 7.1\). A 30-60-90 triangle has a hypotenuse of 14. The short leg is 7 and the long leg is \(7\sqrt{3} \approx 12.1\).

title: Unit 6 Summary
text:
A 45-45-90 triangle is half of a square. The legs are equal. If a leg is \(s\), the hypotenuse is \(s\sqrt{2}\).
A 30-60-90 triangle is half of an equilateral triangle. The short leg \(s\) is across from \(30^\circ\). The long leg is \(s\sqrt{3}\). The hypotenuse is \(2s\).
To go from the hypotenuse to a leg of a 45-45-90 triangle, divide by \(\sqrt{2}\) and rationalize: \(\dfrac{10}{\sqrt{2}} = 5\sqrt{2}\).
The marks on a figure show which pattern to use. A picture alone does not.

title: Unit 6 Summary
text:
6.2 - The Trigonometric Ratios

Name the sides from the angle you are using: the opposite side is across from it, the adjacent side is next to it, and the hypotenuse is across from the right angle.
\(\sin A = \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}\), \(\cos A = \dfrac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}\), \(\tan A = \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}\). Say SOH CAH TOA.
The ratios depend only on the angle, not on the size of the triangle. Similar triangles (AA) have the same ratios.
\(\tan A\) is the slope of a line that makes angle \(A\) with the \(x\)-axis.
Set the calculator to degree mode.






Example: a right triangle has legs 5 and 12 and hypotenuse 13. For the angle across from 5: \(\sin A = \dfrac{5}{13} \approx 0.385\), \(\cos A = \dfrac{12}{13} \approx 0.923\), \(\tan A = \dfrac{5}{12} \approx 0.417\).

title: Unit 6 Summary
text:
6.3 - Solving for a Side

Pick the ratio that has the side you know and the side you want.
If the unknown \(x\) is on top, multiply: \(\sin 40^\circ = \dfrac{x}{12}\) gives \(x = 12 \sin 40^\circ\).
If the unknown is on the bottom, divide: \(\cos 35^\circ = \dfrac{20}{x}\) gives \(x = \dfrac{20}{\cos 35^\circ}\).
Do not round until the last step. Check that the hypotenuse is the longest side.






Example: \(x = 12 \sin 40^\circ \approx 7.7\). And \(x = \dfrac{20}{\cos 35^\circ} \approx 24.4\).

title: Unit 6 Summary
text:
6.4 - Solving for an Angle

Use the inverse ratio when you know two sides and want the angle: \(\sin^{-1}\), \(\cos^{-1}\), or \(\tan^{-1}\).
\(\sin A = \dfrac{7}{13}\) means \(A = \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{7}{13}\right)\). Find the ratio first, then use the inverse key.
The two acute angles add to \(90^\circ\). Subtract to find the other one.
A ramp of \(1 : 12\) has an angle of \(\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{12}\right) \approx 4.8^\circ\).






Example: \(A = \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{7}{13}\right) \approx 32.6^\circ\). The other angle is \(90^\circ - 32.6^\circ = 57.4^\circ\).

title: Unit 6 Summary
section: 6.5 - Sine and Cosine of Complementary Angles
text:
6.5 - Sine and Cosine of Complementary Angles

Two angles are complementary if they add to \(90^\circ\). In a right triangle, the two acute angles are complementary.
\(\sin A = \cos(90^\circ - A)\) and \(\cos A = \sin(90^\circ - A)\).
\(\tan A = \dfrac{\sin A}{\cos A}\) and \(\tan A \cdot \tan(90^\circ - A) = 1\).
Equal ratios do not mean equal angles. \(\sin 40^\circ\) and \(\cos 40^\circ\) are different.






Example: \(\sin 25^\circ \approx 0.423\) and \(\cos 65^\circ \approx 0.423\). They are equal. \(\tan 25^\circ \cdot \tan 65^\circ \approx 1.0\).

title: Unit 6 Summary
text:
6.6 - Angles of Elevation and Depression

Both angles are measured from the horizontal. Elevation is up. Depression is down.
The angle of elevation from \(A\) to \(B\) equals the angle of depression from \(B\) to \(A\) (alternate interior angles).
If the observer’s eyes are above the ground, add the eye height to the height you find.
With two angles, write one equation for each right triangle and solve.






Example: a person stands 80 ft from a tower. Her eyes are 5.5 ft high. The angle of elevation to the top is \(62^\circ\). Height: \(80 \tan 62^\circ + 5.5 \approx 156.0\) ft.

title: Unit 6 Summary
text:
6.7 - Modeling with Right Triangles

Six steps: sketch, label, choose a tool, solve, check, say the answer in a sentence with units.
Two sides and a missing side: Pythagorean theorem. An angle and a side: sine, cosine, or tangent. Two sides and a missing angle: inverse ratio.
A ramp rises 1 inch for every 12 inches of run. A roof pitch of \(\dfrac{7}{12}\) means \(\tan\theta = \dfrac{7}{12}\).
A bearing is measured clockwise from north. North distance \(= d\cos(\text{bearing})\). East distance \(= d\sin(\text{bearing})\).
On a map grid, the bearing is \(90^\circ\) minus the angle from east.






Example: a ship sails 40 nautical miles on a bearing of \(060^\circ\). North: \(40\cos 60^\circ = 20\). East: \(40 \sin 60^\circ \approx 34.6\).

title: Unit 6 Review
text:
6.1 - Special Right Triangles
Example 1: A 30-60-90 triangle has a long leg of 9. Find the short leg and the hypotenuse. Give exact answers.
Long leg \(= s\sqrt{3} = 9\), so \(s = \dfrac{9}{\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{9\sqrt{3}}{3} = 3\sqrt{3}\).
Hypotenuse \(= 2s = 6\sqrt{3} \approx 10.4\).


6.2 - The Trigonometric Ratios
Example 2: A right triangle has legs 8 and 15 and hypotenuse 17. Find \(\sin B\), \(\cos B\), and \(\tan B\) for the angle \(B\) across from the leg 15. Round to the nearest thousandth.
Opposite \(= 15\), adjacent \(= 8\), hypotenuse \(= 17\).
\(\sin B = \dfrac{15}{17} \approx 0.882\), \(\cos B = \dfrac{8}{17} \approx 0.471\), \(\tan B = \dfrac{15}{8} = 1.875\).


6.3 - Solving for a Side
Example 3: A ladder leans on a wall. It makes a \(68^\circ\) angle with the ground and its base is 4 feet from the wall. How long is the ladder? Round to the nearest tenth.
The base is adjacent to \(68^\circ\). The ladder is the hypotenuse. Use cosine.
\(\cos 68^\circ = \dfrac{4}{L}\), so \(L = \dfrac{4}{\cos 68^\circ} \approx 10.7\) ft.


6.4 - Solving for an Angle
Example 4: A ramp rises 22 inches over a run of 240 inches. Find the angle of the ramp. Round to the nearest tenth of a degree.
Rise is opposite and run is adjacent. Use tangent.
\(\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{22}{240}\right) \approx 5.2^\circ\).


6.5 - Sine and Cosine of Complementary Angles
Example 5: Write \(\cos 34^\circ\) as the sine of an angle. Then find \(x\) if \(\sin(x + 4^\circ) = \cos(2x - 1^\circ)\).
\(\cos 34^\circ = \sin(90^\circ - 34^\circ) = \sin 56^\circ\).
The angles add to \(90^\circ\): \((x + 4) + (2x - 1) = 90\), so \(3x = 87\) and \(x = 29\).


6.6 - Angles of Elevation and Depression
Example 6: From the top of a 120-foot lighthouse, the angle of depression to a boat is \(14^\circ\). How far is the boat from the base? Round to the nearest foot.
The angle at the boat is also \(14^\circ\) (alternate interior angles). The height is opposite and the distance is adjacent.
\(\tan 14^\circ = \dfrac{120}{d}\), so \(d = \dfrac{120}{\tan 14^\circ} \approx 481\) ft.


6.7 - Modeling with Right Triangles
Example 7: A house is 32 feet wide. The roof has a \(5/12\) pitch and no overhang. Find the roof angle and the rafter length. Round to the nearest tenth.
The run is \(16\) ft and the rise is \(16 \cdot \dfrac{5}{12} \approx 6.7\) ft.
Angle: \(\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{5}{12}\right) \approx 22.6^\circ\). Rafter: \(\sqrt{16^2 + 6.7^2} \approx 17.3\) ft.

title: Introduction
text:
What You’ll Learn
Welcome to Unit 7! A bike wheel, a pizza, a running track, and the coverage area of a cell tower are all circles.
In this unit you learn how to measure circles: the distance around, the area inside, and the parts in between. You learn a new way to measure angles, called radians. You also learn the angles inside a circle and how to write the equation of a circle on the coordinate plane.
By the end of this unit, you will be able to:

title: Introduction
text:
Find the circumference and area of a circle
Find arc length and the area of a sector
Convert between degrees and radians
Use inscribed angles and tangent lines to find missing angles and lengths
Write and graph the equation of a circle

title: Introduction
text:
Topics in This Unit
Circumference and Arc Length
Find the distance around a circle and around part of it.
Area of Circles and Sectors

Radians
Measure angles with the radius. Convert between degrees and radians.
Inscribed Angles and Tangents
Find angles with their vertex on a circle. Use lines that touch a circle at one point.

Every tool from the unit in one place, to keep beside you.

title: 7.1 - Circumference and Arc Length
text:
🔥 Warm Up
A bike wheel is 26 inches across. Every time the wheel turns once, the bike rolls forward. How far does it go?
The answer is the distance around the wheel. In this lesson you learn the parts of a circle and how to find the distance around it. You also learn how to find the length of just one piece of the edge.

title: 7.1 - Circumference and Arc Length
text:
What fraction of a full turn is \(90^\circ\)? Write it in lowest terms.
Find \(2 \cdot 3.14 \cdot 5\).

title: 7.1 - Circumference and Arc Length
text:
👥 Learn Together

7.1.1 - Parts of a Circle
A circle is all the points in a plane that are the same distance from one point. That point is the center. We name a circle by its center. Circle \(P\) is written \(\odot P\).













Part
What it is
In the figure




radius
a segment from the center to a point on the circle
\(\overline{PA}\)


diameter
a chord that goes through the center
\(\overline{BC}\)


chord
a segment with both endpoints on the circle
\(\overline{EF}\)


arc
part of the circle between two points
\(\overset{\frown}{AD}\)


central angle
an angle with its vertex at the center
\(\angle APD\)




All radii of one circle have the same length. A diameter is two radii in a line, so \[
d = 2r \qquad\text{and}\qquad r = \frac{d}{2}.
\] The diameter is the longest chord of a circle.

An arc has a name too.

A minor arc is less than half of the circle. We name it with its two endpoints: \(\overset{\frown}{AD}\).
A semicircle is exactly half of the circle. We name it with three letters: \(\overset{\frown}{BAC}\).
A major arc is more than half of the circle. We name it with three letters: \(\overset{\frown}{EAF}\) is the long way around from \(E\) to \(F\) through \(A\).


Example 1: Name the parts






Name a radius.
\(\overline{OB}\). (Also \(\overline{OA}\), \(\overline{OC}\), and \(\overline{OD}\).)
Name a diameter.
\(\overline{AC}\). It is a chord that goes through the center \(O\).
Name a chord that is not a diameter.
\(\overline{BD}\). Both endpoints are on the circle, but it does not go through \(O\).
Name a semicircle.
\(\overset{\frown}{ABC}\). Points \(A\) and \(C\) are the ends of a diameter, so the arc from \(A\) to \(C\) through \(B\) is half of the circle.
Name a central angle.
\(\angle BOC\). Its vertex is the center \(O\).



Name another radius that is part of the diameter.
Name the semicircle that goes through \(D\).




\(\overline{OA}\) or \(\overline{OC}\)
\(\overset{\frown}{ADC}\)



Example 2: Radius and diameter

The diameter is \(18\) inches. Find the radius.
\(r = \dfrac{18}{2} = 9\) inches.
The radius is \(7.5\) feet. Find the diameter.
\(d = 2(7.5) = 15\) feet.
A chord goes through the center and is \(26\) centimeters long. Find the radius.
A chord through the center is a diameter. So \(d = 26\) and \(r = 13\) centimeters.



\(d = 11\) meters. Find \(r\).
\(r = 4.2\) inches. Find \(d\).




\(r = 5.5\) meters
\(d = 8.4\) inches





7.1.2 - Circumference and Pi
The distance around a circle is its circumference. Measure some round things. Wrap a string around each one, then measure the string. Divide the circumference \(C\) by the diameter \(d\).



Object

Every answer is close to \(3.14\). The small differences come from measuring. For every circle, \(C \div d\) is the same number. We call it pi and write it \(\pi\). It is about \(3.14159\). It goes on forever without a pattern.

\[
C = \pi d \qquad\text{or}\qquad C = 2\pi r
\] An answer like \(12\pi\) is exact. For a decimal, use the \(\pi\) key on your calculator.


Example 3: Circumference from the diameter
A round fountain has a diameter of \(12\) feet. Find its circumference.
\[
C = \pi d = \pi(12) = 12\pi \text{ feet}
\]
On a calculator, \(12\pi \approx 37.70\). The circumference is \(12\pi\) feet, or about \(37.70\) feet.
Example 4: Circumference from the radius
A circle has a radius of \(5.5\) inches. Find its circumference.
\[
C = 2\pi r = 2\pi(5.5) = 11\pi \approx 34.56 \text{ inches}
\]


\(d = 20\) feet
\(r = 3.5\) centimeters




\(C = 20\pi \approx 62.83\) feet
\(C = 2\pi(3.5) = 7\pi \approx 21.99\) centimeters



Example 5: Find the radius from the circumference

A circle has a circumference of \(28\pi\) centimeters. Find the radius.
\(2\pi r = 28\pi\). Divide both sides by \(2\pi\). Then \(r = 14\) centimeters.
A circle has a circumference of \(50\) inches. Find the radius. Round to the nearest tenth.
\(2\pi r = 50\), so \(r = \dfrac{50}{2\pi} = \dfrac{25}{\pi} \approx 8.0\) inches.



\(C = 36\pi\) feet
\(C = 90\) centimeters. Round to the nearest tenth.




\(r = 18\) feet
\(r = \dfrac{90}{2\pi} = \dfrac{45}{\pi} \approx 14.3\) centimeters



Example 6: The bike wheel
How far does a wheel with a diameter of \(26\) inches roll in one turn? How many turns make one mile? Round to the nearest tenth.
One turn is one circumference:
\[
C = \pi(26) = 26\pi \approx 81.7 \text{ inches}.
\]
One mile is \(5{,}280 \times 12 = 63{,}360\) inches. Divide:
\[
63{,}360 \div 81.68 \approx 775.7 \text{ turns}.
\]
The wheel rolls about \(81.7\) inches in one turn. It turns about \(775.7\) times in one mile.


How far does it roll in one turn? Give the exact answer.
How far does it roll in 5 turns? Round to the nearest tenth.




\(20\pi\) inches
\(5 \cdot 20\pi = 100\pi \approx 314.2\) inches





7.1.3 - Arc Measure and Arc Length
A central angle cuts a piece out of the edge of the circle. We can measure that piece in two different ways.






Arc measure tells how much of a turn the arc is. It is in degrees. It equals the central angle: \(m\overset{\frown}{AB} = 70^\circ\).
Arc length tells how far it is along the arc. It is a distance, in inches, feet, or meters.

The arc is the fraction \(\dfrac{\text{central angle}}{360^\circ}\) of the whole circle. So the arc length is that fraction of the circumference.

\[
\text{arc length} = \frac{\text{central angle}}{360^\circ} \cdot 2\pi r
\]

A semicircle measures \(180^\circ\). A major arc measures \(360^\circ\) minus its minor arc.
Example 7: Arc measure
Use the figure. \(m\angle AOB = 70^\circ\).

Find \(m\overset{\frown}{AB}\).
The arc measure equals the central angle. \(m\overset{\frown}{AB} = 70^\circ\).
Find \(m\overset{\frown}{ACB}\).
\(\overset{\frown}{ACB}\) is the major arc. \(360^\circ - 70^\circ = 290^\circ\).



Find the measure of its minor arc.
Find the measure of the matching major arc.




\(125^\circ\)
\(360^\circ - 125^\circ = 235^\circ\)



Example 8: Arc length
In the figure, the radius is \(9\) feet. Find the length of \(\overset{\frown}{AB}\). Give the exact answer and a decimal rounded to the nearest hundredth.
\[
\text{arc length} = \frac{70}{360} \cdot 2\pi(9) = \frac{7}{36} \cdot 18\pi = 3.5\pi
\]
The arc is \(3.5\pi\) feet, or about \(10.99\) feet.

\(r = 15\) inches and the central angle is \(48^\circ\). Give the exact answer and a decimal rounded to the nearest hundredth.


\(\dfrac{48}{360} \cdot 2\pi(15) = \dfrac{2}{15} \cdot 30\pi = 4\pi \approx 12.57\) inches


Example 9: The same degrees, a different length





Two circles share a center. The inner circle has radius \(3\) and the outer circle has radius \(6\). Both arcs have a \(60^\circ\) central angle. Find each arc length.

Inner arc \(\overset{\frown}{AB}\): \(\dfrac{60}{360} \cdot 2\pi(3) = \dfrac{1}{6} \cdot 6\pi = \pi \approx 3.14\).
Outer arc \(\overset{\frown}{CD}\): \(\dfrac{60}{360} \cdot 2\pi(6) = \dfrac{1}{6} \cdot 12\pi = 2\pi \approx 6.28\).


The two arcs both measure \(60^\circ\). But the outer arc is twice as long. Arc measure says how much of the circle. Arc length says how far. Two arcs with the same measure have the same length only in circles with the same radius.




7.1.4 - Solving with Arcs
The arcs that go all the way around a circle add up to \(360^\circ\).
Example 10: Solve for \(x\)





The four central angles are marked with arc measures. Find \(x\) and each arc.
\[
2x + (3x + 10) + (x + 20) + (4x - 10) = 360
\]
\[
10x + 20 = 360 \quad\Rightarrow\quad 10x = 340 \quad\Rightarrow\quad x = 34.
\]
The arcs are \(2(34) = 68^\circ\), \(3(34) + 10 = 112^\circ\), \(34 + 20 = 54^\circ\), and \(4(34) - 10 = 126^\circ\).
Check: \(68 + 112 + 54 + 126 = 360\).

The arcs measure \(x^\circ\), \((2x + 20)^\circ\), \((3x - 10)^\circ\), and \((4x)^\circ\). Find \(x\) and each arc.


\(x + (2x + 20) + (3x - 10) + 4x = 360\), so \(10x + 10 = 360\) and \(x = 35\). The arcs are \(35^\circ\), \(90^\circ\), \(95^\circ\), and \(140^\circ\).


Example 11: Find the radius from an arc length

An arc of \(150^\circ\) has length \(5\pi\) centimeters. Find the radius.

\[
\frac{150}{360} \cdot 2\pi r = 5\pi \quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{5}{6}\pi r = 5\pi \quad\Rightarrow\quad r = 6.
\]
The radius is \(6\) centimeters.

An arc of \(90^\circ\) is \(20\) feet long. Find the radius. Round to the nearest hundredth.

\[
\frac{90}{360} \cdot 2\pi r = 20 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{\pi r}{2} = 20 \quad\Rightarrow\quad r = \frac{40}{\pi} \approx 12.73.
\]
The radius is about \(12.73\) feet.


An arc of \(120^\circ\) has length \(8\pi\) meters.
An arc of \(60^\circ\) is \(15\) inches long. Round to the nearest hundredth.




\(\dfrac{1}{3}(2\pi r) = 8\pi\), so \(r = 12\) meters.
\(\dfrac{1}{6}(2\pi r) = 15\), so \(\dfrac{\pi r}{3} = 15\) and \(r = \dfrac{45}{\pi} \approx 14.32\) inches.



Example 12: A running track
Each end of a track is a semicircle with radius \(36.5\) meters. The two straight sides are \(84.4\) meters each. How long is one lap? Round to the nearest tenth.
The two ends together make one full circle:
\[
2\pi(36.5) = 73\pi \approx 229.3 \text{ meters}.
\]
Add the two straight sides: \(229.3 + 2(84.4) = 398.1\).
One lap is about \(398.1\) meters.

title: 7.2 - Area of Circles and Sectors
text:
🔥 Warm Up
A pizza shop sells a 10-inch pizza for \(\$8\) and a 14-inch pizza for \(\$14\). Which one is the better deal?
You pay for the pizza that you can eat. That is the area of the circle, not the distance across. In this lesson you learn how to find the area of a circle, the area of one slice, and the area of shapes made from circles.

title: 7.2 - Area of Circles and Sectors
text:
Find the circumference of a circle with radius \(4\). Give the exact answer.
Find \(\pi r^2\) when \(r = 3\). Give the exact answer.
Solve \(\dfrac{x}{360} \cdot 16\pi = 4\pi\).

title: 7.2 - Area of Circles and Sectors
text:
👥 Learn Together

7.2.1 - Area of a Circle
The area of a circle is the number of square units inside it. Here is why the formula works.
Cut a circle into thin wedges, like pizza slices. Then slide the wedges together, one pointing up and the next pointing down.





The new shape looks like a parallelogram. Its base is half of the circumference, \(\frac{1}{2}(2\pi r) = \pi r\). Its height is \(r\). The area of a parallelogram is base times height:
\[
A = \pi r \cdot r = \pi r^2.
\]
If you cut thinner wedges, the shape gets closer to a real parallelogram.

\[
A = \pi r^2
\] Use the radius, not the diameter. Area is in square units.


Example 1: Area from the radius
A circle has a radius of \(5\) inches. Find its area.
\[
A = \pi r^2 = \pi(5)^2 = 25\pi \approx 78.54 \text{ square inches}
\]
Example 2: Area from the diameter
A circle has a diameter of \(12\) feet. Find its area.
The radius is half of the diameter: \(r = 6\) feet.
\[
A = \pi(6)^2 = 36\pi \approx 113.10 \text{ square feet}
\]


\(r = 7\) inches
\(d = 6\) meters




\(A = 49\pi \approx 153.94\) square inches
\(r = 3\), so \(A = 9\pi \approx 28.27\) square meters



Example 3: Find the radius from the area

A circle has an area of \(49\pi\) square meters. Find the radius.
\(\pi r^2 = 49\pi\). Divide both sides by \(\pi\): \(r^2 = 49\). So \(r = 7\) meters.
A circle has an area of \(100\) square feet. Find the radius. Round to the nearest hundredth.
\(\pi r^2 = 100\), so \(r^2 = \dfrac{100}{\pi}\) and \(r = \sqrt{\dfrac{100}{\pi}} \approx 5.64\) feet.



\(A = 144\pi\) square inches
\(A = 150\) square centimeters. Round to the nearest tenth.




\(r^2 = 144\), so \(r = 12\) inches
\(r^2 = \dfrac{150}{\pi}\), so \(r = \sqrt{\dfrac{150}{\pi}} \approx 6.9\) centimeters





7.2.2 - Area of a Sector
A sector is the region inside a circle between two radii and the arc they cut off. A slice of pizza is a sector.





A sector is a fraction of the whole circle. The fraction is the central angle over \(360^\circ\). So the sector is that fraction of the circle’s area.

\[
\text{sector area} = \frac{\text{central angle}}{360^\circ} \cdot \pi r^2
\] Compare with 7.1: arc length uses \(2\pi r\) and is a distance. Sector area uses \(\pi r^2\) and is an area.


Example 4: Find a sector area





The radius is \(10\) inches and the central angle is \(135^\circ\). Find the area of the sector. Give the exact answer and a decimal rounded to the nearest hundredth.
\[
A = \frac{135}{360} \cdot \pi(10)^2 = \frac{3}{8} \cdot 100\pi = 37.5\pi
\]
The area is \(37.5\pi\) square inches, or about \(117.81\) square inches.
Example 5: Another sector
A sector has radius \(6\) feet and a central angle of \(60^\circ\).
\[
A = \frac{60}{360} \cdot \pi(6)^2 = \frac{1}{6} \cdot 36\pi = 6\pi \approx 18.85 \text{ square feet}
\]

\(r = 9\) meters and the central angle is \(120^\circ\). Give the exact answer and a decimal rounded to the nearest hundredth.


\(\dfrac{120}{360} \cdot \pi(9)^2 = \dfrac{1}{3} \cdot 81\pi = 27\pi \approx 84.82\) square meters


Example 6: Find the central angle
A sector of a circle with radius \(6\) inches has an area of \(12\pi\) square inches. Find the central angle.
\[
\frac{x}{360} \cdot \pi(6)^2 = 12\pi \quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{x}{360} \cdot 36\pi = 12\pi \quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{x}{360} = \frac{1}{3} \quad\Rightarrow\quad x = 120.
\]
The central angle is \(120^\circ\).

A sector of a circle with radius \(4\) meters has an area of \(6\pi\) square meters.


\(\dfrac{x}{360} \cdot 16\pi = 6\pi\), so \(\dfrac{x}{360} = \dfrac{6}{16} = \dfrac{3}{8}\) and \(x = 135^\circ\).


Example 7: Find the radius

A \(90^\circ\) sector has an area of \(25\pi\) square centimeters. Find the radius.

\[
\frac{90}{360} \cdot \pi r^2 = 25\pi \quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{1}{4}\pi r^2 = 25\pi \quad\Rightarrow\quad r^2 = 100 \quad\Rightarrow\quad r = 10.
\]

A \(60^\circ\) sector has an area of \(30\) square feet. Find the radius. Round to the nearest hundredth.

\[
\frac{1}{6}\pi r^2 = 30 \quad\Rightarrow\quad r^2 = \frac{180}{\pi} \quad\Rightarrow\quad r = \sqrt{\frac{180}{\pi}} \approx 7.57 \text{ feet}.
\]


A \(60^\circ\) sector has an area of \(6\pi\) square inches.
A \(120^\circ\) sector has an area of \(20\) square meters. Round to the nearest tenth.




\(\dfrac{1}{6}\pi r^2 = 6\pi\), so \(r^2 = 36\) and \(r = 6\) inches.
\(\dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 = 20\), so \(r^2 = \dfrac{60}{\pi}\) and \(r = \sqrt{\dfrac{60}{\pi}} \approx 4.4\) meters.



Use the radius in \(\pi r^2\). If you are given the diameter, cut it in half first. Do not double the answer at the end. Area is in square units, such as \(\text{ft}^2\). Arc length is in plain units, such as \(\text{ft}\).




7.2.3 - Shaded Regions and Composite Shapes
To find the area of a shaded region, add or subtract the areas of simple shapes.
Example 8: A ring





A ring, or annulus, has two circles with the same center. The outer radius is \(10\) feet. The inner radius is \(6\) feet. Find the area of the ring.
Subtract the inner circle from the outer circle.
\[
A = \pi(10)^2 - \pi(6)^2 = 100\pi - 36\pi = 64\pi \approx 201.06 \text{ square feet}
\]

The ring is \(\pi(10)^2 - \pi(6)^2\). It is not \(\pi(10 - 6)^2\). That would be \(16\pi\), which is far too small. Square each radius first, then subtract.


The outer radius is \(8\) inches and the inner radius is \(3\) inches. Give the exact answer and a decimal rounded to the nearest hundredth.


\(64\pi - 9\pi = 55\pi \approx 172.79\) square inches


Example 9: A square with a circle cut out





A square has sides of \(8\) inches. A circle with a diameter of \(8\) inches is cut out of it. Find the shaded area. Round to the nearest hundredth.
The square has area \(8^2 = 64\). The circle has \(r = 4\), so its area is \(\pi(4)^2 = 16\pi\).
\[
A = 64 - 16\pi \approx 64 - 50.27 = 13.73 \text{ square inches}
\]

A square has sides of \(6\) feet. A circle with a diameter of \(6\) feet is cut out of it. Round to the nearest hundredth.


\(36 - 9\pi \approx 36 - 28.27 = 7.73\) square feet


Example 10: A window





A window is a rectangle \(4\) feet wide and \(6\) feet tall, with a half circle on top. The diameter of the half circle is the \(4\)-foot top side. Find the area of the window. Round to the nearest hundredth.

Rectangle: \(4 \cdot 6 = 24\) square feet.
Half circle: \(r = 2\), so \(\dfrac{1}{2}\pi(2)^2 = 2\pi \approx 6.28\) square feet.

\[
A = 24 + 2\pi \approx 30.28 \text{ square feet}
\]

A window is a rectangle \(3\) feet wide and \(5\) feet tall, with a half circle on top. The diameter of the half circle is the \(3\)-foot side. Round to the nearest hundredth.


Rectangle: \(15\). Half circle: \(r = 1.5\), so \(\dfrac{1}{2}\pi(1.5)^2 = 1.125\pi \approx 3.53\). Total: \(15 + 3.53 = 18.53\) square feet.




7.2.4 - Using Area
Example 11: The better deal
A 10-inch pizza costs \(\$8\). A 14-inch pizza costs \(\$14\). Which gives more pizza for each dollar?

10-inch: \(r = 5\), \(A = 25\pi \approx 78.54\) square inches. Per dollar: \(78.54 \div 8 \approx 9.82\) square inches.
14-inch: \(r = 7\), \(A = 49\pi \approx 153.94\) square inches. Per dollar: \(153.94 \div 14 \approx 11.00\) square inches.

The 14-inch pizza is the better deal.

The 14-inch pizza is only \(1.4\) times as wide as the 10-inch pizza. But its area is about \(1.96\) times as big. Area grows with the square of the radius.


An 8-inch pizza costs \(\$6\). A 12-inch pizza costs \(\$12\). Round to the nearest hundredth.


8-inch: \(16\pi \approx 50.27\) square inches, and \(50.27 \div 6 \approx 8.38\) per dollar. 12-inch: \(36\pi \approx 113.10\), and \(113.10 \div 12 \approx 9.42\) per dollar. The 12-inch pizza is the better deal.


Example 12: A sprinkler





A sprinkler sprays water \(15\) feet. It turns back and forth through an angle of \(120^\circ\). How much grass does it water? Round to the nearest hundredth.
\[
A = \frac{120}{360} \cdot \pi(15)^2 = \frac{1}{3} \cdot 225\pi = 75\pi \approx 235.62 \text{ square feet}
\]

A sprinkler sprays \(12\) feet and turns through \(150^\circ\). Round to the nearest hundredth.


\(\dfrac{150}{360} \cdot \pi(12)^2 = \dfrac{5}{12} \cdot 144\pi = 60\pi \approx 188.50\) square feet


Fatima says: “A circle has a diameter of \(10\) inches, so its area is \(\pi(10)^2 = 100\pi\).” What is wrong?
She used the diameter. The radius is \(5\), so \(A = \pi(5)^2 = 25\pi\).
