title: 7.3 - Radians
text:
🔥 Warm Up
Take a piece of string as long as the radius of a pizza. Lay it along the crust. The string covers a piece of the edge. The angle at the center of the pizza is about \(57^\circ\).
That angle is called one radian. It is a way to measure angles that uses the circle itself, not the number \(360\). Math, science, and engineering use radians. In this lesson you learn what a radian is, how to change between degrees and radians, and two short formulas that work with radians.

title: 7.3 - Radians
text:
A circle has radius \(5\). Find its circumference. Give the exact answer.
Simplify \(\dfrac{120}{180}\).
Solve \(\dfrac{x}{180} = \dfrac{2}{3}\).

title: 7.3 - Radians
text:
👥 Learn Together

7.3.1 - What Is a Radian?
Lay the radius along the edge of a circle, again and again. Each time, the string makes the same angle at the center. That angle is 1 radian.





The radius fits around the circle a little more than \(6\) times. In fact, the circumference is \(2\pi r\), so exactly \(2\pi \approx 6.28\) radii fit around. So a full turn is \(2\pi\) radians.

The radian measure of a central angle is the arc length divided by the radius: \[
\theta = \frac{s}{r}
\] where \(s\) is the arc length and \(r\) is the radius. A full turn is \(2\pi\) radians.

A radian has no unit like inches. The inches cancel when you divide \(s\) by \(r\).

Example 1: Find the angle in radians
An arc is \(12\) centimeters long on a circle with radius \(4\) centimeters. Find the central angle in radians.
\[
\theta = \frac{s}{r} = \frac{12}{4} = 3 \text{ radians}
\]
Example 2: A full turn
The whole circle has arc length \(s = 2\pi r\). So
\[
\theta = \frac{2\pi r}{r} = 2\pi \text{ radians}.
\]


\(s = 10\) inches and \(r = 2.5\) inches
\(s = 9\) feet and \(r = 6\) feet




\(\theta = \dfrac{10}{2.5} = 4\) radians
\(\theta = \dfrac{9}{6} = 1.5\) radians





7.3.2 - Degrees and Radians
A full turn is \(360^\circ\), and it is also \(2\pi\) radians. Half of each gives the key fact:

\[
180^\circ = \pi \text{ radians}
\] To change degrees to radians, multiply by \(\dfrac{\pi}{180}\).
To change radians to degrees, multiply by \(\dfrac{180}{\pi}\).






Here are some angles you will use again and again.












Degrees
\(30^\circ\)
\(45^\circ\)
\(60^\circ\)
\(90^\circ\)
\(180^\circ\)
\(360^\circ\)




Radians
\(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\)
\(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\)
\(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\)
\(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\)
\(\pi\)
\(2\pi\)




Example 3: Degrees to radians
Change \(45^\circ\) to radians.
\[
45 \cdot \frac{\pi}{180} = \frac{45\pi}{180} = \frac{\pi}{4}
\]
Example 4: Degrees to radians
Change \(150^\circ\) to radians.
\[
150 \cdot \frac{\pi}{180} = \frac{150\pi}{180} = \frac{5\pi}{6}
\]
Example 5: Radians to degrees
Change \(\dfrac{5\pi}{3}\) radians to degrees.
\[
\frac{5\pi}{3} \cdot \frac{180}{\pi} = \frac{5 \cdot 180}{3} = 300^\circ
\]
The \(\pi\) cancels.
Example 6: A decimal number of radians
Change \(2\) radians to degrees. Round to the nearest hundredth.
\[
2 \cdot \frac{180}{\pi} \approx 114.59^\circ
\]
Example 7: Degrees to a decimal
Change \(70^\circ\) to radians. Give the exact answer and a decimal rounded to the nearest hundredth.
\[
70 \cdot \frac{\pi}{180} = \frac{7\pi}{18} \approx 1.22 \text{ radians}
\]


\(36^\circ\) to radians (exact)
\(225^\circ\) to radians (exact)
\(\dfrac{7\pi}{6}\) radians to degrees
\(1.5\) radians to degrees (nearest hundredth)




\(36 \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{180} = \dfrac{\pi}{5}\)
\(225 \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{180} = \dfrac{5\pi}{4}\)
\(\dfrac{7\pi}{6} \cdot \dfrac{180}{\pi} = 210^\circ\)
\(1.5 \cdot \dfrac{180}{\pi} \approx 85.94^\circ\)





7.3.3 - Arc Length and Sector Area in Radians
In 7.1 and 7.2 you used the central angle in degrees. With radians, the formulas are shorter.
Arc length. From \(\theta = \dfrac{s}{r}\), multiply both sides by \(r\):
\[
s = r\theta.
\]
Sector area. A sector is the fraction \(\dfrac{\theta}{2\pi}\) of the circle:
\[
A = \frac{\theta}{2\pi} \cdot \pi r^2 = \frac{1}{2}r^2\theta.
\]

\[
s = r\theta \qquad\qquad A = \frac{1}{2}r^2\theta
\] Compare with degrees:









Degrees (\(n^\circ\))
Radians (\(\theta\))




arc length
\(\dfrac{n}{360} \cdot 2\pi r\)
\(r\theta\)


sector area
\(\dfrac{n}{360} \cdot \pi r^2\)
\(\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta\)





Example 8: Arc length and sector area





The radius is \(8\) centimeters and \(\theta = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}\). Find the arc length and the sector area. Give the exact answers and decimals rounded to the nearest hundredth.
\[
s = r\theta = 8 \cdot \frac{3\pi}{4} = 6\pi \approx 18.85 \text{ cm}
\]
\[
A = \frac{1}{2}r^2\theta = \frac{1}{2}(8)^2 \cdot \frac{3\pi}{4} = 32 \cdot \frac{3\pi}{4} = 24\pi \approx 75.40 \text{ cm}^2
\]
Example 9: An angle that is a plain number
A sector has radius \(6\) inches and \(\theta = 2.5\) radians. Find \(s\) and \(A\).
\[
s = 6(2.5) = 15 \text{ inches} \qquad A = \frac{1}{2}(6)^2(2.5) = 45 \text{ square inches}
\]
Example 10: Find the angle
An arc is \(14\) feet long on a circle with radius \(8\) feet. Find \(\theta\) in radians. Then change it to degrees. Round to the nearest hundredth.
\[
\theta = \frac{s}{r} = \frac{14}{8} = 1.75 \text{ radians} \qquad 1.75 \cdot \frac{180}{\pi} \approx 100.27^\circ
\]
Example 11: Find the radius
A sector with \(\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\) has an area of \(36\pi\) square meters. Find \(r\).
\[
\frac{1}{2}r^2 \cdot \frac{\pi}{2} = 36\pi \quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{\pi r^2}{4} = 36\pi \quad\Rightarrow\quad r^2 = 144 \quad\Rightarrow\quad r = 12 \text{ meters}
\]

\(r = 10\) inches and \(\theta = \dfrac{2\pi}{5}\). Give the exact answers and decimals rounded to the nearest hundredth.


\(s = 10 \cdot \dfrac{2\pi}{5} = 4\pi \approx 12.57\) inches.
\(A = \dfrac{1}{2}(10)^2 \cdot \dfrac{2\pi}{5} = 50 \cdot \dfrac{2\pi}{5} = 20\pi \approx 62.83\) square inches.


Hnin has a circle with \(r = 5\) and a central angle of \(60^\circ\). She writes \(s = r\theta = 5 \cdot 60 = 300\). What is wrong?
The formula \(s = r\theta\) needs \(\theta\) in radians. Change first: \(60^\circ = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\). Then \(s = 5 \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{5\pi}{3} \approx 5.24\).




7.3.4 - Using Radians
Example 12: A point on a wheel
A wheel has a radius of \(13\) inches. A point on the rim turns through \(3\) radians. How far does the point travel?
\[
s = r\theta = 13 \cdot 3 = 39 \text{ inches}
\]
Example 13: A windshield wiper





A wiper blade covers the part of the arm from \(8\) inches to \(24\) inches from the pivot. The wiper swings through \(110^\circ\). How much glass does the blade clean? Round to the nearest tenth.
The cleaned area is a big sector minus a small sector. First change the angle:
\[
110^\circ = 110 \cdot \frac{\pi}{180} = \frac{11\pi}{18} \text{ radians}.
\]
\[
A = \frac{1}{2}(24)^2\theta - \frac{1}{2}(8)^2\theta = \frac{1}{2}(576 - 64)\theta = 256 \cdot \frac{11\pi}{18} \approx 491.5 \text{ square inches}
\]

A point on the rim of a wheel with radius \(15\) inches turns through \(\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\) radians. How far does it travel? Give the exact answer and a decimal rounded to the nearest tenth.


\(s = 15 \cdot \dfrac{4\pi}{3} = 20\pi \approx 62.8\) inches.

title: 7.4 - Inscribed Angles and Tangents
text:
🔥 Warm Up
A camera stands on the edge of a round stage. It looks at two spotlights, \(A\) and \(B\), on the edge of the stage on the other side. The camera sees the angle between the two lights.
Now move the camera along the edge, to any other seat on the same arc. The angle between the lights does not change. In this lesson you learn why. You also learn what happens when a line just touches a circle.

title: 7.4 - Inscribed Angles and Tangents
text:
A central angle measures \(84^\circ\). What is the measure of its arc?
Find the slope of the line through \((-2, 1)\) and \((4, 5)\).
Solve \(2x + 7 = 4x - 9\).

title: 7.4 - Inscribed Angles and Tangents
text:
👥 Learn Together

7.4.1 - Inscribed Angles
A central angle has its vertex at the center. An inscribed angle has its vertex on the circle, and both sides are chords. The arc that lies inside the angle is its intercepted arc.





In the figure, \(\angle ABC\) is an inscribed angle. It intercepts \(\overset{\frown}{AC}\). The central angle \(\angle AOC\) also intercepts \(\overset{\frown}{AC}\). The arc is \(80^\circ\). The central angle is \(80^\circ\), but the inscribed angle is only \(40^\circ\).

An inscribed angle is half of its intercepted arc. \[
m\angle ABC = \frac{1}{2}\, m\overset{\frown}{AC}
\] Two inscribed angles that intercept the same arc are equal.

Why it works. Look at the case where one side of the angle is a diameter.





\(OA\) and \(OB\) are both radii, so triangle \(OAB\) is isosceles. Its base angles at \(A\) and \(B\) are both \(x\). The angle \(\angle AOC\) is an outside angle of the triangle. It equals the two far angles added together: \(x + x = 2x\). So the inscribed angle \(x\) is half of the central angle \(2x\), and half of the arc.

Example 1: Angle to arc, arc to angle

An inscribed angle measures \(35^\circ\). Find its intercepted arc.
The arc is twice the angle: \(2(35^\circ) = 70^\circ\).
An arc measures \(130^\circ\). Find the inscribed angle that intercepts it.
The angle is half the arc: \(\dfrac{1}{2}(130^\circ) = 65^\circ\).



An inscribed angle measures \(62^\circ\). Find its arc.
An arc measures \(150^\circ\). Find the inscribed angle.




\(124^\circ\)
\(75^\circ\)



Example 2: Two angles on the same arc





\(\overset{\frown}{AB}\) measures \(100^\circ\). Find \(m\angle ACB\) and \(m\angle ADB\).
Both angles intercept \(\overset{\frown}{AB}\). Each is half of \(100^\circ\).
\[
m\angle ACB = m\angle ADB = 50^\circ
\]
This is why the camera sees the same angle from every seat on the arc.

Find the measure of each angle.


\(\dfrac{1}{2}(84^\circ) = 42^\circ\) for each angle.


Example 3: Solve for \(x\)






\(m\angle ABC = (3x + 5)^\circ\) and \(m\overset{\frown}{AC} = (10x - 30)^\circ\). Find \(x\) and both measures.

The angle is half the arc:
\[
3x + 5 = \frac{1}{2}(10x - 30) \quad\Rightarrow\quad 3x + 5 = 5x - 15 \quad\Rightarrow\quad 20 = 2x \quad\Rightarrow\quad x = 10.
\]
The angle is \(3(10) + 5 = 35^\circ\). The arc is \(10(10) - 30 = 70^\circ\).

Two inscribed angles intercept the same arc. They measure \((2x + 14)^\circ\) and \((5x - 4)^\circ\). Find \(x\).

They are equal: \(2x + 14 = 5x - 4\), so \(18 = 3x\) and \(x = 6\). Each angle is \(26^\circ\).


An inscribed angle measures \((2x + 20)^\circ\) and its arc measures \((6x - 20)^\circ\). Find \(x\) and both measures.
Two inscribed angles intercept the same arc. They measure \((3x + 7)^\circ\) and \((5x - 9)^\circ\). Find \(x\).




\(2x + 20 = \dfrac{1}{2}(6x - 20) = 3x - 10\), so \(x = 30\). The angle is \(80^\circ\) and the arc is \(160^\circ\).
\(3x + 7 = 5x - 9\), so \(x = 8\). Each angle is \(31^\circ\).





7.4.2 - Angles in a Semicircle
A diameter cuts a circle into two semicircles. Each semicircle is an arc of \(180^\circ\). An angle that intercepts a semicircle is half of \(180^\circ\).






An angle inscribed in a semicircle is a right angle. If \(\overline{AC}\) is a diameter and \(B\) is on the circle, then \(m\angle ABC = 90^\circ\).

Check it on the coordinate plane. Slopes tell us if two lines are perpendicular (Lesson 2.6).

Example 4: Show it with slopes





The circle has center \((0, 0)\) and radius \(5\). The diameter is \(\overline{AC}\) with \(A(-5, 0)\) and \(C(5, 0)\). Point \(B(3, 4)\) is on the circle. Show that \(\angle ABC\) is a right angle.
First, \(B\) is on the circle. Its distance from the center is \(\sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{25} = 5\).
The slopes of the two sides:
\[
\text{slope of } \overline{BA} = \frac{4 - 0}{3 - (-5)} = \frac{4}{8} = \frac{1}{2} \qquad \text{slope of } \overline{BC} = \frac{4 - 0}{3 - 5} = \frac{4}{-2} = -2
\]
The product is \(\dfrac{1}{2} \cdot (-2) = -1\). The slopes are opposite reciprocals, so \(\overline{BA} \perp \overline{BC}\). The angle is a right angle.

The circle has center \((0, 0)\) and radius \(5\). Point \(B(-4, 3)\) is on the circle. Show that \(\angle ABC\) is a right angle for \(A(-5, 0)\) and \(C(5, 0)\).


Slope of \(\overline{BA} = \dfrac{3 - 0}{-4 - (-5)} = \dfrac{3}{1} = 3\). Slope of \(\overline{BC} = \dfrac{3 - 0}{-4 - 5} = -\dfrac{1}{3}\). The product is \(3 \cdot \left(-\dfrac{1}{3}\right) = -1\), so the sides are perpendicular.


Example 5: Angles of a triangle in a semicircle
\(\overline{AC}\) is a diameter and \(B\) is on the circle.

\(m\angle A = 28^\circ\). Find \(m\angle C\).
\(\angle B = 90^\circ\), so \(\angle A + \angle C = 90^\circ\). Then \(m\angle C = 90^\circ - 28^\circ = 62^\circ\).
\(m\angle A = (4x + 2)^\circ\) and \(m\angle C = (5x + 7)^\circ\). Find \(x\) and both angles.
\((4x + 2) + (5x + 7) = 90\), so \(9x + 9 = 90\) and \(x = 9\). The angles are \(38^\circ\) and \(52^\circ\).



\(m\angle A = 51^\circ\). Find \(m\angle C\).
\(m\angle A = (x + 12)^\circ\) and \(m\angle C = (2x + 3)^\circ\). Find \(x\) and both angles.




\(90^\circ - 51^\circ = 39^\circ\)
\((x + 12) + (2x + 3) = 90\), so \(3x + 15 = 90\) and \(x = 25\). The angles are \(37^\circ\) and \(53^\circ\).





7.4.3 - Inscribed Quadrilaterals
A polygon is inscribed in a circle if all its vertices are on the circle. A four-sided one is an inscribed quadrilateral.





Each angle is half of the arc it intercepts. Angles \(A\) and \(C\) intercept two arcs that together make the whole circle, \(360^\circ\). Half of \(360^\circ\) is \(180^\circ\).

Opposite angles of an inscribed quadrilateral are supplementary. They add to \(180^\circ\). \[
m\angle A + m\angle C = 180^\circ \qquad m\angle B + m\angle D = 180^\circ
\]


Example 6: Find the angles
An inscribed quadrilateral \(ABCD\) has \(m\angle A = 100^\circ\) and \(m\angle B = 85^\circ\). Find \(m\angle C\) and \(m\angle D\).
\(\angle C\) is opposite \(\angle A\): \(m\angle C = 180^\circ - 100^\circ = 80^\circ\).
\(\angle D\) is opposite \(\angle B\): \(m\angle D = 180^\circ - 85^\circ = 95^\circ\).
Example 7: Solve for \(x\)
In the figure above, \(m\angle A = (3x + 10)^\circ\) and \(m\angle C = (5x + 10)^\circ\). Find \(x\) and both angles.
\[
(3x + 10) + (5x + 10) = 180 \quad\Rightarrow\quad 8x + 20 = 180 \quad\Rightarrow\quad 8x = 160 \quad\Rightarrow\quad x = 20.
\]
\(m\angle A = 70^\circ\) and \(m\angle C = 110^\circ\). They add to \(180^\circ\).


An inscribed quadrilateral has \(m\angle A = 71^\circ\) and \(m\angle D = 108^\circ\). Find \(m\angle C\) and \(m\angle B\).
\(m\angle B = (4x - 6)^\circ\) and \(m\angle D = (2x + 24)^\circ\). Find \(x\) and both angles.




\(m\angle C = 180^\circ - 71^\circ = 109^\circ\). \(m\angle B = 180^\circ - 108^\circ = 72^\circ\).
\((4x - 6) + (2x + 24) = 180\), so \(6x + 18 = 180\) and \(x = 27\). The angles are \(102^\circ\) and \(78^\circ\).



A rhombus has angles \(60^\circ\), \(120^\circ\), \(60^\circ\), \(120^\circ\). Its opposite angles are equal, so each pair adds to \(60 + 60 = 120\). That is not \(180\). So this rhombus cannot be inscribed in a circle. A square can, because opposite angles are \(90^\circ + 90^\circ = 180^\circ\).




7.4.4 - Tangent Lines
A line is tangent to a circle if it touches the circle at exactly one point. That point is the point of tangency.






A tangent line is perpendicular to the radius at the point of tangency.


Example 8: Show it with slopes





A circle has center \(O(0, 0)\) and radius \(5\). A tangent line touches the circle at \(T(-3, 4)\). Find the slope of the tangent line and write its equation.
Slope of radius \(\overline{OT}\): \(\dfrac{4 - 0}{-3 - 0} = -\dfrac{4}{3}\).
The tangent is perpendicular to the radius, so its slope is the opposite reciprocal, \(\dfrac{3}{4}\).
Use point-slope form through \(T\):
\[
y - 4 = \frac{3}{4}(x + 3).
\]

A circle has center \((0, 0)\) and radius \(10\). A tangent line touches it at \(T(6, 8)\). Find the slope of the radius and the slope of the tangent.


Radius: \(\dfrac{8}{6} = \dfrac{4}{3}\). Tangent: \(-\dfrac{3}{4}\).


Example 9: Tangent and the Pythagorean theorem





\(\overline{PT}\) is tangent to the circle at \(T\). The radius is \(OT = 5\) and \(OP = 13\). Find \(PT\).
The tangent is perpendicular to the radius, so triangle \(OTP\) has a right angle at \(T\). The hypotenuse is \(OP\).
\[
5^2 + PT^2 = 13^2 \quad\Rightarrow\quad PT^2 = 169 - 25 = 144 \quad\Rightarrow\quad PT = 12.
\]

\(\overline{PT}\) is tangent to a circle at \(T\). The radius is \(6\) and \(PT = 8\). Find \(OP\).


\(6^2 + 8^2 = OP^2\), so \(OP^2 = 100\) and \(OP = 10\).


Two tangents from one point. From a point outside a circle, you can draw two tangent segments. They are equal in length.
Example 10: Equal tangents





\(\overline{PA}\) and \(\overline{PB}\) are tangent to the circle. \(PA = 3x + 4\) and \(PB = 5x - 10\). Find \(x\) and \(PA\).
\[
3x + 4 = 5x - 10 \quad\Rightarrow\quad 14 = 2x \quad\Rightarrow\quad x = 7.
\]
\(PA = 3(7) + 4 = 25\). Check: \(PB = 5(7) - 10 = 25\).

Two tangent segments from one point measure \((2x + 9)\) and \((4x - 3)\). Find \(x\) and the length.


\(2x + 9 = 4x - 3\), so \(12 = 2x\) and \(x = 6\). Each length is \(2(6) + 9 = 21\).


Example 11: A belt around two pulleys





Two pulleys each have a radius of \(3\) inches. Their centers are \(10\) inches apart. A belt goes around both. How long is the belt? Round to the nearest hundredth.
The two straight parts of the belt are tangent to both circles. They are each \(10\) inches long. The two curved parts are half a circle each, so together they make one full circle:
\[
2\pi(3) = 6\pi.
\]
\[
\text{belt} = 10 + 10 + 6\pi = 20 + 6\pi \approx 38.85 \text{ inches}
\]

Two pulleys each have a radius of \(4\) inches. Their centers are \(12\) inches apart. Round to the nearest hundredth.


\(12 + 12 + 2\pi(4) = 24 + 8\pi \approx 49.13\) inches.

Inscribed quadrilaterals.

An inscribed quadrilateral \(ABCD\) has \(m\angle A = 88^\circ\) and \(m\angle B = 104^\circ\). Find \(m\angle C\) and \(m\angle D\).
\(m\angle A = (6x + 4)^\circ\) and \(m\angle C = (4x + 16)^\circ\) in an inscribed quadrilateral. Find \(x\) and both angles.
\(m\angle B = (2x + 30)^\circ\) and \(m\angle D = (7x - 12)^\circ\) in an inscribed quadrilateral. Find \(x\) and both angles.
A parallelogram has angles of \(70^\circ\) and \(110^\circ\). Can it be inscribed in a circle? Explain.


Tangent lines.

The circle \(x^2 + y^2 = 289\) has a tangent line at \(T(8, 15)\). Show that \(T\) is on the circle. Find the slope of the radius and the slope of the tangent.
\(\overline{PT}\) is tangent to a circle at \(T\). The radius is \(9\) and \(OP = 15\). Find \(PT\).

Two tangent segments from one point measure \((4x - 7)\) and \((x + 11)\). Find \(x\) and the length.


Real problems.

Two pulleys each have a radius of \(5\) inches. Their centers are \(18\) inches apart. How long is the belt around them? Round to the nearest hundredth.
Two spotlights \(A\) and \(B\) are on the edge of a round stage. \(\overset{\frown}{AB}\) measures \(110^\circ\). A camera stands at seat \(C\) on the far side of the edge. Another camera stands at seat \(D\), also on the far side. What angle does each camera see?
A road touches a circular track at point \(T\). The track has a radius of \(200\) meters. A bus stop \(P\) is on the road, \(150\) meters from \(T\). How far is the bus stop from the center of the track? How far is it from the nearest point on the track?


Find the mistake.

Amira says: “\(\angle ABC\) intercepts a \(70^\circ\) arc, so \(m\angle ABC = 70^\circ\).” Find her mistake. What is the correct measure?


Test practice

An inscribed angle intercepts an arc that measures \(118^\circ\). What is the measure of the angle?
A. \(59^\circ\)
B. \(62^\circ\)
C. \(118^\circ\)
D. \(236^\circ\)
Quadrilateral \(WXYZ\) is inscribed in a circle. \(m\angle W = 72^\circ\) and \(m\angle X = 95^\circ\). What is \(m\angle Y\)?
A. \(85^\circ\)
B. \(95^\circ\)
C. \(108^\circ\)
D. \(118^\circ\)


Challenge

A circle has the equation \(x^2 + y^2 = 25\). A tangent segment goes from \(P(10, 0)\) to the circle at \(T\). Find \(PT\). Then find \(m\angle OPT\). Hint: triangle \(OTP\) has a right angle at \(T\). Round \(PT\) to the nearest hundredth.
A square is inscribed in a circle with radius \(5\). The diagonal of the square is a diameter. Find the side length and the area of the square.

title: 7.5 - The Equation of a Circle
text:
🔥 Warm Up
A cell tower stands at \((2, 1)\) on a town map. Each unit is one mile. The tower reaches \(6\) miles in every direction. The school is at \((7, 3)\). Does the signal reach the school?
The edge of the signal is a circle. In this lesson you use the distance formula to write the equation of a circle. Then you use it to answer questions like this one.

title: 7.5 - The Equation of a Circle
text:
Find the distance between \((1, 2)\) and \((4, 6)\).
Find the midpoint of the segment with endpoints \((-2, 4)\) and \((6, -2)\).
Write \(x^2 + 8x + 16\) as the square of a sum.

title: 7.5 - The Equation of a Circle
text:
👥 Learn Together

7.5.1 - Where the Equation Comes From
A circle is all the points that are the same distance \(r\) from the center. Let the center be \((h, k)\). Let \((x, y)\) be any point on the circle.





The distance formula (Lesson 2.4) gives the distance from the center to \((x, y)\). It must equal \(r\):
\[
\sqrt{(x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2} = r.
\]
Square both sides to remove the square root:

\[
(x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2 = r^2
\] The center is \((h, k)\). The radius is \(r\). For a circle centered at the origin, \(x^2 + y^2 = r^2\).


Example 1: Build the equation
A circle has center \((2, 1)\) and radius \(6\). Write its equation.
\[
(x - 2)^2 + (y - 1)^2 = 6^2 = 36
\]
Check a point: \((2, 7)\) is \(6\) units above the center. Put it in: \((2 - 2)^2 + (7 - 1)^2 = 0 + 36 = 36\). It works.

A circle has center \((-1, 3)\) and radius \(4\).


\((x + 1)^2 + (y - 3)^2 = 16\)




7.5.2 - Read and Graph
Watch the signs. The equation has \(x - h\) and \(y - k\). A plus sign inside means the center coordinate is negative.

Example 4: From a center and a radius

\[
(x + 2)^2 + (y - 5)^2 = 9.
\]
Example 5: From a center and a point on the circle
A circle has center \((1, -2)\) and passes through \((4, 2)\). Find \(r^2\) with the distance formula. You do not need to take the square root, because the equation needs \(r^2\).
\[
r^2 = (4 - 1)^2 + (2 - (-2))^2 = 3^2 + 4^2 = 9 + 16 = 25
\]
\[
(x - 1)^2 + (y + 2)^2 = 25
\]
Example 6: From the ends of a diameter





A diameter has endpoints \((-3, 2)\) and \((5, 6)\). The center is the midpoint (Lesson 2.5):
\[
\left(\frac{-3 + 5}{2}, \frac{2 + 6}{2}\right) = (1, 4).
\]
The radius is the distance from the center to an endpoint, \((5, 6)\):
\[
r^2 = (5 - 1)^2 + (6 - 4)^2 = 16 + 4 = 20.
\]
\[
(x - 1)^2 + (y - 4)^2 = 20
\]
Check: the distance from \((1, 4)\) to the other end \((-3, 2)\) is also \(r^2 = 16 + 4 = 20\).


Center \((4, -1)\) and radius \(7\).
Center \((-3, 0)\), passing through \((1, 6)\).
A diameter with endpoints \((-2, -1)\) and \((6, 5)\).




\((x - 4)^2 + (y + 1)^2 = 49\)
\(r^2 = (1 + 3)^2 + (6 - 0)^2 = 16 + 36 = 52\). So \((x + 3)^2 + y^2 = 52\).
Center \((2, 2)\). \(r^2 = (6 - 2)^2 + (5 - 2)^2 = 16 + 9 = 25\). So \((x - 2)^2 + (y - 2)^2 = 25\).





7.5.4 - Completing the Square
Sometimes the equation is multiplied out. To find the center and radius, complete the square for \(x\) and for \(y\) (Algebra 1, Lesson 6.5). To complete \(x^2 + bx\), add \(\left(\dfrac{b}{2}\right)^2\).
Example 7: Standard form
Write \(x^2 + y^2 - 6x + 4y - 12 = 0\) in standard form. Find the center and radius.

Group the \(x\) terms and the \(y\) terms. Move the number to the right: \((x^2 - 6x) + (y^2 + 4y) = 12\).
Half of \(-6\) is \(-3\), and \((-3)^2 = 9\). Half of \(4\) is \(2\), and \(2^2 = 4\). Add both numbers to both sides:

\[
(x^2 - 6x + 9) + (y^2 + 4y + 4) = 12 + 9 + 4
\]

Factor and add:

\[
(x - 3)^2 + (y + 2)^2 = 25
\]
The center is \((3, -2)\) and the radius is \(5\).
Example 8: Another one
Write \(x^2 + y^2 + 8x - 10y + 5 = 0\) in standard form.
\[
(x^2 + 8x + 16) + (y^2 - 10y + 25) = -5 + 16 + 25
\]
\[
(x + 4)^2 + (y - 5)^2 = 36
\]
The center is \((-4, 5)\) and the radius is \(6\).


\(x^2 + y^2 + 4x - 2y - 4 = 0\)
\(x^2 + y^2 + 6x + 10y + 18 = 0\)




\((x^2 + 4x + 4) + (y^2 - 2y + 1) = 4 + 4 + 1\), so \((x + 2)^2 + (y - 1)^2 = 9\). Center \((-2, 1)\), radius \(3\).
\((x^2 + 6x + 9) + (y^2 + 10y + 25) = -18 + 9 + 25\), so \((x + 3)^2 + (y + 5)^2 = 16\). Center \((-3, -5)\), radius \(4\).



Try \(x^2 + y^2 + 4x - 6y + 20 = 0\). Completing the square gives \((x + 2)^2 + (y - 3)^2 = -20 + 4 + 9 = -7\). A square cannot add to a negative number. This is not a circle. No points make it true.




7.5.5 - On, Inside, or Outside?
A point is \(r\) away from the center if it is on the circle. Put the point in the left side of the equation and compare with \(r^2\).

Compute \((x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2\) for the point.

equal to \(r^2\): the point is on the circle
less than \(r^2\): the point is inside
greater than \(r^2\): the point is outside



Example 9: Does the signal reach the school?
The tower is at \((2, 1)\) with a reach of \(6\) miles, so the edge is \((x - 2)^2 + (y - 1)^2 = 36\). The school is at \((7, 3)\).
\[
(7 - 2)^2 + (3 - 1)^2 = 25 + 4 = 29
\]
\(29 < 36\), so the school is inside the circle. Yes, the signal reaches the school.
Example 10: Three points





The circle is \((x - 3)^2 + (y + 1)^2 = 25\). Is each point on, inside, or outside?

\(A(7, 2)\): \((4)^2 + (3)^2 = 25\). Equal to \(25\), so on the circle.
\(B(4, 0)\): \((1)^2 + (1)^2 = 2\). Less than \(25\), so inside.
\(C(-2, 5)\): \((-5)^2 + (6)^2 = 61\). More than \(25\), so outside.

Example 11: An earthquake
An earthquake is felt up to \(10\) miles from the epicenter at \((-4, 3)\). The equation is \((x + 4)^2 + (y - 3)^2 = 100\). Which towns feel it?

Town \((4, 6)\): \(8^2 + 3^2 = 73 < 100\). Inside. It feels the earthquake.
Town \((2, -5)\): \(6^2 + (-8)^2 = 100\). On the circle. It is exactly \(10\) miles away, at the edge.
Town \((6, -9)\): \(10^2 + (-12)^2 = 244 > 100\). Outside. It does not feel it.


The circle is \((x + 1)^2 + (y - 2)^2 = 25\). Test \((2, 6)\), \((-3, 5)\), and \((4, -2)\).


\((2, 6)\): \(9 + 16 = 25\), on the circle.
\((-3, 5)\): \(4 + 9 = 13 < 25\), inside.
\((4, -2)\): \(25 + 16 = 41 > 25\), outside.

title: Unit 7 Summary
text:
7.1 - Circumference and Arc Length
Example: \(r = 9\) ft and the central angle is \(70^\circ\). The arc length is \(\dfrac{70}{360} \cdot 18\pi = 3.5\pi \approx 10.99\) ft.

title: Unit 7 Summary
text:
A circle is all the points the same distance from the center. A radius goes from the center to the circle. A diameter is a chord through the center, so \(d = 2r\).
A central angle has its vertex at the center. A minor arc is less than \(180^\circ\). A semicircle is \(180^\circ\). A major arc is more than \(180^\circ\) and has three letters in its name.
Circumference: \(C = \pi d = 2\pi r\). For a circle, \(C \div d = \pi \approx 3.14159\).
Arc measure is in degrees and equals the central angle. Arc length is a distance: \(\dfrac{\text{central angle}}{360^\circ} \cdot 2\pi r\).
The arcs around a circle add to \(360^\circ\).

title: Unit 7 Summary
text:
7.2 - Area of Circles and Sectors

Area of a circle: \(A = \pi r^2\). Use the radius, not the diameter. Area is in square units.
A sector is a slice between two radii. Sector area \(= \dfrac{\text{central angle}}{360^\circ} \cdot \pi r^2\).
A ring (annulus) has area \(\pi R^2 - \pi r^2\). Square each radius first, then subtract.
For a shaded region, add or subtract the areas of simple shapes.






Example: \(r = 6\) in and the central angle is \(60^\circ\). The sector area is \(\dfrac{60}{360} \cdot 36\pi = 6\pi \approx 18.85\) square inches.

title: Unit 7 Summary
text:
7.3 - Radians

One radian is the central angle whose arc is as long as the radius. \(\theta = \dfrac{s}{r}\).
A full turn is \(2\pi\) radians. \(180^\circ = \pi\) radians.
Degrees to radians: multiply by \(\dfrac{\pi}{180}\). Radians to degrees: multiply by \(\dfrac{180}{\pi}\).
With \(\theta\) in radians: arc length \(s = r\theta\) and sector area \(A = \dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta\).

Example: \(r = 8\) and \(\theta = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}\). Then \(s = 8 \cdot \dfrac{3\pi}{4} = 6\pi\) and \(A = \dfrac{1}{2}(64)\dfrac{3\pi}{4} = 24\pi\).

title: Unit 7 Summary
text:
7.4 - Inscribed Angles and Tangents

An inscribed angle has its vertex on the circle. It is half of its intercepted arc. Two inscribed angles on the same arc are equal.
An angle inscribed in a semicircle is a right angle.
Opposite angles of an inscribed quadrilateral are supplementary.
A tangent line touches the circle at one point and is perpendicular to the radius there. Two tangent segments from one outside point are equal.






Example: an inscribed angle that intercepts an \(80^\circ\) arc measures \(40^\circ\). A tangent segment \(PT\) with radius \(5\) and \(OP = 13\) has \(PT = \sqrt{13^2 - 5^2} = 12\).

title: Unit 7 Summary
text:
7.5 - The Equation of a Circle

Standard form: \((x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2 = r^2\). The center is \((h, k)\). The radius is \(r\).
A plus sign inside means a negative coordinate: \((x + 3)^2\) has \(h = -3\).
From a center and a point: find \(r^2\) with the distance formula. From the ends of a diameter: the center is the midpoint.
To change \(x^2 + y^2 + bx + cy + d = 0\) to standard form, complete the square for \(x\) and for \(y\). Add the same numbers to both sides.
Compare \((x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2\) with \(r^2\): equal is on the circle, less is inside, more is outside.






Example: \(x^2 + y^2 - 6x + 4y - 12 = 0\) becomes \((x - 3)^2 + (y + 2)^2 = 25\). The center is \((3, -2)\) and the radius is \(5\).

title: Unit 7 Review
text:
7.1 - Circumference and Arc Length
Example 1: A circle has radius \(15\) feet. Find the length of an arc with central angle \(80^\circ\). Give the exact answer and a decimal rounded to the nearest hundredth.
\(\dfrac{80}{360} \cdot 2\pi(15) = \dfrac{2}{9} \cdot 30\pi = \dfrac{20\pi}{3} \approx 20.94\) ft.


7.2 - Area of Circles and Sectors
Example 2: A sector has radius \(18\) inches and central angle \(50^\circ\). Find its area. Give the exact answer and a decimal rounded to the nearest hundredth.
\(\dfrac{50}{360} \cdot \pi(18)^2 = \dfrac{5}{36} \cdot 324\pi = 45\pi \approx 141.37\) square inches.


7.3 - Radians
Example 3: Change \(330^\circ\) to radians. Then find the arc length for \(r = 20\) and \(\theta = \dfrac{2\pi}{5}\).
\(330 \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{180} = \dfrac{11\pi}{6}\). Then \(s = r\theta = 20 \cdot \dfrac{2\pi}{5} = 8\pi \approx 25.13\).


7.4 - Inscribed Angles and Tangents
Example 4: An inscribed quadrilateral has \(m\angle B = (3x + 9)^\circ\) and \(m\angle D = (7x - 29)^\circ\). Find \(x\) and both angles.
Opposite angles add to \(180^\circ\): \((3x + 9) + (7x - 29) = 180\), so \(10x - 20 = 180\) and \(x = 20\). The angles are \(69^\circ\) and \(111^\circ\).


7.5 - The Equation of a Circle
Example 5: Write \(x^2 + y^2 - 10x + 4y + 13 = 0\) in standard form. Find the center and radius.
\((x^2 - 10x + 25) + (y^2 + 4y + 4) = -13 + 25 + 4\), so \((x - 5)^2 + (y + 2)^2 = 16\). The center is \((5, -2)\) and the radius is \(4\).

title: 8.1 - Area of Polygons and Composite Figures
text:
👥 Learn Together

8.1.1 - Parallelograms, Triangles, and Trapezoids
Area tells how many square units cover a flat shape. A rectangle with base \(b\) and height \(h\) has area \(A = bh\). The other shapes come from the rectangle.
The base is a side you choose. The height is the distance from the base to the opposite side, measured at a right angle. A dashed line with a square mark shows the height.
Parallelogram. Cut a triangle off one end and move it to the other end. You get a rectangle with the same base and height.





Triangle. Two copies of a triangle make a parallelogram. The triangle is half of it.





Trapezoid. Two copies of a trapezoid make a parallelogram. Its base is \(b_1 + b_2\). The trapezoid is half of it.








Shape
Area




rectangle
\(A = bh\)


parallelogram
\(A = bh\)


triangle
\(A = \dfrac{1}{2}bh\)


trapezoid
\(A = \dfrac{1}{2}(b_1 + b_2)h\)




The height makes a right angle with the base. A slanted side is longer than the height, so never use it in these formulas.


Example 1: Area of a parallelogram





Find the area.
The base is \(14\) ft. The height is \(9\) ft (the dashed line). The \(10\) ft side is slanted, so we do not use it.
\[
A = bh = 14 \cdot 9 = 126 \text{ square feet}
\]

\(A = bh = 9 \cdot 6 = 54\) square feet. The \(7\) ft side is not used.


Example 2: Find the mistake
Amira finds the area of the parallelogram in Example 1. She writes \(A = 14 \cdot 10 = 140\) square feet. What is her mistake?
She used the slanted side (\(10\) ft) as the height. The height is the dashed line, \(9\) ft. The correct area is \(14 \cdot 9 = 126\) square feet.

Kofi finds the area of a triangle with base \(10\) cm and height \(6\) cm. He writes \(A = 10 \cdot 6 = 60\) square centimeters. What did he forget? What is the correct area?


He forgot the \(\frac{1}{2}\). The correct area is \(\frac{1}{2}(10)(6) = 30\) square centimeters.


Example 3: A triangle on the coordinate plane





Find the area of \(\triangle ABC\) with \(A(-2, 1)\), \(B(6, 1)\), and \(C(2, 7)\).
Points \(A\) and \(B\) have the same \(y\)-coordinate, so \(\overline{AB}\) is horizontal. Use it as the base.
\[
b = 6 - (-2) = 8
\]
The height goes straight up from the base to \(C\). It is the difference in \(y\)-coordinates.
\[
h = 7 - 1 = 6
\]
\[
A = \tfrac{1}{2}bh = \tfrac{1}{2}(8)(6) = 24 \text{ square units}
\]

\(PQ\) is horizontal: \(b = 5 - (-3) = 8\). The height is \(5 - (-2) = 7\).
\(A = \frac{1}{2}(8)(7) = 28\) square units.


Example 4: A trapezoid





A garden bed is a trapezoid. Find its area.
The parallel sides are \(b_1 = 12\) ft and \(b_2 = 20\) ft. The height is \(8\) ft.
\[
A = \tfrac{1}{2}(b_1 + b_2)h = \tfrac{1}{2}(12 + 20)(8) = \tfrac{1}{2}(32)(8) = 128 \text{ square feet}
\]

\(A = \frac{1}{2}(9 + 15)(6) = \frac{1}{2}(24)(6) = 72\) square feet.




8.1.2 - Regular Polygons
A regular polygon has equal sides and equal angles. The apothem \(a\) is the distance from the center to the middle of a side. It makes a right angle with the side.
Draw lines from the center to every corner. The polygon is cut into triangles. Each triangle has a base that is one side and a height that is the apothem. Add them up:
\[
A = \tfrac{1}{2}a \cdot (\text{side}) \cdot (\text{number of sides}) = \tfrac{1}{2}aP
\]

\(A = \dfrac{1}{2}aP\), where \(a\) is the apothem and \(P\) is the perimeter.


Example 5: A regular hexagon





A regular hexagon has side \(6\) in. Find its area. Give the exact answer and a decimal rounded to the nearest tenth.
The lines from the center to the corners cut the hexagon into \(6\) equilateral triangles. So the distance from the center to each corner is also \(6\) in.
The apothem cuts one triangle into two \(30^\circ\)-\(60^\circ\)-\(90^\circ\) triangles. The short leg is \(3\) in. From Lesson 6.1, the long leg is the short leg times \(\sqrt{3}\):
\[
a = 3\sqrt{3} \text{ in}
\]
The perimeter is \(P = 6 \cdot 6 = 36\) in.
\[
A = \tfrac{1}{2}aP = \tfrac{1}{2}(3\sqrt{3})(36) = 54\sqrt{3} \approx 93.5 \text{ square inches}
\]

Short leg \(= 5\), so \(a = 5\sqrt{3}\) cm. \(P = 6 \cdot 10 = 60\) cm.
\(A = \frac{1}{2}(5\sqrt{3})(60) = 150\sqrt{3} \approx 259.8\) square centimeters.


Example 6: A stop sign





A stop sign is a regular octagon. Each side is \(12.5\) in. The apothem is \(15.1\) in. Find the area of the sign. Round to the nearest square inch.
\[
P = 8 \cdot 12.5 = 100 \text{ in}
\]
\[
A = \tfrac{1}{2}aP = \tfrac{1}{2}(15.1)(100) = 755 \text{ square inches}
\]

\(P = 5 \cdot 8 = 40\) in. \(A = \frac{1}{2}(5.5)(40) = 110\) square inches.




8.1.3 - Composite Figures
A composite figure is made of simple shapes. There are two ways to find its area:

Add the areas of the parts.
Subtract a missing part from a bigger shape.

Always say which shapes you see before you start.

Example 7: An L-shaped room





Diego wants flooring for this room. The flooring costs \(\$3.50\) per square foot. Find the area and the cost.
The room is a \(20\) ft by \(14\) ft rectangle with an \(8\) ft by \(6\) ft corner missing.
\[
A = 20 \cdot 14 - 8 \cdot 6 = 280 - 48 = 232 \text{ square feet}
\]
\[
\text{Cost} = 232 \cdot 3.50 = \$812
\]

\(A = 12 \cdot 10 - 4 \cdot 3 = 120 - 12 = 108\) square feet.


Example 8: Paint for a wall





Moses will paint this wall. He does not paint the window or the door. Find the area he paints.
Wall: \(16 \cdot 8 = 128\) square feet.
Window: \(5 \cdot 4 = 20\) square feet.
Door: \(3 \cdot 7 = 21\) square feet.
\[
128 - 20 - 21 = 87 \text{ square feet}
\]

Wall: \(14 \cdot 9 = 126\). Window: \(12\). Door: \(21\).
\(126 - 12 - 21 = 93\) square feet.


Example 9: A garden with a rounded end





A garden is a rectangle with a semicircle on one end. The rectangle is \(24\) ft by \(10\) ft. The diameter of the semicircle is \(10\) ft. Find the area. Give the exact answer and a decimal rounded to the nearest tenth.
Rectangle: \(24 \cdot 10 = 240\) square feet.
The radius is \(5\) ft. A semicircle is half a circle (Lesson 7.2):
\[
\tfrac{1}{2}\pi r^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}\pi(5)^2 = 12.5\pi \text{ square feet}
\]
\[
A = 240 + 12.5\pi \approx 279.3 \text{ square feet}
\]

Rectangle: \(18 \cdot 8 = 144\). Semicircle: \(r = 4\), \(\frac{1}{2}\pi(4)^2 = 8\pi\).
\(A = 144 + 8\pi \approx 169.1\) square feet.




8.1.4 - Finding a Missing Length
Sometimes you know the area and need a length. Write the area formula with the lengths you know. Put in the area. Then solve the equation.
Example 10: A trapezoid with a missing base





A trapezoid has bases \(x\) and \(x + 4\) and height \(6\) ft. The area is \(66\) square feet. Find \(x\).
\[
\tfrac{1}{2}(x + (x + 4))(6) = 66
\]
\[
3(2x + 4) = 66
\]
\[
6x + 12 = 66
\]
\[
6x = 54
\]
\[
x = 9
\]
The bases are \(9\) ft and \(13\) ft. Check: \(\frac{1}{2}(9 + 13)(6) = 66\).

\(\frac{1}{2}(2x + 6)(5) = 55\), so \(5x + 15 = 55\), so \(x = 8\).
The bases are \(8\) ft and \(14\) ft.


A triangle has three sides. Each one can be the base, with its own height. All three choices give the same area. Try it with a \(3\)-\(4\)-\(5\) right triangle: use leg \(3\) with height \(4\), then use leg \(4\) with height \(3\).

text:
🔥 Warm Up
A baker cuts a round loaf of bread. The cut face is a flat shape. A potter spins a lump of clay on a wheel. The clay becomes a round bowl.

title: 8.2 - Cross Sections and Solids of Revolution
text:
👥 Learn Together

8.2.1 - Solids
A solid is a three-dimensional shape. These are the five solids we study.





A polyhedron has only flat faces. Prisms and pyramids are polyhedrons. Cylinders, cones, and spheres are not, because they have curved surfaces.

A face is a flat surface.
An edge is where two faces meet.
A vertex of a solid is a corner where edges meet.

A prism has two parallel bases that are the same shape. A pyramid has one base and triangle faces that meet at a point. We name each by its base, such as a triangular prism or a square pyramid.

Example 1: Count the parts





Name the solid. Count its faces, vertices, and edges.
The two bases are triangles, so this is a triangular prism.

Faces: \(2\) triangles and \(3\) rectangles, so \(5\) faces.
Vertices: \(3\) on each base, so \(6\) vertices.
Edges: \(3\) on each base and \(3\) going between them, so \(9\) edges.







A square pyramid. Faces: \(1\) square and \(4\) triangles, so \(5\). Vertices: \(4\) at the base and \(1\) on top, so \(5\). Edges: \(4\) at the base and \(4\) going up, so \(8\).


Leonhard Euler saw a pattern in these counts. Look at the last column.



Solid
Faces \(F\)
Vertices \(V\)
Edges \(E\)
\(F + V - E\)




cube
\(6\)
\(8\)
\(12\)
\(2\)


triangular prism
\(5\)
\(6\)
\(9\)
\(2\)


square pyramid

\(8\)
\(2\)


pentagonal prism
\(7\)
\(10\)
\(15\)
\(2\)




For a polyhedron with no holes, \(F + V - E = 2\).


Example 2: Use the pattern
A polyhedron has \(9\) faces and \(14\) vertices. How many edges does it have?
\[
F + V - E = 2
\]
\[
9 + 14 - E = 2
\]
\[
23 - E = 2
\]
\[
E = 21
\]
It has \(21\) edges.

\(8 + 12 - E = 2\), so \(20 - E = 2\), so \(E = 18\).




8.2.2 - Cross Sections
Imagine a plane (a flat sheet) cutting through a solid. The flat shape on the cut is the cross section. The shape depends on how you cut.
Example 3: Slicing a cube





Name the cross section in each cube.

A: the plane is parallel to the top. The cross section is a square.
B: the plane goes through two opposite edges. The cross section is a rectangle that is not a square.
C: the plane cuts off a corner. The cross section is a triangle.
D: the plane cuts through the middle of six edges. The cross section is a hexagon.


No. Cubes A and B are both cube slices, but B is a rectangle that is longer than it is wide. One example like this is a counterexample. It shows that “every slice is a square” is false.


Example 4: Slicing a cylinder and a cone





Name the cross section in each picture.

1: a cut parallel to the base of a cylinder is a circle.
2: a cut straight through the axis of a cylinder is a rectangle.
3: a cut parallel to the base of a cone is a circle (smaller than the base).
4: a cut through the apex and the center of the base of a cone is a triangle.

Every cut of a sphere is a circle.

Parallel to the base: a square, smaller than the base.
Straight down through the apex: a triangle.


Example 5: A slice of a sphere





A sphere has radius \(5\) in. A plane cuts it \(3\) in from the center. Find the area of the cross section. Give the exact answer and a decimal rounded to the nearest tenth.
The cross section is a circle. Look at the side view. The radius of the sphere (\(5\)) is the hypotenuse of a right triangle. One leg is \(3\). The other leg is the radius \(r\) of the cross section.
\[
r^2 + 3^2 = 5^2
\]
\[
r^2 = 25 - 9 = 16
\]
\[
r = 4
\]
\[
A = \pi r^2 = 16\pi \approx 50.3 \text{ square inches}
\]

\(r^2 + 5^2 = 13^2\), so \(r^2 = 169 - 25 = 144\) and \(r = 12\).
\(A = 144\pi \approx 452.4\) square centimeters.


Example 6: Real slices
A deli cuts a round block of cheese. The block is a cylinder. The cut is straight across, parallel to the flat ends. What shape is each slice? Another cut goes at a slant through the block. What shape is that slice?
Parallel to the ends: a circle. A slanted cut makes a longer, rounder shape called an ellipse (an oval).

A circle. Every slice of a sphere is a circle.




8.2.3 - Solids of Revolution
Spin a flat shape around a line. The shape sweeps out a solid. The line is the axis of revolution. The solid is a solid of revolution.








Flat shape
Spin around
Solid




rectangle
one side
cylinder


right triangle
one leg
cone


semicircle
its diameter
sphere




Example 7: Spin a rectangle





The rectangle has vertices \((0, 0)\), \((3, 0)\), \((3, 5)\), and \((0, 5)\). It spins around the \(y\)-axis. Describe the solid.
The \(y\)-axis is the side from \((0, 0)\) to \((0, 5)\). The solid is a cylinder.

The radius is the distance from the axis to the far side: \(r = 3\).
The height is the length along the axis: \(h = 5\).


A cylinder. The side along the \(x\)-axis has length \(3\), so the height is \(h = 3\). The far side is \(5\) away from the axis, so the radius is \(r = 5\).


Example 8: Spin a triangle





The triangle has vertices \((0, 0)\), \((4, 0)\), and \((0, 6)\). It spins around the \(y\)-axis. Describe the solid. Find the slant height. Give the exact answer and a decimal rounded to the nearest tenth.
The solid is a cone. The radius is \(r = 4\) and the height is \(h = 6\).
The slant height \(\ell\) is the hypotenuse of the triangle (the slanted side of the cone):
\[
\ell^2 = 4^2 + 6^2 = 16 + 36 = 52
\]
\[
\ell = \sqrt{52} = 2\sqrt{13} \approx 7.2
\]

\(r = 5\), \(h = 12\). \(\ell^2 = 25 + 144 = 169\), so \(\ell = 13\).

A right triangle has legs \(5\) in and \(12\) in. The triangle spins around its \(12\) in leg. Which describes the solid it makes?

B. a cone with radius \(5\) in and height \(12\) in

A plane cuts a cone parallel to its base, between the base and the apex. Which statement describes the cross section?

C. It is a circle smaller than the base.
D. It is a circle the same size as the base.


Challenge

A polyhedron has \(12\) faces. Every face is a pentagon, and every edge is shared by two faces. How many edges does it have? How many vertices?

text:

Lucía wraps a gift box. She cuts wrapping paper that covers every side of the box, and nothing more. Paper that is too small leaves a gap. Paper that is too big is wasted.
The amount of paper is the surface area of the box. In this lesson you unfold solids into flat patterns, and you find the surface area of prisms, cylinders, pyramids, cones, and spheres.

title: 8.3 - Surface Area and Nets

title: 8.3 - Surface Area and Nets
text:
👥 Learn Together

8.3.1 - Nets
A net is a solid cut open and laid flat. Every face shows. If you fold the net, you get the solid back.





Surface area is the area of the net. Add the areas of all the pieces.

Example 1: Does the net fold into a cube?





A cube has \(6\) faces. All three nets have \(6\) squares, but they do not all fold into a cube.

A folds into a cube. Four squares make a band around the cube. One square is the top and one is the bottom.
B does not fold into a cube. Four squares make a band. The two extra squares are both on the top side. They land on the same face, and the bottom face is empty.
C folds into a cube. One extra square is the top and the other is the bottom.


A triangular prism. The triangles are the two bases. The rectangles are the sides.




8.3.2 - Prisms
The surface area of a prism has two parts.

The lateral area \(L\) is the area of the sides (the rectangles). Unrolled, the sides make one big rectangle with width \(P\) (the perimeter of the base) and height \(h\). So \(L = Ph\).
The two bases each have area \(B\).


\(SA = L + 2B = Ph + 2B\)

For a box, you can also add the area of the three different faces and double it.

Example 2: A box





Find the surface area of the box. It is \(8\) in long, \(5\) in wide, and \(3\) in tall.
Three pairs of faces:

top and bottom: \(2(8 \cdot 5) = 80\)
front and back: \(2(8 \cdot 3) = 48\)
left and right: \(2(5 \cdot 3) = 30\)

\[
SA = 80 + 48 + 30 = 158 \text{ square inches}
\]

\(2(9 \cdot 6) + 2(9 \cdot 4) + 2(6 \cdot 4) = 108 + 72 + 48 = 228\) square inches.


Example 3: A triangular prism





The bases are right triangles with sides \(3\), \(4\), and \(5\) cm. The prism is \(10\) cm long. Find the surface area.
Base area: \(B = \frac{1}{2}(4)(3) = 6\).
Base perimeter: \(P = 3 + 4 + 5 = 12\).
Lateral area: \(L = Ph = 12 \cdot 10 = 120\).
\[
SA = L + 2B = 120 + 2(6) = 132 \text{ square centimeters}
\]

\(B = \frac{1}{2}(12)(5) = 30\). \(P = 5 + 12 + 13 = 30\). \(L = 30 \cdot 8 = 240\).
\(SA = 240 + 2(30) = 300\) square centimeters.




8.3.3 - Cylinders
Take the label off a can. Lay it flat. It is a rectangle. Its width is the distance around the can, \(2\pi r\). Its height is the height of the can, \(h\).





The lateral area is \(2\pi r h\). The two circles each have area \(\pi r^2\).

\(SA = 2\pi r^2 + 2\pi r h\)


Example 4: A cylinder





Find the surface area of a cylinder with \(r = 3\) ft and \(h = 8\) ft. Give the exact answer and a decimal rounded to the nearest tenth.
\[
SA = 2\pi(3)^2 + 2\pi(3)(8) = 18\pi + 48\pi = 66\pi \approx 207.3 \text{ square feet}
\]

\(SA = 2\pi(4)^2 + 2\pi(4)(11) = 32\pi + 88\pi = 120\pi \approx 377.0\) square inches.


Example 5: Paint for a tank





A closed water tank has radius \(10\) ft and height \(12\) ft. One gallon of paint covers \(350\) square feet. How many whole gallons does Samir need to paint the whole outside? Round the surface area to the nearest tenth.
\[
SA = 2\pi(10)^2 + 2\pi(10)(12) = 200\pi + 240\pi = 440\pi \approx 1382.3 \text{ square feet}
\]
\[
1382.3 \div 350 \approx 3.95
\]
He needs \(4\) gallons. (He cannot buy \(0.95\) of a gallon more than he needs, so round up.)

Label \(= 2\pi r h = 2\pi(4)(12) = 96\pi \approx 301.6\) square centimeters.




8.3.4 - Pyramids, Cones, and Spheres
The slant height \(\ell\) is measured along a slanted face. In a pyramid, it goes from the middle of a base edge up to the apex. In a cone, it goes from the edge of the base up to the apex.
The slant height, the height, and half of the base make a right triangle. Use the Pythagorean theorem to find any missing side.

Regular pyramid: \(SA = B + \frac{1}{2}P\ell\)
Cone: \(SA = \pi r^2 + \pi r \ell\)
Sphere: \(SA = 4\pi r^2\)

The triangle faces of a regular pyramid each have base (one edge) and height \(\ell\). All the faces together have area \(\frac{1}{2}P\ell\).

Example 6: A square pyramid with the slant height given





The base is a square with side \(6\) ft. The slant height is \(5\) ft. Find the surface area.
\(B = 6 \cdot 6 = 36\). \(P = 4 \cdot 6 = 24\).
\[
SA = B + \tfrac{1}{2}P\ell = 36 + \tfrac{1}{2}(24)(5) = 36 + 60 = 96 \text{ square feet}
\]

\(B = 100\). \(P = 40\). \(SA = 100 + \frac{1}{2}(40)(8) = 100 + 160 = 260\) square feet.


Example 7: A square pyramid with the height given





The base is a square with side \(10\) in. The height is \(12\) in. Find the surface area.
First find the slant height. Half the base is \(5\). The right triangle has legs \(5\) and \(12\):
\[
\ell^2 = 5^2 + 12^2 = 169, \quad \ell = 13
\]
\(B = 100\) and \(P = 40\).
\[
SA = 100 + \tfrac{1}{2}(40)(13) = 100 + 260 = 360 \text{ square inches}
\]

Half the base is \(6\). \(\ell^2 = 6^2 + 8^2 = 100\), so \(\ell = 10\).
\(SA = 144 + \frac{1}{2}(48)(10) = 144 + 240 = 384\) square inches.


Example 8: A cone





A cone has radius \(4\) in and height \(3\) in. Find the surface area. Give the exact answer and a decimal rounded to the nearest tenth.
Find the slant height: \(\ell^2 = 4^2 + 3^2 = 25\), so \(\ell = 5\).
\[
SA = \pi r^2 + \pi r \ell = \pi(4)^2 + \pi(4)(5) = 16\pi + 20\pi = 36\pi \approx 113.1 \text{ square inches}
\]

\(\ell^2 = 81 + 144 = 225\), so \(\ell = 15\).
\(SA = \pi(81) + \pi(9)(15) = 81\pi + 135\pi = 216\pi \approx 678.6\) square centimeters.


Example 9: Find the mistake
Kofi finds the surface area of the cone in Example 8. He writes \(SA = \pi(4)^2 + \pi(4)(3) = 28\pi\). What is his mistake?
He used the height \(3\) in the formula. The formula needs the slant height \(\ell = 5\). The correct answer is \(36\pi\).

Example 10: A sphere
A basketball has radius \(12\) cm. Find the area of its surface. Give the exact answer and a decimal rounded to the nearest tenth.
\[
SA = 4\pi r^2 = 4\pi(12)^2 = 576\pi \approx 1809.6 \text{ square centimeters}
\]

\(SA = 4\pi(11)^2 = 484\pi \approx 1520.5\) square centimeters.


Peel an orange. Press the peel flat. It covers about \(4\) circles that have the same radius as the orange. One circle has area \(\pi r^2\), so the peel has area \(4\pi r^2\).

title: 8.4 - Volume of Prisms and Cylinders
text:
👥 Learn Together

8.4.1 - Volume of a Prism
Volume is the amount of space inside a solid. We count cubic units. One cubic unit is a cube with edges of \(1\) unit.





This box is \(4\) units long, \(3\) units wide, and \(2\) units tall. Each layer has \(4 \cdot 3 = 12\) cubes. There are \(2\) layers. So the box holds \(12 \cdot 2 = 24\) cubes.
The \(12\) is the area of the base. The \(2\) is the height. This works for every prism, not only boxes.

\(V = Bh\), where \(B\) is the area of the base and \(h\) is the height of the prism.


Example 1: A box





Find the volume of a box that is \(6\) ft long, \(4\) ft wide, and \(3\) ft tall.
\(B = 6 \cdot 4 = 24\) square feet.
\[
V = Bh = 24 \cdot 3 = 72 \text{ cubic feet}
\]

\(B = 7 \cdot 5 = 35\). \(V = 35 \cdot 2 = 70\) cubic meters.


Example 2: A triangular prism





The base is a right triangle with legs \(6\) in and \(4\) in. The prism is \(9\) in long. Find the volume.
The base is the triangle. \(B = \frac{1}{2}(6)(4) = 12\) square inches. The height of the prism is the length, \(9\) in.
\[
V = Bh = 12 \cdot 9 = 108 \text{ cubic inches}
\]

\(B = \frac{1}{2}(5)(12) = 30\). \(V = 30 \cdot 6 = 180\) cubic feet.


Example 3: A base on the coordinate plane





The base of a prism is the trapezoid with vertices \((0, 0)\), \((10, 0)\), \((8, 4)\), and \((2, 4)\). Each unit is \(1\) foot. The prism is \(6\) ft tall. Find the volume.
The parallel sides are horizontal. The bottom is \(10 - 0 = 10\) ft. The top is \(8 - 2 = 6\) ft. The height of the trapezoid is \(4\) ft.
\[
B = \tfrac{1}{2}(10 + 6)(4) = 32 \text{ square feet}
\]
\[
V = Bh = 32 \cdot 6 = 192 \text{ cubic feet}
\]

\(B = \frac{1}{2}(8)(5) = 20\). \(V = 20 \cdot 10 = 200\) cubic feet.




8.4.2 - Volume of a Cylinder
A cylinder is like a prism with a round base. The base is a circle, so \(B = \pi r^2\).

\(V = \pi r^2 h\)


Example 4: A cylinder





Find the volume of a cylinder with \(r = 3\) cm and \(h = 10\) cm. Give the exact answer and a decimal rounded to the nearest tenth.
\[
V = \pi(3)^2(10) = 90\pi \approx 282.7 \text{ cubic centimeters}
\]

The radius is half the diameter, \(r = 5\). \(V = \pi(5)^2(4) = 100\pi \approx 314.2\) cubic inches.




8.4.3 - Slanted Solids (Cavalieri’s Principle)
Make a stack of coins. Push the stack so it leans. You used the same coins, so the volume is the same. The height of the stack did not change.





This idea is Cavalieri’s principle. If two solids have the same height and the same cross-section area at every level, they have the same volume. A leaning prism or cylinder is oblique.

For an oblique solid, the height is the straight-up distance between the bases, at a right angle to them. It is not the slanted side. Look for the dashed line with the square mark.


Example 5: An oblique cylinder





The base has radius \(4\) ft. The slanted side is \(13\) ft. The straight-up height is \(12\) ft. Find the volume. Give the exact answer and a decimal rounded to the nearest tenth.
The slanted side (\(13\)) is not used.
\[
V = \pi r^2 h = \pi(4)^2(12) = 192\pi \approx 603.2 \text{ cubic feet}
\]

\(B = 6 \cdot 5 = 30\). \(V = 30 \cdot 9 = 270\) cubic feet. The \(12\) ft edge is not used.




8.4.4 - Changing Units
Volume units are cubes, so conversion numbers are cubed.



Fact
Why




\(1 \text{ yd}^3 = 27 \text{ ft}^3\)
\(3 \cdot 3 \cdot 3 = 27\)


\(1 \text{ ft}^3 = 1728 \text{ in}^3\)
\(12 \cdot 12 \cdot 12 = 1728\)


\(1 \text{ ft}^3 \approx 7.48\) gallons
measured




Change every length to the same unit before you multiply. A slab that is \(4\) inches thick is \(\frac{1}{3}\) foot thick.


Example 6: Concrete
Moses is pouring a patio. It is \(12\) ft by \(20\) ft and \(4\) in thick. How many cubic yards of concrete does he need? Round to the nearest tenth.
\(4\) in \(= \frac{1}{3}\) ft.
\[
V = 12 \cdot 20 \cdot \tfrac{1}{3} = 80 \text{ cubic feet}
\]
\[
80 \div 27 \approx 3.0 \text{ cubic yards}
\]

\(V = 10 \cdot 15 \cdot \frac{1}{3} = 50\) cubic feet. \(50 \div 27 \approx 1.9\) cubic yards.


Example 7: Water in a pool
A round pool has a diameter of \(24\) ft. The water is \(4\) ft deep. How many gallons does it hold? Use \(1 \text{ ft}^3 \approx 7.48\) gallons. Round to the nearest hundred gallons.
\(r = 12\) ft.
\[
V = \pi(12)^2(4) = 576\pi \approx 1809.6 \text{ cubic feet}
\]
\[
1809.6 \cdot 7.48 \approx 13{,}535 \text{ gallons} \approx 13{,}500 \text{ gallons}
\]

\(V = \pi(3)^2(2) = 18\pi \approx 56.5\) cubic feet. \(56.5 \cdot 7.48 \approx 423\) gallons.




8.4.5 - Finding a Missing Dimension
When you know the volume, write \(V = Bh\) with the numbers you know. Then solve.
Example 8: The height of a tank
A tank is a cylinder with radius \(4\) ft. It holds \(5000\) gallons. How tall is it? Round to the nearest tenth.
First change gallons to cubic feet: \(5000 \div 7.48 \approx 668.4\) cubic feet.
\[
\pi(4)^2 h = 668.4
\]
\[
h = \frac{668.4}{16\pi} \approx 13.3 \text{ feet}
\]

\(2000 \div 7.48 \approx 267.4\) cubic feet. \(h = \frac{267.4}{9\pi} \approx 9.5\) feet.


Example 9: Volume with algebra
A box has length \(x + 3\), width \(x\), and height \(4\). The volume is \(160\) cubic units. Find \(x\).
\[
4x(x + 3) = 160
\]
\[
x^2 + 3x = 40
\]
\[
x^2 + 3x - 40 = 0
\]
\[
(x + 8)(x - 5) = 0
\]
\(x = -8\) or \(x = 5\). A length cannot be negative, so \(x = 5\). The box is \(8\) by \(5\) by \(4\). Check: \(8 \cdot 5 \cdot 4 = 160\).

\(3x(x + 2) = 105\), so \(x^2 + 2x - 35 = 0\), so \((x + 7)(x - 5) = 0\). Length must be positive, so \(x = 5\).

8.5 - Volume of Pyramids, Cones, and Spheres

title: 8.5 - Volume of Pyramids, Cones, and Spheres
text:
👥 Learn Together

8.5.1 - Pyramids and Cones
Take a pyramid and a prism with the same base and the same height. Fill the pyramid with water and pour it into the prism. You need to pour three times to fill the prism. The same is true for a cone and a cylinder.





So a pyramid or cone holds one third as much as the prism or cylinder with the same base and height.

Pyramid: \(V = \dfrac{1}{3}Bh\)
Cone: \(V = \dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h\)
\(B\) is the area of the base. \(h\) is the straight-up height, not the slant height.


Example 1: A square pyramid





The base is a square with side \(6\) ft. The height is \(8\) ft. Find the volume.
\(B = 6 \cdot 6 = 36\) square feet.
\[
V = \tfrac{1}{3}Bh = \tfrac{1}{3}(36)(8) = 96 \text{ cubic feet}
\]

\(B = 5 \cdot 8 = 40\). \(V = \frac{1}{3}(40)(6) = 80\) cubic feet.


Example 2: A cone





A cone has radius \(4\) in and height \(9\) in. Find the volume. Give the exact answer and a decimal rounded to the nearest tenth.
\[
V = \tfrac{1}{3}\pi(4)^2(9) = \tfrac{1}{3}\pi(16)(9) = 48\pi \approx 150.8 \text{ cubic inches}
\]

\(V = \frac{1}{3}\pi(9)(7) = 21\pi \approx 66.0\) cubic centimeters.




8.5.2 - Finding the Height First
Often a problem gives the slant height, not the height. The height, half of the base (or the radius), and the slant height make a right triangle. Use the Pythagorean theorem to find the height. Then use the volume formula.
Example 3: A pyramid with the slant height given





A square pyramid has base side \(10\) in and slant height \(13\) in. Find the volume.
Half of the base is \(5\). The right triangle has leg \(5\), leg \(h\), and hypotenuse \(13\):
\[
h^2 + 5^2 = 13^2
\]
\[
h^2 = 169 - 25 = 144, \quad h = 12
\]
\[
V = \tfrac{1}{3}(10 \cdot 10)(12) = 400 \text{ cubic inches}
\]

Half of the base is \(9\). \(h^2 = 15^2 - 9^2 = 144\), so \(h = 12\).
\(V = \frac{1}{3}(18 \cdot 18)(12) = 1296\) cubic centimeters.


Example 4: A cone with the slant height given





A cone has radius \(6\) in and slant height \(10\) in. Find the volume. Give the exact answer and a decimal rounded to the nearest tenth.
\[
h^2 + 6^2 = 10^2, \quad h^2 = 64, \quad h = 8
\]
\[
V = \tfrac{1}{3}\pi(6)^2(8) = 96\pi \approx 301.6 \text{ cubic inches}
\]

\(h^2 = 15^2 - 9^2 = 144\), so \(h = 12\). \(V = \frac{1}{3}\pi(81)(12) = 324\pi \approx 1017.9\) cubic feet.




8.5.3 - Spheres and Hemispheres

Sphere: \(V = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3\)
Hemisphere (half a sphere): \(V = \dfrac{2}{3}\pi r^3\)

The radius is cubed, not squared. Cube the radius first, then multiply.

Take a cylinder with radius \(r\) and height \(r\). Cut out a cone with the same radius and height. What is left has the same cross-section area at every level as a hemisphere (Cavalieri’s principle). So the hemisphere has volume \(\pi r^3 - \frac{1}{3}\pi r^3 = \frac{2}{3}\pi r^3\).


Example 5: A sphere
Find the volume of a sphere with radius \(6\) cm. Give the exact answer and a decimal rounded to the nearest tenth.
\[
V = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi(6)^3 = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi(216) = 288\pi \approx 904.8 \text{ cubic centimeters}
\]

\(V = \frac{4}{3}\pi(729) = 972\pi \approx 3053.6\) cubic inches.


Example 6: A hemisphere





A bowl is a hemisphere with radius \(5\) in. How much water does it hold when full? Give the exact answer and a decimal rounded to the nearest tenth.
\[
V = \tfrac{2}{3}\pi(5)^3 = \tfrac{250}{3}\pi \approx 261.8 \text{ cubic inches}
\]

\(V = \frac{2}{3}\pi(1728) = 1152\pi \approx 3619.1\) cubic feet.


Example 7: Find the radius
A sphere has volume \(36\pi\) cubic inches. Find its radius.
\[
\tfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3 = 36\pi
\]
Divide both sides by \(\pi\), then multiply by \(\frac{3}{4}\):
\[
r^3 = 36 \cdot \tfrac{3}{4} = 27
\]
\[
r = 3 \text{ inches}
\]

\(\frac{4}{3}r^3 = \frac{500}{3}\), so \(4r^3 = 500\), so \(r^3 = 125\) and \(r = 5\) cm.




8.5.4 - Composite Solids
Break the solid into pieces you know. Find each volume. Then add the pieces (or subtract a piece that was removed).
Example 8: A silo





A grain silo is a cylinder with a hemisphere on top. The cylinder has radius \(6\) ft and height \(20\) ft. Find the volume. Give the exact answer and a decimal rounded to the nearest tenth.
Cylinder: \(\pi(6)^2(20) = 720\pi\).
Hemisphere: \(\frac{2}{3}\pi(6)^3 = 144\pi\).
\[
V = 720\pi + 144\pi = 864\pi \approx 2714.3 \text{ cubic feet}
\]

Cylinder: \(\pi(4)(6) = 24\pi\). Two hemispheres make one sphere: \(\frac{4}{3}\pi(8) = \frac{32}{3}\pi\).
\(V = 24\pi + \frac{32}{3}\pi = \frac{104}{3}\pi \approx 108.9\) cubic centimeters.


Example 9: An ice cream cone





The cone has radius \(3\) cm and height \(10\) cm. A scoop shaped like a hemisphere with radius \(3\) cm sits on top. Find the total volume. Give the exact answer and a decimal rounded to the nearest tenth.
Cone: \(\frac{1}{3}\pi(9)(10) = 30\pi\).
Hemisphere: \(\frac{2}{3}\pi(27) = 18\pi\).
\[
V = 30\pi + 18\pi = 48\pi \approx 150.8 \text{ cubic centimeters}
\]

Cone: \(\frac{1}{3}\pi(4)(8) = \frac{32}{3}\pi\). Hemisphere: \(\frac{2}{3}\pi(8) = \frac{16}{3}\pi\). Total: \(16\pi \approx 50.3\) cubic centimeters.


Example 10: A frustum





A funnel is a cone with the tip cut off. The whole cone has radius \(6\) ft and height \(12\) ft. The tip that was cut off has radius \(3\) ft and height \(6\) ft. Find the volume of the funnel. Give the exact answer and a decimal rounded to the nearest tenth.
Whole cone: \(\frac{1}{3}\pi(36)(12) = 144\pi\).
Tip: \(\frac{1}{3}\pi(9)(6) = 18\pi\).
\[
V = 144\pi - 18\pi = 126\pi \approx 395.8 \text{ cubic feet}
\]

She forgot the \(\frac{1}{3}\). \(V = \frac{1}{3}\pi(9)(5) = 15\pi \approx 47.1\).




8.5.5 - Real Problems
Example 11: A pile of sand
A pile of sand is a cone. The diameter is \(12\) ft and the height is \(5\) ft. How many cubic yards of sand is it? Round to the nearest tenth.
\(r = 6\) ft.
\[
V = \tfrac{1}{3}\pi(6)^2(5) = 60\pi \approx 188.5 \text{ cubic feet}
\]
\[
188.5 \div 27 \approx 7.0 \text{ cubic yards}
\]

\(V = \frac{1}{3}\pi(64)(6) = 128\pi \approx 402.1\) cubic feet. \(402.1 \div 27 \approx 14.9\) cubic yards.

title: 8.5 - Volume of Pyramids, Cones, and Spheres
text:
✍️ Practice On Your Own
Pyramids and cones. Give each volume with units.

title: 8.6 - Density and Modeling
text:
🔥 Warm Up
Moses pours a concrete patio. The truck brings the concrete, but a bigger question is the weight. A cubic foot of concrete is heavy. Will the ground hold it? Will the truck’s load limit allow it?
Volume alone does not answer these questions. You also need density, which tells how heavy a material is for its size. In this lesson you use density to find weight, population density to compare places, scale factors to compare models with real things, and you plan real jobs.
crumbs: Unit 8: Area, Surface Area, and Volume

title: 8.6 - Density and Modeling
text:
Find the volume of a box \(4\) ft by \(2\) ft by \(2\) ft.
A rectangle is \(12\) ft by \(20\) ft. Find its area.
Two similar triangles have scale factor \(3\). A side of the small triangle is \(5\). What is the matching side of the large triangle?
crumbs: Unit 8: Area, Surface Area, and Volume

title: 8.6 - Density and Modeling
text:
👥 Learn Together

8.6.1 - Density and Weight
Density compares mass (or weight) to volume:
\[
\text{density} = \frac{\text{mass}}{\text{volume}}
\]
Rearranged: \(\text{weight} = \text{density} \times \text{volume}\).



Material
Density




water
\(62.4\) lb per ft\(^3\) (or \(1\) g per cm\(^3\))


concrete
about \(150\) lb per ft\(^3\)



An object floats in water if its density is less than the density of water. It sinks if its density is greater.

Example 1: Weight of a slab





A concrete slab is \(12\) ft by \(20\) ft and \(4\) in thick. Concrete weighs about \(150\) lb per cubic foot. Find the weight.
\(4\) in \(= \frac{1}{3}\) ft.
\[
V = 12 \cdot 20 \cdot \tfrac{1}{3} = 80 \text{ ft}^3
\]
\[
\text{weight} = 150 \cdot 80 = 12{,}000 \text{ pounds}
\]
That is \(6\) tons.

\(V = 10 \cdot 15 \cdot \frac{1}{3} = 50\) cubic feet. Weight \(= 150 \cdot 50 = 7500\) pounds.


Example 2: Weight of water
An aquarium is \(4\) ft long, \(2\) ft wide, and \(2\) ft tall. It is full of water. Find the weight of the water.
\(V = 4 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 = 16\) cubic feet.
\[
\text{weight} = 62.4 \cdot 16 = 998.4 \text{ pounds}
\]

\(V = 3 \cdot 1.5 \cdot 2 = 9\) cubic feet. Weight \(= 62.4 \cdot 9 = 561.6\) pounds.


Example 3: Will it float?





A wood block is \(10\) cm by \(6\) cm by \(4\) cm. Its mass is \(168\) g. Does it float in water? (Water has density \(1\) g per cm\(^3\).)
\(V = 10 \cdot 6 \cdot 4 = 240\) cm\(^3\).
\[
\text{density} = \frac{168}{240} = 0.7 \text{ g per cm}^3
\]
\(0.7 < 1\), so the block floats.

\(V = 5^3 = 125\) cm\(^3\). Density \(= \frac{1000}{125} = 8\) g per cm\(^3\). \(8 > 1\), so it sinks.




8.6.2 - Population Density
Population density is people per square mile:
\[
\text{population density} = \frac{\text{number of people}}{\text{area in square miles}}
\]
Example 4: Compare two cities
City A has \(120{,}000\) people in \(40\) square miles. City B has \(75{,}000\) people in \(15\) square miles. Which is more crowded?
A: \(120{,}000 \div 40 = 3000\) people per square mile.
B: \(75{,}000 \div 15 = 5000\) people per square mile.
City B is more crowded, even though City A has more people.

C: \(90{,}000 \div 36 = 2500\). D: \(48{,}000 \div 20 = 2400\). Town C has the greater density.


Example 5: A county on a map grid





Each unit on the grid is \(1\) mile. The county has \(22{,}400\) people. Find the population density.
Split the county into two rectangles. The bottom one is \(10\) by \(4\). The top one is \(6\) by \(4\).
\[
A = 10 \cdot 4 + 6 \cdot 4 = 40 + 24 = 64 \text{ square miles}
\]
\[
\text{density} = \frac{22{,}400}{64} = 350 \text{ people per square mile}
\]

Bottom rectangle \(9 \cdot 3 = 27\). Top rectangle \(5 \cdot 4 = 20\). \(A = 47\) square miles.
\(14{,}100 \div 47 = 300\) people per square mile.




8.6.3 - Scaling Lengths, Areas, and Volumes
In Lesson 5.2 you learned that if lengths scale by \(k\), then areas scale by \(k^2\). Volumes scale by \(k^3\).

Lengths: \(\times k\)
Surface areas and other areas: \(\times k^2\)
Volumes (and weights of the same material): \(\times k^3\)

Example 6: Two cubes





A cube has edge \(2\) in. A larger cube has edge \(6\) in. The scale factor is \(k = 3\).




Small cube
Large cube
Ratio




edge
\(2\)
\(6\)
\(3\)


surface area
\(6 \cdot 4 = 24\)
\(6 \cdot 36 = 216\)
\(9 = 3^2\)


volume
\(2^3 = 8\)
\(6^3 = 216\)
\(27 = 3^3\)




\(k = 2\). Small: \(\pi(9)(5) = 45\pi\). Large: \(\pi(36)(10) = 360\pi\). Ratio \(= 8 = 2^3\).


Example 7: A model boat
A model boat is \(\frac{1}{20}\) of the size of the real boat. The real boat has \(600\) square feet of hull to paint. The real boat holds \(2400\) gallons of water. Its mass is \(3000\) pounds.
The scale factor from the real boat to the model is \(\frac{1}{20}\).

Hull area: \(600 \cdot \left(\frac{1}{20}\right)^2 = 600 \cdot \frac{1}{400} = 1.5\) square feet.
Volume: \(2400 \cdot \left(\frac{1}{20}\right)^3 = 2400 \cdot \frac{1}{8000} = 0.3\) gallon.
Mass, if made of the same material: \(3000 \cdot \frac{1}{8000} = 0.375\) pound.


\(k = \frac{1}{12}\). Weight \(= 2400 \cdot \left(\frac{1}{12}\right)^3 = \frac{2400}{1728} \approx 1.4\) pounds.


Samir says, “If I double every side of a box, the volume doubles.” Test his claim on a box \(2\) by \(3\) by \(4\).
The box has volume \(24\). The doubled box is \(4\) by \(6\) by \(8\) and has volume \(192\). That is \(8\) times larger, not \(2\) times. The volume is multiplied by \(2^3 = 8\).


Make an animal \(10\) times as tall in every direction. Its weight grows like volume, so \(10^3 = 1000\) times. The strength of a leg grows like the area of its cross section, so only \(10^2 = 100\) times. The legs must be thicker than a simple enlargement, or they will break.




8.6.4 - Modeling and Design
Real jobs combine area, volume, density, and unit conversion. Plan in steps: draw it, make the units match, find the volume, then use what you need (cost, weight, bags, or trips).
Example 8: Bags of concrete





A slab is \(12\) ft by \(10\) ft and \(4\) in thick. One \(80\) lb bag of mix makes about \(0.6\) cubic feet of concrete. How many bags are needed?
\(V = 12 \cdot 10 \cdot \frac{1}{3} = 40\) cubic feet.
\[
40 \div 0.6 \approx 66.7
\]
Round up: \(67\) bags. The bags weigh \(67 \cdot 80 = 5360\) pounds.

\(V = 12 \cdot 16 \cdot \frac{1}{3} = 64\) cubic feet. \(64 \div 0.6 \approx 106.7\), so \(107\) bags. They weigh \(107 \cdot 80 = 8560\) pounds.


Example 9: Which can uses less metal?





Two soup can designs each hold \(500\) cm\(^3\). Design A has radius \(4\) cm. Design B has radius \(5\) cm. Which uses less metal? Round to the nearest tenth.
Find the height from \(V = \pi r^2 h\):

A: \(h = \dfrac{500}{16\pi} \approx 9.95\) cm. \(SA = 2\pi(4)^2 + 2\pi(4)(9.95) \approx 350.5\) cm\(^2\).
B: \(h = \dfrac{500}{25\pi} \approx 6.37\) cm. \(SA = 2\pi(5)^2 + 2\pi(5)(6.37) \approx 357.1\) cm\(^2\).

Design A uses less metal.

A: \(h = \frac{400}{16\pi} \approx 7.96\), \(SA \approx 300.5\) cm\(^2\). B: \(h = \frac{400}{36\pi} \approx 3.54\), \(SA \approx 359.5\) cm\(^2\). Can A uses less.


Example 10: How many trips?
A pickup truck carries at most \(2000\) lb. Dry sand weighs about \(100\) lb per cubic foot. A play area is \(12\) ft by \(10\) ft and the sand is \(6\) in deep. How many trips does the truck make?
\(V = 12 \cdot 10 \cdot 0.5 = 60\) cubic feet.
\(\text{weight} = 100 \cdot 60 = 6000\) pounds.
\(6000 \div 2000 = 3\) trips.

\(V = 10 \cdot 9 \cdot \frac{2}{3} = 60\) cubic feet. \(6000 \div 2000 = 3\) trips.

Test practice

A. 24,000 lb
B. 36,000 lb
C. 288,000 lb
D. 1,440,000 lb

C. 1,350 cm\(^3\)

Challenge

text:
8.1 - Area of Polygons and Composite Figures

title: Unit 8 Summary
text:
Parallelogram: \(A = bh\). Triangle: \(A = \dfrac{1}{2}bh\). Trapezoid: \(A = \dfrac{1}{2}(b_1 + b_2)h\). The height is perpendicular to the base.
Regular polygon: \(A = \dfrac{1}{2}aP\). The apothem \(a\) goes from the center to the middle of a side. \(P\) is the perimeter. Use a \(30^\circ\)-\(60^\circ\)-\(90^\circ\) triangle to find \(a\) for a hexagon.
A composite figure is made of simple shapes. Add the parts, or subtract a missing part from a bigger shape.
To find a missing length, put the known numbers in the formula and solve.

title: Unit 8 Summary
section: 8.2 - Cross Sections and Solids of Revolution
text:
8.2 - Cross Sections and Solids of Revolution

A polyhedron has flat faces, edges and vertices. Euler’s formula: \(F + V - E = 2\).
A prism has two matching bases. A pyramid has one base and a point (the apex). A cylinder and a cone have circular bases. A sphere is all the points the same distance from the center.
A cross section is the shape a plane makes when it cuts a solid. A cut parallel to the base of a cylinder or cone is a circle. A cut through the axis of a cylinder is a rectangle. A cut through the apex of a cone is a triangle. Every cut of a sphere is a circle.
A solid of revolution is made by spinning a flat shape about an axis. A rectangle makes a cylinder. A right triangle makes a cone.






Example: a solid has \(6\) faces and \(8\) vertices. \(6 + 8 - E = 2\), so \(E = 12\).
crumbs: Unit 8: Area, Surface Area, and Volume

title: Unit 8 Summary
text:
8.3 - Surface Area and Nets

A net is a solid unfolded flat. Surface area is the area of the net.
Prism: \(SA = 2B + Ph\). The lateral area \(L = Ph\) is the sides only.
Cylinder: \(SA = 2\pi r^2 + 2\pi r h\).
Pyramid: \(SA = B + \dfrac{1}{2}P\ell\). Cone: \(SA = \pi r^2 + \pi r \ell\). The slant height \(\ell\) is along a face, not the inside height. Find \(h\) or \(\ell\) with the Pythagorean theorem.
Sphere: \(SA = 4\pi r^2\).






Example: a cylinder with \(r = 3\) and \(h = 10\) has \(SA = 2\pi(9) + 2\pi(3)(10) = 78\pi \approx 245.0\).
crumbs: Unit 8: Area, Surface Area, and Volume

title: Unit 8 Summary
text:
8.4 - Volume of Prisms and Cylinders

Volume is the number of cubic units that fill a solid.
Prism: \(V = Bh\). Cylinder: \(V = \pi r^2 h\). \(B\) is the area of the base.
Cavalieri’s principle: solids with the same height and the same cross-section area at every level have the same volume. A slanted (oblique) prism or cylinder uses the vertical height.
Change units with a ratio: \(1\) yd\(^3\) = \(27\) ft\(^3\). \(1\) ft\(^3\) \(\approx\) \(7.48\) gallons.






Example: a slab is \(30\) ft by \(12\) ft by \(\dfrac{1}{3}\) ft. \(V = 120\) ft\(^3\), and \(120 \div 27 \approx 4.4\) yd\(^3\).
crumbs: Unit 8: Area, Surface Area, and Volume

title: Unit 8 Summary
section: 8.5 - Volume of Pyramids, Cones, and Spheres
text:
8.5 - Volume of Pyramids, Cones, and Spheres

Pyramid: \(V = \dfrac{1}{3}Bh\). Cone: \(V = \dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h\). Each is one third of the prism or cylinder with the same base and height.
Sphere: \(V = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3\). A hemisphere is half: \(V = \dfrac{2}{3}\pi r^3\).
Use the height, not the slant height. If you are given the slant height, find \(h\) first.
A frustum is a cone or pyramid with the top cut off. Subtract the small solid from the large one.
For a composite solid, add or subtract the volumes of the parts.






Example: a cone with \(r = 6\) and \(\ell = 10\) has \(h = 8\) and \(V = \dfrac{1}{3}\pi(36)(8) = 96\pi \approx 301.6\).
crumbs: Unit 8: Area, Surface Area, and Volume

title: Unit 8 Summary
text:
8.6 - Density and Modeling

Density \(= \dfrac{\text{mass}}{\text{volume}}\). Weight = density \(\cdot\) volume. Water: \(62.4\) lb per ft\(^3\), or \(1\) g per cm\(^3\). Concrete: about \(150\) lb per ft\(^3\). An object floats if its density is less than water.
Population density \(= \dfrac{\text{people}}{\text{square miles}}\).
If lengths are multiplied by \(k\), areas are multiplied by \(k^2\) and volumes by \(k^3\).
For a plan: draw it, make the units match, find the volume, then find the cost, weight, bags or trips. Round up for whole items.






Example: a slab is \(10\) ft by \(15\) ft by \(\dfrac{1}{3}\) ft. \(V = 50\) ft\(^3\) and the weight is \(150 \cdot 50 = 7500\) lb.

title: Unit 8 Review
text: 👥 Learn Together

title: Unit 8 Review
text:
8.1 - Area of Polygons and Composite Figures
Example 1: A regular hexagon has sides of \(6\) in. Find its area. Give the exact answer and a decimal rounded to the nearest tenth.
The apothem is the long leg of a \(30^\circ\)-\(60^\circ\)-\(90^\circ\) triangle with short leg \(3\), so \(a = 3\sqrt{3}\). The perimeter is \(36\). \(A = \dfrac{1}{2}aP = \dfrac{1}{2}(3\sqrt{3})(36) = 54\sqrt{3} \approx 93.5\) square inches.


8.2 - Cross Sections and Solids of Revolution
Example 2: A solid has \(8\) faces and \(12\) vertices. How many edges does it have?
Euler’s formula: \(F + V - E = 2\). So \(8 + 12 - E = 2\) and \(E = 18\).


8.3 - Surface Area and Nets
Example 3: A cylinder has radius \(5\) ft and height \(12\) ft. Find its surface area. Give the exact answer and a decimal rounded to the nearest tenth.
\(SA = 2\pi r^2 + 2\pi r h = 2\pi(25) + 2\pi(5)(12) = 50\pi + 120\pi = 170\pi \approx 534.1\) square feet.


8.4 - Volume of Prisms and Cylinders
Example 4: A tank is \(20\) ft by \(12\) ft by \(5\) ft. Find its volume in cubic feet and in cubic yards. Round the yards to the nearest tenth.
\(V = 20 \cdot 12 \cdot 5 = 1200\) ft\(^3\). \(1200 \div 27 \approx 44.4\) yd\(^3\).


8.5 - Volume of Pyramids, Cones, and Spheres
Example 5: A cone has radius \(6\) and slant height \(10\). Find its volume. Give the exact answer and a decimal rounded to the nearest tenth.
\(h = \sqrt{10^2 - 6^2} = 8\). \(V = \dfrac{1}{3}\pi(36)(8) = 96\pi \approx 301.6\) cubic units.


8.6 - Density and Modeling
Example 6: A model tank is \(\dfrac{1}{10}\) of the size of a real tank. The real tank holds \(5000\) gallons. How much does the model hold?
Volume scales by \(k^3 = \left(\dfrac{1}{10}\right)^3 = \dfrac{1}{1000}\). The model holds \(5000 \div 1000 = 5\) gallons.
